en: In the section on *Śrāddha*, the daily *śrāddha* (*nityaśrāddha*) has been described in the daily ritual manual (*āhnika*). Now, following that context, the chapter on *śrāddha* (*śrāddhaprakaraṇa*) is commenced. First therein is the majesty of *śrāddha*. Regarding this, Sumantu says:
Nothing else is declared to be more conducive to supreme welfare than the śrāddha;
therefore, a wise person should perform the śrāddha with every effort.
Devala also says: "In this world,
one who desires to perform the *śrāddha* shall be free from disease, established in his natural state, long-lived, possessed of sons and grandsons, wealthy, and successful in his worldly aims."
Furthermore, the man who performs a *śrāddha* attains supreme satisfaction in the hereafter, various auspicious worlds, and vast renown.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"The ancestors, when pleased, bestow upon men longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, happiness, and likewise sovereignty."
Yama also says:
"Those who worship the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins together with the sacrificial fires,
they indeed worship Viṣṇu himself, the inner self of all beings."
Through the worship of the ancestors, one shall obtain long life, sons, fame, heaven, renown, nourishment, strength, prosperity, cattle, happiness, wealth, and grain.
Also in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—
these three persons are to be known as those connected by the rice-ball (piṇḍa)."
But others, related by lepasaṃbandha, are said to begin from the great-grandfather of the grandfather;
with these three, the sacrificer is the seventh.
Likewise, other ancestors who dwell in heaven, those others who inhabit the hells,
those who have entered the state of animals, and those who exist as spirits and so forth— [all these were saved].
O child, listen to that by which the sacrificer, performing the śrāddha according to the rules, nourishes all of them.
Whatever scattering of food is performed on the ground by human beings,
by that those who have fallen into the state of Piśācas attain satisfaction.
O son, by that water which falls upon the ground from the bathing garment,
those who have attained the state of trees find satisfaction.
And those droplets of scented water that fall upon the surface of the earth—
by means of them, there is nourishment for those in the family who have attained the state of gods.
But when the rice-balls have been offered, whatever grains remain there on the ground,
by those may there be nourishment for those in the family who have gone to the state of animals.
And those who are toothless, children in the family, unfit for ritual action, and unconsecrated—
they perish by eating scattered grains, sweepings, and water.
The water used for rinsing the mouths after eating, as well as that used for washing the feet of the Brahmins— by that indeed do others attain satisfaction.
Therefore, O child, having passed through various other wombs within those many families, they receive full nourishment from those who perform the śrāddha rites correctly.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"The wise man who understands this shall obtain the fruit of the śrāddha;
both the instructor and the one who gives consent are recorded in the world as having equal merit."
Whoever performs or even recites this meritorious ritual for the ancestors shall fulfill all desires and indeed attain immortality.
The fault in acting otherwise has been shown by that very same [author]:
"Neither heroes are born there, nor those free from disease, nor those with a lifespan of a hundred years;
nor do they attain the highest good where the *śrāddha* is avoided."
In the Āditya Purāṇa as well: "If a man, thinking in his mind that the ancestors do not exist,
does not perform a śrāddha ceremony there, they drink his blood."

Likewise, the fault regarding impure wealth is also shown in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "The śrāddha that is performed by men with wealth acquired through unjust means—by that, Cāṇḍālas, Pulkasas, and other such low-born beings are satisfied. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the section on the greatness of the Śrāddha in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, the classifications of the Śrāddha.
In this regard, Viśvāmitra says:

"The daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), the optional (kāmya), the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the *sapiṇḍana*, the *pārvaṇa*, and the *gauṣṭhya* for the sake of purification— these are to be known as the eight [types of śrāddha]."
The ninth is declared to be the limb of ritual action (karmāṅga), and the tenth is remembered as the divine (daivika).
The eleventh is declared for journeys (yātrā), and the twelfth is remembered for the purpose of nourishment (puṣṭi).
Regarding that, the definition of the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites has been stated by Pāraskara:
"That *śrāddha* which is performed day after day is proclaimed as obligatory;
even when one is incapable, it may be performed with water alone, though devoid of the Vaiśvadeva offering."

"But that *śrāddha* which is performed for a single person is called *naimittika* (occasional). That too should be performed without [invoking] the gods; one should feed an odd number of twice-born [brahmins]. Thus [it is said]. The definitions of the *kāmya* (optional) and other types of *śrāddha* have been stated by Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:
The *kāmya* śrāddha is prescribed for the sake of accomplishing a desired object, like the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha;
the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is declared for occasions such as the birth of a son or a marriage.
The vessel for the arghya water is new, and the rice-ball (piṇḍa) is scattered;
that indeed is the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite performed with the vessels and rice-balls of the ancestors.
Because it occurs on every *parvan* (lunar node), it is called *pārvaṇa*.

That *śrāddha* which is performed in a social gathering (*goṣṭhī*) is called a *goṣṭhī-śrāddha*, for the purpose of providing comfort to many learned men and for the satisfaction of the ancestors. Thus it is said.
The definition of that which is for the purpose of purification was stated by Pracetas:
"That which is performed for the sake of purification, namely the feeding of Brāhmaṇas, is declared to be for the purpose of purification; it is a Śrāddha performed according to the Pārvaṇa rite."
The definition of the *karmāṅga* (subsidiary) and other types of *śrāddhas* has been stated by Pāraskara:

"At the time of the *niṣeka* (conception rite), at the *soma* sacrifice, likewise at the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair), and at the *puṃsavana* (male-impregnation rite)— the *śrāddha* performed according to rule is to be known as *karmāṅga*."
Whatever is performed with reference to the gods is called *daivika*;
one should perform that diligently on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) and other such occasions, just like the daily *śrāddha*.

"For when one going to another country performs a *śrāddha* with clarified butter (*sarpiṣā*), that is declared to be for the purpose of the journey; and likewise upon returning, there is no doubt. Here, the mention of it being "an auxiliary to the rite" (*karmāṅga*) is for the purpose of making known that the rite would be deficient if not performed. "With clarified butter" (*sarpiṣā*) means "with clarified butter as the primary substance. Otherwise, since satisfaction [of the ancestors] would be impossible by means of [butter] alone.
Thus concludes the section on the varieties of Śrāddha in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the determination of those entitled to perform the Śrāddha (Śrāddhādhikārinirṇaya). Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"Upon the death of a father, the Śrāddha should be diligently offered by his sons, as well as by kinsmen, relatives, friends, disciples, officiating priests, servants, and family chaplains.

The phrase "in the absence of sons" is to be understood as the remainder [of the statement]. The mention of the "father" is intended to indicate the "mother" as well. For this very reason, Sumantu says:
"The legitimate son of the body (aurasa) should perform [the rites] for his deceased mother and father.
This must be performed even by one who has not yet been initiated (anupanīta). Regarding this, Sumantu said:
"He whose father has died must certainly perform the śrāddha."
Whether established in a vow or not established in a vow, if he should be alone;
"One who does not abide by the vows" refers to one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*). For this very reason, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"Even one who is uninitiated should perform the *śrāddha*, for he who is the only son;
he should offer the oblation of the *pitṛyajña* into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa."
Regarding this, Vyāghra states a specific rule:
"One who has undergone the *caula* ceremony should offer water and the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*),
and should employ the utterance 'svadhā,' but he should not be made to recite the Veda."

The words "of the mother and father" are to be supplied [to the verse]. It is also stated in another Smṛti: "One who has undergone the tonsure ceremony but has not yet been initiated should perform the Śrāddha for his parents;
he may utter the word *svadhā*, but he must not pronounce the syllables of the Veda."
He states that even the syllables of the Veda should be employed [only at specific times]:
"Indeed, no ritual action is appropriate for him prior to the tying of the girdle;
he should not utter the Veda, except for the offering of the *svadhā*. Thus it is said.
In this regard, the following distinction should be understood: in the absence of a son, however, it is stated by Śaṅkha:
"The offering of rice balls (piṇḍas) and the performance of water-libations (udaka-kriyā) for the father must be performed by the son;
in the absence of a son, the wife shall do so; and in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother. Thus it is said.

Here, by the term "son," both the primary and secondary types are included, according to the traditional teaching of Yājñavalkya: "Among these, the giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and the taker of the share shall be each subsequent one in the absence of each preceding one. Therefore, the meaning of the statement "In the absence of sons, however, the wife [shall inherit]" applies when there is an absence of both types of sons. That too refers to a situation where there is an absence of even a grandson (pautra).
[7] Now, both the grandson and the son of an appointed daughter bring about the attainment of heaven;
they are declared to be equal in regard to inheritance and the offering of funeral cakes.

Thus, because Bṛhaspati speaks of the general category of "secondary sons" (gauṇaputra), one should not suspect that there is an option between a son and a grandson regarding the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa);
for the Smṛti of Ṛśyaśṛṅga states: "While sons exist, one should certainly not have another perform the ancestral rite (svadhā)."

"This [offering] should not be performed by the grandson if the grandfather has a son," according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) of Kātyāyana. However, the statement that "in the absence of a son, the wife shall [perform it]" refers specifically to the case of the sacrificer's wife, because she is the heir to the estate; otherwise, whoever is the heir to the estate should alone perform the offering. For this very reason, Viṣṇu and Āpastamba state: "Whoever takes the wealth, he is the giver of the *piṇḍa*; in the absence of paternal wealth, the son should give the *piṇḍa*. For this same reason, Yājñavalkya also says:
"The giver of the *piṇḍa* and the taker of the share among these [heirs] is each subsequent one in the absence of the preceding."

Thus, the coexistence of the status of being an offerer of the funeral ball (*piṇḍada*) and the status of being an inheritor of the share (*aṃśahara*) has been stated. This should be understood to apply likewise to a uterine brother (*sodara*). And so it was said by Manu: "Among brothers born of one father, if even one should have a son, Manu declared them all to be possessed of a son through that son."

Thus, it should be understood that the mention of the "son" (*putra*) there is for the sake of praise, just as one says "the father of the village. Otherwise, the sequence beginning with "the wife, the daughters," and so forth, would be inconsistent. With this very intention, Gautama also states: "In the absence of his son, his kinsmen (*bāndhava*), the *sapiṇḍas*, the *mātṛ-sapiṇḍas*, and the disciples shall offer [the funeral cake]; in their absence, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*). The *mātṛ-sapiṇḍas* are the maternal uncles and others. In the absence of *sapiṇḍas*, those who share the same water (*samānodaka*) shall offer the *piṇḍa*. And so it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
In the absence of a son, the sapindas [shall perform the rites]; in their absence, the sodakas;
or those who are the mother’s sapindas, or those who are the mother’s sodakas.
The sons of a sonless man are declared to be those who should properly perform this rite for him;
likewise, the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should perform it for his maternal grandfather.
In the absence of all these, women should perform [the rites] for their own husbands without mantras;
and in their absence, the king should cause it to be performed by his own householders.
All the rites, such as cremation and others, should be properly performed by men of the same caste;
for the king is the kinsman of all social classes.
In the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Parāśara also says:
"O King, the son, the grandson, the great-grandson, or likewise the lineage of a brother,
or even the lineage of a *sapiṇḍa*, becomes eligible to perform the funeral rites."
In the absence of all these, the sapinda-relationship extends to those of the same water-lineage (samānodaka),
whether they are connected to the maternal side by means of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) or by means of water.
O King, the funeral rites for the deceased must be performed by women from both families even if they have passed away;
or else, the rites for the deceased must indeed be performed by those belonging to their [the deceased's] own group.
"The king shall cause the rites to be performed for those whose relatives have perished and who possess no inheritance.
Having raised the doubt as to which of the aforementioned sons and others has authority over which rite, that same author says:
"The prior rites, the middle rites, and likewise the subsequent rites..."
These actions are indeed of three kinds; hear from me their subdivisions.
Those rites which are considered to occur between the first day and the twelfth day are the "prior" and "intermediate" ones; they are performed month after month and are designated as *ekoddiṣṭa*.
When the deceased has attained the status of a *pitṛ* following the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
those ancestral rites (*pitryāḥ kriyāḥ*) which are performed thereafter are designated as the "later" rites (*uttarāḥ*), O King.
But by the father’s and mother’s sapindas, as well as those who share the same water (samānodaka),
and by those included in their respective groups, or by the king who takes away the wealth;

"The preliminary rites (*pūrvāḥ kriyāḥ*) must be performed by the [deceased’s] sons and others, and the subsequent rites (*uttarāḥ kriyāḥ*) by the daughters' sons (*dauhitra*), O best of kings, or likewise by their [the daughters'] sons. The meaning is that the preliminary and intermediate rites must be performed by those beginning with the *sapiṇḍas* and ending with the king (i.e., the state authorities), whereas the subsequent rites must be performed only by the sons and others, by those within the brotherly lineage, and by the daughters' sons and others—not by those beginning with the *sapiṇḍas* and ending with the king. Regarding the daughter's son (*dauhitra*), however, there is a specific rule stated in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
"Just as a son, even if he is under a vow, O King, should perform the rites for his father—such as the water libations and so forth, O mighty-armed one—a daughter's son likewise deserves to do so.

Now, an objection may be raised: does this not contradict the Purāṇic statement, "In the absence of a son, the wife shall [perform the rites]," which says, "In the absence of all [others], women should perform the rites for their husbands without mantras"?

It is not so; the statement, "In the absence of a son, the wife shall [inherit]," refers specifically to women wed according to the Brāhma and other approved forms of marriage, because the term *patnī* (wife) is applied to her alone due to her participation in the sacrificial rites (*yajñānvitatva*). As for others, however: "A woman who has been purchased by means of a price is not ordained as a *patnī*.
She is neither at the rites for the gods nor at those for the ancestors; the wise know her to be a slave. [10]

Thus, because of the absence of the status of wife (*patnītva*), the Purāṇic statement that [the rite] for one's own husbands is "without mantras" refers to that specific case. Alternatively, the statement "In the absence of a son, the wife shall [perform the rite]" refers to a woman who is a knower of Brahman (*brahmavādinī*), since she is capable of using mantras due to her possession of Vedic study. It should be understood, however, that the Purāṇic statement intends those newly married women who are devoid of Vedic study. One should accept whatever is logical in this matter. Regarding the wife, Vṛddha-Manu states a special rule:
"A sonless wife, guarding the bed of her husband and remaining steadfast in her vows..."
"The wife, however, should offer that *piṇḍa* and receive the entire share," so it is said. This means she should remain well-restrained while guarding the bed. Viṣṇu also says:
"Likewise, the wife, being well-restrained, should offer the *piṇḍa* to her mother-in-law and the other [elders]."
As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana:
"The son, the pupil, or the wife, the father, the brother, or the teacher,
as well as the taker of the wife and the taker of the wealth, shall perform the rites of the funeral cake and the water libation."
Thus, as it was stated by Vṛddha-Śātātapa: "The maternal uncle [is the teacher] of the sister's son, and the sister's son [is the teacher] of the maternal uncle;
likewise, the father-in-law, the preceptor, the friend, and the maternal grandfather [are teachers]."
For these very wives, as well as for one's sister, mother, and father, a śrāddha with raw food (āmāśrāddha) must be performed; such is the settled rule of those who know the Vedas.
Thus, even in this case, the settled rule should be understood in accordance with the statement of the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "But as for what was stated by Kātyāyana:
'In the case of a woman without sons, the husband shall give; but never in the case of one who has sons.
A father shall not perform [the rite] for his son, nor likewise an elder brother for his younger brother.'"

Thus, that [rule] refers to cases such as a father who is devoid of affection. For this very reason, Bodhāyana states: "A father should by no means perform the Śrāddha for his sons, nor should a brother perform it for his younger brothers."
"Out of affection, they may perform [the rite] even without the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*;
however, at Gayā especially, even the elder brother should perform it.

Regarding this, Vṛddha-Śātātapa states that prosperity (*abhyudaya*) results even when the rite is performed in the absence of causes such as being the inheritor of the wealth: *atra dhanahāritvādinimittābhāve 'pi kṛte 'bhyudaya ity āha vṛddhaśātātapaḥ |*
"The Śrāddha for the father must be performed by all those belonging to the [four] castes and the [four] stages of life (liṅgins).

A man who performs it correctly in this manner shall attain great prosperity. Here, "liṅgins" refers to those in the [four] stages of life (āśramins). And this is intended with respect to those of the same caste (savarṇas), because otherwise a fault is heard [in the scriptures]. Thus says Marīci:
For a Brāhmaṇa who performs the funeral rites for one of a different caste attains the status of that caste both in this world and in the next.
Pāraskara also says:
"A Brāhmaṇa must never perform the funeral rites for a Śūdra,
nor should a Śūdra perform them for a Brāhmaṇa, except in the case of a Pāraśava son."
Thus ends the determination of those entitled to perform the *śrāddha* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
[12] Now follows the determination of those entitled to perform the *mātāmaha-śrāddha*.
In this regard, Pulastya says: "Three maternal grandfathers are traditionally recognized, beginning with the mother’s father;
the sons of daughters should perform the śrāddha for them just as they do for their paternal ancestors."
"Pitṛvat" means the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha; and that śrāddha is obligatory. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
"A twice-born man should satisfy both his paternal ancestors and his maternal grandfathers with the śrāddha;
being free from debt to his ancestors, he goes to the world of Brahmā."
Also in the Purāṇa:
"Having performed the ancestral Śrāddha for the three beginning with the father,
one should likewise perform it for the maternal grandfathers for the sake of discharging those debts."
The mention of "freedom from debt" is for the purpose of making known its obligatory nature. For this very reason, the fault incurred by non-performance is shown in the Purāṇa:
"He who performs the Pārvaṇa rite solely for the sake of his father, but does not perform it for his maternal grandfather, is born as a slayer of his father."
"Wherever the fathers are worshipped, there the maternal grandfathers must certainly be worshipped without distinction; otherwise, one goes to hell.

The meaning is that in whatever rite the fathers are worshipped, there the maternal grandfathers must also be worshipped without exception. By this, it is stated that in every *pitṛ-śrāddha*, the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* must also be performed. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states an exception in certain cases:
"Excluding the first *śrāddha* accompanied by the *karṣū*, as well as the annual *pratyābdika* [śrāddha], there shall be six *piṇḍas* in the remaining [sixteen]; such is the established rule. [13]

The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha is accompanied by the *karṣū* (the sacrificial pit). The mention of the sixteen [śrāddhas] is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *ekoddiṣṭa*. And thus, since the discharge of debt and the removal of faults are specified only in connection with that *mātāmaha* śrāddha which is prescribed among the paternal (*pitṛ*) śrāddhas, that alone is common to all grandsons (*dauhitra*). However, a grandson who inherits the wealth must certainly perform even the nine *śrāddhas* (*navaśrāddha*) and so forth, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*): "Whoever takes from whom, he should perform the śrāddha for him. With this very intention, Skanda also says: "The śrāddha for the maternal grandfathers must necessarily be performed by the one who inherits the wealth."
"A daughter's son (dauhitra) must always perform [the rites] according to the rules for the sake of expiating the debt.

This means that whichever daughter's son inherits the wealth, he must necessarily perform the *nava-śrāddha* and other post-mortem funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*). He states the justification for this as follows: "That which is proclaimed as wealth is but the impurity of human beings."
By grasping that, one takes on impurity which is difficult even for the wise to break through.
"The sages have prescribed for him a supreme expiation that purifies:
until the fall of the body, one should perform for him the rites of offering rice-balls and water.
But surely, [one might object]:
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikāsuta) must perform the śrāddha for his maternal grandfather according to the rule;
being connected to both families, he should perform it for both.

Thus, according to Yama, it is only the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) who is subject to a restriction, and no other restriction is observed outside of that. This is not so, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the statement. Its meaning is as follows: there are indeed two kinds of sons of an appointed daughter; one is connected to the maternal grandfather alone, while the other is connected to both the father and the maternal grandfather. Among these, the first must perform the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather as a rule, whereas the *śrāddha* for the father may be performed at his own discretion. As for the one connected to both, he must perform the *śrāddha* for both. Therefore, no restrictive rule is understood from this passage. Furthermore, as for what was stated by Manu:
For the daughter’s son shall take the entire inheritance of a father who has no [other] son;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his own father and one to his maternal grandfather.

Thus, even that [text] intends only to mean that the daughter’s son who inherits the wealth shall perform the *nava-śrāddha* and other post-mortem rites for his father and maternal grandfather, and no one else; it does not, however, aim at a total prohibition of the *śrāddha* for others, as that would contradict the previously cited statements establishing [the son's] freedom from debt (*anṛṇya*) and so forth. Consequently, the claim made by some—that the maternal grandfather’s *śrāddha* is mandatory for the daughter’s son who inherits the wealth and for no one else—is to be disregarded, as it is based on a failure to observe the aforementioned texts. Manu states a specific rule regarding the *śrāddha* of the daughter’s son:
"The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) should first offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa) to his mother,
the second to her father, and the third to his own father.
Regarding the son of an appointed daughter who belongs to two lineages (dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa), there is a specific rule stated by Uśanas:
"However, for the maternal grandfather, the order begins with the mother and so forth;
for the paternal [lineage], it begins with the father and so forth, because according to the Dharma, there is a right of succession from the mother and from the father.
Regarding the *kṣetraja* son who belongs to two lineages (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*), that which was stated by Devala is as follows:
"Those who belong to two lineages (dvyāmuṣyāyaṇakas) should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water separately to both [fathers].
This means "to both paternal and maternal groups. Regarding this, Marīci states the specific order:
"Whether he be of the same lineage or of a different lineage, whoever becomes a son according to the prescribed rule..."
One should first offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and the performance of the śrāddha rite to the owner of the field (kṣetrin).

"But if, after that, the owner of the field should somehow survive while the owner of the seed has died, they should first give [the inheritance] to the owner of the seed; it is given later [to the owner of the field]. The word "to the owners of the field" (*kṣetriṇaḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the performance of the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* and other rites in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination regarding the *śrāddha* for one whose father is living (*jīvapitṛka-śrāddha*).
On this matter, Kātyāyana states:
"One has no authority over the ancestral rites of one's father;

according to the Śruti, one should not give anything while bypassing a living person. This means that in ancestral rites (*pitṛkṛtya*), such as *śrāddha* ceremonies involving the grandfather and others, [the son has no authority]. Regarding this, an exception is shown in certain cases in the *Maitrāyaṇīyapariśiṣṭa*.

"At a wedding, at the birth of a son, at a *pitryeṣṭi*, at a *saumika* sacrifice, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and when a Brāhmaṇa has arrived—these six [are occasions for a Śrāddha] while the father is still living. This means that these six are the times for a son to perform a Śrāddha while his father is alive. Regarding the *pitryeṣṭi*, this refers to the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices; regarding the *saumika* sacrifice, it refers to the *piṇḍadāna* performed from the *puroḍāśa* cake at the Soma sacrifice and others. This is intended to include those [rites] where the Soma is present. For this very reason, Sumantu says:
A twice-born man whose father is still living shall not perform a śrāddha rite without the sacred fire;
however, one who maintains the sacred fire should perform it for those same ancestors to whom his father would have offered oblations.
"The grandfather also should act in this very same way while the father is alive and maintains the sacred fires;
even one who maintains the sacred fires should not perform it while the great-grandfather is alive. Thus it is said.

The mention of the *prapitāmaha* (great-grandfather) is for the purpose of indicating the great-grandfather together with the father and grandfather. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "If the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are all living, one should not perform the offering at all. When it is asked how the rite should be performed when both the father and grandfather are living, he himself says: "He who performs the *śrāddha* while his father is living should perform it for those for whom his father would have performed it; [likewise] when the father and grandfather are living, [he should perform it] for those for whom his grandfather would have performed it. Similarly, even when two or one out of the three beginning with the father has died, it has been stated by that same author: "He whose father is deceased should, having placed the *piṇḍa* for the father, offer to the two beyond the grandfather. He whose grandfather is deceased should, having placed the *piṇḍa* for him, offer to the two beyond the great-grandfather. And he whose grandfather and great-grandfather are deceased, or he whose father and great-grandfather are deceased, should, having placed the *piṇḍa* for the father, offer to the two beyond the grandfather. In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*, the *śrāddha* for only two is prescribed when the father is living.

"O best of the Bharatas, because [the rite] should not be given while [the father] is alive, therefore one whose father is living should perform [the Śrāddha] with only two [invitations]; of this there is no doubt.
But Manu says that one should feed at the Śrāddha only him among the three who is living.
While one's father is still living, however, one should perform the offerings for the ancestors alone;
at the śrāddha, one should cause one's own father—who has been mentally envisioned—to partake as if he were a Brahmin guest.
But if one's father has passed away while the grandfather is still living,
he should pronounce his father’s name and then proclaim the name of the great-grandfather.
"Or the grandfather may eat that *śrāddha*," so Manu declared.

This refers to the ancestors beginning with the grandfather. There is also a *nigama*: "Some say that one should feed the one among the ancestors who is living, as he occupies the place of the *pitṛ*s; Hiraṇyaketu says it should be given whether they are living or not. This should also be understood to apply to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states:
"The *pitṛyajña* is performed by means of the *homa*, provided the father is living."
Or, having fed his father, he should offer two funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for his father.
"But if both [the father and grandfather] have passed away, yet the great-grandfather lives,
one should offer two rice-balls for the former ancestors and feed the great-grandfather.
Yama, however, states that even the fire-oblation (*homa*) is optional.
The ancestral rite (pitrya) is not prescribed for one whose father is still living; even the oblation into the fire is optional.
Or rather, he should offer it to those same ancestors to whom his father would have offered it during the Vedic sacrificial ritual.
"One should give to them [the ancestors] and to those beyond; however, one may live [off the offerings] if the triad [of ancestors] is alive.

Here, *pitrya-piṇḍadāna* refers to the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) in the ancestral rites, specifically the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* performed during the Vedic fire-sacrifice (*vaitānakarman*). Āpastamba, however, states that when the father is alive, the offering of rice balls is not obligatory: "If the father is alive, one should not offer until the oblation (*homa*); having omitted [the rice balls], one should desist. In this matter, the settled rule is according to one's own *śākhā*. It is also stated in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* that direct worship (*pratyakṣārcana*) is forbidden in the *śrāddha*:
"Manu declared that direct worship in the *śrāddha* is not appropriate."
[18] "The offering of the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is also equal to a great sin.
In this context, Manu is the authoritative knower, for it was Manu himself who prescribed the direct worship.
Thus concludes the determination of the eligibility for the *śrāddha* performed while the father is still living, in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follow the times for the *śrāddha*;
regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:

The new moon day, the Aṣṭakās, a time of prosperity, the dark fortnight, the two solstices, the availability of materials, the excellence of Brahmins, the equinoxes, and the sun’s transit— these are the occasions for [performing] ancestral rites.
"Vyatīpāta, Gajacchāyā, the eclipses of the moon and the sun, and a personal inclination toward performing a śrāddha—these are proclaimed as the times for śrāddha.
On whichever lunar day (tithi) the sun and the moon are in close conjunction, that is the new moon (amāvāsyā). On that lunar day, the śrāddha is mandatory. And so says Laugākṣi:
"One whose father has died must himself perform the *śrāddha* necessarily every month on the new moon (*indukṣaya*), as well as on the full moon (*vṛddhi*) and annually.

Here, *indukṣaya* refers to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). The *aṣṭakās* are the eighth days of the dark fortnights of the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, according to the traditional teaching of Śaunaka: "The *aṣṭakās* occur on the eighth days of the dark fortnights of the four [months] of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. In this case as well, the *śrāddha* is mandatory.
On the new moon day, during the vyatīpāta yoga, on the full moon day, and on the aṣṭakā days,
a learned man who does not perform the śrāddha rite incurs the need for expiation.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Pitāmaha. "Vṛddhi" refers to the birth of a son and other such occasions. Here too, the Śrāddha is obligatory: "If the deities are not gratified by those householders during a Vṛddhi ceremony, all that gift is demonic; it is indeed a demonic rite."

Thus, according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Vṛddha-Śātātapa. The "dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is the latter half of the month (*aparapakṣa*). Here too, the *śrāddha* is obligatory, because of the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana: "One should not let the latter fortnight pass even with mere vegetables. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states a specific rule: "In the latter fortnight, one should give [offerings] to the ancestors after the fourth day. The meaning of "after the fourth day" is starting from the fifth day. Gautama also says: "Now, regarding the *śrāddha*: one should give to the ancestors on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), or starting from the fifth day of the latter fortnight as prescribed for the *śrāddha*, or on every day of it. The meaning is that one should give to the ancestors starting from the fifth day of the latter fortnight, or on every day of the latter fortnight beginning from the first day (*pratipad*). Kātyāyana also says: "One should perform the *śrāddha* in the latter fortnight on whichever day [the necessary materials] may be available after the fourth day. The meaning is that one should perform it on whichever day after the fourth the materials and so forth become available; by this, it is stated that one should perform the *śrāddha* on a single day. And it has been said by Gautama: "Or on every day, or when the materials, the place, and the Brāhmaṇas are all present. In this case, the arrangement depends on one's capacity. For this very reason, Gautama says: "The restriction of time is according to one's ability. The meaning here is that the restriction of time occurs according to one's capability. When it is performed on a single day, then the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha* must be performed separately, because of the separate mention [in the texts]: "The new moon, the *aṣṭakā*s, the prosperity rites (*vṛddhi*), and the dark fortnight," and because of the restrictive traditional teaching: "On whatever day of the latter fortnight [the *śrāddha*] may be available, especially on the new moon day. Likewise...
The twice-born man whose father has died who does not perform the Śrāddha rite every month at the waning of the moon must undergo penance.

This is because Vyāghra prescribes an expiation for its non-performance; likewise, Hārīta declares its obligatory nature by stating, "One should perform the obligatory rites somehow or other on the new moon day and so forth. Therefore, the claim made by some—that "the *amāvāsyā* śrāddha is optional with respect to the *aparapakṣika* śrāddha"—is refuted. Furthermore, regarding the fortnight of the waning moon (*aparapakṣa*), there is a specific rule stated by Āpastamba: "It should be performed month after month; the afternoon of the *aparapakṣa* is best, as are the later days of the *aparapakṣa*. The "later days" refer to the tenth day onwards. For this very reason, Manu says:
"In the dark fortnight, starting from the tenth day and excluding the fourteenth, these lunar days (tithis) are praised for the *śrāddha*, whereas others are not so.
This means that among the lunar days beginning with the tenth, the fourteenth is to be excluded. However, the fourteenth is [suitable] only for those killed by weapons. As Yājñavalkya said:
"Starting from the first day [of the lunar fortnight], excluding the fourteenth day, this is offered by you for those who have indeed been slain by a weapon.
The mention of "weapon" (*śastra*) is intended to indicate poison and so forth as well. For this very reason, Marīci says:

For those who have killed a Brahmin, or for those who have committed suicide by means of poison, weapons, wild beasts, fire, or animals, the funeral rites should be performed on the fourteenth day; for others, however, they are censured.
Pracetas also says:

"For those who die by climbing trees, through iron and the like, or by water, poison, and so forth, as well as for those killed by clawed or fanged beasts and venomous snakes, the fourteenth day is prescribed. [21]
Regarding this, Garga states the specific rule:
"The Śrāddha performed on the fourteenth day after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa for one slain by a weapon must be conducted according to the Ekoddiṣṭa procedure."

The meaning is that when the *aparapakṣika-śrāddha* (the ancestral rite of the dark fortnight) for one who was killed by a weapon is performed on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), it must be done according to the procedure for a single offering (*ekoddiṣṭa*) and not otherwise. For this very reason, Sumantu states: "But for those whose *piṇḍas* have been unified (*sapiṇḍīkṛta*), a separate performance is not appropriate after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, except on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight."
As for that which is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "The first lunar day (pratipad) leads to the acquisition of wealth; the second bestows bipeds;
the third is for those seeking the welfare of others; and the fourth destroys enemies."
On the fifth [day] one attains prosperity; on the sixth, a man becomes worthy of worship;
on the seventh, lordship over the Gaṇas; and on the eighth, supreme supernatural power.
On the ninth day one attains prosperity; on the tenth, the fulfillment of all desires;
and on the eleventh, one devoted to ritual action likewise attains all the Vedas.
On the twelfth day, the worshiper of the ancestors obtains the fruit of recitation,
as well as desired progeny, pure cattle, independence, and supreme intelligence.
A man devoted to the ancestral rites who performs the Śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day attains long life as well as sovereignty; of this there is no doubt.
He whose deceased ancestors were young men, or who were slain by a weapon,
should perform [the rite] on the fourteenth day if he desires their success.
[22] A pure man who performs a *śrāddha* with effort on the new moon day attains all his desires and enjoys infinite heaven.

Thus, this [statement] is not intended to refute its permanence, but rather aims to show that a specific fruit arises from a specific time. For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "By performing [the rite] on any day of the dark fortnight, one pleases the ancestors; however, for the performer, there is a distinction of fruit due to the restriction of time. Now, the subject at hand is discussed: the two solstices (*ayana*) are the transits (*saṃkrānti*) of Capricorn (*makara*) and Cancer (*karkaṭaka*). Here too, the *śrāddha* is obligatory. For this very reason, Parāśara states in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, during the three Aṣṭakās, and during the two solstices..."
A self-controlled man should also offer water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors here.
By him a śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years; this is a secret that the ancestors declare.
From the statement, "There is water here as well," it is understood that the *ayana-śrāddha* (ancestral rite performed during the solstices) is obligatory (*nitya*). Jātūkarṇya also says:

"During an eclipse of a planet, at the equinoxes, when the Maghā asterism occurs, during both solstices, and likewise when the *śaṅkha* and *padma* [yogas] arise—whatever is given at these times becomes equal to a thousand gold coins (*niṣka*)."

The syntactical connection here is: "What is given constantly here is equal to a thousand *niṣkas*. The meaning is: "In the fortnight of the latter half of the month of Nabhasya, on that which is the *Maghā* [nakṣatra]. The nature of the *śaṅkha* and other [vessels] has been stated by that very same author:
"The best of the twice-born call the new moon day the *śaṅkha*, when the moon has waned;
on the *aṣṭakā* days it is the *padma*; what is given there becomes inexhaustible" [23].
Alternatively, the *padma* is as stated by Śaṅkha:
"Just as *viṣṭi*, *vyatīpāta*, and likewise Sunday, that is declared to be named *padmaka*; and it is four times more [efficacious] than the *ayana*."

As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "The transit of the sun, the two equinoxes, the Vyatīpāta yoga, one's own birth-star, and a time of prosperity—Prajāpati has declared these to be the optional times for Śrāddha;
the Śrāddha given on these occasions conduces to infinity."

This [statement] also does not serve to refute its permanence (*nityatva*), because there is no contradiction between its being permanent and its being optional (*kāmyatva*), as in the case of the *agnihotra* and other rites, according to the two statements. "The acquisition of substance and a Brāhmaṇa" means that the time when there is the acquisition—that is, the obtaining—of the substance or of a Brāhmaṇa worthy of the *śrāddha*, as will be described, is the time for the *śrāddha*. Here too, the *śrāddha* is obligatory. As Hārīta says:
"But when a substance is available at a sacred site (*tīrtha*), one need not wait for a specific time;
having obtained a worthy Brāhmaṇa as a recipient, the *śrāddha* is properly prescribed."

A *tīrtha* refers to the Gaṅgā and other such sacred sites. The *viṣuvat* is the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*) into Aries and Libra. Regarding this, there is a specific rule stated by Pulastya: "The *śrāddha* should be performed during the two solstices (*ayana*), likewise during the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), and on all *yugādi* days, except for the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nirvāpaṇa*)."

The *sūryasaṃkrama* is the Sun’s transition from one zodiac sign (*rāśi*) to another. Although the term *sūryasaṃkrama* alone would suffice to establish the occurrence of any transit, the separate mention of "the solstices (*ayana*) and the equinoxes (*viṣuva*)" is for the purpose of indicating a greater abundance of merit. For this very reason, Śaṅkha states: "Whatever is given during the 'elephant-shadows' (*hasticchāyā*), whatever is given at the sight of Rāhu, and likewise at the equinoxes and solstices—all that attains infinity."

Vyatīpāta is a specific astrological conjunction (yoga) described by Vṛddha-Manu: "If the new moon day (amāvāsyā) occurs on a Sunday in conjunction with the asterisms Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, or Abhijit, it is called Vyatīpāta."

The meaning is that if the new moon (amāvāsyā) is joined with Sunday and the asterism Śravaṇa or others, that is called Vyatīpāta. Nāgadaivata is the asterism Āśleṣā; Mastaka is Mṛgaśiras. On these occasions also, the Śrāddha is obligatory:
"On the new moon, on Vyatīpāta, on the full moon, and on the Aṣṭakās—the learned man who does not perform the Śrāddha becomes liable to penance."

Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Pitāmaha: "Gaja-chāyā" means the shadow of an elephant; one should offer the Śrāddha during that [shadow]. Likewise, the Kāṭhaka Śruti states: "For this is the path of the gods and ancestors—that one should offer the Śrāddha in the shadow of an elephant. Also in the Mahābhārata:
"With a goat entirely made of copper, during the rainy season, one whose vows are restrained should [offer it] according to rule in the shadows of elephants, fanned by ear-fans."
One should offer the *śrāddha*—this is the ellipsis. By the phrase "fanned with the ears as a fan," it is understood that this refers specifically to the shadow of an elephant. Manu also says:
"May he be born in our lineage who would give us milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth lunar day, when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east. [25]

The meaning is: "in that region which has its shadow cast toward the east" (*prākchāya*). Alternatively, it refers to the technical term *gajacchāyā*. This is shown in another Smṛti: "When the Moon is in the constellation presided over by the ancestors (Maghā) and the Sun is situated in the hand (Hasta), and the lunar day is that of Vaiśravaṇa (the third day of the dark fortnight), that is known as *gajacchāyā*."

On the thirteenth lunar day dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛdaivatyā*), when the sun is in the constellation *Haṃsa* (i.e., *Śravaṇā*) and the moon is in the constellation *Kara* (i.e., *Hasta*), it is the *Vaiśravaṇī* Trayodaśī. As it is stated in the *Purāṇa*:
"That thirteenth day which occurs when the sun is in *Hasta* and conjoined with the *Makhā* (i.e., *Pūrvaphalgunī*) constellation is called *Vaiśravaṇī*; it is the shadow of the elephant."
When the moon is situated in the constellation Haṃsa and the new moon day is joined with the Hasta nakṣatra, that is the Kuñjaracchāyā; thus Bodhāyana has declared.

"When the moon has entered the *vanaspati* [constellation] and the shadow falls facing eastward, that is declared to be 'elephant-shadow' (*gajacchāyā*); one should perform the *śrāddha* at that time.
This means on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) in the afternoon.
When the son of Siṃhikā (Rāhu) eclipses the sun at the junctions of the lunar phases, that is called Gajacchāyā; one should perform a Śrāddha ceremony during that time.
Rāhu is the son of Siṃhikā. Regarding this, a specific result is shown in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"One should feed the Brahmins with ghee and pour ghee upon the ground;
having performed the Śrāddha in the shade of an elephant, one does not grieve."
Also in the *Śrī-Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"At Gayā, during an eclipse of Rāhu, one should feed a yogin with rhinoceros meat; and [one should do so] under the shadow of an elephant for the sake of our lineage."
But that satisfaction shall be lasting for us;
the donor shall become one who acts at will throughout all worlds.
"If even this group of five were not present, we would always attain infinite satisfaction; how much more so with all these riches! Thus, the fault of the eater is also shown in another Smṛti:
Whether one accepts a black antelope skin as a gift or sells it,
if that person eats while seated in the "elephant's shadow" (the shadow of an elephant), he shall not be born as a human again.
"An eclipse of the moon and the sun" means that an eclipse is an *uparāga*. In this case as well, the *śrāddha* is obligatory. For this very reason, Śātātapa says:
"The *śrāddha* must indeed be performed even at the cost of one's entire property during the appearance of Rāhu;
he who does not perform that *śrāddha* sinks like a cow in the mud."
Likewise, the specific fruit [of this] has been shown by Viṣṇu:
"A śrāddha offered at the sight of Rāhu remains as long as the moon and stars;
endowed with all virtues, it reaches the ancestors and fulfills every desire. Thus it is said.
And Ṛṣyaśṛṅga also says:
"But when the sun is seized by Rāhu, whoever performs a śrāddha—
by him indeed the entire earth is placed into the hand of the brāhmaṇa."
Regarding this, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha states the rule for the timing:
"The gods are satisfied at the moment of contact, likewise the ancestors;
humans, however, at the middle time, while the rākṣasas are satisfied at the time of release. [27]

As for that which is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "Upon obtaining a distinguished Brāhmaṇa, during solar and lunar eclipses, at the solstices (*ayana*), at the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), at the sun's passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*), during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, and on the *putraka* day..."
Upon obtaining materials suitable for a *śrāddha*, as well as upon seeing an evil dream,
or when one's birth-star (*janmarkṣa*) is afflicted by malefic planets, one may perform a *śrāddha* according to one's desire.

Thus—this [statement] "one should perform the *śrāddha* even when there is desire (*kāma*)" is intended to mean that one should perform it even then, and not to say that it is exclusively for the sake of a specific desire (*kāmya*). For this very reason, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states:
"But the occasional (*naimittika*) rite must be performed during the eclipses of the moon and sun, and upon the death of a relative; otherwise, one would become a denizen of hell."
"And optional *śrāddhas* are commended during eclipses and other such occasions.

Regarding the phrase "a desire for *śrāddha*": the meaning is that whenever there is a desire—that is, a wish—for *śrāddha*, at that very time it should be performed. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to indicate other times for *śrāddha* as well. For this very reason, Yama says:
"On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Māgha, [one should feed] three or five twice-born men."
One should satisfy the ancestors first; for that [offering], it is said to be inexhaustible.
Devala also says:
"The third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha joined with Rohiṇī,
and the thirteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya joined with Maghā."
Likewise, on the day of Śatabhiṣaj, on the ninth day of Kārttika, during the waning of the moon,
on the Gajacchāyā, on the Vaidhṛti yoga, and on the Yugādi days.
"These times have been specified as those which increase the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, the beginnings of the Yugas are shown in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"The third day of Vaiśākha and the ninth of Kārttika..."
"The fifteenth day of the month of Māgha and the thirteenth day of Nabhasya are indeed remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas (yugādi), which cause what is given to be inexhaustible.
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well.
The third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa), and the fifteenth day of Māgha.
A self-controlled man should also offer water mixed with sesame seeds here to the ancestors;
by him a Śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years—this is a secret that the ancestors declare.
The grammatical connection here is: "the third day of the bright fortnight [of Vaiśākha] and the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight [of Kārttika]. For this very reason, the *Nāradīya Purāṇa* states:
"The wise know the beginnings of the Yugas to be two in the bright fortnights and two in the dark fortnights.
However, in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, it is stated that the full moon day of Māgha is the beginning of the Yuga.
The Kṛta Yuga was established on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,
and the Tretā Yuga on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
Then, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Dvāpara Yuga begins;
and likewise, on the full moon day of Māgha, the terrible Kali Yuga begins.
The lunar days (tithis) at the commencement of the yugas are therefore renowned as Yugādyas;
for at the sun's entry into Leo, there is the end of the Kṛtayuga.
Now, at the transit of Scorpio, the end of the Tretā Yuga is to be known;
and by calculation, the end of the Dvāpara Yuga is to be known at the transit of Taurus.

"And likewise, it is recorded that within the Kali Yuga, at the transit of the sun into Aquarius (Kumbha-saṃkrānti), as well as on the beginnings and ends of the Yugas, a Śrāddha is said to yield inexhaustible merit. Thus it is stated; and also in the Purāṇa:
The third day of Vaiśākha, the ninth of Kārttika,
the full moon of Māgha, and the thirteenth of Nabhasya.
"For these are remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas, which cause what is given to be inexhaustible;
likewise, at the beginning of a Manvantara, a Śrāddha should be offered by one who possesses knowledge.
Regarding this, some maintain that the arrangement depends on the distinction between Kalpas. In this regard, there is a specific rule stated by Pulastya:
One should perform the Śrāddha at both solstices, likewise at both equinoxes,
and on all the Yugādi days, except for the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa).
The beginnings of the Manvantaras are shown in the Matsya Purāṇa:
the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
the third day of the month of Caitra, and likewise that of Bhādrapada.
The new moon of Phālguna and the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Puṣya.
The tenth day of Āṣāḍha, the seventh of the month of Māgha,
the eighth of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise the full moon day of Āṣāḍha.
The fifteenth day of the bright fortnight in the months of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha—
these are the beginnings of Manvantaras, which cause whatever is given to be inexhaustible.
Thus ends the section on the times for *śrāddha* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination of the two types of new moon days (*amāvāsyā*).

Regarding this, Gautama states: "Now, one should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). The new moon day is the fifteenth lunar day (*tithi*) of the dark fortnight; the meaning is that the *śrāddha* should be performed on that day. In this regard, there is a specific rule stated by Kātyāyana: "The *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* *śrāddha* is recommended when the moon has waned, during the third part of the day, but not too close to the time of twilight."

The *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* Śrāddha is so called because it is brought forth—that is, performed—subsequent to (*anu-paścāt*) the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) that constitute a part of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Its meaning is that it should be performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), when the moon—the "king"—has waned. When it is asked at what time that waning of the moon occurs, he himself says:
"The moon becomes waned during the eighth part of the fourteenth [lunar day];
and again, it is said to become minute during the eighth part of the new moon. Thus.
Thus, it is stated that when there is a conflict between two lunar days (*tithi*), the *śrāddha* should be performed specifically on the *sinīvālī*. And it has been said by Vyāsa:

"Sinīvālī is considered to be that [lunar day] on which the moon is visible; Kuhū is considered to be that on which the moon has disappeared. Sinīvālī is for the ancestral rites (*pitrya*), while Kuhū is for the divine rites (*daiva*)."
Hārīta also says: "In that twilight when the moon appears like a lotus stalk, it is certain that the offering of rice balls (piṇḍas) should be performed in the afternoon. [31]

On whichever lunar day, during the night, the moon is seen as if subtle while at twilight in the eastern direction, on that very day the waning of the moon occurs in the afternoon; the meaning is that the *śrāddha* should be performed then. And this is to be understood as occurring on a *sinīvālī* that extends through the time of the ritual; otherwise, a fault is heard [in the scriptures]. Thus says Bodhāyana:
"Where the fourteenth day continues beyond midday, that should be known as *sinīvālī*, but it is fruitless for rites dedicated to the ancestors."

The meaning is that *sinīvālī*, as defined by the aforementioned characteristics, should be understood as fruitless for rites dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*). Bṛhaspati also says: "That new moon which begins after midday should be known as pierced by the fourteenth day (*bhūta*); it shall not be considered the fifteenth day."
The meaning is that one has exceeded the time for the ritual after midday. With this very intention, Kārṣṇājini also said:
"Those who perform the śrāddha rite on a new-moon day pierced by [the previous lunar day], whether out of delusion or even through ignorance, their lifespan is diminished."

Therefore, the meaning is that *sinīvālī* alone, which extends throughout the time of the ritual action, is to be accepted. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Manu says: "The ancestors attend to that lunar day on which the sun sets, because the afternoon was personally assigned to them by the Self-Existent One."

But when such a *sanīvālī* (the day on which the new moon occurs while the sun is still visible) cannot be obtained, then Hārīta says that the *kuhū* (the actual new moon) itself must be accepted, provided it extends through the time of the ritual:

"For the ancestors, however, the afternoon is prescribed; therefore, for ancestral rites, that [new moon] which follows into the afternoon is to be accepted, not that which follows into the setting of the sun."

The meaning is that *kuhū* (the new moon), which follows the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), is the one to be accepted, and not *sinīvālī* of such a nature. Thus, it is stated that when there is a conflict between two lunar days (*tithidvaidha*), the one that pervades the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*) is the one to be accepted. And it has been said by that very same [author]: "Even if the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is pierced by the fourteenth day (*bhūta*) or mixed with the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipat*), it should be accepted for rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*) by the wise, provided it occurs during the *kutu-pa* period."
"Bhūtaviddhā" means pierced by the fourteenth day. Also in another Smṛti:

"Whichever lunar day (tithi) extends across midday, whether it be the preceding or the following one, on that day one should perform the ritual; its waning or waxing is no cause [for concern]. Thus it is said.
But when [the new moon] does not pervade the time of the ritual on either of the two lunar days, then one should accept that which is pierced by the fourteenth day (bhūta); thus says Bodhāyana:

"If even a single ghaṭikā of the new moon does not likewise exist on the first day (pratipad), then it should be performed—even if pierced by the fourteenth day—for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors."
The meaning is that if even a single *ghaṭikā* of the *pratipad* is not connected with the time for the performance of the rite. For this very reason, Jābāli states:

"Even among the *pratipads*, if the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) extends into the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), it should always be employed in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), even if it is pierced by the fourteenth day (*bhūta*)."
And thus, as it has been stated by Hārīta:
"If the new moon occurs in the forenoon or in the afternoon,
those who know the śrāddha rites understand that the śrāddha should be performed even on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad)."

[33] Thus, where the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is postponed because the moon cannot be seen on the previous day, it is for the purpose of enjoining the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* on the first lunar day (*pratipad*); otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the previously cited statement. Furthermore, he himself stated:
"In the signs of Libra, Capricorn, and Pisces, as well as in Virgo and Gemini, even if the new moon is pierced by the fourteenth day (*bhūta*), it should be diligently honored."

Thus, some have explained this as referring to the subject of vows, fasts, and the like. However, when [the lunar day] pervades the time for the ritual (*karmakāla*) during two lunar days (*tithi*), then that which was stated by Pracetas applies: "Sinīvālī and Kuhū are both declared in the Śruti for the rite of Śrāddha;
if they both occur at midday, how then should one offer the Śrāddha?"
When there is a decrease in the lunar day (tithi), it is Sinīvālī; likewise, when there is an increase, it is Kuhū;
and when there is equality, it should be known as Kuhū by those who know the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.

"In equality" means in the absence of decrease or increase. Thus, since the *śrāddha* would apply to all [lunar days] without distinction when there is no decrease, Laugākṣi states for the sake of specification:
"The *sinīvālī* day should be used by the twice-born who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) for ancestral rites;
the *kuhū* day should be used by women, by Śūdras, and likewise by the twice-born who do not maintain the sacred fires (*anagnika*)."

And thus, on the occasion of a death (kṣaya), those who maintain the sacred fires (sāgnika) should perform the śrāddha on the day of Sinīvālī; however, on the occasion of a prosperity-rite (vṛddhi), it should be understood that it must be performed by everyone on the following day.

Now, even so, should Sinīvālī not be accepted by those with sacred fires on every mere occasion of death? [The answer is: Only in that case where, on the day of death falling on Sinīvālī, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is to be performed. Otherwise, as it is said:
"But having completed the Pitṛyajña, a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fire [should perform the śrāddha] when the moon has waned."
One should perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month.

[34] Thus, since the performance of the *śrāddha* is not established by Manu as occurring after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* has been performed by those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), it follows that wherever the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* takes place on the new moon day (*khuḥvām*) during the waning period, that very same day must be adopted even by those who maintain the sacred fires.

It is not so. For even if [the new moon] spans both days, if there is a decrease [of the lunar day], the moon might be visible on *sinīvālī* itself; thus, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* would never be obtained. This is because Āpastamba ordains the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* only when the moon is not seen, stating: "On that day when they do not see the moon, one should perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Furthermore, it is well known in the *jyotiḥśāstra* that the non-appearance of the moon occurs only where the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) concludes within three *muhūrtas* [of the new moon]. Therefore, Manu restricts the rule: "Where the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is obtained on the day of the *śrāddha* due to the non-appearance of the moon, one who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimān*) should perform the *śrāddha* only after having performed the *pitṛyajña*. This was stated by accepting that the word *pitṛyajña* refers specifically to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, rather than asserting that one who maintains the sacred fires has the entitlement to perform a *śrāddha* only if he has already performed the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* in every case. In reality, however, the word *pitṛyajña* refers only to the *pitṛyajña* known as the libation (*tarpaṇa*). As it is said in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: [text follows]
"However, having performed the *pitṛyajña* known as *tarpaṇa*, one who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimān*) should always perform the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka-śrāddha* on the new moon day (*indukṣaye*).
Thus ends the determination of the two-fold nature of the new moon day in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some other statements concerning the new moon day (amāvāsya) are also written here; regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"The new moon day [conjoined] with Monday, or the seventh lunar day [conjoined] with Sunday..."
The fourth [tithi] on a Tuesday yields fruit equal to that of the equinox.
[35] *Amā* is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Śaṅkha also says: "The new moon is associated with the Moon; the seventh [lunar day] is with the Sun;
the fourth is with the Son of Earth (Mars); and the eighth is with the Son of the Moon (Mercury)."
These four lunar days are equal to the times of eclipses and the like;
everything performed here, such as bathing, giving gifts, and recitation, is said to be inexhaustible.
Maṅgala is the son of Bhūmi; Budha is the son of Soma. Also in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"When the new moon (amāvāsyā) is conjoined with Anurādhā, Viśākhā, or Svātī, the host of ancestors attains satisfaction for eight years through the śrāddha."
Anurādhā is Maitra.
When the new moon occurs under Puṣya, Raudra, or Punarvasu,
then the ancestors, being honored, attain satisfaction for twelve years.
The Raudra [constellation] is Ārdrā;
the Vāsava and Ajaikapāt constellations are for those desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors;
and the Amāvāsyā [day] under the Vāruṇa [constellation] is difficult to obtain even for the gods.

Vāsava is the constellation Dhaniṣṭhā, presided over by the Vasus; Ajaikapād is the constellation Pūrvabhādra; and Vāruṇa is the constellation Śatabhiṣaj. If the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha ever coincides with the Vāruṇa constellation, that is the supreme time for the ancestors, which cannot be attained by those of little merit.
O King, if at that time Dhaniṣṭhā should indeed be present,
then water and food offered to the ancestors provides satisfaction for ten thousand years to the men born in that lineage.
[36] At that time— meaning on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha—
if the Śrāddha for the ancestors is performed right there during the period of the former Bhādrapadas,
then by that, having attained supreme satisfaction, the ancestors sleep for a thousand Yugas.
The meaning is: "in that very place," that is, on that very fifteenth day.
Thus concludes the section on the New Moon (Amāvāsyā) in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now, by way of digression, the Full Moon (Parvan) is also determined.

Regarding this, Gobhila states: "That which is the greatest distance between the sun and the moon is the Paurṇamāsī; that which is the closest proximity is the Amāvāsyā. These two are of two kinds, as stated in the Purāṇa.
"Rākā and Anumati are remembered as the two kinds of Paurṇamāsī;
Sinīvālī and Kuhū are likewise the two kinds of Amāvāsyā. Thus it is said.

In this context, *Anumati* and *Sinīvālī* are associated with the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), while *Rākā* and *Kuhū* are associated with the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*). Thus says the Śruti: "That which is the earlier full moon is *Anumati*; that which is the later is *Rākā*. That which is the earlier new moon is *Sinīvālī*; that which is the later is *Kuhū*. Regarding this, Gobhila states the determination of the ritual procedure according to the specific rule: "The ends of the fortnights (*pakṣāntāḥ*) are to be observed as fasts (*upavastavyāḥ*); the beginnings of the fortnights (*pakṣādayaḥ*) are to be sacrificed upon (*abhiyaṣṭavyāḥ*). The meaning is this: the fifteenth days (*pañcadaśyaḥ*) are the ends of the fortnights; on those days, the preparatory rites such as the placing of the sacred fires (*anvādhāna*) and so forth are to be performed. The first days of the fortnights are the *pratipads*; on those days, the sacrifice itself is to be performed, including acts such as the washing of the hands (*hastāvanejana*) and the formal offering (*abhījyā*). In this matter, there is a specific distinction stated by Laugākṣi.
[37] They know that there are three parts of the fast and four parts of the sacrifice;
one should omit the last two parts in both the sacrifice and the ritual of Vratakarma.

The meaning is that the final quarter of the fifteenth day must be avoided for the preparatory rites such as the *anvādhāna* when fasting (*aupavasta*), and the final quarter of the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pakṣādi*) must be avoided for the sacrifice (*yajña*). How then, when the requirement for "four [days] for the sacrifice" arises, does Yajñapārśva explain it? "The last quarter of the fifteenth day and the first three quarters of the beginning of the fortnight constitute the time for the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice; otherwise, it does not exist."
Vṛddha-Śātātapa also says:
"The fourth part of the full moon day (parvan) and the first three parts of the following new moon day (pratipad)—
this is to be known as the time for sacrifice, declared by the wise to be the morning."
By this, it is stated that one must not perform a sacrifice during the fourth part of the *pratipad*. And it has been said by Kātyāyana:
"One must never perform sacrifices with offerings during the fourth part of the *pratipad*;
the Rākṣasas plunder them—this is the eternal Vedic injunction."

As for the scriptural injunction, "One should sacrifice at the junction (*saṃdhi*)," since the junction is extremely subtle and a sacrifice is impossible there, when it is established that the word indicates a time proximate to it, there is no contradiction because the word "junction" refers generally to the two periods of time consisting of the [end of the] *parvan* and the [beginning of the] *pratipad* which are in close proximity. For this very reason, another scripture states: "One should sacrifice on both sides of the junction. The meaning is that one should sacrifice on both sides, that is, around the junction of the *parvan* and the *pratipad*. Therefore, where the sacrifice takes place during the fourth part of the *parvan*, the completion of the sacrifice occurs precisely on the first day (*pratipad*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural injunction, "On both sides of the junction. And so it was said by Garga:

"But when the *iṣṭi* is completed on the *pratipad* without having entered [the conjunction], then the entire *iṣṭi* must be performed again by those most skilled in sacrifice, after having re-consecrated the fires. Thus, there is no contradiction, for [the re-consecration] takes place before the *agnyanvādhāna* at the junction (*saṃdhi*) with the *pratipad*. Regarding the precise determination of that junction, however, a specific rule is shown in another *smṛti*:

"Whatever ghaṭikās may remain after the tenth part [of the day], whether they be fewer or more, half of them should be subtracted or added respectively; that [correction] applies on the first day, both in the case of decrease and increase. Thus it is said.

The meaning is as follows: whatever *ghaṭikās* of the preceding lunar day (*pratipad*) may belong to the succeeding lunar day—whether they be fewer or more—their half is to be subtracted from the previous day in the case of a decrease (*hrāsa*), but added in the case of an increase (*vṛddhi*). By this, it is stated that one should combine the total number of *ghaṭikās* of the full-moon (*rākā*) and new-moon (*kuhu*) days with those of the subsequent day, divide that sum by two, and thereby determine the exact moment of the conjunction (*saṃdhi*). Furthermore, one should understand that the sacrifice must be performed on that very day when the conjunction of the *parvan* occurs, or on the following morning when the conjunction falls within the fourth part of the *parvan* as prescribed, and not elsewhere. For this very reason, Laugākṣi says: [The verse of Laugākṣi follows.]
If the festival day (parvan) concludes either in the forenoon or at midday, one should fast on the preceding day;
the sacrifice is prescribed for that [following] day.

"If the [sacrificial] joint (parvan) concludes in the afternoon or at night, one should fast on that day; the sacrifice is prescribed for the following day. The meaning is that the prescribed time is possible precisely in that case. This is also stated in the *Gṛhyakārikā*:
[39] "If the fifteenth and the first day of the lunar fortnight coincide on a single day, that [day] is great;
on that day, if the fifteenth is the primary [time], there is fasting, and if the fifteenth here is the secondary [time], there is sacrifice. Thus it is said.

The meaning of *samete* is "joined together. With this very intention, Āpastamba also says: "On whichever day the moon should rise full in the east, one should observe that as the *paurṇamāsī*; or [one may observe] the day [thinking] 'it will be full tomorrow. The Vājasaneyins prescribe the third [lunar day] as the *kharvikā*. On whichever day the moon is not seen, that day is the *amāvāsyā*; or [one may observe] the day [thinking] 'it will not be seen tomorrow. Among these, the meaning of the *kharvikā*-sūtra will be explained later. The meaning of the two sūtras—"on whichever day the moon should rise full in the east"—and "on whichever day the moon is not seen"—is as follows: In every case, it is well known in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*) that fullness and non-appearance belong respectively to the *rākā* (the full moon) and the *kuhū* (the new moon). In that regard, on whichever day the moon should rise full in the east, or should not be seen at sunrise—if at that time the junction of the lunar phases (*parvasaṃdhi*) occurs in the afternoon or at night—then one should observe that as the *paurṇamāsī* or the *amāvāsyā*. But when the junction of the phases occurs in the forenoon or at midday, then one should observe that day as *anumati* or *sinīvālī*, which is the day on which the moon will be full or the day on which people will not see it. This is the meaning of the two sūtras: "it will be full tomorrow" and "people will not see it tomorrow. And so it has been stated by the author of the *Bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha*:
If the lunar festival (parvan) concludes in the afternoon or at night,
then that full moon day (rākā) should be observed as the fast-day, characterized by the "overflowing" of the full disk.
If the lunar festival (parvan) concludes either in the forenoon or at midday, Anumati is to be observed as the fast there; it is characterized by being fulfilled on the following day.

[40] If the junction of the lunar phases (parvasandhi) should occur in the afternoon or at night, then the new moon day (kuhū) on that very day— provided it does not possess the characteristics of the following day— is to be observed as the fast-day.

"If the junction of the lunar phases (parvasandhi) should occur either in the forenoon or at midday, one should fast on that day [when] Sinīvālī is characterized by not being visible tomorrow. In this context, it should be understood that the words "forenoon" (pūrvāhṇa) and "afternoon" (aparāhṇa) denote the prior and posterior halves of the day divided into two parts, while the word "midday" (madhyāhna) denotes the junction between those two.
Now, one might argue that in this case, let the words *pūrvāhṇa* and so forth refer respectively to the three parts of a day divided into three equal portions.

This is not so; for on that view, since the midday (*madhyāhna*) would extend only as far as five *ghaṭikās* beyond the turning point (*āvartana*), if the junction (*saṃdhi*) occurred therein, the sacrifice would necessarily have to take place on that very same day. Nor can it be said, "Let it be so," because in that case, the prescribed time consisting of the fourth part of the *parvan* and so forth would be impossible, which would contradict such scriptural injunctions as, "That which is the fourth part of the *parvan*... and so on.

[Objection: But surely, since there is a division into two parts, where the *parvasaṃdhi* (the junction of the lunar phases) occurs only one *ghaṭikā* after [the end of the previous day], the sacrifice must take place on the very next day; thus, even in that case, the contradiction regarding the time is exactly the same due to the impossibility of the [prescribed] time. [Response: Not so. Since the time specified in such passages as "the fourth part of the *parvan*" is understood to be connected with the sacrifice, it must be accepted that the sacrifice itself is connected with that time. Consequently, if the sacrifice were performed on the next day in that situation, the sacrifice would not be connected with the [prescribed] time; therefore, the sacrifice must take place on the previous day, and thus there is no contradiction. This should be understood in all cases.
But in that case, would not the injunction for the sacrifice on the following day at the juncture of the afternoon be contradicted?

This is not so. Where the *parvan* conjunction occurs in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) and the sacrifice does not take place on the following day during the fourth quarter of the first lunar day (*pratipad*), it is precisely such an afternoon that is intended here; thus there is no contradiction. This is also logical. Otherwise, in the winter season, because the days are very short, the *āvartana* (midday) would occur at only slightly less than fourteen *ghaṭikās*. Likewise, in that same season, due to the increase of the lunar day (*tithi*), the fourth quarter might sometimes consist of sixteen *nāḍikās*. In that case, if the *parvan* conjunction occurred only one *ghaṭikā* after the *āvartana*, the sacrifice would necessarily fall on the following day. But this is not tenable, because of the prohibition stating that one should not sacrifice when the prescribed time is impossible, and because the time is possible on the preceding day. In this view, a mere restriction of the word "afternoon" used here would be preferable. Furthermore, in the summer season, because the days are very long, the *āvartana* occurs at a time consisting of sixteen and a quarter *ghaṭikās*. Likewise, in that same season, due to the decrease of the lunar day, the fourth quarter of the *parvan* might sometimes consist of only thirteen and a half *nāḍikās*. In that situation, when the *parvan* conjunction occurs before the *āvartana* by a quarter of a day, the conjunction would fall in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), and the sacrifice would have to take place on that very day. But this is not tenable, because the prescribed times—such as the fourth quarter of the *parvan* in the morning—are impossible then. According to this position, however, the sacrifice takes place on the following day alone, since the prescribed time is possible only then. For this very reason, Āpastamba also stated: "The followers of the Vājasaneyi school recite [the rule regarding] the *kharvikā* third [quarter]. *Kharvikā* means "small.
