Its smallness is due to its not being half a day. And this has been stated by the author of the *Bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha*.
"In this case, that day on which the junction (*saṃdhi*) of the *parvan* occurs before midday is the third [type].
Regarding the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), however, the sacrifice must certainly take place on the following day, because its commencement there occurs precisely before sunrise.
[Objection: But if that is so, would it not contradict the injunction for the sacrifice to take place on that very day when the junction occurs in the forenoon?
Not so; for there is no contradiction, since that [other injunction] can apply to a different object distinct from this one.
[42] But then, by the force of the statement of Laugākṣi, "In the forenoon or at midday," let the sacrifice take place at that very time even in the absence of the prescribed time.
Not so.
The final quarter of the fifteenth day and the first three quarters of the new moon are the time for the Pārvaṇa sacrifice; otherwise, it does not exist.

This is because of the traditional teaching that there is no other time apart from the time indicated by the half-quarter portion [of the moon] mentioned in such statements. Furthermore, were this the case, scriptures prescribing times such as "the fourth quarter of the *parvan*" would be rendered entirely useless due to the impossibility of their having any scope. Therefore, the claim made by some—that "if the conjunction occurs in the afternoon, there is no fault in performing the sacrifice even during the fourth quarter of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) on the following day"—is refuted. And thus, as stated by Kātyāyana:
"If the moon is visible in the western direction on the day of sacrifice..."
Having offered oblations there with the Vyāhṛtis, one should give a staff to a twice-born man.
Thus, as for another Smṛti text:
"If the second [lunar day] lasts for three muhūrtas and the first [day] occurs in the afternoon,
the anvādhāna should be performed on the fourteenth day, because the moon would be visible thereafter."
Thus, it should be understood that this refers to the junction of the morning and the parvan. Furthermore, there is another statement:
"The desired *iṣṭi* is on the sixteenth day; the middling is on the fifteenth day;
the inferior *iṣṭi* is on the fourteenth day; and the wretched one is on the seventeenth day."

Thus, by the statement "on the seventeenth day one should neither perform the *iṣṭi* nor add fuel to the fire," it is specifically the adding of fuel (*anvādhāna*) that is prohibited there, not the sacrifice itself. If that were the case, then in the event of an increase in the lunar days (*tithi-vṛddhi*), distinguished practitioners would simply fail to perform the rite altogether. Therefore, it must be understood that starting from the day of sacrifice, the *aupavasathika* ritual should not be performed on the seventeenth day. For this very reason, Bodhāyana says: "Where the *aupavasatha* ritual would fall on the thirteenth or even the seventeenth day from the day of sacrifice, one should avoid it with great care."

But surely, since the decrease or increase of two days is possible, the ritual for the fast-day (aupavasathya-karman) might sometimes not fall on the thirteenth or seventeenth day; how then can there be a prohibition?

It is said: if there is non-attainment [of the time], then—just like the statement "not in the intermediate space, not in heaven"—this is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*), and thus everything is faultless. However, regarding the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), there is a specific rule stated by Āpastamba: "On the full moon day, [the rites] beginning with the placing of fuel (*anvādhāna*), the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*), and the fasting (*upavāsa*) are performed either immediately or on the same day; or, in the case of an immediate-time [full moon], everything is performed [on that very day]. The meaning of this is: on an immediate-time full moon day, the placing of fuel for the fires and so forth are performed either immediately—that is, on the same day—or on the preceding day; in that case, everything up to the satiating of the Brahmins is performed. It has been stated by the author of the *Bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha* that [the rites] ending with the *iḍā* portion do not [apply].
"The placing of the anvāhiti fire, the spreading [of the grass], and the fasting—these indeed take place on the previous day at the full moon.
However, if the junction of the lunar phases (parvasandhi) occurs before the turning point (āvartana), then the entire rite is performed on that very day.
The phrase "before the turning point" implies "after the time of saṅgava."
If the conjunction occurs after the time of sunrise and before the sun's turning back [at midday],
that lunar day is to be known as the full moon (paurṇamāsī) for the rite to be performed on the same day.
[44] Thus, according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Kātyāyana.

However, some maintain that the portion beginning with "on the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsyām*) and ending with "or immediately" (*sadyo vā*) constitutes one single sūtra, while another [portion], "in the case of an immediate time (*sadyaḥkāla*), everything is performed," is a separate sūtra. In this regard, the meaning of the first sūtra is that on every full moon day, the rite beginning with the placing of fuel on the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) is performed either immediately or on the preceding day. As for the second, however, it refers to a modification (*vikṛti*) performed at an immediate time; in that case, everything up to the satiation of the Brahmins (*brāhmaṇatarpaṇa*) is performed, but not the concluding *iḍā* offering and so forth.

This is not correct. In the view that the *sadyaskāla* (immediate) period applies when the junction (*saṃdhi*) occurs in the afternoon, there is a contradiction with the Vedic injunction: "One should sacrifice around the junction. This has been stated regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*). As for the ectype (*vikṛti*), although it appears that the same time—characterized by the fourth part of the *parvan* day and so forth—should apply here as well due to the extension (*atideśa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual procedure according to the rule, "The Darśapūrṇamāsa are the archetype of sacrifices," nevertheless, Āpastamba prescribes the time again for the ectype: "If one should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, with an animal, or with Soma, one should sacrifice on the new moon or full moon day. Therefore, the completion of the sacrifice must occur on the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) itself. Consequently, where the fifteenth day and the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) are both complete, one should conclude the ectype on the fifteenth day itself, and immediately thereafter perform the preparatory rites (*agnyanvādhāna*, etc. for the archetype. When the junction of the *parvan* occurs in the forenoon during a fragmented lunar day (*khaṇḍatithi*), then because the prescribed time is impossible on the previous day—even if it were possible, it would be impossible at the stage of commencing the rite—it does not pervade both the primary and auxiliary parts. For Āpastamba states: "The primary rite together with its auxiliaries is designated as being performed at a specific place, time, and agent," thereby enjoining the connection with the prescribed time only for the rite together with its auxiliaries. It has also been stated regarding the following day: since the archetype was mentioned previously, Āpastamba himself ordains the archetype before the ectype with the rule, "The unprecedented [rite] should be at the end. Thus, immediately after the archetype, the performance of the ectype is to be understood as occurring within the three parts of the *pratipad* and so forth, which are obtained through extension (*atideśika*), provided that the primary and auxiliary rites can be completed therein. However, when the junction of the *parvan* occurs in the afternoon or at night, then the sacrifice takes place on that very day, because the prescribed time is possible precisely then. Having all this in mind, it was said: [45] When the junction of the *parvan* occurs in the afternoon or at night, the sacrifice is on that very day, because the prescribed time is possible then. All this was intended [by the author].

"If the junction of the lunar phase (parvasaṃdhi) occurs before the time of turning back (āvartana), one should perform the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) after having first performed the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti). If it should occur later than that, then the sacrifice of the modified rite is on that very day, and that of the archetypal rite is on the following day. This should be understood to apply to the animal sacrifice (paśu) as well; for this very reason, it has been stated there too.
The joint of the lunar day (parvasandhi) occurs before the end of the day;

having performed the preliminary rites on that day, one should then commence the animal sacrifices either immediately or after two days, provided the joint of the lunar day falls later [in the following day]. If it were otherwise, the procedure would be according to the archetype.
"Having performed [the preliminary rites] upon that [altar], one should then become a *paśu* (sacrificial victim) immediately.

Since the prescribed time is impossible on the following day during the morning twilight (*pūrvāhṇasaṃdhi*), the word "immediately" (*sadya eva*) is used. However, the oral instruction (*upadeśa*) there also states that the duration is two days; therefore, since that contradicts such scriptural statements as "one should not sacrifice," it must simply be disregarded.

Thus concludes the determination of the lunar festivals (*parvanirṇaya*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now, as an incidental topic, follows the determination regarding the conflict between two lunar days (*tithidvaidha*).
On this matter, the *Skandapurāṇa* states:
"All [days] beginning with the *pratipad*, from sunrise to sunrise, are renowned as 'complete' (*sampūrṇā*), provided they exclude the day of Hari (the eleventh day). Thus it is said.

In these "complete" days, the performance of the ritual is indeed beyond doubt. However, where there is a twofold division of the lunar day (*tithi*) due to its waning or waxing, that which is declared in the *Nigama* applies.
The second, third, fourth, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, fourteenth, and fifteenth lunar days are auspicious when conjoined with the moon on those respective dates.
Specifically, the twelfth is joined with the eleventh, and the full moon is joined with the fourteenth.
"The first lunar day (pratipad) and the new moon (amāvāsyā)—this pair of lunar days yields great fruit.
If these are reversed, it is a great fault that destroys previously accumulated merit. Thus [it is said].

In this context, by the words "pair" (*yugma*) and so forth, ending with "aperture" (*randhra*) and "end" (*antya*), there is a sequential reference to the lunar days beginning from the second and ending with the ninth, because of the definition that "a pair consists of two lunar days. *Rudra* refers to the eleventh day. The meaning is that among the lunar days beginning from the second and ending with the first (*pratipad*), a mutual pairing of each successive pair of lunar days yields great fruit; however, a pair consisting of non-sequential lunar days does not. By this, it is stated that within the aforementioned seven lunar days of the "pair," the preceding lunar day should be taken when overlapped by the following one, while the subsequent lunar day should be taken when overlapped by the preceding one. Like the third day and others, the tenth and thirteenth days are also [to be taken] when overlapped by the preceding day. And thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
"The fifth, the seventh, the tenth, the thirteenth, as well as the first and the ninth— these lunar days (tithis) should be observed as 'saṃmukhā'.
Here, "saṃmukhā" means "preceded by [the previous day]."
"Face-to-face" (*saṃmukhā*) is seen as that which extends through the evening;

thus it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*. As for the statement in the Vedic text regarding the third lunar day and the full moon being "preceded by" (*pūrvaviddha*), that refers to specific types of vows. For this very reason, the *Brahmakai varta* states:
"O best of the twice-born, with the exception of the third lunar day called Rambhā..."
In all other matters, she is praised when accompanied by her attendants.

[47] "The new moon day (*amā*) pierced by the [preceding] lunar day (*bhūta*) should never be used for the *pūrṇā* [observance], O best of sages, with the exception of the supreme *Sāvitrī-vrata*. Thus, the third lunar day called *Rambhā* refers to the vow known as the *Rambhā-tṛtīyā*. "Joined with the *gaṇa*" means joined with the fourth lunar day; "the new moon" (*amā*) refers to the *amāvāsyā*. And so it is stated in the *Nāradīya-purāṇa*:
One who performs the New Moon sacrifice (Darśa), the Full Moon sacrifice (Pūrṇamāsa), or the anniversary day of a father's death on a date overlapping with the previous lunar day,
falls into hell.

Thus, that [rule] also should be understood as referring specifically to the Sāvitrī-vrata; however, for a fast (upavāsa), only that [lunar day] conjoined with the following day is to be taken. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"The eleventh, eighth, sixth, full moon, fourteenth, new moon, and third—these are to be observed as fasts when conjoined with the following day."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha also says:
"The second, fifth, tenth, thirteenth,
and fourteenth lunar days, through piercing, destroy the preceding and succeeding days for the purpose of fasting."
"Regarding the fast, however, the seventh [lunar day] destroys the following day by its conjunction."

The meaning is that the lunar days (tithis) beginning with the second destroy their own preceding and succeeding days due to piercing (vedha) in the context of fasting; however, the seventh destroys only its own succeeding day. By this, it is stated that the first and third lunar days should not be accepted when pierced by the second. This should be understood to apply to the fifth and subsequent days as well. Furthermore, it should be understood that what is stated in the Nigama text regarding the fourth day being pierced by the following day refers to occasions other than fasting, because in this [present] statement, the acceptability of a day pierced by the preceding one is prescribed. Moreover, as for what is stated in the Brahmakaivarta:
[48] "O best of the twice-born, the second [lunar day] should be made face-to-face with the *pratipad*.

Thus, the acceptability of a *pratipad*-pierced [second] has been stated; however, that too refers to occasions other than the fast (*upavāsa*), because it is traditionally remembered that for the fast, only the completely pierced [second] is acceptable. And so it is said in the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"The eleventh, the eighth, the sixth, the second, and the fourteenth..."
"The new moon day and the third lunar day should be observed as fasts when they are joined with the following [day].
In this context, the quality of being "joined with the following" (*paraviddha*) regarding the fourteenth day refers to the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). For this very reason, the *Nigama* states:
"The eleventh, eighth, sixth, and the fourteenth days of the bright fortnight..."
"The meritorious [days] are joined with the subsequent, and the subsequent are joined with the preceding.
Here, "subsequent" means immediate;
however, that sixth lunar day which is pierced by the Nāga (the fifth), and the Sun (the seventh) which is pierced by Rudra (the eleventh).
Even Viṣṇu would be pierced by desire; therefore, those days should not be observed.
When the ninth and the eleventh lunar days are pierced by the tenth,
they must be especially avoided, just as one avoids the water of the Gaṅgā when it has been touched by a dog.

Thus, from the recollection of the Purāṇas: "The Nāga is the fifth; Rudra is the eighth; the Sun is the seventh; Kāma is the thirteenth; Viṣṇu is the twelfth; the Direction (Dik) is the tenth. In this same manner, the eighth should also be understood. For this very reason, another Smṛti states:

"The eighth of the dark fortnight and the fourteenth of the dark fortnight should be observed when joined with the preceding [tithi]; they are never to be observed when joined with the following [tithi]."

The eighth day of the bright fortnight and the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight should not be observed when overlapped by the preceding day; they should be observed when joined with the following day.
"For this is the eternal law regarding rites such as fasting.
The fact that the thirteenth day is "pierced" by the following [fourteenth] refers specifically to the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa). For this very reason, the Nigama states:
"The sixth, the eighth, the new moon (darśa), and likewise the thirteenth of the dark fortnight..."
These should be worshipped joined with the supreme, and likewise the supreme joined with the prior.
The meaning is "the subsequent" or "the next. And thus, as it was stated by Mārkaṇḍeya:
"In the bright fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun rises is to be taken;
in the dark fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be taken."

Thus, it should be understood that this refers specifically to the fourteenth day and other such dates as determined by the distinction between the bright and dark fortnights. Furthermore, as stated by Devala: "The lunar day upon which the sun rises is to be known as complete for the purposes of bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, and so forth."

Thus, that which was stated regarding the acceptability of lunar days (*tithis*) overlapped by the subsequent day refers to that specific context. Furthermore, it was stated by that same authority: "The lunar day upon which the sun sets should be known as complete for the performance of rites such as giving gifts and Vedic study."

Thus, that [statement] also refers to those lunar days (*tithi*) which are to be accepted as being joined with the previous day (*pūrvaviddhā*). "Entire" (*sakalā*) means complete. And this is said in order to explain that because the lunar day extending over the sunrise is short, even when the ritual is performed on the subsequent lunar day, it is nonetheless considered to have been performed on that very same lunar day. With this very intention, it is also stated in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: "When there is even a single *ghaṭikā* [of a lunar day] remaining at the time of the vow, fast, or observance, that lunar day is to be known as 'entire' (*sakalā*); for rites concerning the ancestors (*pitṛ*), it is that which occurs in the afternoon."
Therefore, it is the settled conclusion that in the performance of other rites, the lunar day (tithi) is utilized according to its increase or decrease. And it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"That is the lunar day, and that is the day-and-night, during which the sun sets;
at that time one should perform the rites; the decrease or increase [of the lunar day] is not the cause [for determining the timing]."

But when [the Ekādaśī] does not extend into the next day, and instead on the previous day it is indeed overlapped by a prohibited lunar day (tithi), then that which is stated in another Smṛti applies:
"The Ekādaśī, the Tṛtīyā, the Ṣaṣṭhī, and the Trayodaśī— these should be observed as overlapped by the previous day, provided they do not exist on the following day."
And thus it has been said:
"A lunar day (tithi) is honored when the fortnight is waxing because of its increase;
when the fortnight undergoes waning, then [the tithi] shall belong to the afternoon."

Thus, since it is generally impossible for [the Ekādaśī] to extend into the following day when the [preceding] lunar day has ended, the rule that "only the one joined with the previous day" (*pūrvaviddhā*) should be accepted is identical in meaning to the previous statement. Regarding this, Ṛśyaśṛṅga states a specific distinction: "If days not pierced by forbidden [times] are not obtained, then the lunar day of Ekādaśī, even if pierced by five *muhūrtas*, must indeed be accepted."

The meaning is that if days unblemished by prohibited days cannot be obtained, then those possessing the aforementioned characteristics should be accepted. And when even such a lunar day (tithi) is not available, it has been stated by that same authority: "But when unblemished days are unavailable, one should eat only a small amount once, using milk, curd, or ghee; this indeed shall constitute a fast."
Regarding the statement, "that lunar day (tithi) is to be known as complete," Vasiṣṭha states an exception to this in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"In the case of breaking the fast (pāraṇa) or the death of men, the lunar day is considered to be that which exists at that very moment;
for rites pertaining to the ancestors (pitrya), it is declared to be full when touched at the time of sunset."

The meaning is this: whether at the conclusion [of a vow] or at death, only the lunar day (tithi) prevailing at that specific moment is relevant; it is not to be understood as if that entire lunar day were to be taken into account. This same principle is to be observed regarding the beginnings of the Manvantaras and the Yugas as well. For this very reason, the *Skanda Purāṇa* states: "At the beginning of a Manvantara, at the beginning of a Yuga, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, and during the Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti yogas, the lunar day is valid only as far as it extends at that particular time."
"And when the *nakta-vrata* has arrived, the lunar day (*tithi*) that pervades that time [is to be taken].
This means that for that *nakta-vrata*, the lunar day that pervades its specific time—known as *pradoṣa* (the evening)—is to be accepted. And so says Vasiṣṭha:
"In the *nakta-vrata*, the lunar day that always pervades *pradoṣa* is to be accepted."
"Except for Ekādaśī, all [tithis] in the bright and dark fortnights are considered equal. The duration of *pradoṣa* (the evening twilight) is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The period of three *ghaṭikās* prior to sunrise is called *saṃdhyā*."
"The evening twilight consists of three *ghaṭikās* above the setting sun;
thereafter, for three *muhūrtas*, it is *pradoṣa* once the sun has set.

The intention here is that whatever rites such as observing silence (*mauna*) are to be performed during the two twilights, they should be performed within this duration of time. However, when the lunar day (*tithi*) does not extend into the *pradoṣa* period on either of the two days, then the rule stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa* applies.
If it does not extend into the evening (pradoṣa), the rite is prescribed as being performed during the day;
this occurs when the sun has passed its double shadow.

Regarding that, they say "naktaṃ naktaṃ" (nightly meal), yet eating at night during the darkness is not what is meant. Having understood this, the wise man should therefore perform the act of eating in the evening.
"One who observes the *nakta-vrata* shall certainly obtain the fruit of the *nakta* fast.
Regarding the fast associated with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra-upavāsa*), Viṣṇu has stated:
"The lunar mansion upon which the sun sets is the one that should be observed as the fast."
"Or rather, O Rāma, [that day] on which the midnight is joined with the moon.

This means that on whichever day the midnight—the half-night—is joined with the moon, that is, with the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) that has begun its conjunction after sunset, that very mansion is to be observed for the fast. And so Sumantu says:
"On whichever lunar day (*tithi*) a lunar mansion is reached even before midnight..."

"One should perform that lunar mansion vow (*nakṣatravrata*); the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) should take place when [the vow] has passed. This means that [the vow] is attained or commenced. "When it has passed"—the word "in that lunar mansion" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. In this same way, it should be understood for a fast occasioned by a lunar day (*tithi*) as well.
Regarding the rule for lunar days and lunar mansions, the breaking of the fast occurs at the end of the lunar day.
Otherwise, by breaking the fast in a different manner, one would incur a violation of the vow.

[53] Thus it is stated in the *Smṛti*. This refers specifically to the subject of fasting (*upavāsa*) associated with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Regarding a lunar day (*tithi*) conjoined with a lunar mansion, the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* states:

"Whatever lunar days are declared to be meritorious by virtue of their conjunction with a lunar mansion, one should perform that vow on those very days, with the exception of the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī. Thus it is said.
When it is asked, "How then [should one observe] Śravaṇa-dvādaśī?", the Matsya Purāṇa states:
"If on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight the asterism Śravaṇa occurs,
one should fast on the eleventh day and worship Hari on that twelfth day."

Thus concludes the determination regarding the conflict of lunar days (*tithidvaidhanirṇaya*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now, in connection with the lunar days, the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is also determined.
Regarding that, first is the majesty (*mahimā*) of Ekādaśī. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says in the *Nāradīyapurāṇa*:
O King of kings, by the fire arising from Ekādaśī, the fuel of sin— even that produced over a hundred lifetimes— is reduced to ashes.
O King, there exists nothing for men so purifying as this day of Padmanābha, which brings about the destruction of sins.
O lord of men, sins remain in this body for as long as a living being does not observe the auspicious day of Padmanābha by fasting.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the eleventh day.
O Lord, whatever sin has been committed by means of the eleven senses,
all of that one shall render void through fasting on the eleventh day.
There exists no means of protection equal to Ekādaśī;
for she indeed bestows heaven and liberation, and grants sovereignty and sons.
For she is the bestower of a virtuous wife and the giver of health to the body;
O King, neither the Gaṅgā, nor Gayā, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara is equal to her.
Neither the Kaurava-kṣetra, nor the Revā, nor the Devikā,
nor the Yamunā, nor the Candrabhāgā is equal to a single day of Hari.
O Indra among kings, the state of Viṣṇu is indeed attained without effort;
for this [knowledge] is like the wish-fulfilling gem, or even like a treasure-trove.
She was like a wish-fulfilling tree, or rather, comparable to a celestial cow.
Nārada also said:
"By fasting on even a single Ekādaśī and worshipping Janārdana,
even out of desire, one shall attain liberation from saṃsāra."

"Or else, O Lord of the Thirty-three, even one who fasts on the eleventh day out of attachment, hypocrisy, or greed is liberated from all suffering. Thus ends the section on the greatness of Ekādaśī in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination of the eleventh day (ekādaśī). Regarding this, Devala says:
"One should not drink water from a conch shell, nor should one eat the meat of tortoises or pigs."
One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight.
[55] Kātyāyana also says:
Whatever sins there may be, even those equal to the murder of a Brahmin,
they remain dependent upon food when the day of Hari has arrived.
"O fair-faced one, the ancient texts proclaim again and again here:
'One must not eat, one must not eat when the day of Hari has arrived. 'One must not eat' means that one must observe a fast. For this very reason, Nārada says:"

"Those men who are devoted to Viṣṇu and endowed with constant devotion must observe the fast on Ekādaśī every fortnight. Here, the grammatical connection is that the fasting must be performed as a mandatory duty (*nitya*). By this, the obligatory nature of the Ekādaśī vow is stated. For this very reason, the fault incurred by its non-performance is shown in the Purāṇa.
O best of gods, that twice-born man who eats on the eleventh day eats food morsel by morsel that is as sinful as the excrement of a dog.
If one who is capable and free from affliction eats on the eleventh day, his sin will be equal to the drinking of liquor; of this there is no doubt.
"O best of gods, from drinking liquor one surely goes to hell;
but he who desires the food of the Ekādaśī sinks into [hell] along with his ancestors.

Therefore, the sense is that one should fast on the Ekādaśī of both fortnights. And this injunction for fasting during both fortnights refers to forest-dwellers (*vanastha*) and others. For this very reason, Gobhila says:
"One should not eat on the eleventh day of both fortnights; this is the duty of forest-dwellers and ascetics, but a householder should always observe the bright fortnight alone.
Thus it should also be understood for the student (*brahmacārin*) and others. For this very reason, another *smṛti* states:

"One should not eat on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) of either fortnight; the celibate student (brahmacārī), the woman, and the householder (gṛhī) [should observe it] always during the bright fortnight alone. The term "householder" here implies one who has sons, because there is a traditional injunction prohibiting his fasting on the dark eleventh day (kṛṣṇaikādaśī).
A householder who has sons should not observe a fast on the day of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, or during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, as well as on the sun's transit (saṃkrānti),
a householder who has sons should neither break his fast nor observe a fast.
Also in another Smṛti: "On a Sunday, on the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight,
or during the Vyatīpāta yoga— if a Śrāddha has been performed, a householder who has sons should not fast."
O Yudhiṣṭhira,
even for one who observes a fast on the day of the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti) and breaks it [immediately],
or on the dark eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), an eldest son perishes.

This being the case, one should not suspect that for a householder who has sons, there is no fasting on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight when it coincides with a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) or similar occasions. For Jaimini says:
"On a Sunday, during a solar transit, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, a householder who has sons should neither perform a fast nor break his fast."

[57] This prohibition of fasting on account of that [occasion] has been cited; it should not be understood as applying to incidental [occasions], since fasting is obligatory [on those days]. Thus it is said.

This is a prohibition of the *nimitta* (the occasion), such as Sunday and so forth; it is not, however, a prohibition of fasting based on the conjunction of Sunday and other such days with the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*), because the meaning is that fasting on the eleventh day is obligatory. Some explain this as follows: since this is read within the section on the eleventh day, the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the eleventh day proximate to that context; and since the phrase "due to the connection" (*anuṣaṅgakṛta*) refers to fasting obtained through hardship, this passage is intended to prohibit fasting for a householder with children when the eleventh day is joined with a *saṃkrānti* or similar occasion. That is weak, because syntactic proximity (*vākya-saṃnidhi*) occurs more rapidly than contextual proximity (*prakaraṇa-saṃnidhi*). Otherwise, since an eclipse of the moon (*rāhudarśana*) is impossible on the eleventh day, how could the word "that" be applicable there? If it were intended to refer merely to an eclipse of the moon, then there would be the fault of inconsistency (*vairūpya*), as a single uttered word would have two distinct meanings; therefore, the previously stated explanation alone is superior. For this very reason, Nārada says:
The Ekādaśī occurring on a Sunday, as well as that joined with a Saṃkrānti, should be observed with a fast; it increases one's sons and grandsons.
Also in the Purāṇa:
"O child, when the day of Āditya falls on the eleventh lunar day, one should diligently observe a fast thereon; it increases sons and grandsons."

Others say that for householders who have sons, there should be a fast on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-ekādaśī*), while on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-ekādaśī*) there is merely the abstention from food without specific observances (*niyama*); this should be disregarded as it is merely a fabrication of their own intellect. As for the statement of Yama to a Brāhmaṇa in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa* regarding Rukmāṅgada—who possessed sons and grandsons—prohibiting a fast on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) alone: "Men together with their fathers, and likewise with their grandfathers, and even the fathers of those [grandfathers], and the fathers of those fathers."
Then the maternal grandfathers go, as do those who are their fathers;
likewise, the fathers of those [grandfathers], and the ancestors of those progenitors.
Having fasted on the day of Hari, they indeed go to the world of Viṣṇu;
this is the staff, and this is the cloth, which has been placed at your feet.
O best among speakers, tell me of that one king who, on the arrival of the day of Hari, attained incomparable status as a guardian of the world.
If you can move me from my steadfastness, then I shall be your servant.

Thus, even in that context, the mention of "Harivāsara" (the day of Hari) should be understood as referring to the Ekādaśī specifically prescribed for Rukmāṅgada. Therefore, it is established that for a householder who has sons, the fast is on the bright (Śukla) Ekādaśī, whereas for others, it is on both. And so it is said in the Viṣṇudharmottara: "He who, out of delusion, discriminates between the white and the dark Ekādaśīs, becomes a killer of a Brahmin, a thief, a drinker of liquor, or a violator of the Guru’s bed."
Thus it is said; and also in the Purāṇa:
"A killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a killer of a brother, and likewise a killer of a guru—whoever eats on the eleventh day of both fortnights [is as such]."

Thus, it should be understood that this refers to householders who have sons and excludes others. Even though such an arrangement is possible according to the manner stated above, some—interpreting passages such as "A householder with sons shall not fast," etc., as referring specifically to optional (kāmya) fasting—describe even a householder with sons as being permitted to fast on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇaikādaśī). One should accept whatever among these views is logically sound. Furthermore, as stated by Āpastamba: "The maintainer of the sacred fires (āhitāgni), the bull (anaḍvān), and the student (brahmacārī)—these three attain perfection only while eating; for them there is no perfection through fasting."
Thus, that [rule] refers to occasions other than Ekādaśī. For this very reason, the Agni Purāṇa states:
"A householder, a student, and likewise one who has consecrated the sacred fires, shall not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight."
Furthermore, it is stated in the Purāṇa:
"One should not observe a fast on the day of a Śrāddha, on one's birthday, on the day of a Saṃkrānti, or during the Rāhusūtakam, if one desires one's own welfare."
And there is also a statement regarding the prohibition of fasting during a *śrāddha*: "That too refers to occasions other than Ekādaśī. For this very reason, another *smṛti* states:
"When fasting is obligatory and a *naimittika-śrāddha* occurs, one should then perform the fast after having smelled that which was partaken by the ancestors."
The definition of fasting (upavāsa) has been stated in detail:
"That which is the dwelling together with virtues by one who has turned away from sins, devoid of all enjoyments—that is to be understood as fasting. Thus it is said.

The meaning of *upavāsa* is the dwelling together with virtues—such as the rules of eating once a day and so forth—of one who has turned away from evil deeds, being devoid of enjoyments such as betel and the like. And those virtues are shown in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*:
"O King, while Rukmāṅgada was thus sporting with Mohinī, the sound of a drum reached his ears."
Abiding by the doctrine of Dharmāṅgada, which rests upon the frontal globes of intoxicated elephants,
people should observe the day of Hari in the morning and remain restricted to a single meal.
All were abstaining from pungent and salty foods, subsisting on sacrificial oblations (haviṣya),
sleeping on the bare ground, and avoiding the company of their beloveds.
Remember the Lord Īśāna, the ancient Puruṣottama;
by taking food only once, you shall be as if fasting.
Indeed, no mortal who is more than eight years old and less than eighty—
who commits evil while eating in my kingdom on the day of Viṣṇu— ever reaches full completion.
"He is to be slain by me, or punished, or banished from the realm.
This means that [the fast] is to be observed on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*). Devala also says:
"On the tenth day, one should eat only once, abstaining from meat and sexual intercourse."
One should fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights.
Celibacy, purity, truthfulness, and the avoidance of meat—
these four are determined to be the most excellent among religious observances.
But through looking at women, touching them, or even conversing with them, one's celibacy flows away; it does not flow away, however, from union with one's own wife during her season.
Fasting is invalidated by drinking water more than once, by chewing betel that has not been cut,
by sleeping during the day, and by sexual intercourse.
Vyāsa also says: "Flowers, ornaments, garments, perfumes, incense, and ointments—these do not cause a fault during a fast; likewise, cleaning the teeth and applying collyrium are permitted."

Some have stated that this [rule] regarding the fast for generating merit pertains to women. In this case, the cleaning of the teeth is to be done with leaves and the like, not with wood; for it is said:
"During a fast and likewise at a śrāddha, one should not use a tooth-stick;
the contact of the teeth with wood destroys even seven generations."
For it has been stated by that very [author]: Viṣṇu also says, "One should avoid conversing with outcasts or heretics, as well as falsehood, theft, and so forth. Also in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"While fasting, one should abandon bell-metal, meat, lentils, chickpeas, millet, beans, vegetables, honey, food belonging to others, and women."
"Upavasat" means "intending to fast. Therefore, these observances pertain to the tenth day. As it is stated in another Smṛti:
"A man intent on fasting should not engage in speaking untruths, gambling, sleeping during the day, or sexual intercourse on the eleventh day."
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa as well: "Bell-metal, meat, liquor, honey, oil, false speech, sexual intercourse, travel abroad, sleeping during the day, and the application of collyrium."
Sesame paste and lentils—these twelve things a devotee of Viṣṇu should always avoid on the twelfth lunar day; by doing so, he is liberated from all sins.
Bṛhaspati also says:
On the twelfth lunar day, one should avoid these eight things: sleeping by day, food from others, eating a second meal, sexual intercourse, honey, eating from a bronze vessel, meat, and oil.
Aṅgiras also says: "One who desires the fruit of fasting should omit four meals— twice at the beginning and end of the day, that is, in the evening and morning, and twice in the middle."

Nor should it be suspected that this refers to optional fasting because of the mention of a fruit here, for even in the case of the obligatory [fast], there is a connection with fruits such as the destruction of accumulated sins. However, some say: "Since there is no fruit in the obligatory [fast], those [verses] which speak of eating only one meal per day refer to the following:
'He who desires union with Viṣṇu, prosperity, and even progeny, should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight.'"

They explain that these [rules] refer to optional fasts (*kāmyopavāsa*) prescribed in such passages. Whatever is appropriate here should be accepted. Regarding this, Devala states the rule for undertaking the fast:
"Facing north, holding a vessel made of *udumbara* wood filled with water, a wise man should either undertake the fast or make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)."

Taking a vessel made of udumbara wood or copper and filled with water while facing north, one should undertake the fast; or rather, one should form the intention (*saṃkalpa*), which means one should merely perform the mental resolve. Regarding this, some have stated that the mention of the "vessel" pertains to the first type of resolve and to optional (*kāmya*) fasting. The mantra for the resolve has also been shown by that same author: "Having remained without food on the eleventh day, O Lotus-eyed One, I shall eat on the following day; may you, O Acyuta, be my refuge."
Viṣṇu, however, stated another mantra:
"O Lotus-eyed One, having remained without food on the eleventh day, I shall eat on the following day; O Acyuta, be my refuge."
After the recitation of the mantra, Kātyāyana says:
"Having uttered this, the wise man should then offer a handful of flowers.
In the same way, the offering of the fast (*upavāsa*) should also be understood. To that effect, Nārada says:
Having recited the mantra with effort, one should then offer a handful of flowers, [saying]:
"O Keśava, for me who am blinded by the darkness of ignorance, through this vow..."
"Be gracious, O Lord of benevolent countenance; become the bestower of the vision of knowledge.
Having thus offered [the vow], the wise man should immediately perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*).
And this should be performed even during periods of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*) and so forth. This is stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"Even when one has fallen into the greatest calamity, or when joy has arisen,
or during birth-impurity or death-impurity, the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī) must not be abandoned.
In this regard, there is a specific rule stated in the Varāha Purāṇa:
During a period of birth-impurity, however, a man should bathe, mentally bow to Hari, and not eat on the Ekādaśī; thus, this vow is not violated.

Then, on the twelfth day, having eaten at the end of the period of impurity and having worshipped Janārdana according to the prescribed rite, one should also worship the most excellent of the twice-born.

"A man should never eat on the eleventh day (ekādaśī), even if there is a death-impurity; however, he should eat on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) after bathing and bowing to Viṣṇu. Regarding the inability to observe a fast, that which is stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya* is as follows:
If the body lacks the capacity and a religious vow has been undertaken,
one should have the lawful wife or a disciplined son perform it.
Kātyāyana also says:
"One who observes a fast for the sake of his father, mother, or brother, and especially for the sake of his teacher, shall obtain a hundredfold merit."
The learned man for whose sake this rite is performed shall also obtain the full reward.
When a woman fasts on the Ekādaśī day for the sake of her husband,
the sages who perceive the further shore declare that she gains a hundredfold merit.
"Her husband undoubtedly obtains the fruit of that fast. Alternatively, as stated in another Smṛti:
"For those who are unable to fast and are over eighty years of age..."
The sage Bodhāyana states that the practice of eating once a day and so forth should be performed.
With this very intention, Mārkaṇḍeya also said: "By eating once a day, by eating only at night, likewise by eating what is unasked for,
and by fasting or giving gifts, one should not fail to observe the twelfth day."
Regarding the night meal, Vyāsa states the specific rule:
"One who eats at night should practice eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), bathing, truthfulness, moderation in food, performing fire-rites, and sleeping on the ground. [65]
Vasiṣṭha states in the Nāradīya Purāṇa the fruit for one who acts in this way:
"The living being who passes the day of Hari in fasts does not enter again the womb of his mother, which is filled with feces and urine."
Even one burdened with much evil and overcome by sensual passion goes to the infinite abode of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World.
Thus concludes the determination of Ekādaśī in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the determination regarding the conflict between two Ekādaśīs; in this regard, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"All [days] beginning with the *pratipad* (first lunar day) are known as 'complete' (*saṃpūrṇa*) from sunrise until sunrise, excluding the day of Hari (*harivāsara*).
When it is asked what kind of day, then, is a "complete" *harivāsara*, the *Garuḍapurāṇa* states:
O Brahmin, when [the Ekādaśī] is joined with two muhūrtas before sunrise, it is called "Saṃpūrṇaikādaśī"; on that very day, the householder should fast.
Furthermore, when one *ghaṭikā* remains of the morning time,
fasting is prescribed here for those dwelling in the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*).
"And for a widow, in that very case, if there is no twelfth day thereafter" (66).

By this, it is stated that where there is no twelfth day on the thirteenth, but rather the eleventh alone spans two days, a householder should observe the fast on that which is the complete eleventh day, while ascetics and others should do so on the other. And it is said in another Smṛti:
"Where the eleventh day is complete and it occurs again at dawn..."
If the twelfth day is lost [to the thirteenth], how can there be a fast on that day?
"In that case, those intent on pleasing Viṣṇu should fast on two lunar days.

This means that when the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) is absent on that thirteenth day, two lunar days are to be fasted upon according to the previously mentioned distinctions of qualified persons, and not just one alone. For this very reason, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states:
"Where the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is complete [on the first day] and it occurs again at dawn..."
"A renunciant (yati) should perform the fast on the latter [Ekādaśī], but a householder (gṛhī) should observe the fast on the former.
Regarding this very subject, when there is a twelfth [tithi] even on the thirteenth day, then the fast is observed on the second Ekādaśī alone. And so says Bhṛgu:
"Where the Ekādaśī is complete and it occurs again at dawn..."
"In that case, one should fast on the second [day], provided there is a twelfth day following it.
Regarding this very subject, when the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) does not exist on the twelfth day, then the fast is observed on the twelfth day itself. And so says another *smṛti*:
"If the eleventh day should be full, and the twelfth day follows after it..."

"Having abandoned the Ekādaśī, one should observe the fast on the Dvādaśī. Thus, it is stated that where the remnant of the Daśamī does not enter into the two muhūrtas preceding sunrise, the fast should be observed there. However, if there is such entry, that which is stated in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa applies:
"When the Ekādaśī extends for three ghaṭikās before sunrise..."
The Ekādaśī known as Saṃviddhā should be avoided by those who desire merit, wealth, and pleasure.
For the sake of the prosperity of one's sons and kingdom, one should fast on the twelfth day;
by doing so, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices, and the breaking of the fast should take place on the thirteenth day.
The sixty *nāḍikās* that begin at the time of sunrise are called "mixed Ekādaśī"; they should be avoided by those who desire the fruits of dharma.
"One should fast on the twelfth day for the sake of the increase of sons and grandsons;
therein lies the merit of a hundred sacrifices if the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) occurs on the thirteenth.

Thus, since the Ekādaśī does not extend into the twelfth day, and the twelfth day does not extend into the thirteenth—because of the entry of the remaining portion of the tenth day into the two muhūrtas preceding sunrise—it is stated that one should abandon the Ekādaśī, fast on the twelfth, and break the fast on the thirteenth. With this very intention, Kaṇva also [says]:
If the tenth lunar day coincides with the time of dawn,
then the twelfth lunar day should be observed as the fast, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth lunar day.
If the tenth lunar day is joined with the time of sunrise,
even by a measure of half the sun’s orb, one should observe the fast on the twelfth day.
[68] In that regard, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices for one who breaks the fast on the thirteenth day.
If a certain [day] is pierced by the time of dawn and one fasts upon it, her hundred sons are lost; therefore, one should avoid such a day.
Also in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"If the tenth lunar day exists at the time of dawn,
it should always be known as the root of sin for those observing the fast on the eleventh."
Nārada also says: If the tenth lunar day is seen at the time of dawn,
the eleventh day should not be observed then, for it destroys virtue, desire, and wealth.
Even Gobiha said:
"If the tenth lunar day (daśamī) should coincide at the time of dawn with the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), the Lord granted the merit of that combined [day] to Mohinī."
When the tenth lunar day pierces the eleventh from sunrise onwards,
Indra, the subduer of Pāka, gave it [as a fast] for the sake of pleasing the Dānavas.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid the Saṃkīrṇa Ekādaśī;
here, the fast is observed on the Dvādaśī, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) takes place on the Trayodaśī.
In the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*, near the time of dawn, there is the speech of Mohinī:
"At the time of the fire's ritual movement, likewise when the bride is being raised up,
at the time of milking the cows, and likewise upon the warbling of birds."
When departing, when gathering the broom,
at the time of opening the door, and when the time for bathing has arrived;
[69] Likewise, when there is the sound of musical instruments for those observing vows and those who have been initiated,
as well as the end of the tenth day which is joined with the eleventh;
"O best of the wise, let a period of time be granted for the purpose of dwelling.
Having heard those words of Mohinī, all the gods were greatly delighted.
Having deliberated for a very long time, led by Digambara,
they set out for the purpose of seeing Yama and for the destruction of Vaikuṇṭha.
For the sake of increasing the heretics and for the generation of sin,
those gods spoke to Mohinī indeed for the purpose of deluding the world.
"O Mohinī, this place was indeed granted to you at the time of dawn;
it is defective when joined with the day of Hari (Ekādaśī), for it must be the very end of the tenth.
The meaning is that one should avoid [the Ekādaśī] pierced by the dawn (aruṇodaya-viddhā). The dawn is also described in the Purāṇa:

"Four *ghaṭikās* in the morning are called *aruṇodaya*; for ascetics (*yatayaḥ*), this is traditionally held to be the time for bathing, equal to the waters of the Gaṅgā. Here, "ascetics" refers to those who are self-restrained. "The time for their bathing"—by this it is stated that the four *ghaṭikās* preceding sunrise constitute *aruṇodaya*. With reference to *aruṇodaya*, Nārada also says:
Where the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is followed by the tenth (daśamī),
there is the destruction of one's offspring and one goes to hell after death.
This is also stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*.
Having fasted on the eleventh day joined with the remainder of the tenth,
a man is indeed liberated here from the merit accumulated over a year.
The fast observed on the eleventh day conjoined with the remainder of the tenth day was undertaken by Gāndhārī;
her hundred sons perished because of it, therefore one should avoid it.
In the *Brahmakaivarta*:
"The fool who observes [the fast] joined with the remainder of the tenth day shall not obtain the fruit of Ekādaśī for twelve years."

Thus, it should be understood that all those [scriptural passages] which are intent on prohibiting the piercing (*veda*) by the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) refer to the piercing occurring at dawn (*aruṇodaya*). For this very reason, the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa* states:
"When the dawn is pure, free from the piercing of the tenth day, and liberated from all defects—that day is declared to be fit for fasting."

But when one knows that the pure dawn is free from *vedha* (piercing by the previous lunar day), then the meaning is that that day, being devoid of all defects, is to be observed as a fast (*upoṣyam*). Thus, the claim made by some—that "those [scriptural passages] which prohibit fasting on a pierced day refer to cases occurring after sunrise"—is refuted. Consequently, it is established that where a *daśamī*-pierced eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) does not exist on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), one should fast on the twelfth day and perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*). As for what was stated by Hārīta:
"When on the thirteenth day there is not even two *ghaṭikās* of the twelfth day..."
When the eleventh lunar day is pierced by the tenth, that very tithi is always to be observed as the fast-day.
Even according to Rṣyaśṛṅga:
"If, on the day of breaking the fast, even a single moment of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) cannot be obtained,
then one should observe the fast on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) even if it is pierced by the tenth (daśamī)."
Thus it is said; and also in the Viṣṇurahasya:
"Likewise, one should fast on the Ekādaśī that is joined with the remainder of the Daśamī, provided that there is not even a Muhūrta of the Dvādaśī lunar day on the Trayodaśī."
Thus, all of this refers to the case where the Ekādaśī day is diminished. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"The lunar day of Ekādaśī should not be observed as a fast when it is joined with the remainder of the tenth day;
[however], if the twelfth day is not seen at the end of the night of Ekādaśī, [it may be observed]."

The meaning is that when there is no *kṣaya* (diminution) on the day of Ekādaśī, then the Ekādaśī tainted by Daśamī (*daśamī-viddhā*) is not to be observed as a fast. By this, it is implied that when there is *kṣaya* of the Ekādaśī day, the Ekādaśī tainted by Daśamī is to be observed as a fast. And it has been stated by that very same authority:
"If, by chance, the three lunar days should coincide on the Ekādaśī, then the merit of a hundred sacrifices is attained; the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) should take place on the Dvādaśī."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Wherever Ekādaśī is touched by two [days], Hari is present there; one who is devoted to Viṣṇu, whether having desires or being desireless, should fast on that very day."
That [tithi] which touches both the tenth and the twelfth is called *dvispṛk* (touching two). It is also stated in the Purāṇa:
"O Goddess, except in the case of a loss of a day (*dinakṣaya*), a [tenth tithi] joined with the tenth should not be observed for fasting;
rather, that [eleventh tithi] should always be observed as meritorious, provided the thirteenth [tithi] follows."

When there is a loss of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and there is no twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*), only then should one observe the fast on the day pierced by the tenth (*daśamī-viddhā*); not otherwise—this is the meaning. By this, it is stated by implication that on a day when there is a loss [of the *ekādaśī*], if there is a twelfth day even on the thirteenth, one should certainly not fast. For this very reason, Vyāsa says: "When the eleventh day is lost and the twelfth follows, one should fast on the twelfth if one desires the supreme goal."
"Luptā" means gone to destruction; that is to say, on the thirteenth day thereafter. As for what was stated by Gobhila:
"O Brahmin, when the day of the *dinakṣaya* (the loss of a lunar day) occurs on the eleventh, one should then abandon the eleventh and observe the fast on the twelfth."
In that regard, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices for one who breaks the fast on the thirteenth day.
Thus it was said; and furthermore, by the Grandfather (Brahmā):
"O child, when the Ekādaśī coincides with a *dinakṣaya* tithi, one should fast on that [Ekādaśī] and the Dvādaśī, while the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) should take place on the Trayodaśī."
Thus, that [rule] pertains to householders who have sons, because for such a person alone is fasting on the day of *dinakṣaya* (the waning of the day) forbidden. And so says the Matsya Purāṇa:
"On the waning of the day (*dinakṣaya*), at the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*), and during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should not observe a fast if accompanied by sons and grandsons."
Vyāsa also says: "When the Ekādaśīs have been lost and during the solar transits (saṃkrāntis),
a householder who has sons should perform neither the breaking of the fast nor the fasting itself."
The Grandfather (Brahmā) also said:

"If one observes a fast on the day of Ekādaśī when it coincides with the waning of the lunar day, his sons perish, just like one who offers the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) under the asterism Maghā. Thus [it is said].

Thus, it should be understood that all those [scriptural] passages which prohibit fasting on a *viddhā* (pierced) day refer to occasions other than the loss of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī-dinakṣaya*). And it is said in a Purāṇa:
"O Goddess, except for the loss of the day, one should not fast when [the Ekādaśī] is joined with the tenth.
With this very intention, it is also stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
When the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is pierced by even half a digit of the tenth day (Daśamī),
one should then abandon that Ekādaśī and observe the fast on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī).
In this case, the fast is observed on the twelfth day, while the breaking of the fast takes place on the thirteenth day.
Vyāsa also says:
"O one of great wisdom, if the twelfth day is lost because it is mixed with the tenth, how can the fast be observed on the eleventh?"
O King, the twelfth day alone, being pure, should be observed as a fast by those desiring liberation;
however, the breaking of the fast should take place on the thirteenth day after having worshipped Janārdana.
Also in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"If the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) should not be pure, one should then observe the Dvādaśī;
on this occasion, the fast is on the Dvādaśī, while the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) takes place on the Trayodaśī."
"By performing it thus with devotion, a man shall attain union (*sāyujya*) with Viṣṇu;
but he who performs it otherwise certainly goes to hell.
This should also be understood to apply even when there is doubt regarding the creator (Brahmā). For this very reason, the *Kūrma Purāṇa* states:

"When a doubt arises due to the contradiction of many statements, then the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is to be accepted, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should be on the thirteenth day. Thus, it is stated that when the eleventh day (ekādaśī) is overlapped by the tenth (daśamī-viddhā) and the twelfth day does not exist on the twelfth day but exists on the thirteenth, one should fast on the twelfth day and perform the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth. In this very context, when the eleventh day also exists on the twelfth day, then the fast should be observed on the second eleventh day alone. And so says Nārada:
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, when the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is joined with the twelfth (dvādaśī),
one should fast on that [eleventh] and then perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) on the thirteenth (trayodaśī). Thus says Bodhāyana as well.

Where even a single *kalā* of the eleventh day exists and the twelfth day does not follow, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices; however, the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) must be done on the thirteenth day.
Also in the Purāṇa:
"In all cases, the Ekādaśī lunar day should be accepted when it is conjoined with Dvādaśī;
provided that Dvādaśī exists on the Trayodaśī [the following day], whether it be present or not."

In this matter, when the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) extends even into the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*), the fast should be observed on the second *ekādaśī* alone. Accordingly, the *Nāradīya Purāṇa* states:

"Where the *ekādaśī* overlaps with the *dvādaśī*, or where the *dvādaśī* continues even further, one should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) on the *dvādaśī*; that shall yield the fruit of ten million sacrifices."
Also in the Purāṇa:
"O King, what need has he who has fasted on the twelfth day joined with even a single digit of the eleventh for many sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha?"
"Both the eleventh and twelfth days are present there; Hari is personally present therein.
By fasting for a single night, one destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Regarding this very subject, when the eleventh day does not exist on the twelfth day, then the fast is observed on the twelfth day itself. And so says the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"One should fast on a pure *dvādaśī* and conclude the vow on that very same *dvādaśī*,
even if a single digit (*kalā*) or even two digits remain on the *trayodaśī*.
Thus it is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* regarding the waning of the *dvādaśī* day.
When the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), the twelfth day (Dvādaśī), and the thirteenth day (Trayodaśī) overlap at the end of the night,
that lunar day (Tithi) mixed with all three is remembered as the remover of all sins.
Fasting observed on that [Ekādaśī] destroys even great sins;
when Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī coincide, and Trayodaśī remains at the end of the night.
In that regard, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices for one who breaks the fast on the thirteenth day.
Also in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Wherever the lunar day of Ekādaśī is joined with Dvādaśī, even if it occurs on a *dinakṣaya* (the loss of a day), that [Ekādaśī] is meritorious and must not be discarded under any circumstances."
As for that which was stated by Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
"When the eleventh [lunar day] is pierced by the tenth and the twelfth has come to an end, that twelfth should be known as 'diminished' (kṣīṇā); in that case, the nakta fast is prescribed."
Furthermore, it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"When the Ekādaśī is overlapped and the Dvādaśī has reached its end, that Dvādaśī is to be known as 'waning' (kṣīṇā); in that case, the Naktavrata is prescribed."

[76] Thus, this refers to householders who have sons, because for such a person alone is the fasting on the day of the waning of the moon (the fourteenth) prohibited. And so says the Matsya Purāṇa: "One should not observe a fast on the eleventh, the twelfth, and especially the thirteenth, if he is accompanied by sons and grandsons."

[Objection: Surely by this [verse], the fast (*upavāsa*) is prohibited, not the injunction for eating at night (*nakta*). [Response: Not so; for even though the fast has been prohibited, the *Vāyupurāṇa* prescribes eating at night:
"When the fast is prohibited, one should arrange some food to eat;
one does not incur fault by means of the fast, and one obtains the fruit of the fast."
The preparation of food is also stated immediately thereafter in that same work:
"At night, sacrificial food (haviṣya), or rice-free grain, barley, sesame seeds, milk, water, or clarified butter;
or the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), or even air—each subsequent one among these is more highly praised."
Thus it was said by Vyāsa: "If the eleventh and twelfth lunar days [overlap] such that the thirteenth day remains at the end of the night,
one destroys twelve twelfth-day observances by performing the ritual breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day."

Thus, it should be understood that this refers to householders who have sons. Now, one might object: since the rewards such as "the merit of a hundred sacrifices" are heard in those very texts that are intent upon breaking the fast on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*), those passages must refer to optional (*kāmya*) fasting; whereas those passages concerned with the injunction for fasting on the overlapping day (*viddhā*) must refer to obligatory (*nitya*) fasting. This is not so. For it is said: "If by chance three lunar days (*tithitraya*) should coincide on the Ekādaśī, and the fast is broken on the Dvādaśī, therein lies the merit of a hundred sacrifices."

[77] Where the eleventh day is the twelfth, and the twelfth day follows after it as well, one should perform the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day; the fruit thereof shall be equal to ten million sacrifices.
Thus, because there is no difference in the scriptural declaration of the fruit even regarding the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī-pāraṇa*), furthermore:
"In all cases, men should observe the Ekādaśī mixed with the Dvādaśī;
whether it occurs in the morning or not, for the breaking of the fast is indeed obligatory."

Furthermore, because the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day is heard of as being mandatory even for those seeking liberation in such passages as, "But the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day bestows liberation upon those free from desire," it should be understood that this [mention of results] is not a statement of fruit (*phalaśruti*), but rather an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Some, however, say:
"O King, a pure twelfth day alone should be observed as a fast by those desiring liberation."
On the thirteenth day, having worshipped Janārdana, one should perform the breaking of the fast.

Based on such statements, they establish the following distinction: since ascetics alone desire liberation (*mokṣa*), the rules concerning the fast on the pure twelfth lunar day (*śuddhadvādaśī*) pertain exclusively to them; however, the rules concerning the fast on the overlapping day (*viddhā*) pertain only to householders. This is weak, because since the fruits such as heaven are transitory, all people alike desire liberation without distinction. Furthermore: "The pure twelfth lunar day should always be observed as a fast by the best of the twice-born, as well as by Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—what else do you wish to hear?"
Thus, since it is seen that even those other than ascetics (*yati*) have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for the fast on the pure twelfth day (*śuddhadvādaśī*), so too:
"When the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is pierced by the tenth (*diśā-viddhā*) and does not cease on the following day,
that very lunar day (*tithi*) must always be observed as a fast by both householders (*gṛhin*) and ascetics (*yati*)."
[78] Thus, because even for ascetics (*yatīnām*) the rule for fasting on the pierced day (*viddhopavāsa*) is prescribed in the *Matsyapurāṇa*, it contradicts what has been stated by others:
"Where the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) is complete and recurs again at dawn,
the ascetic should observe the later day, but the householder (*gṛhī*) should fast on the earlier."

In this regard, the claim that because ascetics (*yatis*) are seen breaking their fast on the thirteenth day, the texts prescribing a fast-break on the thirteenth apply only to them, whereas those prescribing a fast on the [pierced] day apply only to householders (*gṛhasthas*), is also refuted by the two previously cited statements and should therefore be disregarded. Others, however, maintain that the rules concerning the pierced day refer to the piercing at dawn (*aruṇodaya-vedha*), while the rules for fasting on the twelfth day refer to the period after sunrise; this too should be disregarded as it contradicts the injunction for breaking the fast on the thirteenth day. Now, how can there be a fast-break on the thirteenth day, given that in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*...?
Having fasted on the eleventh day, the breaking of the fast is prescribed on the twelfth;
one should not do so on the thirteenth, because of the loss of twelve twelfth-day periods.

Thus, because of the prohibition against breaking the fast on the thirteenth day; and also in the *Śrī Viṣṇurahasya*: "Those men who desire the increase of dharma must never break their fast on the thirteenth day after having observed the Ekādaśī vow."
Also in another Smṛti:
"Breaking the fast on the tenth destroys [the merit of] twelve twelfth-days;
however, breaking the fast on the thirteenth destroys dharma, progeny, wealth, and lifespan."

It is said: This is indeed true; nevertheless, this refers to cases where there is the occurrence of a *dvādaśī* on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*), meaning that one should not break the fast on that thirteenth day by bypassing the *dvādaśī*, but not in the case of a pure *trayodaśī*. For this very reason, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states: "When the *dvādaśī* is very short on the day of breaking the fast, one should perform both rites—the morning and the midday—at the time of dawn."
Also in the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "O best of Brahmins, when the Dvādaśī is short, one should perform the rites of bathing and worship at dawn, accompanied by gifts, fire-offerings, and so forth."
On the pure thirteenth day, however, breaking the fast yields the fruit of the earth;
a man undoubtedly obtains even more than the merit of a hundred sacrifices.
For this reason, O Brahmins, one should perform the ritual bath at dawn,
accompanied by the libations to the ancestors, as soon as one perceives that the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is only slightly remaining.
For this twelfth day, when neglected by men, causes great ruin;
it effects the destruction of dharma, just as the Sarasvatī river does for one who fails to bathe in her.
Furthermore,
whichever lunar day the sun reaches at its rising,
that lunar day is to be known as complete for the purposes of bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and so forth.

Based on this statement by Devala, one should not suspect that there is no fault even when the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) has passed; for Vasiṣṭha says in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*: "In the case of breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*) or death, the lunar day (*tithi*) is recorded as being momentary. The meaning is this: at whatever time the breaking of the fast or death occurs, the lunar day is considered to exist only at that specific moment; it does not mean that the entire lunar day is to be understood as present. Furthermore, regarding a case where only a single digit (*kalā*) of the twelfth day remains on the thirteenth day, it is stated in the Purāṇa:
"O King, when there is even a fraction of the twelfth day on the thirteenth, that lunar day is considered complete; so said Vasiṣṭha, the knower of dharma.

Thus it is established that those [texts] which prohibit breaking the fast on the thirteenth refer to cases where a portion of the twelfth day occurs on the thirteenth. Furthermore, as for those [texts]:
If, on the following day, even for a *kalā*, a *kāṣṭhā*, or a *muhūrta*,
twelve twelfth days (*dvādaśīs*) are destroyed, then the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) must take place on the thirteenth day.
Thus, these passages—which, by referring to the occurrence of the twelfth day on the thirteenth day, are intended to prohibit breaking the fast—state:
"Even if the Ekādaśī is overlapped [by the next tithi], it should be accepted provided there is no twelfth day thereafter;
for breaking the fast on the thirteenth day destroys twelve twelfth days."

Thus, since these [passages] have the same meaning as the aforementioned ones, there is no fault. And in this way, that which was stated by some—namely, that even if the twelfth day occurs on the thirteenth, breaking the fast on the thirteenth day is not a fault—is refuted.

Thus concludes the determination regarding the conflict of the Ekādaśī in the *Smṛticandrikā*, as well as the determination of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). Having thus completed the relevant and incidental discussions, the determination of the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) is now undertaken in connection with the main subject. Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
That which is declared as the Darśa-śrāddha is proclaimed as the Pārvaṇa;
therein, a gift to the ancestors in the afternoon is highly praised.
Vyāsa also states that the afternoon is the fourth part of the day divided into five parts:
"The morning consists of three muhūrtas, and the saṅgava period is of the same duration;
midday shall consist of three muhūrtas, and the afternoon is likewise."
"The period of three muhūrtas at the end of the day, however, is excluded from all ritual acts. Thus [it is said].

The *Vājasaneyi-śruti* also states: "The sun, indeed, is all the seasons: when it rises, it is spring; when it is the time of the cows returning (*saṅgava*), it is summer; when it is midday, it is autumn; when it is afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), it is the rainy season; and when it sets, it is winter. In another *śruti*, however, the word *aparāhṇa* is used for the third part of the day divided into three: "Forenoon belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and afternoon to the ancestors. Manu, on the other hand, uses the term *aparāhṇa* for the second part of the day divided into two.
Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight,
so too the afternoon is superior to the forenoon for a śrāddha ceremony.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa* as well, it is stated:
"The forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) is indeed until the turning point (*āvartana*), and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is after that.

The meaning is that the period up to the turning point constitutes the forenoon. Thus, although the term *aparāhṇa* is employed in various ways, the very definition of the word *aparāhṇa* as stated by Manu is accepted.
The best of the twice-born should perform the śrāddha in the forenoon during the bright fortnight;
however, during the dark fortnight, he should perform it in the afternoon, but must not let the time of Rauhina pass.

Thus, because Mārkaṇḍeya prescribes the performance of the *śrāddha* during the second part of the day—divided into two parts—and because he likewise ordains its completion before the fourth part, stating, "One must not let the *rauhiṇa* [muhūrta] pass," and since the *rauhiṇa* is the ninth *muhūrta*; furthermore: "But the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) pierced by the [preceding] *bhūta-tithi*, or even mixed with the first lunar day (*pratipad*), should be accepted for ancestral rites (*pitrya-karman*) by the learned, provided it occurs at the time of *kutapa*."

Thus Hārīta prescribes the *kutapa* period as an ancillary (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*; that too would not be correct. [Objection: But the status of the *kutapa* period as an ancillary of the *śrāddha* is not understood from this [text]. [Reply: Not so; because the injunction for taking [the food] at the time of the *kutapa* serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), it is more appropriate that it be an ancillary. And it is said in the Purāṇa: "At whatever moment the sun (*gopati*) heats the earth (*kuṃ*) completely with its rays (*gobhiḥ*), that time is called *kutapa*; there the *śrāddha* is offered. Thus it is said.

*Kuḥ* is the earth; *gopatiḥ* is the sun. Regarding this, the claim made by some—that because of the statement, "The *ekoddiṣṭa* [rite] is at midday," the prescription of the *kutapa* time applies exclusively to the *ekoddiṣṭa*—is refuted by this very [text], which prescribes the *kutapa* time even for the *darśaśrāddha*. Nor should it be suspected that, this being the case, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) between the prescriptions of the *kutapa* and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), for the latter half of the *kutapa* is included within the afternoon. For the *kutapa* is indeed the eighth *muhūrta* of the day, which consists of fifteen *muhūrtas*. Thus says the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Fifteen muhūrtas are always renowned as the divisions of the day;
among them, that which is the eighth muhūrta is known as the time called *kutapa*.
Thus it is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa* as well.

"The period beginning from the seventh *muhūrta* up to the ninth *muhūrta* and so on is called *kutapa*; what is given to the ancestors during that time is inexhaustible. Thus, there is no contradiction in the rule that whatever is prescribed for the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) should be performed during the *kutapa* included within that afternoon. This also refers to the commencement [of the rite]. To this effect, the Matsya Purāṇa says:
Since at midday the sun becomes sluggish,
therefore an undertaking made then is distinguished by yielding infinite fruit.
Gautama also says:

"A wise man, knowing the ritual procedure, should perform the *śrāddha* beginning at the *kutapa* hour and continue until the *rauhiṇa*; having undertaken the rite, he must not let the *rauhiṇa* pass."

And this procedure for the *śrāddha* beginning with the *kutapa* vessel pertains to one who maintains no sacred fire (*anagnika*), because Manu has prescribed the *śrāddha* ritual specifically for one who possesses the sacred fire and has already performed the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*:
"Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors, a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fire should, on the waning of the moon, perform the monthly *śrāddha*, known as the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka*."

The sense is that, since the Piṇḍapitṛyajña also takes place in the afternoon, it is impossible for the Śrāddha to occur during the Kutapa period and so forth. Nor [can it be argued that this is not a problem] because of the following: "But he who maintains the sacred fires, having performed the Pitṛyajña known as Tarpaṇa, should always perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha on the new moon day."

Based on this statement from the *Matsya Purāṇa*, one might suspect that the term "pitṛyajña" refers specifically to the ancestral sacrifice known as *tarpaṇa* (libation), and thus even for one who maintains a sacred fire (*sāgni*), the *śrāddha* must begin at the *kutapa* hour. However, this is not the case, for it is said: "Having completed the rites up to the end of the fortnight and having performed the *vaiśvadeva*, the wise one who maintains a sacred fire should then perform the *piṇḍayajña*, and after that, the *anvāhāryaka*."

Thus, because Laugākṣi prescribes the Śrāddha immediately after the Piṇḍapitṛyajña for one who maintains the sacred fire (*sāgni*), it should be understood that the term *tarpaṇa* (libation) also refers, in some sense, to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. Consequently, where the Piṇḍapitṛyajña occurs on the day of the Śrāddha due to the appearance of the moon, one who maintains the sacred fire should perform the Śrāddha only after having performed the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. Otherwise, however, it should be noted that even for one who maintains the sacred fire, the Śrāddha begins at the *Kutapa* hour and so forth. Now, an objection may be raised: since the time for the Śrāddha extends from the *Kutapa* until the end of the *Rohiṇī* [nakṣatra], and since that duration is insufficient to accommodate two separate rites, how can the Śrāddha of one who maintains the sacred fire follow immediately after the Piṇḍapitṛyajña? This is not so; for the *Matsyapurāṇa* prescribes the time for the Śrāddha as extending even beyond the *Rohiṇī*.
The four muhūrtas that follow the Kutapa muhūrta,
making five muhūrtas in total, are indeed desired as the time for the offering of Svadhā.
Thus, the meaning is that the five muhūrtas beginning with Kutapa constitute an essential limb (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*. As for that which was stated by Yama:
"When the fourth watch has arrived, the man who performs a *śrāddha*—that *śrāddha* shall become demonic (*āsura*), and the giver shall go to hell."
