Thus, this refers to the fault incurred by one who performs a *śrāddha* during the final three *muhūrtas* when the fourth watch (*prahara*) has arrived; it does not, however, intend to prohibit the entire watch, as that would contradict the previously cited statement from the *Matsya Purāṇa*. For it is said in that very same text: "The evening consists of three *muhūrtas*; one should not perform a *śrāddha* at that time, for that period is called 'Rākṣasī' and is censured in all ritual acts."
As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana:
"The Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha is recommended when the moon has waned,
during the third part of the day, and not in the vicinity of the twilights."

Thus, even that statement from the *Kūrma Purāṇa*—"In the third part of the day, not too close to the twilight"—is intended to mean that the rite should not be performed during the final three *muhūrtas* of the day; it does not, however, specifically intend to enjoin its performance in the third part of the day. As for the statement of Vyāghrapāda:
"One who knows the rules, is endowed with faith, and properly employs worthy recipients, attains spiritual welfare without doubt, provided he performs it at other times than night."

Thus, by the very reasoning already stated, that [text] also does not have the purpose of enjoining merely the day; therefore, everything is faultless. Viṣṇu states an exception to the prohibition of performing [śrāddha] at night:
"Śrāddha should certainly not be performed by the wise during the two twilights (saṃdhyā) or at night;
however, it may be performed even during those two times if there is the sight of Rāhu (an eclipse). Thus he says.
Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"Whatever śrāddha, fire-oblation, or recitation one performs after the proper time has passed—
all that becomes useless, just like poison mixed with nectar."
Thus concludes the determination of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some other statements regarding the times for *śrāddha* are also recorded.
In that regard, Mārkaṇḍeya says in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
O King, the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is superior to the northern course;
for during that four-month period of the sun's southern path, Keśava is indeed asleep.
The second fortnight of the month of Proṣṭhapada;
and especially therein, from the fifth day onwards, and even beyond that, from the tenth day onwards.
"O King, even when conjoined with the Maghā constellation, the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) is likewise praised there."

Among the times for *śrāddha*, the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) is superior to the northern solstice (*udagayana*); that is to say, it is superior to the path of Yama (*yāmyāyana*). Within that southern solstice, when Keśava is asleep, the four-month period is superior; even within the southern solstice, the four months beginning from the full moon of Āṣāḍha are superior—this is the sense. Even therein, the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) of the month of Proṣṭhapada is especially superior. Even therein, the days ending with the new moon (*darśānta*) after the fifth day are superior. Even therein, the five days after the tenth are superior. Among those as well, the thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the *Makhā* asterism is most highly praised—this is the meaning. Also, in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
Taking the full moon day of Āṣāḍha as the limit, whichever shall be the fifth fortnight—
therein one should perform the Śrāddha, whether the sun enters Virgo or not.

In the fifth alternative, the meaning is whether or not the sun enters the zodiac sign of Virgo (*kanyārāśi*). Here, the phrase "or not" is not stated as an option to enjoin that one should perform the *śrāddha* even in the absence of the sun’s entry into Virgo; rather, it should be understood as intended to show that the fifth alternative is excellent even when devoid of the sun’s entry into Virgo, let alone when it is accompanied by it. For this very reason, Śāṭyāyani says: "The sixteen lunar days in the latter fortnight of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), if they are joined with the sun’s presence in Virgo—that is the time for the rite of *śrāddha*."

Regarding the phrase "sixteen lunar days" (*tithiṣoḍaśaka*): it is stated so to show that, due to the occasional increase of a fortnight (*pakṣavṛddhi*), even the second fortnight of the month of *nabhasya* may consist of sixteen days and is still the time for the *śrāddha* rite; it is not the case that it must consist of exactly fifteen days. Alternatively, the term "sixteen lunar days" is used to include the first lunar day (*pratipad*) immediately following the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), because the *pratipad* is equal to the latter fortnight insofar as the moon is waning therein. Nor should it be argued that this implies the sixteen lunar days beginning from that specific day constitute the time for *śrāddha* whenever the sun is in Virgo (*kanyā*) during the second fortnight of *nabhasya*. For Vṛddhamanu says: [The text continues with the citation from Vṛddhamanu.]

"Whether in the middle or even at the end, whichever fortnight the Sun enters [the sign] of Virgo, that entire fortnight is to be honored; therein the Śrāddha is ordained. This means that in whichever fifth fortnight, whenever the Sun has entered Virgo, that entire fortnight is the most highly recommended time for the Śrāddha. By this, it should be understood that the Śrāddha must be performed there either every day or on a single day, according to one's capacity. And so says the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
Even in the other fortnight, when the sun is situated in Virgo, the Śrāddha is praised;
however, one should perform it especially when the sun has entered the fifth [sign] from Virgo.

"In another alternative" (*pakṣāntare*) means even in an alternative other than the fifth alternative. The fact that the fifth alternative is more praiseworthy is stated by the phrase "one should especially cause [it] to be performed. With this very intention, Jātūkarṇya says: "The ancestors, having resorted to the fifth alternative, longed for it;
therefore, the gift should be given right there, for what is given elsewhere is fruitless."

The meaning is that what is given at an auspicious time brings about exceedingly great fruit. When it is asked what, then, is the fruit of what is given at an even more auspicious time, Kārṣājini states: "By giving a *śrāddha* on the fifth lunar day, one obtains sons, long life, health, incomparable sovereignty, and abundant fulfillment of desires."
Also in the Purāṇa:
"Those sixteen days when the sun has entered Virgo are equal to sacrificial rites; what is given to the ancestors during them becomes inexhaustible."
This should be explained as having the same meaning as the statement of Śāṭyāyani. Kārṣṇājini has also shown the fault incurred by the transgression of the most recommended time:
"The deceased indeed harm him who would neglect the fifth [day];
therefore, a wise man should not bypass the ancestral rite on the fifth day."
But when, for some reason, this *śrāddha* has not been performed during the fifth fortnight, then Sumantu says: "O Great King, as long as the sun remains in the zodiac sign of Virgo (*kanyā*),
from that time until it has entered Scorpio (*vṛścika*), the offering should be made."
"O King, on this fifteenth day of the month known on earth as Dīpānvitā, if one does not give [offerings] to the ancestors during the Mahālaya, it is as if nothing has been given."

If [the śrāddha] has not been offered to the ancestors on the fifth fortnight known as Mahālaya, then one should offer it even during another fortnight, for as long as the sun remains in the zodiac sign of Virgo (Kanyā). After that time—that is, after the period when the sun has entered the sign of Libra (Tulā)—the śrāddha must still be offered. If, for some reason, it has not been offered even at that time, then the meaning is that one should offer it on the fifteenth day (Pañcadaśī) known as Dīpāvalī. Thus it is stated in the Purāṇa as well.
[89] When the sun has entered the sign of Virgo, the ancestors indeed go toward their sons;
the city of the departed remains entirely empty until the appearance of Scorpio.
Then, having encountered the scorpion, the ancestors departed in despair;
yet, after pronouncing a most terrible curse, they returned once more to their own abode.
If a householder does not perform the śrāddha when the sun has entered Virgo, how can he have wealth or sons? For he is tormented by the sighs of his ancestors.
In the *Āditya Purāṇa* as well: "During the rainy season, Yama, having released the deceased ancestors from his own abode and having emptied his city, [returns] to the world of men."
Afflicted by hunger and confessing their own misdeeds,
they long for milk-rice mixed with honey for the sake of their sons and grandsons.
Therefore, one should satisfy them there according to the prescribed rite with milk-rice mixed with honey, sesame seeds, and rice, as well as with cool water.
The man who obtains from another's house food only the size of a mouthful,
or who sustains his own life by means of mere alms;
"Or, he who would nourish his body day by day by selling himself must also perform the *śrāddha* with those various materials well-accumulated. Thus it is said.

Having dismissed the *preta*s and the ancestors (*pitṛ*s) from the abode of Yama, and having made his own city empty, he causes them to dwell in the world of men during the rainy season, starting from the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada until the appearance of the scorpion; this is the connection with the ellipsis [supplied]. The connection with the ellipsis is that "the *preta*s and ancestors, afflicted by hunger, remain. The remainder [of the sentence] is "the son should satisfy them according to the rule. Also in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "To the teachers, gurus, disciples, as well as to friends and kinsmen..."
And likewise, he offered handfuls of water to all of their wives as well.
A man should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to them during the month of Bhādrapada,
as well as at all sacred fords (tīrthas) and likewise in the month of Māgha.
One should honor all the teachers and others through a single Brahmin;
one should offer ten or twelve rice-balls, for there is no option of not performing them.
"The restrictive rule is certainly remembered as applying specifically to the fifth fortnight;
an oblation offered during that time will surely become inexhaustible for the ancestors. Thus it is said.

The phrase "in one Brāhmaṇa" refers to a case where [the capacity] is insufficient. However, one who has sufficient capacity should, according to his own ability, worship all [the guests], beginning with the teacher, either on each individual Brāhmaṇa [separately] on a single day, or he may worship each individual person, such as the teacher, on a separate day. In that regard, when the first option is adopted, one should perform the worship by relying on a common ritual procedure (*samānatantra*) using a single cooking (*ekapāka*). And so it was said by Bhṛgu:
"When many, or even two, have died at the same time, having performed the cooking by means of a common ritual procedure (*tantra*), one should perform the *śrāddha* separately for each."
First for the one who died previously, then again for the second, and then for the third; thus one should perform [the rites].

Having said this, it was stated: "This is the procedure for simultaneous occurrences. The meaning is that when various *śrāddhas* fall to be performed at the same time, this is the sequence: having performed the cooking once by way of a single ritual framework (*tantra*), one should follow the order of performing the *śrāddhas* according to the seniority of the ancestors. Regarding this, what is stated in the *Smṛtyarthasāra* is: "There is a single cooking, a single *vaiśvadeva* ritual framework, a single funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), and a single sacrificial grass (*barhis*)."

Thus, in that regard, one must consider whether "the Vaiśvadeva rite is part of the procedure. For it has been stated in Smṛti texts that "the Śrāddha for teachers, gurus, disciples, friends, kinsmen, and so forth, should be performed according to the Ekoddiṣṭa rule alone," because the Vaiśvadeva is impossible there; and because it has been stated that "Ekoddiṣṭas are of three kinds—those mixed with new [grain], those with old [grain], and those [with neither]," and the *Smṛtyarthasāra* itself declares that the rite for the gods (*daiva*) does not exist in any Ekoddiṣṭa. We shall show the Smṛti passages shortly. Yama also speaks regarding one who is unable [to perform the full rite]:
When the sun is in the constellation Haṃsa (Śravaṇā) during the rainy season, while the moon is in Kanyā, one may dwell even on vegetables at home;
during the interval between the two Pañcamīs, one should give gifts in both fortnights.

The meaning is that during the rainy season (*varṣā*), specifically in the *prāvṛṭ* period when the sun is in the constellation of Haṃsa (the Swan) and situated in the sign of Virgo (*kanyārāśi*), the householder should offer [the funeral cakes] to the ancestors on any one of the days from the fifth day of the second fortnight until the fifth day of the subsequent fortnight, as circumstances permit. The phrase "between the two fiths" implies, with the exception of the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*). Regarding this, Marīci says:
"For those who have killed by means of poison, weapons, wild beasts, fire, animals, or Brahmins, the rite should be performed on the fourteenth day; for others, however, it is censured."

Those who have committed the killing of these—namely, those who kill poisoners and so forth, up to Brāhmaṇas—are "killers of poisoners, those with weapons, beasts of prey, fire, animals, and Brāhmaṇas. The ritual action (*kriyā*) refers to the performance of the *śrāddha* rite; the remainder of the sense is that it is to be performed according to the rules for the *ekoddiṣṭa*. And so says Sumantu:
"Even for a father who has attained equality [with the gods] but was killed by a weapon, the sons must perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the fourteenth day during the *mahālaya*."

[92] The meaning is: even for one who has attained equality and oneness (*ekatva*), that is, even after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed; for a father killed by a weapon, even when the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha has been performed on the fourteenth day during the *mahālaya*, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha must still be performed on another day, because the satisfaction (*tṛpti*) of the grandfather and others is not accomplished by the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha alone. Now, one might object: "In that case, even on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), once the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha has been performed, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha would also have to be performed for the sake of accomplishing the satisfaction of the grandfather and others. This is not so. For it is traditionally taught (*asmaraṇa*) that on the anniversary of the father's death, the grandfather and others are not to be offered libations (*tarpaṇīya*); therefore, a śrāddha for their satisfaction need not be performed. This is stated in the section concerning the *mahālaya*:
They desire milk-rice mixed with honey for their sons and grandsons;
therefore, one should satisfy them there according to the ritual rule with that milk-rice.
With [an offering] mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds...

Thus, since there is a traditional injunction (*smaraṇa*) that even the grandfather and others are to be offered libations (*tarpaṇīya*), a *pārvaṇa* Śrāddha must indeed be performed on another day for their satisfaction. However, for one whose grandfather was also killed by weapons or other means, a Śrāddha for the grandfather in the form of an *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) during the Mahālaya. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "The rule of the *ekoddiṣṭa* applies to one or to two. This means that when one father is killed by weapons or the like, or when both the father and grandfather are so killed, a Śrāddha for each must be performed individually on the fourteenth day according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure. When the Śrāddhas for the two have been performed individually by prescribing the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, a *pārvaṇa* Śrāddha must be performed on another day to ensure the satisfaction of the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), because of the statement "to one or to two. It is understood that the *ekoddiṣṭa* rule does not apply when all three—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—have been killed by weapons or other means. When those three have been killed by weapons or the like, the *pārvaṇa* rite alone applies on the fourteenth day. And this is logical: although the prescribed time (the fourteenth day) occurs for all three who were killed by weapons and have undergone *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite—which is contingent upon the occurrence of that specific prescribed time—does not apply. With this very intention, Aparārka also stated: "In that case, if only one has been killed by weapons, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is prescribed; but if all three are likewise [killed], then the *pārvaṇa* alone applies. The meaning of this is that when all three are killed by weapons, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is not prescribed, but rather the *pārvaṇa* alone. Devasvāmin, however, stated: "Even when all three have been killed by weapons, only three separate *ekoddiṣṭas* should be performed; the *pārvaṇa* is not [prescribed], as there is no explicit scriptural statement to that effect. One should accept whichever of these views is logically consistent. Furthermore, as for what was stated by Śākaṭāyana:
For those who have perished by water or fire, or for those who died while in the state of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), at home, or on a journey,
one should indeed perform their Śrāddha, avoiding the fourteenth day (caturdaśī).

Thus, this refers to cases involving death by water, fire, and so forth, as prescribed for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). For those who die an "evil death" (*pāpamṛtyu*), the fourteenth lunar day (*caturdaśī*) is to be observed specifically for those who have perished by water, fire, and the like—those killed by climbing trees, by iron [weapons], lightning, flames, poison, and so forth;
for those killed by clawed or fanged beasts, the fourteenth day is likewise recommended.

Thus, from the statement of Pracetas and the mention of lightning, flames, and so forth, it is understood that for those who die by such [violent] means, the fourteenth day is recommended. For these individuals as well, the *śrāddha* performed on the anniversary of death and other such occasions must be conducted according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure;
however, the *śrāddha* performed on the fourteenth day after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for one killed by weapons must be performed according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure.

This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Gārgya: "When the *aparapakṣika* śrāddha for those killed by weapons is performed on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), it should be done there alone according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure, and not otherwise. Nor should it be argued that if those killed by weapons somehow miss the fourteenth day, the śrāddha must simply not be performed due to the lapse of the prescribed time; for it has already been shown previously that even when a more excellent time is unavailable, the performance of the *mahālaya* śrāddha is mandatory. Consequently, even for those killed by weapons, if the fourteenth day of the fifth fortnight—the most excellent time—is missed, the rite must be performed on another day according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure.
At the transit of the sun, during an eclipse, at the festival of the rains, and at the Mahālaya ceremony,
one should offer three rice-balls (piṇḍas) here.
This is because of the traditional teaching of Prajāpati. Even on occasions such as the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), one who is sonless is entitled only to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. As Garga has said:
"For those who have died without sons—whether they be women or men—an *ekoddiṣṭa* must be offered for them, and not a *pārvaṇa*."
Women include sisters and so forth; men include brothers and so forth. And thus Sumantu says:
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, wherever [an offering] is given—to a brother, a sister, a son, a husband, or a maternal uncle..."

"For a friend or for a guru, the *śrāddha* is the *ekoddiṣṭa*, not the *pārvaṇa*. This means that whenever offerings are made to brothers and others on occasions such as the *saṃkrānti*, eclipses, festivals at the end of the year (*varṣotsava*), the *mahālaya*, or at Gayā, it must be performed according to the rules of the *ekoddiṣṭa*. Kātyāyana also states:
"For relatives, kinsmen, and others, however, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is always [the rule]."
As for that which was stated by Jātūkarṇya concerning the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*:
"From this point forward, the *ekoddiṣṭa* should never be performed;
Mudgala has declared that [the rite] ends with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."
Having crossed over the state of being a preta, he indeed attained the company of the ancestors;
yet, through the offering of separate funeral cakes (piṇḍas), he falls away from the world of the ancestors.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, separation is no longer possible;
however, if separation has been performed, the *sapiṇḍatā* must be performed again.
Thus [it was said]; and as for that which was stated by Kārṣṇājini:
"Henceforth, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should never be performed;
this [rite] is inauspicious for the deceased until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."
And as for that which was stated by Yama:
"He who should join a deceased person who has already been made a *sapiṇḍa* with a separate *piṇḍa* becomes a destroyer of the ritual procedure and is born as a slayer of his ancestors."
That gift which is given directed toward a single individual is called a *pretakarma*;
the best of the twice-born say that what is given to the ancestors is called a *śrāddha*.
Thus it is said; and as for that which is stated in the Purāṇa:
"In whatever case the offering of these [ancestors] occurs after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, there the wise man should abandon the Ekoddiṣṭa śrāddha and perform it according to the Pārvaṇa rule."

Thus, all of this should be understood as applying only in the absence of a specific injunction for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. Now, one might object: "O King, even in that case, the thirteenth day joined with the Maghā asterism is praised" (Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa 96). By this previously cited statement of Mārkaṇḍeya, the excellence attributed to the thirteenth day conjoined with the Maghā asterism appears to be inconsistent.
If a man performs a śrāddha on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should know for certain that his eldest son will meet his death.

"By one performing a *śrāddha* during the *Maghā* [nakṣatra], the eldest son perishes"—from such statements, a fault is recorded for the performance of a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight when the *Maghā* nakṣatra is present. This is true; however, the aforementioned excellence refers to the *śrāddha* for the group of ancestors (*pitṛvarga*) together with the group of maternal ancestors (*mātāmahavarga*), whereas the statement declaring the fault regarding "the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight," etc., refers to the *śrāddha* for the group of ancestors alone. Thus, because the subject matters differ, the excellence of the thirteenth day conjoined with the *Maghā* nakṣatra is indeed appropriate. For this very reason, another *smṛti* states:

"One who possesses sons and desires the increase of both his offspring and their longevity should not offer the *trayodaśī-śrāddha* for only one [lineage]; rather, he should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite.

This means that he who possesses sons and desires the prosperity of his children and their lives should not offer the *trayodaśī-śrāddha* for a single group; instead, he should perform the *pārvaṇa* for both groups. This very meaning has been clarified by Kārṣṇājini:
"One should never commence a *śrāddha* for a single class [of ancestors] on the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*).
Those who remain unsatisfied therein will indeed harm his progeny.
By this, the intention is that the *śrāddha* should be performed for two classes [of ancestors]. Śaṅkha states its fruit:
When the month of Proṣṭhapada has passed, having reached the thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the Maghā asterism,
one should perform a Śrāddha ceremony with honey and milk-rice (pāyasa).
When pleased by the śrāddha, the ancestors always bestow upon men desired offspring, fame, heaven, health, and likewise wealth.
Also in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "One who observes the thirteenth [lunar day] attains desired offspring, sacrificial animals, independence, supreme intelligence, long life, and likewise sovereignty."
The meaning is that one performing the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth lunar day of the month of Māgha obtains progeny and other blessings. The *Mahābhārata* also states:
"By performing the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day, one becomes preeminent among the wise;
moreover, young men do not necessarily die in his house."

The meaning here is that in the house of one who performs the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the month of Māgha, young men certainly—meaning inevitably—do not die. In this *śrāddha*, the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) should not be performed by those who have sons nor by those who are sonless, because the thirteenth day of Māgha is a *yugādi* (the beginning of a Yuga). Thus says Pulastya: "Just as in the two solstices and the two equinoxes, so too in all *yugādi* days, [the *śrāddha*] is performed without the casting of rice-balls."

The word "should be performed" is the ellipsis. However, for a householder with sons, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) should especially not be performed because of the conjunction with the Maghā asterism; [as it is said]:
"O Bhārata, by fasting and breaking the fast on the day of the sun's passage (*saṃkrānti*), and by the offering of rice-balls during Maghā, the eldest son perishes."

[98] Thus, because of the hearing of faults in the Purāṇas, therefore, on the thirteenth day of the month of Maghā, a householder—whether he has sons or is without sons—should perform the Śrāddha for both lineages (varga), with the exception of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) alone. Nor should it be said:
"One should not commence the Śrāddha for only one lineage on the thirteenth day;
those who are not satisfied there will indeed harm his progeny."

Because of this statement, since the group of maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) is mentioned separately [in the injunction for the *śrāddha*], it follows that a separate *śrāddha* for the group of mothers (*mātṛvarga*) on the thirteenth day of the month of Māgha is mandatory. However, even in the absence of a separate mention, the satisfaction (*tṛpti*) of the group of mothers is possible. Thus says the *Smṛti*:
"The sages have not prescribed a separate *śrāddha* for the mothers;
a virtuous wife who does not act otherwise partakes in the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and the water-offering (*udaka*) intended for her father."

Bṛhaspati also says: "The mother eats at the Śrāddha together with her own husband, along with the deities; likewise always the paternal grandmother with her own [husband], and the great-grandmother with her own."

"Accompanied by the deities" means a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha. This refers to the case of women performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite together with their husband. However, in the case of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* performed together with her father-in-law, she partakes in the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha along with him. Thus says Śātātapa:
"When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, the wife attains a single form with the ancestors of her husband; therefore, she is a sharer in their portions."

The distinction is that when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed for the husband together with his father, she becomes a sharer in her husband’s paternal portion. Also, in another *smṛti*: "After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, whatever is offered to the ancestors, the mother is a recipient of a share in all cases; such is the certainty in the *dharma* scriptures."

Because of the statement "in all cases," it is understood that even though the *pārvaṇa* rite performed during the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada known as the *mahālaya*, or in the specific region called Gayā, generates extreme satisfaction, the mother still possesses a share of the inheritance; thus, even in the *mahālaya*, at Gayā, and so forth, the son should not perform a separate *śrāddha* for the mother by designating her individually. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "Excluding the sixth day, there is no separate ritual for women. Furthermore, regarding what was stated in that same work:
Some great seers maintain that women should have a separate śrāddha ceremony.

Thus, this refers to the case where the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed for women together with their paternal grandmothers and others; for in that case, there is an absence of entitlement to a share in the *piṇḍas* of the [husband's] fathers. And so, apart from the annual *śrāddha*, even in the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* performed with intent for the father and others, a *śrāddha* should not be performed separately for those who have been *sapiṇḍīkṛta* with the husband and others. It is established that for those *sapiṇḍīkṛta* with the paternal grandmother and others, the *śrāddha* must be performed separately. How then is it that in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and the *anvaṣṭakya*, a separate performance of the *śrāddha* is carried out for mothers and others, even though they have been *sapiṇḍīkṛta* with the husband and others, given that there is no separate *śrāddha* for those who are entitled to a share? It is said:

On the Anvaṣṭakā days, at a rite for prosperity (vṛddhi), and likewise on the anniversary of death, the śrāddha for the mother is performed separately; on other occasions, it is performed together with her husband.
Thus, by the force of the statement in another Smṛti:
"In the Anvaṣṭakā, likewise in the Śrāddha for the Mothers, and on the anniversary of death—
excluding the Ekoddiṣṭa— in these three cases, no other rite should be performed separately."

And by the force of this statement of Śaṅkha, there is a separate performance [of the rite] at the Anvaṣṭakā and other occasions; [this refers to] the Mātṛ-śrāddha and the Nāndī-śrāddha. Thus, it should be understood that this concerns cases where the women’s entitlement to a share of the husband’s portion in the śrāddha is not possible, or even when it is possible, the injunction for a separate śrāddha is prescribed by specific scriptural authority. This is to be understood as referring to the statement of the Caturviṃśati-mata: "Some great sages desire a separate śrāddha for women. Others, however, think as follows:
When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed, she attains a single death [with them];
therefore, the wife is a sharer in the portions of her husband’s ancestors.

By this statement, it is merely ordained that in a Śrāddha dedicated to the deities beginning with the husband, the mothers attain the status of deities by virtue of their association; however, it does not mean that they attain the status of deities by association in a Śrāddha dedicated to that specific person with whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* was performed, because no such specific distinction is understood from this text. Consequently, even for a mother who has been *sapiṇḍīkṛta* together with the paternal grandmother and others, there is no separate Śrāddha. Furthermore, this non-separate Śrāddha for the mother is optional (*anitya*).

Some great sages maintain that there should be a separate *śrāddha* for women, because the *Caturviṃśatimata* mentions the position of a separate *śrāddha*: "Thus, in the three [rites] beginning with the *Anvaṣṭakā*, the *śrāddha* for the mothers is indeed separate. Consequently, while there is an option—either separately or together with their husbands—at those *śrāddhas* which produce an excess of satisfaction due to the excellence of place and time, such as Gayā and the *Mahālaya*, this is not the case for all occasions, including the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and others. One should accept whatever is logical in this matter.

It has been stated that when the sun has entered Virgo (kanyā), during the fifth fortnight of the dark half known as Mahālayā, the śrāddha must be performed. However, when there is an absence of the sun’s entry into Virgo, then the śrāddha should not be performed. As Jyotiḥparāśara says:
"The śrāddha fortnight is proclaimed to be when the sun is in the month of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada) while situated in Virgo;
but when the sun, having passed beyond Sinīvālī, enters Virgo [only after that], [the śrāddha is not to be done]."
At that time, because of the advanced age, the ancestral rites for the father were already past.

Because of the advanced age of the time—that is, because it is characterized by such advancement—the ancestral rite (*pitṛkriyā*) has indeed passed, having already exceeded the fifth fortnight, since the *mahālaya-śrāddha* is prohibited therein. And so says Bhṛgu: "When two new moon days (*darśa*) occur while the sun remains in a single zodiac sign (*ekarāśi*), that intercalary month (*adhimāsaka*) should be known as the destroyer of rites for the gods and ancestors (*havya-kavya*)."

"One should not perform the *vṛddhiśrāddha*, the *soma* sacrifice, the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the *mahālaya*, the royal consecration, or rites for specific desires when the sun has transgressed [its proper path]," it is said. Here, "mahālaya" refers to the *mahālaya-śrāddha*. The Grandfather of Astronomy (*jyotiḥpitāmaha*) also states:
Sixty days constitute a month, as stated by the followers of Bādarāyaṇa;
having omitted the first half, the ritual action should be performed in the latter half.

The meaning is that, having omitted the first half of the month consisting of sixty days, the performance of the *śrāddha* rites should be carried out at the proper time during the second half. Jyotiḥparāśara also states: "When the month dear to the *yātudhānas* occurs with the sun in Virgo (*kanyā*), the ancestral (*pitrya*) and divine (*daiva*) rites are joined to the subsequent month."

"When the sun has entered Virgo, the month dear to the *yātudhānas* arises"—the meaning is that the month of Bhādrapada arises without a solar transit (*asaṃkrāntika*). This is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*: "The intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) belongs to the *naiṛtas* and *yātudhānas*. It is explained in this way because the name of the month without a solar transit is derived from its connection with the *rākṣasas* residing in the southwest direction (*naiṛtadig*). The phrase "it is joined in the subsequent month" has this meaning: "A month is said by the followers of Bādarāyaṇa to consist of sixty days."

According to this view, when the month of Bhādrapada is doubled, since a fortnight consists of thirty days, the latter month constitutes the latter half (aparapakṣa) of the sixty-day Bhādrapada month, comprising the subsequent thirty days. Furthermore, if it coincides with the *kanyā* transit (*saṃkrānti*), the ancestral rites (*pitrya-karma*) and other duties to be performed during the *mahālaya* are appropriately joined to that very period; moreover, it should be understood from other scriptures that within that [month], the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is more highly recommended than the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). As for what was stated by that same author:
"When the month occurs while the sun has entered Virgo (*kanyā*) and there is no solar transit (*asaṃkrānta*)," etc.
Likewise, ancestral rites (pitrya) should be performed when the sun is in Libra; for the performer, such action yields inexhaustible merit.

Thus, this [rule] is to be understood as applying when the *śrāddha* is somehow not performed at the previously mentioned times, because it refers to a subsequent time in comparison to those previously mentioned.
Thus ends the section on the times for *śrāddha* in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now, some other statements concerning the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) are also written down.
Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"All rites pertaining to the Śruti and Smṛti are prescribed for the twelfth month;
however, in the thirteenth month, they are all designated as fruitless."

"Therefore, one should by no means perform those [rites] in the thirteenth month. The meaning of "those" is the rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti. The meaning of "in the thirteenth month" is in the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). For this very reason, Gabhasti says: "One should never perform any ritual action during that intercalary month."
The intention is that, because the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) is impure in nature, it is unfit for ritual action (*karman*). Thus, it is stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:

"Those who know time call the intercalary month the impurity of time. The grammatical construction is: "They call the intercalary month the impurity of time. When it is asked when such a month occurs, it is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"There is no intercalary month prior to Caitra, but after it, one may occur.
This means "prior to Caitra" refers to starting from the *saṃkrānti* (sun's passage) into Virgo. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Jyotiḥsiddhānta*:
"When the sun has entered Aquarius, Virgo, Scorpio, or Sagittarius..."
An intercalary month is not ordained when the sun is in Capricorn or Aquarius.

When the Sun has entered the signs of Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, or Aquarius, an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) does not occur; rather, the implication is that it occurs only when the Sun has entered the remaining signs, provided there is an increase in the duration of time. Thus it is stated in the *Vāsiṣṭhasiddhānta*:
"An intercalary month falls after thirty-two months have passed, along with sixteen days and four *ghaṭikās*."

The meaning is that an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) occurs when, starting from a previous intercalary month, thirty-two months have passed and sixteen days plus four *ghaṭikās* have elapsed. As for what is stated in the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya*: "That month in which there is no solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), or in which there are two transits, should be known as an intercalary month; it occurs in the thirtieth month."
Thus, that [statement] intends to show that [the occurrence of an intercalary month] is not possible within thirty months. As for what is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"When no solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) occurs within two months during the course of a year, the former is the natural (*prākṛta*) month, and likewise the latter is the intercalary (*adhimāsa*) month."

Thus, in this context, it should be understood that the mere point intended is as follows: a month that is devoid of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) occurring after the thirtieth month is an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*); whereas a month lacking a solar transit occurring prior to that is an ordinary month and not an intercalary month. It is not, however, intended that there be a fixed sequence of priority between them. Furthermore, when two months without solar transits occur in a single year, or a month containing two solar transits occurs, one should understand that among those, the month without a solar transit occurring after the thirtieth month is the intercalary month, while the remaining two are designated as *saṃsarpa* and *āṃhaspati*. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Bāhaspatya-jyotiḥ-śāstra*: [The Sanskrit text follows: iti, atra triṃśanmāsād ūrdhvaṃ yaḥ saṃkrāntirahito māsaḥ so 'dhimāsaḥ | tato 'rvāg yo 'saṃkrānto māsaḥ sa prākṛtaḥ nādhimāsa ity etāvanmātraṃ vivakṣitaṃ na punaḥ paurvāparyam iti mantavyam | yadā tv ekasmin saṃvatsare asaṃkrāntamāsadvayaṃ saṃkrāntidvayayuto māsaḥ tatrāpi triṃśanmāsād ūrdhvaṃ yo 'saṃkrānto māsaḥ so 'dhimāsaḥ | śeṣau tu saṃsarpāṃhaspatisaṃjñakāv iti boddhavyam | tathā ca bāhaspatye jyotirgranthe 'bhihitam ||
"In whichever month there is no solar transit (saṃkrānti), or even two transits,
those months— known as Saṃsarpi, Hāyana, and Adhimāsa— are censured."

The two months in which no solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) occurs after Caitra, or in which exactly two transits occur, are designated as *saṃsarpa* and *āhaspati*. The month that occurs after Caitra without a transit is designated as *adhimāsa*. The meaning is that these three months are censurable; among them, the *adhimāsa* is most censurable because it is of the nature of temporal impurity (*kālamala*). Thus it has been stated in that very same work: "The *adhimāsa* is extremely defiled" (105). For this very reason, its designation as *malimluca* was shown by Laghuhārīta.
Where Indra and Agni are invoked, that is proclaimed as the beginning of the month;
Agni and Soma are remembered for the middle, and the Pitṛs and Soma for the conclusion.

"If one should ever pass over that [lunar month] and proceed into another month, the first is to be known as *malimluca* (the intercalary), and the second is recorded as *prākṛta* (the ordinary). Thus it is said.

By the phrase "where Indra and Agni are invoked," the first day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-pratipad) is indicated. By the phrase "Agni and Soma are remembered in the middle," the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad) is indicated. By the phrase "at the conclusion, the Pitṛs and Soma-drinkers," the new moon (amāvāsyā) is indicated. By this, the lunar month is characterized. Starting from the previous intercalary month (adhimāsa), when the sun enters another zodiac sign after thirty months have passed, that month which has been bypassed is to be known as the intercalary (malimluca) month. The meaning is that the subsequent month, containing the solar transit (saṅkrānti), is to be known as the natural (prākṛta) month. Parāśara also says:
When a lunar month is overtaken by the solar month, that first month is called *malimluca* (intercalary).
Whatever rite has been prescribed for it, one should perform it in the subsequent month.
Also in another Smṛti:
"In this manner, sixty days constitute a month, and half of that is the intercalary month (malimluca).
Having omitted that [half], one should perform the rites for the ancestors, the gods, and so forth, in the subsequent [month]."
Bṛhaspati states that even in the case of an *malimluca* [intercalary] month, half of certain rites for the ancestors and gods must be abandoned:
"One who is purified should perform the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites during the *malimluca*."

That obligatory (*nitya*) rite for the non-performance of which an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed on account of the lapse of time is as follows: "One who, being a performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), should omit either the new moon day or the full moon day, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt. It is such an obligatory rite that is intended here, not merely any obligatory rite in general. Therefore, the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Agnihotra, the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), and so forth, must be performed during the intercalary month (*malimluca*), because an expiation is prescribed for their performance after the lapse of their own proper time. And likewise, even the obligatory act of the Soma sacrifice must be performed in the intercalary month; for even if the intercalary month itself is passed over, there is no possibility of incurring an expiation here, since the time of spring and so forth—which constitutes an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Soma sacrifice—has not been transgressed. Similarly, regarding occasional (*naimittika*) rites such as the *Gṛhadāheṣṭi* (the sacrifice for a house fire), which are to be performed immediately after the occurrence of the cause (*nimitta*) but for which the prescribed time is not available in another month—it is precisely with respect to such necessary acts that the injunction "one should perform [them] in the intercalary month" is intended. As for occasional rites like the *Jāteṣṭi* (the sacrifice upon a child's birth), which, though occasional, are to be performed at a different time rather than immediately after the cause in order to protect the child—for instance, it is improper to perform them during the period of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*) lasting ten nights or more—the same applies to the intercalary month; thus, they are not to be performed during the intercalary month. In this way, the terms "obligatory" and "occasional" are not intended to be restrictive. The purport of the statement of Bṛhaspati is to be understood as follows: one should perform in the intercalary month all those rites for the omission of which an expiation is incurred, and all those necessary rites for which the performance in the intercalary month is required because the prescribed time is unavailable in another month. Likewise, it is stated in another Smṛti:
"One should always perform that which has no other recourse, as well as that which is occasional. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"Those who know time declare the month to be the primary impurity of time; the additional [period] is likewise [impure]."
"One should not perform any sacrifice here [in the intercalary month], except for that rite which is mandatory.
By this, it is implied that the mandatory rite must be performed during the intercalary month. And it has also been stated explicitly in that very same place:
"The oblations without the *vaṣaṭ* call, the *parvan*, and likewise the *āgrayaṇa*."
But [the following] should be performed during an intercalary month: ... || Thus.

The *avaṣaṭkāra* rites are the *agnihotra*, *aupāsana*, *vaiśvadeva*, and so forth. The *parvan* rites are the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and the *sthālīpāka* performed on those occasions. Regarding the *āgrayaṇa*: although the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi* is prescribed for the season called "rainy," specifically by the rule "one should sacrifice with *śyāmāka* grains during the rains"—which lasts for two months—it is not the case that this rite lacks an alternative application simply because it occurs during an intercalary (*amalimluca*) month. Nevertheless, in the event of famine, when other grains besides new *śyāmāka* are unavailable, one must not consume new *śyāmāka* for the sake of survival without having performed the *āgrayaṇa*. Thus, it is rightly stated that "the *āgrayaṇa* is likewise [necessary]" insofar as its performance is essential for survival. However, when it is not necessary due to the absence of famine, then the *āgrayaṇa* of new *śyāmāka* need not be performed in an intercalary month. It was with this very intention that Paiṭhīnasi said:

"Whether one performs the Āgrayaṇa rite or not in a month devoid of a solar transit (saṃkrānti)—thus an option has been stated. Furthermore, Yama has stated that certain other rites are also to be performed during an intercalary month (*malimluca*):
"In the case of a pregnancy, a usurer, a servant, or a monthly *śrāddha* ceremony..."
In the obligatory Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, one should not avoid the intercalary month.
Bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), the recitation of mantras (japa), burnt offerings (homa) with barley, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth,
the birth rites (jātakarma), the final rites (antyakarma), and likewise the first funeral feast (navaśrāddha).
The *makhā-trayodaśī-śrāddha*, the sixteen *śrāddhas*,
bathing during lunar and solar eclipses, as well as *śrāddha*, giving gifts, recitation (*japa*), and so forth.
"Ritual duties—both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*)—are to be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).

This refers to rites such as the *puṃsavana* and *sīmantonnayana*, which are prescribed on account of pregnancy, being occasioned by pregnancy, and performed solely for the sake of the fetus. Regarding usury: "The interest shall be one-eighth part [of the principal] every month when there is a pledge."

Regarding the inclusion of "interest" as stated in such passages: *bhṛtye* refers to a servant engaged for a period lasting up to a year; *māsike śrāddhakarmaṇi* means in the monthly *śrāddha* rite, that is, the *śrāddha* performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Others, however, hold the view that the new moon *śrāddha* is prohibited even in the thirteenth month according to the statement of Ṛśyaśṛṅga; therefore, they argue that the word *māsika* does not refer to the new moon *śrāddha*, but rather to the monthly *śrāddha* prescribed during the first year. They cite the following statement of Ṛśyaśṛṅga: "The thirteenth month which occurs is indeed an excess over the year."
"Therefore, one should not perform a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth [lunar day] when the moon has waned.
Others, however, say:
"Therefore, one should not perform a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth; it does not stand [in favor]."

Thus they recite. This reading alone is appropriate. For if the reading were *indusaṃkṣaye* ("at the waning of the moon"), there would follow the undesirable consequence of prohibiting the New Moon *śrāddha*, which—like the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*—must necessarily be performed immediately thereafter and is not fit for prohibition. [As it is said: "The *śrāddha* performed at birth (*jātakarman*), as well as the New Moon *śrāddha*, that which is performed annually, and that which is prescribed for the preceding month..."

This is also because it would result in a contradiction with that statement. Therefore, the interpretation that the phrase "in the monthly *śrāddha* rite" refers specifically to the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha* (new moon *śrāddha*) is indeed the correct one. The meaning of the verse of Ṛśyaśṛṅga will be explained below. "In the obligatory [rites]" (*nitye*) means in the daily giving of gifts. Here, "oblation" (*homa*) refers to the *aupāsana-homa*, because of the reference to the substances to be offered there in the words "with barley, rice, sesame, and so forth. "Exceedingly important rites" (*atyantakarmāṇi*) include cremation, the offering of water and funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), the collection of bones, and so on. The rest is clear. The mention of the *jātakarman* (birth rite) is intended as an illustration for the *jāta-śrāddha* and other such rites; for this very reason, another *smṛti* states:

The *Śrāddha-jātaka* rites and those sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) accompanied by vows (*savrata*) should be performed even during the intercalary month (*malimluca*), but one should avoid optional sacrifices (*iṣṭi*) and optional rites (*kāmya*). The term "sacramental rites" refers to the *annaprāśana*, *niṣkramaṇa*, and others. "Accompanied by vows" means those undertaken with a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) such as, "Starting from the Lord's lying down (*janārdana-śayana*) until his rising (*utthāna*), I shall observe the vow, including the wearing [of the sacred thread] and its breaking. The mention of "optional" is intended to include optional animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*) and other such rites, because all optional acts are to be avoided since they are not mandatory. For this very reason, Hārīta says:

"One should not perform the *śrāddha* for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), nor likewise any optional (*kāmya*) rite during an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). This means that all optional rites, such as the *iṣṭi* sacrifice and so forth, must not be performed during the intercalary month. The *śrāddha* for prosperity should be understood as excluding the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* prescribed for the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) prior to the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), since the specific injunction for the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* in rites such as the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*) has already been demonstrated previously. Vṛddha-Manu also mentions other things to be avoided:
The establishment of the sacred fires, consecrations, sacrifices, gifts, and vows;
Vedic observances, the release of a bull, the tonsure ceremony, and the girdle ceremony.
One should avoid auspicious rites and consecrations during the intercalary month (malamāsa),
as well as when Venus is either heliacally set or has reached its setting point, whether it be during childhood or old age.
"One should avoid these [actions], such as visiting a deity, as one would during an intercalary month."

Regarding the statement, “The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the installation [of an image], sacrifices, gifts, and vows,” one should understand the qualification “provided they are not obligatory. Consequently, even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), the *agnyādheya* performed as a penance (*prāyaścitta*) after the extinction of the fires is not prohibited. Likewise, the re-installation (*punar-pratiṣṭhā*) of an image upon its destruction is not prohibited. Similarly, sacrifices such as the *saṃsargeṣṭi* performed as penances are not prohibited. Furthermore, the giving of gifts required for penance, as well as vows such as “one should not detain a Brahmin for lodging,” are permitted. There is a prohibition against the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) on the eleventh day and so forth, because like the sixteen *śrāddhas*, that too serves to benefit the deceased. Even during the setting of Venus (*śukrāstamaya*) and similar occasions, the *agnyādheya* and other rites are prohibited only when they are not obligatory; this is because the term used is specifically “intercalary month” (*malamāsa*). Regarding the prohibition, “one should avoid visiting a deity,” they say that this refers exclusively to the first visit. Hārīta also says:
[111] Except for the first year,
whatever śrāddha may occur after the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite—
"One should not perform either *iṣṭa* (sacrificial rites) or *pūrta* (charitable works) during the intercalary month (*malimluca*).

To state that the monthly *śrāddha* for three ancestors (*traipuruṣika*), which is performed every month during the first year after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, must be performed even in an intercalary month, it is said: "except for [the rites of] the first year. On this very point, Vasiṣṭha also says: "If an intercalary month should occur within the year, one should increase the duration by one day for the sake of the monthly [śrāddha]. This is also stated in another Smṛti.
"Even when a year has elapsed, the monthly rite is performed every month.
Regarding the monthly rites performed prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, Gabhasti has stated:
"The *śrāddha* that is offered as an *ekoddiṣṭa* is called occasional (*naimittika*)."
"That rite should be performed in the previous month, even if there is an excess of time, according to dharma.

By the use of the word "ca" (and), it is understood that it may also be performed in the subsequent month. This refers to the monthly rites (*māsika*) preceding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, as they take the form of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. As for that which was stated by Ṛśyaśṛṅga: "The thirteenth month, which exceeds the year..."
But this is the month of the Asuras; therefore, it is censured by the gods.
Therefore, one should not perform the thirteenth ancestral rite (śrāddha), nor does it take effect.

Thus, regarding the monthly *śrāddhas* prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*: if those performed before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* have somehow not been performed, they must be performed after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* by the force of the scriptural injunction. However, this applies to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites performed every month; it concerns the monthly *śrāddha* that falls due in the thirteenth month. Since a rite performed in a censured month does not take effect unless there is a specific counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), the meaning is that one should not perform the thirteenth-month *śrāddha*. Deva Svāmin has demonstrated the established scope of this statement: "In the case of one for whom, due to varying circumstances, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* and other rites are more urgently required, and because of the lack of materials or Brahmins according to place and time, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed before the completion of the year without having first performed the sixteen *śrāddhas*—for such a person, even though the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed..."
A monthly offering and a water-pot should also be given to him for a year.

By the statement, "Thus, by this verse of Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the thirteenth *śrāddha*—which is the *preta-śrāddha* known as the monthly (*māsika*)—is prohibited," [it is established]. And thus, for one who has died in a year consisting of thirteen months, there are thirteen monthly *śrāddhas*. However, when the monthly *śrāddhas* are performed only after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* due to the unavailability of materials, Brahmins, or other such factors, it should be understood that they then become twelve. And regarding what has been said by some: "One performing the monthly *śrāddhas* until the end of the year's release (*saṃvatsaravimoka*) should not perform them in an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), but must certainly perform them in the subsequent [regular] month; likewise, one performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* at the end of the year and the *saṃvatsaravimoka*, even while performing the monthly *śrāddhas* at their proper times, should not perform them in an intercalary month, but must certainly perform them in the subsequent [regular] month"—this refers to the principle: "one should extend the day by one for the sake of the monthly [rite]."
Even when the year has increased [in length], the monthly rite must be performed every month;
and according to dharma, it must be performed in the preceding month even if there is an excess of time.
Thus, it should be understood that this is based on the non-observation of two such statements. Vṛddhavasiṣṭha has also spoken with reference to the monthly *śrāddha*:
"If an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) should occur when the day for the *śrāddha* has arrived, one should perform two *śrāddhas*; by acting thus, one does not err. [113]
One should perform two *śrāddhas*: the monthly *śrāddha* (*māsika-śrāddha*) in the intercalary month and in the following month; this is the meaning. As for that which was stated by Jyotiḥparāśara:

"The ritual of commencing Vedic study (*upākarma*), the ritual of its conclusion (*utsarga*), births, festivals, and the *aṣṭakā* rites—when there is an increase in the number of months, these should be performed in the subsequent [month], with the exception of those pertaining to the ancestors (*paitṛka*)."

Thus, "the subsequent [rites] are to be performed" means they are to be performed in the following month. In this context, by the term *prasavāhotsava* (the festival of birth), only the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice is intended; it does not include the *ābhyudayika* śrāddha or the *jātakarma*, for if those were also included, [the verse would read]:

"The śrāddha, the naming ceremony (*jātakarman*), and those sacraments accompanied by vows (*savratāḥ*)—these should be performed even during an intercalary month (*malimluca*), but one should avoid optional (*kāmya*) sacrifices."
For otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Smṛti: "By the word *paitṛka*, the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) is intended, not the general [ancestral rite];
one should not avoid the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) in the annual Śrāddha;
even in a *malamāsa*, that Śrāddha which is performed every year must be performed."
And that which was proclaimed previously for the first month of every year.

Because that very [meaning] is clearly stated in such passages as these. All these statements are to be understood as referring to one who has died during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) and that same intercalary month occurs again; for it is said: "On whichever day of a month, fortnight, or lunar date a person dies, they declare that corresponding day each year to be his *kṣayāha* (anniversary of death)."

This is because of such a traditional injunction (*smaraṇa*). And thus, when an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) occurs for one who has died during an intercalary month, the annual *śrāddha* must be performed specifically on the day of the death that falls within that intercalary month; it should not be performed on the day of death falling in the pure (*śuddha*) month, because that [latter] is not of such a nature. However, when an intercalary month does not occur, it should be understood that the *mṛtāha-śrāddha* must indeed be performed even on the day of death that is untouched by an intercalary month, according to the principle of the omission of secondary qualities (*guṇalopa-nyāya*). As for what was stated by Satyavrata:
"The annual *śrāddha* for mother and father on the day of their death should not be performed in an intercalary month; such is the word of Vyāghra."

Thus, this refers to the *mṛtāha-śrāddha* (the annual death-day rite) for one who has died other than during an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*). For one who dies in a pure (*śuddha*) month, the death-day is one that is touched by that same pure month, and not one touched by an intercalary month, because the day of death occurring in an intercalary month is not a prescribed time [for such rites]. For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi states: "The annual *śrāddha* for those who have died in an intercalary month must indeed be performed in the intercalary month, but never for others."

The meaning is: for those who died at a time other than during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). The intention is that the rite must be performed even during an intercalary month, because the prescribed time for it exists precisely therein. Bhṛgu also says: "But for those who died during an intercalary month, the annual *śrāddha* should be performed even in the intercalary month; however, for others, it should never be performed [then]."

[115] As for that which was stated by Vṛddhavasiṣṭha: "If an intercalary month (adhimāsa) should occur when the day of a Śrāddha has arrived, one should perform two Śrāddhas; acting thus, one does not go astray."

Thus, this does not refer to the annual *śrāddha* (*sāṃvatsarika-śrāddha*), because in the case of an annual *śrāddha*, it is impossible for the day of death (*kṣayāha*) to fall within an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) in the subsequent month. Therefore, this statement refers to the monthly *śrāddha* (*māsika-śrāddha*). Consequently, the monthly *śrāddha* should be performed both in the intercalary month and in the following month. Regarding the annual *śrāddha*, however, it should be performed in one of the two months: in that case, for those who died during an intercalary month, it is in the first [regular] month; for those who died in the other month, it is in the subsequent month—this is how it should be understood. As for the prohibition, "but by no means for others," this refers to occasions other than the first annual *śrāddha*, because the first annual *śrāddha* must be performed in the intercalary month by the force of the scriptural injunction. And so says Hārīta:
"But the first annual rite (ābdika) must be performed by the twice-born even when [the anniversary] has not shifted," so it is said. Also, in another Smṛti:
"That which is the first annual rite, one should perform that during the intercalary month (malimluca)."
And when the thirteenth year has arrived, one should perform the annual śrāddha once again.
The meaning is that one should perform the *punarābdika* (the second anniversary rite) when the thirteenth month has arrived following the first year. Laghuhārīta also says:
"The twice-born should perform the *piṇḍa* rites every year in the twelfth month;
however, in some cases it may take place in the thirteenth month, excluding the very first year."

The *piṇḍakriyā* (the performance of the funeral rice-ball offerings) and the *mṛtāha-śrāddha* (the anniversary śrāddha rite) are to be performed when the twelfth month is completed—that is, in the thirteenth month. In some cases, in a year containing an intercalary (*adhika*) month, they are performed when the thirteenth month is completed—that is, in the fourteenth month. However, the first annual (*ābdika*) rite must be performed when the twelfth month is completed even in a year containing an intercalary month; the meaning is that it is to be performed in the thirteenth month. As for what was stated by Śātātapa: "When two months have the same name in a certain year..."
Among those, the rites for the ancestors are in the first [half], and the rites for the gods are in the latter.
Thus it is said; and as for that which was stated by Paiṭhīnasi:
"If two months should have the same name within a year, the rites for the ancestors are to be performed in the former, and the rites for the gods in the latter."

Thus, it should be understood that this refers specifically to those ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*) for which the rule applies during the *malimluca* month, and those divine rites (*devakārya*) for which the rule applies in the subsequent month. Even if a month known as *saṃsarpa* or *aṃhaspati*—characterized by either no solar transit (*asaṃkrānti*) or two transits (*saṃkrāntidvaya*)—should occasionally occur prior to Caitra, nevertheless, the previously mentioned injunctions and prohibitions do not apply there as either prescriptive or prohibitive rules, because those statements concern the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). Furthermore, the months designated as *saṃsarpa* and *aṃhaspati* are not themselves intercalary months.
There is no intercalary month prior to Caitra, but one may occur after it;
for in all the scriptures, the thirteenth lunar day is seen to correspond to that [intercalary] form.

By this statement, since the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is recorded as occurring only after Caitra, the meaning is that in all treatises on calculation (*gaṇitaśāstra*), the thirteenth form—that is, the form of the intercalary month—is observed precisely subsequent to Caitra. Furthermore, it should be understood that those months designated as *saṃsarpa* and *anhaspati* are not eras unfit for ritual action (*karma*), but rather are indeed praiseworthy.
Thus ends the section on the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some other statements concerning the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) are also written here;
regarding this, Garga says:

The solar month is prescribed for marriage and similar rites; the sāvana month is prescribed for sacrifices and the like; and the lunar month is praised for annual śrāddha ceremonies and other ancestral rites.

The meaning is: "at the beginning of a sacrifice," that is, in sacrifices, vows, expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), and other such acts accomplished over a month or a year. Among these, sacrifices accomplished over a month are those prescribed by such scriptural injunctions as, "One should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*," and "For a month, one should sacrifice with the *Vaiśvadeva*. Vows accomplished over a month include the month-long fast (*māsopavāsa*) and others. Expiatory rites accomplished over a month are as follows:
"Dwelling in a cow-pen, practicing celibacy, and observing a milk-vow for one month, one who is devoted to the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* is liberated from [the sin of] accepting gifts."

These are prescribed by such scriptural statements as these. Sacrifices accomplished over the course of a year include *satra* sacrifices such as the *Gavāmayana*. Vows to be accomplished over a year are those prescribed in the Śruti, such as "one should not eat," and so forth. Expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) to be accomplished over a year, such as the twelve-year penance (*dvādaśavārṣika*), are also to be understood here. Regarding the annual (*ābdika*) or yearly *śrāddha*, and regarding ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*) such as the six-monthly *śrāddha*, the lunar month is praised for all divine rites (*devakārya*) other than sacrifices that are accomplished over months or years—this is indicated by the word "also" (*api*). And it has been stated by Pitāmaha:
"In rites for the gods and rites for the ancestors, the lunar month is prescribed.
When it is asked what, then, is the distinction between the lunar, solar, and civil months, it is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"The interval from new moon to new moon is the lunar month; the month consisting of thirty days is the civil (sāvana) month."
The solar month is declared by those who know it to be that which is marked by the sun's transit (saṃkrānti).
The meaning of this has been clarified in another Smṛti:
"The lunar month begins with the bright fortnight and ends with the new moon; the solar month is the period during which the sun remains in a single zodiac sign, measured by thirty solar days."

The lunar month (*cāndra-māsa*) is that which begins with the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*) and ends with the new moon (*darśa*); this is to be understood as the practice in the southern region (*dakṣiṇāpatha*). However, in the northern region (*uttarāpatha*), it should be known that the lunar month begins with the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pratipad*) and ends with the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), because there the conventional usage of the lunar month concludes with the full moon. Therefore, for the purpose of including both types of lunar months, [it is said]:
"In whichever month and on whichever day a death occurs, that month should be known as the one determined by the occasion (*naimittika*) until the next [lunar] junction (*parvan*)."

Thus, Gārgya has stated generally that "the end of the lunar day" (*parvānta*) is the time; the meaning is with reference to the occasional *pratisāṃvatsarika-śrāddha*. However, a specific rule regarding the day is shown in another Smṛti:

"On whichever day a person dies, characterized by a particular month, fortnight, and lunar date, they know that corresponding day of the same nature each year to be his *kṣayāha* (anniversary of death)."

By the word *tithi*, only the lunar day-and-night (*ahorātra*) is denoted, and not the solar or the civil (*sāvana*) day-and-night; for Amarasiṃha has taught the usage of the word *tithi* specifically for lunar days-and-nights in the rule: "The *tithis* beginning with that [first day] belong to both [fortnights]. The meaning is that those beginning with the first day (*pratipad*), etc., are what are designated by the term *tithi*. When the question arises as to what the distinction is between the civil, solar, and lunar day-and-nights, it is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:

"A civil day-and-night (*sāvana*) is from sunrise to sunrise. A solar [day-and-night] consists of thirty degrees of a zodiacal sign. A lunar day (*tithi*) is a conjunction [of the moon with the sun]. (Brahmasiddhānta 1.12)

This is because of such a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*). However, when [the moon] does not become thus, it is understood through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*) that it is a "deficient lunar day" (*khaṇḍatithi*). In order to state that even in the absence of a time touched by the month, fortnight, and lunar day of death for each year, the time for the annual *śrāddha* is precisely a time similar to that, [the text says]:
"But they know that for him, the day of death (*kṣayāha*) is one that occurs in such a manner every year."

Thus it has been stated. "Of such a nature" means corresponding to the time touched by the month, fortnight, lunar day (*tithi*), and so forth of the death. However, when two days are of such a nature—such that on the first day there is a conjunction of the lunar day (*tithi*) during the time for the rite, while on the second day there is no conjunction of the lunar day during the time for the rite—then the first day is the time for the *śrāddha*. Regarding this, Sumantu says: "If the lunar day of the day of death should span two days, one should offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) on the former; thus was it spoken by Āṅgirasa."

"In the preceding [day]" means that which extends over the previous day. By this, it is stated that the annual *śrāddha* must be performed on the previous day during the afternoon—specifically at the time conjoined with the lunar date (*tithi*)—excluding the latter half of the fourth watch (*prahara*). However, when the conjunction with the lunar date occurs in the final *muhūrta* of the afternoon on the previous day (excluding the latter half of the fourth watch), then even though the fifth *muhūrta* starting from *Kutapa* on the following day is conjoined with the lunar date of death, one should begin the *śrāddha* at the time of the conjunction on the previous day and complete it before nightfall. This is because the rule implies that once a rite has begun at its proper time, it must be completed without delay even if the specific time for its conclusion has passed. And thus is the statement of Vyāghrapāda:
One who knows the rules, is endowed with faith, and properly employs worthy recipients,
attains unsurpassed excellence by performing [this rite] at any time other than night.

Thus, it should be understood that this refers to *śrāddha* rites commenced at their own specific time. Having intended all of this, Aparārka has also stated: "The annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) and other *śrāddhas* should be performed at any place during the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) conjoined with the lunar day (*tithi*). If that [lunar day] should extend only into the evening (*sāyāhna*), then the *śrāddha* must be performed in the evening itself by the force of Vyāghrapāda’s statement; it is not, however, [performed] on a day that extends from sunrise until the end of the afternoon. But when the lunar day on the previous day does not touch the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*) yet sets [during the day], while on the following day it touches the time of the ritual and does not set, then the previous day alone is the time for the *śrāddha*, because of the traditional law (*smaraṇa*): "In the case of *śrāddha* and the like, [the lunar day] that sets [during the day] is [to be taken]. The meaning is that the lunar day which sets [during the day] is to be accepted for the annual *śrāddha* and so forth. Nor is it proper here, as in the previous case, to commence the *śrāddha* at the time conjoined with the lunar day and complete it before nightfall, because the latter half of the fourth watch (*prahara*) is not the time for *śrāddha*. Thus it is said in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"That which consists of four *muhūrta*s after the *muhūrta* of Kutapa—
this group of five *muhūrta*s is indeed desired as the abode of *svadhā*.
Thus it was also stated by Kātyāyana.

"In the third part of the day, not too close to the twilight. Nor should it be argued that the *śrāddha* cannot be performed because the conjunction with the lunar day (*tithi*) is impossible at any time other than the latter half of the fourth watch of the day, and thus the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) endowed with the lunar day is absent; for Vasiṣṭha states in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*:
"In the case of breaking a fast or the death of men, the lunar day is considered to be that which exists at the very moment [of the event]."
"In the rite for the ancestors (pitrya), the lunar day that touches the time of sunset is declared to be complete.

This means that the lunar day of death which touches the time of sunset is declared to be complete for the ancestral rites to be performed on that day, such as the annual śrāddha and others. By the phrase "touches the time of sunset," it should be understood that the lunar day of death is considered complete even if only a minute fraction of it exists at the moment of sunset. As for another Smṛti text:
"The five nāḍīs at the end of the day are declared by the wise to be meritorious."
And likewise at the time of sunrise, during rites for the ancestors, and in rites for the gods.

Thus, the meaning is as follows: in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya-karma*), the five *nāḍīs* (fifteen minutes) occurring at the end of the day associated with the lunar day (*tithi*) prescribed as the time are meritorious; the *nāḍīs* preceding them do not bestow the merit arising from the conjunction with that lunar day, nor are those following them less so. In rites for the gods (*daiva-karma*), the five *nāḍīs* occurring at sunrise associated with the lunar day prescribed as the time are meritorious; the *nāḍīs* following them also bestow the merit arising from the conjunction with that lunar day, and none are less so than those. This is expressed by the verse: "The second lunar day bestows two feet for the sake of obtaining a full foot."
By such means as these, a pure man who diligently performs the śrāddha on the new moon day attains all his desires... [and so forth].

Up to this point, [the text] concerns the duality of lunar dates (tithi) beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) as prescribed for the time of the optional *śrāddha* (*kāmya-śrāddha*), but not the duality of dates prescribed for the time of other types of *śrāddha*. This is because this statement is intended to specify a particular detail within that very context, having introduced the subject with the words: "The ancestral *śrāddha* should be performed in the dark fortnight on a day joined with sunset. Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the previously cited statement of Vasiṣṭha. Furthermore, in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:

"When even a single *ghaṭikā* remains of the vow, fast, or observance, that lunar day (*tithi*) is to be known as complete for ancestral rites (*pitrya*), provided it falls in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*).

The meaning is this: when a single *ghaṭikā* remains in the afternoon near the time of twilight (*saṃdhyā*), that lunar day is to be known as complete for the purpose of ancestral rites. And thus, in such a case:
Having begun the Śrāddha during the Kutapa period, a wise man should perform it until the Ārauhiṇa period.

Thus, the very meaning of the scriptural injunction must be followed, for there is no reason to transgress it. However, in the case of the *ekoddiṣṭa* Śrāddha on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), even if the day of death does not coincide with the period after the ninth *muhūrta*, the rite should not begin at *kutapa* and be completed in *rauhiṇa*—despite the rule that "that lunar day (*tithi*) is to be known as whole [if it extends through the day]"—because it must occupy the midday (*madhyāhna*). This is because of the traditional law (*smaraṇa*): "But the *ekoddiṣṭa* is at midday. When, however, the conjunction of the lunar day occurs on the previous day before sunset, while on the following day it lasts for three *muhūrtas* after sunset, then Sumantu declares the latter day to be the time for the Śrāddha.
When the sun has risen, it is the time for offerings to the gods; when the sun has set, it is the time for offerings to the ancestors.
That lunar day (tithi) which lasts for two muhūrtas during the three divisions of the day is the one prescribed for offerings to the gods and the ancestors.

The meaning of this is as follows: When the sun has risen, whichever lunar day (*tithi*) connected with the day and constituting a part of a rite for the gods (*daiva-karma*) lasts for two *muhūrtas*, it brings about the status of being the time for offering the oblation (*havya*) for the entire day, just like a complete lunar day. Therefore, one should perform the rite for the gods on that day.
