When the sun has set, whichever lunar day constituting a part of a rite for the ancestors (*pitṛ-karma*) continues for three *muhūrtas*, it brings about the status of being the time for offering the ancestral oblation (*kavya*) for the day with which it is connected. Therefore, one should perform the ancestral rites—such as the annual *śrāddha* and others—on the day connected with that [lunar day]. By this, it is stated that if on the following day the [lunar day] does not continue for three *muhūrtas* after sunset, then the preceding lunar day, even if it is setting, is the one to be accepted. And thus, what was stated in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*:
One who performs the New Moon sacrifice, the Full Moon sacrifice, or the anniversary day of a father’s death while it is overlapped by the preceding lunar day, falls into hell.

Thus, this should be understood to apply when, on the following day, the lunar day (tithi) does not persist for three *muhūrtas* after sunset. However, when the lunar day on the previous day does not reach sunset, and on the following day it likewise does not extend for three *muhūrtas* after the sun has set—yet instead reaches sunset—then that very same day is to be taken, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*) which states: "In the case of *śrāddha* and other rites, that which reaches sunset [is to be taken]. But when the lunar day does not reach sunset on either of the two days, then the annual *śrāddha* must be performed on the following day alone—even in the absence of the specific quality of reaching sunset—by applying the principle of omitting secondary qualities (*guṇalopa-nyāya*), since the time of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) conjoined with the lunar day is possible then. Furthermore, by failing to perform it, one incurs sin due to the transgression of what is prescribed.
Thus ends the section concerning the day of death in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the rules concerning cases where the month, fortnight, lunar day, or the exact day of death is unknown;
regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:

If the day of death is not known when someone has died while living abroad, but the month is known, then the rite should be performed on the new moon day of that month. If the day of death is known, it should be performed on that very day.
When the month is not known but the day alone is known,
then that day shall fall in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha.
"When the day and month of death are not known, however, the day and month of departure should be taken according to the previously stated method. Thus it is said.

By the word *dina* (day), the very lunar day (*tithi*) of death is to be understood. When a father or other relative has died while abroad, and because of the proximity of timid kinsmen the specific time of death cannot be known—if the exact day of death is not ascertained but only the month is known—then whatever rite is to be performed on the day of death must all be performed on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) of that month; this is the meaning of the first verse. In the phrase "that new moon shall be on the day of death," the mention of the new moon is intended to indicate the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) belonging to that same month. For this very reason, Marīci says:
When an obstacle to the Śrāddha has arisen and the day of death is unknown,
it should be performed on the eleventh day, especially during the dark fortnight.

The meaning of the phrase "by the direction previously stated" is as follows: If only the month of departure is known, then the annual *śrāddha* should be performed on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) of that month. If only the lunar fortnight (*pakṣa*) and the lunar day (*tithi*) of departure are known, then it should be performed on a day touched by that fortnight and lunar day within the months of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha. However, when even the day and month of departure are unknown, then it should be performed on a day touched by the month, fortnight, and lunar day of hearing the news of death; for it has been stated by Parāśara: "When [the details] are unknown, [it should be done] on the new moon day or on the day of hearing [the news]. But when there is an absence of even hearing the news of death, Jātūkarṇya says:
If a father has gone abroad and there is neither news of him nor his return,
after fifteen years have passed, one should create a representative image of him.
"Then one should perform its consecration according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, one should carry out all the remaining rites, beginning with that [consecration].

From the use of the word "all," it is understood that even the rite for the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) must be performed on the day touched by the month, fortnight, lunar date, and [specific] day associated with the cremation.
Thus ends the section concerning the non-recognition of the month, fortnight, lunar day, and the exact day of death in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
[126] Now, the times for optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddha* rites.
In that regard, Viṣṇu states: "The Saṃkrānti, the Viṣuva, especially the two Ayanas,
the Vyatīpāta, one's own birth-star (janmarkṣa), as well as lunar and solar eclipses."
"Thus Prajāpati has declared these times for the Śrāddha as being conducive to desired results;
whatever Śrāddha is offered on these occasions conduces to infinity. Thus [it is said].

By the statement, "He declares the times for *śrāddha* that are for the sake of desired results (*kāmya*)," he shows that the quality characterized by the time of the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*) and so forth is the means for accomplishing the fruit of the desired result, and not the ritual action characterized as *śrāddha* itself. As for the fruit of the ritual action characterized as *śrāddha*, it is shown by the scriptural injunction: "One should satisfy the ancestors with *śrāddha*. Just as the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice, when performed by the father, produces for the son fruits such as purity (*pūtatva*), based on the authority of the scripture which states, "He becomes pure, radiant, an eater of food, possessed of sensory power, and rich in cattle," so too must it be accepted that *śrāddha* performed even by a son or others accomplishes for his ancestors the fruit consisting of satisfaction (*tṛpti*), based on the authority of the scripture stating, "One should satisfy the ancestors with *śrāddha*. The fruit accomplished here by the quality characterized by the time of the sun's transit and so forth should be understood—by way of the *Rātrisatra* principle—to consist in an increase in excellence based upon the satisfaction of the ancestors accomplished through the *śrāddha*.
The ancestral offering (śrāddha) given on these [days] conduces to infinity.

Because the supplementary portion of this statement declares the infinity of the satisfaction of the ancestors (*pitṛs*) accomplished through the *śrāddha*. Since infinity is impossible for a physical object, the word "infinity" refers here to an abundance of excellence residing in that satisfaction. Thus, what is meant is this: on occasions such as the *saṃkrānti*, at a time when the satisfaction of the ancestors is especially great, a *śrāddha* should be performed by a son or other descendant. By the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the word *saṃkrānti* here refers to solar transits other than the two equinoxes (*viṣuva*) and the two solstices (*ayana*). When it is asked what these equinoctial and other transits are, Jyotir-Vasiṣṭha says:
The two transits of Capricorn and Cancer are the northern and southern solstices;
the equinoxes are those of Libra and Aries, and the others [the remaining transits] occur between them.

The phrase "solar transits" (*sūryasaṃkrāntayaḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. The meaning is: "in the middle of those two," namely, the two solstices (*ayana*) and the two equinoxes (*viṣuva*). Among these, one should know that there are eight solar transits: two between the southern solstice and the equinox following it; two between the equinox and the northern solstice following it; two between the northern solstice and the equinox following it; and two between the equinox and the southern solstice following it. Among those, the transits occurring after the equinoxes and solstices, which are not separated by another transit, are to be known by the name *viṣṇupada*; however, those occurring after them are to be known by the name *ṣaḍaśītimukha*. And thus says that very same [author]:
When the sun is in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, or Leo, this is called Viṣṇupada; its fruit is even greater than that of the equinoxes.
"The Sun's transit through Virgo, Gemini, Pisces,
and Sagittarius is declared to be the 'mouths of the sixty-four' (ṣaḍaśītimukha), which possess the qualities of the sixty-four through their fruits."

The construction of the first *śloka* is as follows: when the Sun enters Taurus, Scorpio, Capricorn, and Leo, those four transits are designated as *viṣṇupada*. Although the periods named equinoxes (*viṣuva*), solstices (*ayana*), *viṣṇupada*, and *ṣaḍaśītimukha*, thus described, are indeed shorter than even a *nimeṣa*, nevertheless, being supported by the preceding and following times associated with them, they are prescribed for the performance of rites accomplished over long durations; therefore, it should be understood that they are not invalidated by [the objection of] unsuitability. Thus it has been stated by that very same author:
"The moment of transition (saṃkrānti) is subtle and difficult to perceive even for those with the eyes of a seer;
yet through its conjunction, thirty channels—both below and above—are purified.

Thus, in statements such as "one should perform a śrāddha at the time of transition," it is understood by implication that the śrāddha and other rites should be performed during the purified period resulting from the conjunction with the subtle time denoted by the word "transition. As for that which was stated by Jyotirbṛhaspati:
"In the southern transit (ayana), there will be exactly thirty meritorious *nāḍīs*;
in the past northern [transit], so say the wise.
This is its meaning: "Exactly thirty *nāḍīs* are more meritorious—that is to say, more sacred. And thus:
And through that conjunction, thirty channels (nāḍīs) below and above are purified;

there is no contradiction with this [statement]. Although in the passage "in the past and in the north, the channels," the connection appears to be with "thirty" by way of ellipsis (anuṣaṅga), nevertheless, in order to avoid contradicting other statements, one should supply "twenty" and connect it with that. Otherwise:
"In Cancer, thirty channels are recorded; in Capricorn, twenty."
In the current [solar transits] of Libra and Aries, there are ten nāḍīs on both sides.

This is because it contradicts the statement of Vasiṣṭha. The meaning is that when Cancer has not yet arrived, thirty *nāḍīs* are most pure, and when Capricorn has passed, twenty *nāḍīs* are most pure; for he himself stated: "The two solstices, northern and southern, are meritorious when past and future. In the phrase "ten on both sides," one should also understand that the word "most pure" (*pavitratamāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Furthermore, that which was stated by him immediately thereafter:
During an eclipse, at that time, and during the northern course of the sun;

Thus, by the use of the word *ca* (and) there, it is indicated that twenty *nāḍīs* are meritorious during the future *uttarāyaṇa* as well; therefore, it was stated again, "and in the past *uttarāyaṇa*," not to say that the twenty *nāḍīs* are meritorious only in the past *uttarāyaṇa*. Consequently, there is no contradiction with what was previously stated. And so it should be understood: at the time of the transit (*saṃkrānti*) during the *dakṣiṇāyana*, thirty *nāḍīs* prior [to the transit] bring about an abundance of merit; at the time of the transit during the *uttarāyaṇa*, thirty *nāḍīs* subsequent [to the transit] bring about an abundance of merit; at the time of the transit during the *uttarāyaṇa*, twenty *nāḍīs* on both sides [of the transit] bring about an abundance of merit; and at the time of the transit during the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), ten *nāḍīs* on both sides bring about an abundance of merit. As for what is stated in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*: "They say that during the *uttarāyaṇa*, forty *ghaṭikās* after [the transit] are meritorious, and forty *ghaṭikās* before [the transit] are meritorious," its source must be investigated, since no such foundational statement is seen in the collection of well-known *smṛti* texts. As for what was stated by Marīci:
Sixteen nāḍīs before and sixteen after the transit [of the sun] constitute the meritorious time, as proclaimed by the mere sight of Rāhu.

Thus, although in that context the phrase "of the transition" (*saṃkrānteḥ*) appears to indicate the general transition as the temporal limit (*avadhi*), it should nevertheless be understood—by the principle of the general and the particular—that it refers to cases other than the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*) and the two solstices (*ayana*). For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha stated:
"The period known as meritorious (*puṇya*) lasts sixteen [nāḍīs] both before and after the *Viṣṇupadī*.
By the use of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the verse],...

And in the case of the *ṣaḍaśītimukha*, sixteen [days] are understood to be [auspicious] both before and after; this means they are called "meritorious" (*puṇya*) or "even more meritorious" (*puṇyatara*). As for that which was stated by Garga:
"When the sun is in the solstice (*ayana*), in Viṣṇu, and likewise in the *viṣuva*..."
And likewise at the commencement of the six-month period, and when the northern course has passed.

Thus, "when the equinox is occurring" means in its midst; this is intended to indicate the abundance of the fruit, and not as a restrictive rule, so there is no contradiction with what was stated previously. Therefore, another Smṛti says: "A gift given in the midst of the equinox (viṣuvat), at Viṣṇupada, at the beginning of the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana), when the six-aśīti-mukha has passed, and also during the northern solstice (udagayana), yields abundant fruit."

Thus, regarding these channels (*nāḍī*) as meritorious and most meritorious, one should understand that there is a gradation in their status as causes for superior results—namely, the first, second, third, and so forth—according to the degree of proximity to the subtle moment (*sūkṣmasamaya*) designated by each respective transit (*saṃkrānti*). For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha stated:
"Those channels which are in close proximity are remembered as the most meritorious.
Furthermore, he said:

"Regarding the statement, 'On the day of the transit [of the sun], the entire day is proclaimed meritorious,' it should be understood that this is intended merely as a negative corollary (vyatireka) to show that there is no merit in the extremely distant nāḍīs.
And by association with that [meritorious time], thirty nāḍīs above and below are also purified."
Regarding this, he himself states an exception in a certain case:
"When the sun enters a new sign at night, the merit for bathing and giving belongs to the half-day.

The meaning is that even though it is separated in time, the merit belongs specifically to the half-day, and not to the moments occurring during the proximate night. And this refers to cases other than the solstices (ayana). As he himself says:
If the transit occurs below midnight, the rite is performed above midday;
if it occurs above [midnight], it is two watches after sunrise.
If the sun’s transit occurs exactly at midnight,
they say that both days are meritorious, with the exception of the transits in Capricorn and Cancer.
This, however, refers exclusively to the equinoxes (viṣuva) other than the Viṣṇupada and the two Ṣaḍaśītimukha periods; for it is said:
"When the sun's transition occurs in Sagittarius, Pisces, Gemini, or Virgo, it always takes place at night, whether the sun is moving northward or southward."
The wise have declared that five *nāḍīs* in the forenoon and likewise five in the afternoon are auspicious for rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti*.

Thus, because Viṣṇu has stated it otherwise on the occasions of the *ṣaḍaśīti* and the *mukha*, the term *nṛyuk* refers to the zodiac sign of Gemini (*mithuna*). Regarding the time situated in the eastern or western part—that is, when the sun is in the eastern or western half—if the transit (*saṃkramaṇa*) occurs at midnight, it should be understood that five [periods] are meritorious across both days, due to the equality of the underlying logic characterized by the absence of any specific distinction in proximity. However, in the case of the two solstices (*ayana*), whether by day or night, there is no discarding of the proximate *nāḍīs* (fifteen-minute intervals) as long as they are possible. But surely:
"One should not perform a ritual bath at night, nor especially a gift."

Since bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts are prohibited at night by statements such as these, one must either avoid the *nāḍīs* (lunar mansions) occurring during the night even in the solstice (*ayana*), or a specific exception must be stated. It is said:

"At the sight of Rāhu (an eclipse), during a solar or lunar transit (*saṃkrānti*), at weddings, on days of calamity or prosperity (*atyayavṛddhi*), and during optional vows (*kāmyavrata*), one should perform bathing, giving gifts, and other rites even at night."

By this statement, there is indeed a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) even for the transits (*saṃkrānti*) and so forth. However, this counter-exception is not applicable to all transits; for if it applied to a transit occurring at night other than the two solstices (*ayanadvaya*), it would result in a contradiction with the scriptural injunctions that prescribe the performance of the transit-rites during the day alone. Therefore, one must conclude that this counter-exception pertains specifically to the two solstices. Consequently, during the two solstices, even if they occur at night, there is no abandonment of the proximate *nāḍīs*.

The subject at hand is now stated: the optional times for *śrāddha*, such as the *saṃkrānti* (transits), are to be combined with the *kutapa* and other prescribed times for *śrāddha* whenever possible, because it is necessary to perform all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha* when they can be so performed. However, when such combination is impossible—as in the case of lunar or solar eclipses—there is no contradiction regarding the attainment of the fruit even if they are not combined; for the non-performance of auxiliary parts due to impossibility is permitted by the injunction itself. As for the *vyatīpāta* yoga, that which coincides with the *kutapa* and other times should be accepted, provided it is possible. A birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*) that coincides with the *kutapa* and other times should likewise be accepted when possible. Regarding an asterism that spans two days for the purpose of *śrāddha*: in the bright fortnight, one should take that which occurs at sunrise, according to Devasvāmin’s statement: "That which extends into the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) is to be accepted. In the case of a lunar or solar eclipse, however, the *śrāddha* must be performed precisely during the time of the eclipse.
The gods are satisfied at the moment of contact, as are the ancestors;
humans, however, at the middle of the time, while the rākṣasas are satisfied at the moment of release.
Because of the injunction regarding the timing of eclipses for rites for the gods and rites for the ancestors, the times for optional *śrāddhas* are also shown in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"By worshipping the ancestors under the asterism Kṛttikā, a man attains heaven;
one desiring offspring [should worship] under Rohiṇī, and under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras) he shall obtain vigor."
Under Ārdrā one attains valor; under Punarvasu, land and the like;
under Puṣya, prosperity; and by worshipping the ancestors under Āśleṣā, one obtains excellent sons.
In the month of Māgha, one attains preeminence among kinsmen; in Phalgunī, good fortune;
and by being disposed toward generosity, one becomes possessed of offspring in the Uttarās.
A man who bestows funeral offerings (śrāddha) in the month of Hasta attains preeminence among the virtuous;
likewise, he shall obtain beautiful offspring under the asterism Citrā.
Svāti bestows profit from trade; Viśākhā grants the desire for sons;
and for those who practice them, Anurādhā bestows the turning of the wheel.
In Jyeṣṭhā, one attains sovereignty over heaven; in Mūla, supreme health;
in Āṣāḍhā, the attainment of prosperity; and in Uttarā, freedom from sorrow.
By hearing [the teachings] under Śravaṇā one attains auspicious worlds; under Dhaniṣṭhā, great wealth;
one becomes a knower of the Vedas under Abhijit; and under Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), there is success as a physician.
One finds goats and sheep under the Pūrva-proṣṭhapadās, cattle under the Uttarā-proṣṭhapadās;
likewise, one finds base metals under the Revatīs and horses under the Aśvinīs.
"By performing a *śrāddha* under the *bharaṇī* asterism, one likewise obtains excellent longevity;
therefore, the knower of reality should perform rites for specific desires under these asterisms. Thus it is said.

*Saumyam* refers to that which has Soma as its deity, namely the *mṛgaśīrṣa* constellation. *Ojas* is the excellence of one's own power. *Śauryam* is conduct characterized by fearlessness. "Fields and so forth" means the fruits of the fields. *Puṣṭiḥ* is prosperity; *apuṣṭiḥ* is lack thereof. *Varān sutān* means sons endowed with excellent qualities. *Saubhagyam* is being beloved by the people. *Sāpatyaḥ* means he becomes possessed of offspring. *Satsu* means among virtuous persons. *Rūpavanti* means handsome. *Cakrapravartanam* is the exercise of command without obstruction. *Abhijit* is the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) named Abhijit, which is described in the Veda: "The lunar mansion named Abhijit is above the Āṣāḍhās and below Śroṇā. *Bhiṣaksiddhiḥ* is the attainment of the results of medicinal herbs. *Vāruṇam* is the Śatabhiṣaj lunar mansion. *Kupyam* refers to base metals such as tin, lead, and so forth. *Ṛkṣeṣv eteṣu* means in these aforementioned lunar mansions. *Tattvavit* is one who knows the proper procedure for performing the *śrāddha*. This is also stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Health, as well as good fortune, victory in battle,
and likewise all desires, knowledge, wealth, and even long life.
"A man who always performs the śrāddha in this manner on the days of Āditya and the others, attains these [results] in succession; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that a man performing the respective *śrāddha* on those specific days in the sequence of the sun and other planets obtains these results, such as health and so forth. This is what is being said: one desiring health should perform the *śrāddha* on Sunday; one desiring good fortune on Monday; one desiring victory in battle on Tuesday; one desiring all desires on Wednesday; one desiring knowledge on Thursday; one desiring wealth on Friday; and one desiring long life on Saturday. Yājñavalkya also has shown the times for optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddha*: "A daughter, those who seek a daughter, cattle, and even sons..."
Gambling, agriculture, trade, as well as animals with cloven and uncloven hoofs;
The giver of a Śrāddha always obtains sons endowed with Vedic luster, gold, silver, and base metals, as well as preeminence among kinsmen and all desired objects.
"Starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight, excluding the fourteenth day. Thus it is said.

A maiden who possesses beauty, auspicious marks, and good character—since such a girl is generally most desirable. A suitor seeking a bride should be learned and free from disease. One should seek cattle endowed with good character and auspicious marks, for only such animals are desirable. Regarding the desired results, one desiring a daughter should perform the *śrāddha* on the first day (*pratipad*) of the dark fortnight; on the second day, one desiring a son-in-law; on the third, one desiring cattle; on the fourth, one desiring a son; on the fifth, one desiring victory; on the sixth, one desiring the fruits of agriculture; on the seventh, one desiring profit from trade; on the eighth, one desiring cloven-hoofed animals such as cows; on the ninth, one desiring single-hoofed animals such as horses; on the tenth, one desiring a son rich in conduct and Vedic study; on the eleventh, one desiring gold and silver; on the twelfth, one desiring substances such as tin and lead; on the thirteenth, one desiring preeminence among kinsmen; and on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), according to the principle stated in the section on the accomplishment of yoga, one may gradually obtain all desires. In this regard:
During the dark fortnight, in the afternoon, one must not cross the Rohiṇī constellation.

Thus, the specific rule mentioned in another *smṛti* should be observed. *Rauhiṇa* is the ninth *muhūrta* of the day. Consequently, it should be understood that the optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddha* must be performed on a lunar day such as the first (*pratipad*), when it is conjoined with the three *ghaṭikās* beginning with *kutapa*, and not when it is not so conjoined. In the case of a conflict between two lunar days (such as the first), the *śrāddha* should be performed on whichever day—either the earlier or the later—is conjoined with the three *ghaṭikās* beginning with *kutapa*. As Devasvāmin has stated: "At whatever time an action is prescribed, that rite, including both its commencement and conclusion, should be undertaken on that day and at that time; whichever [day] makes it possible to perform it, whether it be the later or the earlier, should be accepted. If it is possible to perform it on both days, then the earlier day should naturally be accepted; however, if for some reason the performance cannot take place there, the later day should be accepted. Regarding the situation where neither the commencement nor the conclusion is possible on either day, Devasvāmin says: "On the day when the completion occurs, having commenced on that day even if it is not the proper time, it should be completed at the proper time. Here, "completion" means the conclusion. The meaning is: having commenced on that day even if it is not the proper time, it should be completed at the proper time. This is incorrect, because since time is a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārin*), one lacks the entitlement to the rite if the proper time has not arrived; furthermore, commencing a rite at an improper time is unjust. Therefore, in this case, one should commence at the proper time and complete it at an improper time. For when a rite has been commenced at the proper time, the rule implies that its completion may occur at another time. However, when even commencement at the proper time is impossible, then the rule from another *smṛti* should be followed: "The ancestral *śrāddha* should be performed on a day in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) that is joined with sunset."
"In the bright fortnight, however, when conjoined with sunrise, [one should perform] giving, sacrifice, and so forth.

Regarding the dark fortnight, the *śrāddha* prescribed by such statements as "the first lunar day (*pratipad*) is for the acquisition of wealth" should be performed on a day conjoined with the first lunar day at sunset. In the bright fortnight, the meaning is that giving, rites for the gods, and so forth, which are prescribed by the mention of specific lunar days, should be performed on a day conjoined with that specific lunar day at sunrise. The distinction regarding conjunction with sunset and conjunction with sunrise is stated in that very same source:
"The five *nāḍīs* (twenty-four minutes) at the end of the day are declared by the wise to be meritorious."
"And likewise at the rising [of the sun], in rites for the ancestors (paitrya), and in rites for the gods (daiva). [137] Thus it is said.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: for rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*), five *nāḍīs* at the end of the day are declared auspicious; for rites pertaining to the gods (*daiva*), five *nāḍīs* at sunrise are declared auspicious. Regarding a fragmented lunar day (*khaṇḍatithi*), it should be avoided at the initial commencement of an optional rite (*kāmyakarman*), because the commencement is only possible on a complete lunar day (*saṃpūrṇatithi*). However, once an optional rite such as a *śrāddha* has been commenced, it must necessarily be performed on that very day—even if it falls on a fragmented lunar day—whenever its performance is required again during its own proper time, either until the fulfillment of the desired object or for a period of one year. Accordingly, Devasvāmin, citing the *nakṣatra-śrāddha*, stated: "In the case of optional *śrāddhas* performed under specific asterisms (*nakṣatra*), when the asterism that grants the desired object arrives, one should perform the *śrāddha* in that asterism for as long as the desire persists, or for one year. On this point, Hārīta says:
One who desires specific results should properly perform the optional *śrāddhas* with great effort;
however, one who seeks liberation should not perform them, as they are causes for the initiation of a new body.
Those śrāddhas which have been prescribed as pertaining to the realm of desire,
one should perform them for the sake of heaven and liberation, because they are enjoined by another rule.
One should perform the obligatory rites by any means possible during lunar eclipses and similar occasions;
when the necessary vessels, materials, and other requisites are available, one shall obtain the fruits of optional rites.

Regarding the phrase "because it is stated in another injunction": "Sanskara (purificatory rite) is indeed of two kinds: the Brāhma and the Daiva. That which begins with *garbhādhāna* (conception) and is prescribed by the Smṛtis is the Brāhma; while the *pākayajña*, *haviryajña*, and *saumya* sacrifices constitute the Daiva. One who is purified by the Brāhma saṃskāras attains equality with the Ṛṣis, that is, the same world and union (*sāyujya*). Purified by the subsequent Daiva rites, one attains the same world and union with the Devas. By such other injunctions as these, [it is said]: "Even a householder who performs *śrāddha* and speaks the truth is liberated."
Because it has been stated in such a manner and by means of another injunction as well.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, [are concluded] the times for optional Śrāddhas; now follow the secondary times for Śrāddha. Regarding this, Ṛśyaśṛṅga says:
If impurity (āśauca) should arise during a śrāddha for the gods or for the ancestors,
the śrāddha is offered to them once that period of impurity has passed.

The meaning is as follows: when an impurity (*āśauca*) arises for those entitled to perform the *śrāddha* prior to the commencement of the cooking at the primary time, then—since that primary time has drawn near and is defiled by the impurity—the ancestral rite (*paitṛka-karma*) must be performed only after the impurity has ceased. As for another Smṛti text: "If that day should be defiled by something such as birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), one should perform it after the birth-impurity has ended, or else on that very same day again."

Thus, regarding the view that "if the day of the *śrāddha* is defiled by *sūtaka* (birth-impurity), one should perform it after the *sūtaka* has ended," this is indeed not in contradiction with the statement of Ṛśyaśṛṅga. However, the alternative view—"or on that very same day"—must be understood as referring to a situation where the primary time prescribed by other causes mentioned by the word "etc. (*ādi*) is unavailable; this is to be so construed in order to avoid contradicting the preceding statement. Furthermore, this alternative option pertains specifically to the monthly *śrāddhas* performed on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*). In that case, even if the time corresponding to the entire month is unavailable, the lunar day (*tithi*) alone associated with that fortnight (*pakṣa*) is to be accepted. For this very reason, another *Smṛti* states:
[139] But when the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite has arrived and an obstacle arises,
one should diligently perform the *śrāddha* on another day of that same lunar date.

"In another month immediately following" means on that lunar day—the day of death—in whichever fortnight (whether bright or dark) he died; the meaning is that one should perform the *śrāddha* in that same fortnight if it was passed over due to an obstacle. Even here, regarding the phrase "if there is an obstacle," a supplementary clause must be understood—"due to a cause other than ritual impurity (*aśauca*)"—in order to avoid contradicting the statement of Ṛśyaśṛṅga. However, when an obstacle arises due to the cause of *aśauca*, even in the case of the monthly rites, the performance of the *śrāddha* immediately after the period of impurity has ended should be followed according to what was stated by Ṛśyaśṛṅga. For this very reason, Devasvāmin also said: "This statement of Ṛśyaśṛṅga concerns the subject of impurity due to birth or death (*sūtaka-aśauca*). If, due to another cause, that day is obstructed..."
"But if an obstacle arises when the *ekoddiṣṭa* has arrived," and so forth—this is a statement from another *smṛti*. Furthermore, as for another *smṛti*:
"When an obstacle to the *śrāddha* has arisen, or if there is death or birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) in the interval..."
Some wise men say that one should perform it on the new moon day when it is pure.

Thus, regarding "death or birth occurring in the interval": if a birth or death occurs prior to the commencement of the cooking during the performance of a *śrāddha*, then purification occurs on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) or upon subsequent purification. This refers specifically to the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) *śrāddha*. The mention of the new moon is intended as an illustration for the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇaikādaśī*) as well. For this very reason, Marīci states:
"When an obstacle to the *śrāddha* arises and the day of death is unknown, it should be performed on the eleventh day, especially in the dark fortnight."

The syntactical connection is: "On that Ekādaśī which falls in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), [the rite] should especially be performed. Since for rites dedicated to the ancestors (pitṛkārya) the dark fortnight itself is naturally to be preferred, it should be understood that the superiority of the new moon (amāvāsyā) over even the dark Ekādaśī for ancestral rites is established by the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (daṇḍāpūpikā-nyāya). As for the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "When a monthly or annual [ancestral rite] has arrived, but an impurity due to death or birth occurs in the interval, the wise say that it should be performed upon purification or on the new moon day."

Thus, this [rule], namely "one should perform those very same [rites] again," refers to the *anvaṣṭakya* Śrāddha as prescribed. This is because, regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa* monthly Śrāddha, an alternative time has already been stated previously. In that context, the period immediately following purification is superior, as it is the primary time (*mukhyakāla*). The time of the new moon (*darśa*) is inferior to that, because it lacks proximity to the primary time; so it should be understood. And likewise, Ṛśyaśṛṅga says: "The day on which the lunar date (*tithi*) arrives for one who has become pure—that date should be observed by him, and never any other."

The meaning is this: first, one should perform the rite having become pure. If purity is impossible at the primary time, then the lunar day (*tithi*) following purification is obtained; that *tithi* is to be performed by him prior to the commencement of the ritual action, being accomplished through some means of performance, and no other. The primary *tithi*, when defiled by impurity (*āśauca*), must never be performed. He himself states that the primary *tithi* defiled by impurity is not to be performed:
"The interruption of the *tithi* must not be made arbitrarily, except on account of impurity."
The funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and the ancestral offering (śrāddha) must be given; one must never cause their interruption.

"Yadṛcchayā" means by one's own will. "Śrāddha" refers to the satiation of Brāhmaṇas. By the word "ca" (and), it is implied that the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) must also be performed. Here, the term "śrāddha" is used figuratively (*upacāra*) to denote merely the satiation of Brāhmaṇas, and not in its primary sense; for the primary meaning of the term consists of the triad of rites comprising the *agnaukaraṇa*, the satiation of Brāhmaṇas, and the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍadāna*). Accordingly, Devasvāmin has correctly defined the meaning of the word "śrāddha" in this very way:
because the term "śrāddha" is employed even in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and others when the funeral cakes are absent.
The word *śrāddha* refers neither to the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) nor to the feeding of the twice-born.
Because the term *śrāddha* is not applied when eating occurs during guest-reception (*atithyādi*) and the like,
it is certainly not merely the giving away of wealth and so forth for the sake of the ancestors.
Even in the case of libations and other such rites, their abandonment is observed despite their being otherwise established;
having considered the opinions of the learned, this is what remains fixed in my heart.
"The fire-oblation (homa), the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍadāna), and likewise the satiation of Brahmins—
these may be designated by the single term 'śrāddha' in a figurative sense."

The meaning of the statement by Ṛśyaśṛṅga, "one should never cause an interruption," is as follows: even if it is impossible to perform the entire ritual denoted by the term *śrāddha*, one should perform at least a portion of it according to one's capacity; in no case should one cause an interruption in the performance of the rite. For this very reason, the *Nigama* states: "For one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the worship of the ancestors should be performed with the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) alone, or else one should feed Brāhmaṇas. In this matter, the arrangement depends on one's capacity. Consequently, if one lacks the capacity for the second option, the first-mentioned option applies.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, the secondary times for *śrāddha* [142]. Now, the locations for *śrāddha*.

In that regard, the Viṣṇudharmottara states: "One should diligently perform the Śrāddha in a region sloping toward the south, or at a sacred ford (tīrtha), or even in one's own home, provided it has been prepared with the proper consecration of the ground and other rites."

A *tīrtha* is water frequented by sages; "near it" means in its vicinity. By the word "etcetera," hermitages and other places frequented by sages are included. It should be "endowed with the purification of the ground and so forth"; the purification of the ground refers to smearing it with cow dung and the like. By the word "etcetera," the removal of impure substances such as hair is included. And thus it has been stated in that very same work: "And one should perform the *śrāddha* according to the rules, always in these [places]: in secluded houses smeared with cow dung."
The meaning is that one should always perform the *śrāddha* in these aforementioned houses and dwellings that have been smeared with cow dung and cleared of substances such as hair. Manu also says:
"One should smear a clean and secluded place with cow dung, and one should diligently ensure that it slopes toward the south."

The meaning is as follows: having made a naturally pure place—such as a sacred bathing site (*tīrtha*) or a portion of one’s own house—secluded by removing impurities caused by others and free from hair and the like, one should smear it with cow dung for the sake of providing an excellence of purification to the ground. Even if it is not naturally inclined toward the south, one should diligently ensure that it is inclined toward the south through such means as digging it up, in order to achieve the status of a *pitṛyajana* (place of sacrifice for the ancestors). Regarding this, Yama says:
"If one should perform the offering to the ancestors on grounds belonging to another, the *śrāddha* rite is obstructed by the ancestors of the owner of that land."

The intention is that one should not perform a *śrāddha* ceremony there. "Places belonging to others" refers to places such as houses or cow-pens occupied by others, but not sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and the like. Thus says the *Purāṇa*:
"Forests, mountains, and riverbanks which are holy—all these are said to be without an owner, for there is no private possession over them."

"Forests, mountains, rivers, sacred fords, sanctuaries, and both divine excavations (*devakhāta*) and natural hollows (*garta*): no owner is found among them. (Viṣṇudharmottara). The compound *devakhātagartāḥ* means "divine excavations and natural hollows," because it is impossible for there to be a restrictive rule regarding the lack of ownership for artificial hollows. Since there is an absence of possession by others in these places, it is therefore stated that one should offer the *śrāddha* in these locations as if in one's own home. (Viṣṇudharmottara).
"Therefore, funeral offerings (śrāddhas) should be given with diligence at sacred sites, on the banks of rivers, at holy fords (tīrthas), and on one's own land.
Even on one's own land, they should be given in a place other than an artificial area, because of the prohibition regarding that. And so says Śaṅkha:
One should not perform a śrāddha on the backs of oxen, elephants, horses, and so forth, nor on artificial ground, nor on these types of land belonging to others or that is impure.

The meaning is: "on an altar-platform constructed on the ground. By this, it is implied that the satisfaction of the ancestors occurs only on ground that is not artificially prepared. And it has been stated directly by Devala:
"On bare ground, on mountain ridges, at sacred fords, and in sanctuaries;
likewise, in cow-pens and in secluded places, the ancestors are satisfied."

"On *sthalīṣu* means on places that are naturally elevated; for by the Pāṇinian sūtra *jānapadakuṇḍagolasthala-* (Pāṇ 6.2.129), the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed after the word *sthala* in the sense of being non-artificial. Śaṅkha also states a prohibition regarding artificial ground: 'One should not offer libations to the ancestors on ground paved with bricks. Yama, however, describes the locations to be avoided:
'In the performance of a *śrāddha*, one should avoid a place that is parched, infested with worms, damp, crowded, foul-smelling, or characterized by unpleasant sounds.'"

"Rūkṣa" means dry and lacking oiliness; "klinna" means muddy with mire; "saṃkīrṛṇa" means strewn or crowded with other objects; "aniṣṭagandhika" means having a foul odor; "aniṣṭaśabda" means having an unpleasant sound or an unhearable sound, including even speech that is slurred by intoxication. In the performance of a Śrāddha rite, ground that is infested with living creatures, dry, scorched by fire, possessing unpleasant or wicked sounds, fierce, or foul-smelling, should be avoided.
"Scorched by fire" means burnt; "fierce" means being in close proximity to tigers and other such beasts.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, [the section on] the places for *śrāddha* has been concluded.
Now, the places for optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddha*: regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"At Puṣkara, however, a śrāddha, as well as recitation, fire-oblations, and ascetic penances, are inexhaustible;

likewise at the great ocean, at Prayāga, at Kāśī, and in Kurujāṅgala. Here, "Puṣkara" refers to the sacred site named Puṣkara. "Kāśī" is Vārāṇasī. The words "Kuru" and "Jāṅgala" denote specific regions. Śaṅkha also says:
In Vārāṇasī, at Kurukṣetra, on Bhṛgutuṅga, in the Himālaya,
and on the banks of the Narmadā and Bāhudā, one enjoys all eternity.
Whatever is given at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, or likewise at Puṣkara, at Saṃnihati, or at Gayā, shall attain imperishability.

Naimiṣa is located on the banks of the Sarasvatī in the Naimiṣa forest. Saṃnihati is a specific sacred site (tīrtha) situated in Kurukṣetra. Gayā is well known. Furthermore, the measurement of the Gayā-kṣetra is shown in the Purāṇa: "The region between the Mahānadī and the Devanadī, extending northward from the Kanakhalā river, is proclaimed as the center of Gayā."
The sacred field of Gayā extends for five krośas, while Gayāśiras measures one krośa.

The meaning is that within the Gayā-kṣetra, which measures five *krośas*, the essential portion of one *krośa* is known as Gayāśiras; and this has been defined in that very same place: "From the west of the Mahānadī river as far as Mount Gṛdhreśvara, and from the north of the Brahmayūpa as far as the Dakṣiṇamānasa."

"This is known as Gayāśiras, renowned throughout the three worlds. Thus it is said. Just like Gayāśiras, other famous sites for *śrāddha* rites in Gayā, such as the Mahānadī and others, are also indicated in that very same place:
"The Mahānadī, Brahmasadas, the Akṣaya Vaṭa, Prabhāsa, Udyanta, and also Gayāśiras."
"Sarasvatī, Dhenuka, and Dharmapṛṣṭha—these are equal to Kurukṣetra at Gayā.
Udyantākhya is a particular mountain. The Sarasvatī is renowned as the Prācī Sarasvatī. Vyāsa also says:
"Brahmāraṇya, Dharmapṛṣṭha, and Dhenukāraṇya..."
By worshipping the ancestors in these three, one uplifts seven generations of one's lineage.
In the Brahmakaivarta [Purāṇa] as well:
"By seeing Muṇḍapṛṣṭha at Gayā, the mountain Aravinda,
and thirdly Krauñcapāda, one is liberated from sins."
The greatness of Gayā, of its peak, and of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is shown in that very place:
"In heaven, in the netherworld, and among mortals, there is no sacred site equal to Gayā;
the ancestors attain divinity when the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) are offered at Gayāśiras."
When one offers the funeral rice-ball at Gayāśīrṣa by the names of those [ancestors],
those residing in hell go to heaven, and those residing in heaven proceed to liberation.
On Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, the wise Mahādeva set down his foot after performing most rigorous austerities for many thousands of years.
"Even by a short time spent here, a person devoted to dharma quickly liberates himself from evil, just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
Thus is the greatness of the Akṣayavaṭa tree demonstrated in that very place.
There, O Lord, is the one known as Akṣayavaṭa, renowned throughout the three worlds; whatever is given there to the ancestors becomes indeed inexhaustible.
Having approached a banyan tree, even if one feeds a single Brahmin with only vegetables or water, it is as if ten million have been fed.
The greatness of Dhenukāraṇya is shown in another Purāṇa:
"From there, O king of kings, one should go to the world-renowned Dhenukā;
for even today its sign is clearly visible there, of this there is no doubt. [147]
O best of the Kurus, the five well-formed footprints of the tawny cow with her calf are seen as she wanders about.
O lord of men, by touching those footprints of Kapilā,
whatever sin a man has committed is completely destroyed upon seeing them.
The majesty of Gṛdhreśvara is revealed in that very place.
Thereafter, one should go to Gṛdhranaga, the abode of the wise deity;
having bathed there with sacred ash, one should approach Maheśvara.
"A twelve-year vow shall have been performed by a Brāhmaṇa;
for the other castes, however, there shall be the destruction of all sins.
Thus is the majesty of Gṛdhreśvaragiri shown in that very place.
From there, O bull of the Bharatas, one should go to the level mountain known as Annaparvata, which is surrounded by hills; there the footprints of Sāvitrī are visible.
There, a Brahmin of firm vows should perform the twilight worship;
by that, the twilight worship is considered performed for twelve years.
The greatness of Dharmapṛṣṭha is also shown in that very place.
Therefore, O king of kings, one should go to Dharmapṛṣṭha with a concentrated mind.
O great king, best among warriors, wherever Dharma eternally resides,
O lord of kings, one shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice upon reaching that place.
The majesty of other famous sacred sites at Gayā has thus been shown.
Then, having reached the river Viśālā, renowned throughout the three worlds,
one obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
Then, having reached the abode of Maheśvara, a pure man obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice and uplifts his entire lineage.
Having reached the lotus pond of the gods, a pure man does not fall into an evil state of existence, but goes instead to the world of Viṣṇu.
In that place, O bull of the Bharatas, there is a world-renowned confluence of holy fords,
O King, which was [occupied] by a wicked-souled Dānava in the form of a tortoise.
O King, best among warriors, when it was being carried away and then recovered by the powerful Viṣṇu, one should perform an ablution there; it is equal to ten million sacred fords (tīrthas).
One obtains the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
there are mango trees established by Brahmā situated near the pasture for cows.
When those [offerings] are attached to him, the ancestors of the man here obtain liberation.
A single sage, with a water-pot in his hand, constantly gives water to the mango trees;
the mango trees are watered and the ancestors are satisfied—thus one action has become the performer of two purposes.
That river known as Vaitaraṇī, renowned throughout the three worlds,
has indeed descended at Gayāśīrṣa for the sake of delivering the ancestors.
Having bathed there, O Great King, he who bestows the gift of a cow shall deliver twenty-one generations of his lineage; of this there is no doubt.
"In that regard, by the gift of a cow, the ancestors shall attain liberation" (149). Thus it is said.
*Pauṇḍarīkam* refers to the fruit of the sacrifice known as the *Pauṇḍarīka*. Also in the *Brahmakaivarta*:
"The killer of a Brahmin, the ungrateful person, the killer of a cow, and the one who commits the five great sins—"
All attain liberation through the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā.
The slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, and those who betray children, the elderly, or their gurus—
their sin indeed goes to destruction if they go to Gayā.
Just as one who has obtained the status of a son at the bank of the Gaṅgā [performs the rite],
by uttering whose name one should cast the funeral ball (piṇḍa), he shall lead that person to eternal Brahman.
Thus it is said:
"When an eclipse of the moon or the sun occurs while the moon is in Capricorn,
the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā— which is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds— is [attained]."

The meaning is that he shall lead [the deceased] to the eternal world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), which brings about the attainment of Brahman, together with Brahmā himself. Vyāsa also says: "Whatever man goes to Gayā and satiates his ancestors, he purifies ten generations of his lineage—both preceding and succeeding—and himself as well."
In another Purāṇa:
"Bathing and the renunciation of the body are especially distinguished when performed in the Gaṅgā;
however, the Śrāddha and the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) are especially distinguished at Gayā."
Knowledge of Brahman, the Śrāddha rite at Gayā, death in the house of a cow,
and residence for men in Kurukṣetra— these four kinds of liberation have been declared.
One should dwell constantly at Gayāśīrṣa and perform one’s ablutions in the Phalgu;
at Gayāśīrṣa, one should always offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa), for this is difficult to obtain even in heaven.
Having bathed at Phalgutīrtha and beheld the god Gadādhara,
and having circumambulated Gayāśiras, a man is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
At Gayā, Janārdana himself exists in the form of the ancestors;
having seen that lotus-eyed one, Janārdana himself [is attained].
Having seen that lotus-eyed one, one is released from the three debts,
by whomsoever even once the back of the Dharma at Gayāśiras has been trodden.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin perish; there is no doubt about this.
Yet, even by bestowing the entire earth three times, one would not be released from the debt owed to the ancestors.
As long as a son has not gone to Gayāśiras,
to Dharmapṛṣṭha in Gayā, and likewise to the assembly hall of Brahmā, he cannot truly perform the ancestral rites.
What is given to the ancestors at Gayāśīrṣa and at Pade is inexhaustible;
one should offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa) on the crest of Gayā even if it is only the size of a Śamī leaf.

"Those dwelling in hell go to heaven; those dwelling in heaven attain liberation. The mention of taking *śamī* leaves is for the purpose of making it known that the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) is mandatory according to one's own means; therefore, it is said in that very same place:
"Upon reaching Gayā, a man should never practice stinginess regarding his wealth."
And one who practices stinginess regarding wealth shall not partake in the fruit of the sacred ford.
Therefore, the *gayāśrāddha* should be performed according to one’s wealth and according to the strength of one’s body. This too has been stated in that very same source:
"Having thus performed the *śrāddha* according to one's capacity and according to one's strength, one obtains divine desires; for it is remembered as the gateway to heaven. [151]

Therefore, if possible, one should out of compassion give the offering of the *piṇḍa* and so forth even to those of the same caste (*savarṇa*) and others; this too has been stated in that very same place:
"To those of the same caste, to kinsmen, and to those who are relatives and friends—to them, moreover, the *piṇḍas* should be offered according to the rule on the ground of Gayā."
And from all his daughters' sons and sons— even those younger than himself—
he should offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) to those who have died in other births as well.
"They all go to heaven when a funeral ball (piṇḍa) is offered"—such is the sacred tradition (śruti).

If the lineage (*gotra*) and other details of those belonging to the same class (*savarṇa*) and so forth are unknown, the mantra for the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is also shown in that very [text]:
"Those born in the paternal line, and likewise those in the maternal line;
those who are the gurus, fathers-in-law, and kinsmen, and whatever other twice-born men [there may be]."

Those in my family for whom the funeral offerings have been interrupted, those deprived of sons and wives, the deformed, those who died as miscarriages, and likewise those known and unknown; [may they all attain satisfaction].
To those who have reached the state of being cast away, and to others who are situated within the womb—to them I have given this punishment; may it abide as inexhaustible.

"Unripe embryos," "uncooked embryos," and "incomplete embryos"—this is what it means. Just as in the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) for those of the same lineage and so forth, one should offer a rice ball devoid of sesame seeds even for one's own sake in the presence of the deity Janārdana, like placing a deposit of wealth. This too has been stated in that very same place:
"O one of great intelligence, for oneself at Gayā, the offering of the rice ball should be performed without sesame seeds; however, for the deceased, it should be performed with sesame seeds."

Wherever the *śrāddha* and other rites are performed at Gayā, the Brahmins of that very locality—even those who subsist on their caste alone—are to be accepted for the sake of the *brāhmaṇa* rite. Thus says another Purāṇa: "If a son should go to Gayā at some point in the course of time, he should feed those very Brahmins who have been designated as such."
Their abode consists of Brahman and likewise the drinking of Soma;
these Brahmins, established in the conduct prescribed by Brahman, are remembered as being equal to Brahman itself.
The Brahmins of Gayā are superhuman; when those appointed Brahmins are satisfied, the deities together with the ancestors are fully gratified.
Having worshipped the Brahmins of Gayā, who are the very forms of his ancestors, with a concentrated mind,
one whose self is purified of all sins is glorified in the heavenly world.
And whatever is given by their own hands, especially at Gayā, that becomes inexhaustible for their ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
"One need not consider family, character, learning, or even asceticism;
for when these are honored, the gods, along with the ancestors and the Guhyakas, are satisfied.

Thus, in the passage "If a son should go to Gayā," the mention of the "son" is intended as an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all those who go to Gayā, such as grandsons and others, who desire the welfare of their fathers and ancestors. For this very reason, in the *Brahmakaivarta*:
Having performed the śrāddha according to the prescribed rules and completed the remaining ritual duties, one who is intent on going to Gayā should circumambulate the village.
Then the man should go to another village and eat the remnants of the śrāddha food;
thereafter, he should travel day by day, avoiding the acceptance of gifts.

[153] Thus it has been stated in general. For this very reason, Vyāsa also stated in the Mahābhārata in a general manner: "A wise man, having properly formed a resolve, should perform the *śrāddha* at home, designating the *pitṛ-tīrtha* and forming the resolve in the presence of the ancestors."
"Acceptance of gifts, food from others, and quarreling—these [should be avoided], O best of the twice-born.

The meaning is that, in the presence of the ancestors—that is, in the presence of the Brāhmaṇas invited for the sake of the ancestors—one should perform the *saṃkalpa* properly with devotion, intending: "I shall perform the Śrāddha for the purpose of the pilgrimage to Gayā, directed toward the *pitṛtīrtha*," and then perform the Śrāddha for the pilgrimage in one's own home. "Quarreling" (*kali*) means a dispute. Other things to be avoided have also been stated by that same author: "The shaving of the hair, beard, nails, and so forth, is not recommended."
Therefore, one who desires to perform the *śrāddha* at Gayā should never undergo the shaving of the head.
Thus, the fruit for one performing the pilgrimage to Gayā is also stated in that very same place:
"Those in this land of Bhārata who are devoted to the rites for their ancestors, maintaining their hair while being bowed down with great devotion..."

"Those who have come to the Pitṛtīrtha for the sake of discharging their debts—certainly their debt shall be extinguished. Thus [it is said]. In the Bhārata, that is, in Bhāratavarṣa, Pitṛtīrtha is Gayā, for the purpose of discharging debts—that is, for the purpose of discharging the debts owed to the gods, sages, and ancestors.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, [section 154]: The Locations for Optional Śrāddhas;
and the Description of Brāhmaṇas to be Feasted at a Śrāddha.

Regarding this, Manu says: "In that regard, I shall explain in its entirety who those best of the twice-born are who are to be fed, who are to be avoided, how many there are, and with what kinds of food."

In this context, the meaning is "at the rite for the ancestors" (*śrāddhakarmaṇi*). "The best of the twice-born" (*dvijottamāḥ*) refers to those who are the best among the twice-born of the three *varṇas*, that is to say, Brāhmaṇas. He (the same author) states that one must perform an examination of qualities, defects, and so forth, in order to discern which Brāhmaṇas are worthy of being fed and which are not:
"One should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.

The "examination from afar" (*dūrāt parīkṣā*) refers to the investigation of a Brāhmaṇa worthy of being fed, starting from his great-grandfather down to himself. The mention of "one who has mastered the Vedas" is intended as an illustration of the desirable qualities [to be examined]. For this very reason, Chāgaleya says:

One should perform every śrāddha with those endowed with the characteristics already described, possessed of learning, virtuous conduct, and good qualities, and renowned among three generations of their lineage.

The meaning is that one should "prepare"—that is, perform—all *śrāddha* rites, such as the *pārvaṇa* and *ābhyudayika*, by means of Brahmins possessing the characteristics already described. Also in the *Purāṇa*: "He who has been purified by the sacraments beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), who is pure, perfected in the study of the Veda, and established in the six duties..."
One who stands firm in the wheel of purity, eats only the remains of the meal, is dear to his teacher, is constantly observant of vows, and is devoted to truth— he indeed is called a Brāhmaṇa.
Austerity, sacred learning, and noble birth—these are the causes of Brahminhood;
as are truth, charity, austerity, freedom from malice, kindness, forbearance, and compassion.
"And where austerity is seen, he is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa. Thus it is said.

The six [occupations] consist of sacrificing for oneself, officiating as a priest for others, studying, teaching, giving gifts, and receiving gifts. *Vighasa* is the remnant of a sacrifice, as well as the remnant of what has been eaten by guests and others. *Yoni* refers to purity of lineage (*anvaya-śuddhi*). *Ānṛśaṃsya* is the absence of cruelty. Hārīta also says: "Those who are of noble birth, possessed of learning and good character, established in right conduct, speakers of truth, free from physical defects, and worthy of the *pāṅkta* (the row of diners). He himself explains the qualities of lineage and so forth: "Stability," which consists of an uninterrupted knowledge of the Vedas, freedom from the confusion of castes (*ayoni-saṃkara*), and descent from a lineage of seers (*ārṣeya-tva*)—these are the qualities of lineage. The Vedas, their auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), Dharma, metaphysics (*adhyātma*), specialized knowledge (*vijñāna*), and tradition (*smṛti*) constitute the sixfold "learning" (*śruta*). Devotion to Brahman, devotion to the Vedas and ancestors, equanimity, gentleness, not causing pain to others, lack of envy, lack of arrogance, absence of harshness, friendliness, speaking kindly, gratitude, being a refuge for others, tranquility—these are the thirteen kinds of "good character" (*śīla*). Forgiveness, compassion, self-restraint, charity, non-violence, honoring teachers, purity, recitation, burnt offerings (*homa*), austerity, Vedic study, truthfulness, contentment, firmness in vows, and observance of minor vows—these are the sixteen qualities of "right conduct" (*vṛtta*). "Stability" also implies the persistence of the lineage over time. In the phrase "uninterrupted knowledge of the Vedas," the word *vedi*—which denotes a specific place for placing the sacrificial oblation—indirectly indicates the sacrifice accomplished by that oblation. What is meant is this: the existence of Vedic study and the performance of sacrifices among one's ancestors constitutes the qualities of lineage. "Descent from a lineage of seers" means being born from the *ṛṣis* included in one's own *pravara*. "Dharma" refers to the treatises on law (*dharma-śāstra*). "Specialized knowledge" is the knowledge of systems such as Vaiśeṣika. "Tradition" is the non-forgetting of the Vedas and other sacred texts. "Observance of minor vows" is the practice of eating only one meal a day on the tenth lunar day and other such occasions. Viṣṇu also [says]:
[156] Those who are patient and self-controlled, whose throats are filled with sacred learning, who have conquered their senses and desisted from killing living beings,
and whose hands are restrained from accepting gifts—
"Those Brahmins are capable of delivering [others].
Thus it is said; and also in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"One who knows the meaning, a knower of the Vedas, a performer of sacrificial sessions (*satrin*), one whose lineage is known, and one endowed with noble birth."
He was a knower of the Purāṇas, omniscient, and devoted to the private recitation and chanting of the Vedas.
“A devotee of Śiva, one devoted to the ancestors, a devotee of the Sun, or a Vaiṣṇava;
one who is devoted to Brahman, a knower of yoga, tranquil, self-conquered, and virtuous”—the ellipsis here is that such persons “should be appointed at the śrāddha. Manu also says:
A Brahmin who is well-restrained, even if his essence consists only of the Gāyatrī,
is better than one who is unrestrained, though he may know the four Vedas, eat all things, and sell all things.
Matsya also says:
One should employ a person devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī in offerings to the gods and ancestors;
sin does not remain in him, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.
Vyāsa also says: "O King,
those who have observed their vows, who are described as virtuous,
who are cultivators, who know the Sāvitrī, and who are observant of sacred rites— they are worthy of being invited."
O bull of the Bharatas, he who recites the Sāvitrī twice daily,
subsisting on alms and performing his duties, is worthy of being invited as a guest, O King.
An invitation (*ketana*) is an act of summoning. "Worthy" (*kṣama*) means suitable; it also implies self-restraint (*yama*).
[157] One should examine the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas even beforehand—those who are purified from defects arising from the body and who have observed their vows.

"Even before the invitation" means prior to the formal invitation. [He should invite] those who have completed their vows, the *snātakas*. And so says that same [author]: "A householder, a student (*brahmacārī*), and one who knows the *Yajurveda*—a Brāhmaṇa who has bathed after completing his Vedic study and vows is a purifier of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*)."

By the word *ca* (and), the ascetic (*yati*) is also mentioned. And it has been stated directly by Vasiṣṭha: "Ascetics, householders, or those with wives"—the ellipsis being "one should feed them. Also in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "One should cause [food] to be given to those with topknots (*śikhin*), to those dyed with mineral pigments (*dhāturuakta*), and to triple-staffed ascetics (*tridaṇḍin*). Here, "those with topknots" refers to celibate students (*brahmacārin*); "those dyed with mineral pigments" refers to forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) who wear garments dyed with mineral pigments. Among these, each subsequent one is superior. For this very reason, Nārada says:
If one who knows the truth should, out of disrespect for ascetics, feed other twice-born men while they are residing in his village, that offering to the ancestors goes to the Rākṣasas.

The meaning is this: even if one knows that ascetics (*yatis*) are residing in one’s own village, if one disregards them and feeds other twice-born men such as forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) and so forth, then that *kavya*—the food and other offerings intended for the ancestors—goes only to the *rākṣasas*. Therefore, when possible, one should feed the ascetics; in their absence, the forest-dwellers; in their absence, the celibate students (*brahmacārins*); and in their absence, the householders (*gṛhasthas*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "In the absence of meditating mendicants, one should feed a celibate student."
Indeed, if these are unavailable, one may feed even a neutral householder.

A *dhyānī* is a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who possesses meditative concentration; a *bhikṣu* is an ascetic (*yati*). An *udāsīna* is one who has no connection with the donor. And so says Āpastamba: "One should feed Brāhmaṇas who know the Brahman, provided they are not related by birth, lineage, mantra, or pupilage. By "related by birth" are meant maternal uncles and the like; by "related by lineage" are meant sapinda-relatives and the like; by "related by mantra" are meant Vedic teachers and the like; and by "related by pupilage" are meant disciples, fellow students, and sub-teachers. One should feed Brāhmaṇas who are householders and free from such connections. The meaning is that one should diligently feed those Brāhmaṇas who possess knowledge of the Brahman. And so [runs] the verse of the ancestors (*pitṛgāthā*).
There may be such a being in this world who would diligently feed a yogi—a brahmin—at a śrāddha ceremony; by him we are satisfied.

By the phrase "one should feed with effort," the supreme excellence of the yogin is stated. And this has been very clearly stated in the Purāṇa: "A yogin excels over a thousand householders, a hundred forest-dwellers, and a thousand celibate students."
Also in the Padma Purāṇa:
"He who has studied the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, who is refined and knows their meaning,
and who is purified in birth, speech, and action— he is considered the foremost [guest] at a Śrāddha."
A man who has taken refuge in yoga is superior to ten thousand such [others].
Vṛddha-Śātātapa also says:
"One should always feed a wise yogin who has perceived reality."
There is no doubt that what is given to them becomes inexhaustible.

The meaning is that those who correctly observe the conduct of their caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) are the supreme recipients, as stated in the first half of that [verse]. This is merely a praise of yogins, because Śātātapa specifies [the recipient] as "one who has seen reality and is wise";
for those who are always established in right conduct, who possess knowledge, and likewise practice meditation—

Thus, because the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* declares that only those who are established in their conduct—whether they be possessors of knowledge (*jñānin*) or practitioners of meditation (*dhyāyin*)—are worthy of being fed: "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the discernment of the true nature of the Self and so forth; "meditation" (*dhyāna*), however, is the direct realization of the nature of the Self and so forth, through the setting aside of all other cognitions. And so it has been said by Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
"In whosever house a man of knowledge eats, or even if he drinks water, whatever duty was to be performed here has been fulfilled by him, and three lineages have been delivered."
If one should bypass a yogin and feed a householder instead, one does not obtain the fruit of that act; rather, one causes even a resident of heaven to fall.
But if they bypass the yogin and honor one another instead,
then the eaters as well as the givers, along with their kinsmen, shall dwell in hell.
All this should be understood as referring to a yogin who abides in his conduct and has perceived reality. Regarding this, Manu says:
"If any one of these, being honored, should eat at someone's *śrāddha*, the satisfaction of that person's ancestors shall be eternal for seven generations."
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*;
however, this secondary rule (*anukalpa*) should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.

"One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister's son, the father-in-law, the teacher, the daughter's son, the husband of a sister, a relative, as well as the officiating priest and the one for whom he performs sacrifices."

Among these previously mentioned individuals, such as those who have mastered the Vedas and so forth, this distinct group of Brahmins is the first and most excellent. It is a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*), an inferior option compared to the primary one (*prathamakalpa*), according to the definition of Amarasiṃha: "The primary option should be the first; the secondary alternative is inferior to that. This inferior option, which will be described by the words "the maternal grandfather and the maternal uncle," etc., is the sense of what has been "always practiced by the virtuous. Here, "preceptor" (*guru*) refers to the teacher of knowledge (*vidyāguru*) and not the father, according to Devasvāmin’s statement: "The husband of a sister, the son-in-law, or the guest [is meant]; others say it is the guest. He himself states the fault in performing a secondary alternative when the primary option is available.
The master of the primary rule who conducts himself by means of a secondary rule—
no fruit pertaining to the next world exists for that person of evil intellect.

The Lord is capable of accomplishing [this]. *Sāmparāya* refers to the subsequent time; for Amarasimha states, "In the words *sāmparāya*, it means battle or the future. Thus, the meaning is this: in the future (*sāmparāye*), such fruits as heaven and the like do not exist—that is, they are not attained. An alternative practice (*anukalpa*) is also stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:

"One should honor with offerings to the gods and ancestors (*havya-kavya*) paternal uncles, preceptors, daughters' sons, officiating priests, sisters' sons, maternal uncles, elders, and those who are not distant kinsmen."

[161] A sister’s son (*svasrīya*) is a nephew (*bhāgineya*). In this context, one should honor the paternal uncle (*pitṛvya*) and the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) with *havya* (offerings to the gods); the connection should be made that others, such as the teacher’s daughter’s son (*gurudauhitrādi*), are to be honored with *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors). This is because Atri prohibits the honoring with *kavya* of those within six generations prior, such as the paternal uncle, stating: "But those of the same lineage (*gotrin*) who are within six generations are not fit for the *śrāddha*. Likewise:
"The father, grandfather, brother, or even a sapinda relative—these should not offer the *arghya* to one another; likewise, officiating priests are not [to be honored] at a *śrāddha*."
For these—the officiating priest, the son, and so forth—are Brahmins of the same lineage;
they should be appointed at the Vaiśvadeva rite if they are more distinguished by their qualities.

This is because the eligibility for worship with the *havya* (offering) is prescribed by that very same [text]. Furthermore, Kātyāyana has stated under the rule *yady āmantrayīta* ("if he should invite"): "In the absence [of others], [one may invite] students or one's own teachers. Here too, the phrase "for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*" is to be understood as the ellipsis. For Āpastamba, after stating, "If those possessing [excellent] qualities are unavailable, even a uterine brother (*sodarya*) should be fed," immediately adds: "By this, students (*antevāsinaḥ*) are explained. It has already been established that even a uterine brother is to be fed in the place of the *vaiśvadeva*, but not in the place of the Brahmins representing the ancestors and so forth. Therefore, students also are prohibited from occupying that specific place. As for what Bodhāyana stated after describing those who sanctify the row (*paṅktipāvana*), namely: "In their absence, one should feed a *sapiṇḍa*—even if he knows the secret *ṛc*s, *yajus* verses, and *sāmans*, and the greatness of the *śrāddha*—provided he possesses such knowledge," this also refers to a *sapiṇḍa* who is within six generations, in accordance with the statement of Atri; it does not refer to a *sapiṇḍa* who is more remote than that. Rather, it refers to a *samānodaka* (a kinsman connected by water-libations), since the term *sapiṇḍa* can be used figuratively for a *samānodaka*. This was indeed stated explicitly by Atri.
"But beyond six, even those belonging to the same lineage (*gotra*) may be fed at the *śrāddha*.

Alternatively, let the word *sapiṇḍa* be taken in its primary sense; however, the meaning should be understood as follows: in the absence of a superior *samānodaka* (distant relative), one should feed that superior *sapiṇḍa* who stands beyond the three *sapiṇḍa* persons. And thus, with the term *sapiṇḍa* recurring, Gautama states: "One should feed a virtuous person beyond the three. Manu, however, mentions another secondary option (*anukalpa*).
"One may, if one wishes, honor a friend at a *śrāddha*, even if he is not learned, but never an enemy; for an oblation consumed by one who hates becomes fruitless after death.

The phrase "even if he is not learned" means "even if he is a scholar (*abhirūpa*). Because of the use of the word "if one wishes" (*kāmaṃ*), it is understood that this is a secondary option (*anukalpa*). This secondary option, however, is to be understood as applicable only in the absence of the previously mentioned secondary options.
One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*; rather, one should win him over with wealth.
That twice-born man whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend—one should feed him at the *śrāddha*.
For one whose śrāddha rites and sacrificial oblations are dominated by friends,
there is no fruit after death for those śrāddhas or those oblations.

Thus, because a friend who has been prohibited by [the author] himself through a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is subsequently accepted as an alternative through the statement, "One may, at will, honor a friend at a *śrāddha*," it is understood that such a person is inferior even to other secondary options (*anukalpa*). Vasiṣṭha also states that when secondary options involving those with qualities are unavailable, one should accept those without qualities as secondary options: "Compassion is the highest duty; whatever is given to one who asks should be given.
To those who do not ask but are suffering, one should invite them by all possible means."

Compassion (*ānṛśaṃsya*) is the supreme, most excellent dharma. By that [principle], even in the absence of qualified substitutes (*anukalpa*), whatever is given to one who asks—even if they lack qualities—constitutes a substitute. Regarding those who do not ask but are suffering, and who suffer precisely because of their habit of not asking: even if they lack qualities, since qualified substitutes are unavailable, the meaning is that one should invite them by all possible means—by whatever means they will accept the invitation. By stating "one should invite by all possible means," he expresses that the invitation must be made with earnestness; thus he shows that when those who do not ask are suffering due to lack of gain, one should give even when asked. He says the same thing to show that one should not utter reproach toward such Brahmins, even when observing a deficiency in their virtuous conduct.
Whatever duties exist in each respective age, and whatever twice-born ones exist in those duties—
one must not criticize them, for those twice-born ones conform to the nature of the age.

In every age, however, those dharmas which are appropriate to that age—whether they be untruthful speech and other such evil natures based on the varying degrees of passion, hatred, and so forth—one must not censure the twice-born who practice them. Even among the Brahmins suited to a particular age, one should accept only those who are excellent as far as possible. For this very reason, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states that those Brahmins who are unworthy are not to be accepted for gifts and other rites: "Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and abandoned by the duty of hospitality—all those should be known as *vṛṣalas*, even if they have acquired the Vedas."
