"O Lord of the People, he who possesses neither the Veda, nor the recitation [of mantras], nor sacred knowledge, should be regarded as a Śūdra; so said the Blessed, All-pervading Lord."
O Bhārata, one should not accept gifts from those who are without vows, without mantras, and devoid of compassion; nor should one strike a stone with a stone.
There is no transgression against a Brahmin who is a fool and devoid of the Vedas;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire.

The mention of the *vaiśvadeva* is intended as an illustration for the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). "From stone to stone" means that even when one fails to provide food and other offerings to a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of Vedic knowledge, there is no transgression against a Brāhmaṇa; this refers to a Brāhmaṇa with whom one has absolutely no connection. Regarding a Brāhmaṇa with whom one has some connection, it is stated in that very same place: "A Brāhmaṇa who possesses the essence of the Gāyatrī alone has attained honor;
he does not become fallen merely because he dwells in a cave."

A "neighbor" (*prātiveśya*) is one who dwells near the house. By using the word "especially," [the author] shows that even if one has some slight connection, such a person must not be bypassed. Regarding the bypassing of a superior neighbor, a fault is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"He who bypasses a nearby Brāhmaṇa who is studying, whether in a meal or in a gift, destroys his family for three generations."
One who is physically near but unlearned incurs no fault even if he is bypassed. And so it is said in that very same place:

"If there is a fool in one's own house and a man endowed with virtues resides far away, the gift should be given to the one endowed with virtues; there is no transgression in this regard toward the fool."

The meaning is that there is no transgression, nor any fault of transgression. The mention of a "fool" (mūrkha) is intended as an illustration for one who is devoid of merit (*nirguṇa*), because it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "There is never any fault for the transgressor with respect to one who is devoid of merit. Furthermore, as for what has been stated in another *Purāṇa*:
But that fool who, bypassing a Brahmin standing nearby— provided he is not an outcast—
should instead feed one who is far away though rich in virtues, shall go to hell.
Therefore, one should honor him and not consider his virtues;
one should always consider only his birth and never his possession of good qualities.
But if one [approaches] a nearby twice-born man who is of suitable caste and speaks kindly—
even if he be a fool, or an outcast, or even devoid of good conduct—
A wise man should not transgress against one who is likewise afflicted by poverty.

Thus, that [statement] regarding the body mentioned as a secondary option (*anukalpa*) refers to those who are proximate by blood relation, such as a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) or a son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*). However, what was stated previously refers to those who are proximate by location, such as a neighbor (*prātiveśya*) and so forth; therefore, there is no contradiction. For this very reason, having cited one who is proximate by blood relation as an example, Manu has said: "One should feed even a daughter’s son who is observing a vow at a *śrāddha*."

"Established in a vow" means standing merely in the vow, that is to say, devoid of Vedic study. Even regarding the two types of proximate objects, if one passes over a superior person on account of qualities and so forth, a fault certainly occurs. This too has been stated in the Purāṇa:
"O Bird, by passing over an excellent twice-born man, one causes seven ancestors, seven descendants, and oneself as well, to fall into hell."
Therefore, a wise man should not bypass his neighboring Brahmins,
nor any of his relatives, nor his daughter's son, nor his brother-in-law.
O Lord of Birds, O Lord of Cows, a man should especially not bypass his sister’s son nor his other kinsmen,
even if they are not wise.
"Having bypassed it, one would go to the most terrible Raurava hell.
Here, the word "api" (even) in the phrase "even those who are not fools" is for the purpose of completing the meter.
[166] One whose family and name are unknown, who has arrived at that very moment—
A hungry person who has arrived for a śrāddha ceremony, being destitute and begging for alms.
They call a Brahmin a guest...

Even a Brahmin who is characterized by the aforementioned definition of a guest must not be bypassed; for the Smṛti of Śātātapa states: "That Śrāddha is not praised in which the guest does not eat. Furthermore, one should not examine the qualities or learning of a guest who has arrived, just as one would not do so for one who is already present. Thus says the Purāṇa.
A wise man should never examine an unknown Brahmin at a śrāddha;
for perfected beings (siddhas) wander here upon the earth in the form of Brahmins.
"Unknown" means a guest whose family, name, and so forth are not known; "perfected ones" (siddhas) refers to those who have realized the true nature of the self.
Thus concludes the section on the description of Brāhmaṇas fit for the Śrāddha meal in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, among those Brāhmaṇas such as the *Śrotriya* who have been declared fit for the meal, those who are to be avoided due to the presence of defects are described.
On this point, Manu says:
"Those who are thieves, those who are outcasts, those who are eunuchs, and those who follow the lifestyle of atheists—
Manu has declared these Brahmins to be unworthy of offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya)."
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who have matted hair but do not study the Vedas, nor those with shaggy hair, nor gamblers, nor those who officiate as priests for large groups.
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers,
and those who live by trade— these should be avoided at offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth,
one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer;

One afflicted by consumption, a cattle-herder, one who marries before his elder brother, one who has been expelled from the Veda, a hater of Brahmins, an elder brother whose younger brother has married before him, and one who belongs to a social guild— these are excluded.
One who is of bad character, one who has broken his vows, the husband of a low-caste woman,
the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour— these are excluded.
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught for a fee,
one whose pupil is a Śūdra, one whose teacher is a Śūdra, one of foul speech, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka.
One who has abandoned mother, father, or teacher without cause;
and one who has entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial connections.
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats from a vessel made of a human skull, a seller of Soma,
one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger;
One who quarrels with his father, one who squints, a drunkard,
one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids (or flavors).
One who performs abortions, one who is the husband of an agredidhiṣū,
a betrayer of friends, one who lives by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher of his own son;
One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one with leucoderma, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and likewise a reviler of the Vedas— these should be avoided.
One who trains elephants, horses, or camels; one who lives by means of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras);
one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare.
He who damns the watercourses and delights in obstructing them,
he who constructs houses, acts as a messenger, and likewise plants trees;
One who sports with dogs, one who lives by falcons, a defiler of maidens,
a violent man, the son of a Śūdra, and a priest for the Gaṇas.
One devoid of proper conduct, a eunuch, a constant beggar,
one who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis, and one censured by the virtuous— these are likewise [excluded].
One who raises sheep, one who raises buffalo, a husband of a woman previously married to another, and a carrier of corpses— these must be avoided with great effort.
"A learned man, the best among the twice-born, should avoid both here and hereafter those of censurable conduct, those unworthy of sitting in the row for meals, and the lowest of men.

Regarding this, whatever is to be understood through explanation shall now be explained. "Thieves" (*stenāḥ*) are those who steal property other than the gold of a Brāhmaṇa; for the avoidance of those who steal the gold of a Brāhmaṇa is already expressed by the term "outcastes" (*patita*). Alternatively, "thieves" may refer to those who abandon their own duties.

"Those who have strayed from their own duties are proclaimed to be thieves," according to the traditional teaching of Yama. "The fallen" (patita) refers to those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātakin). As for the impotent (klība), Devala has shown that they are of six kinds:
the eunuch (ṣaṇḍaka), the one born of wind (vātaja), the ṣaṇḍa, the klība, and the neuter (napuṃsaka).
And the *kīlaka*; thus, this sixfold classification of the neuter has been explained.
He himself shows the characteristics of the *ṣaṇḍaka* and others:
"Among them, one who has speech and gestures equal to a woman and possesses female characteristics is a *ṣaṇḍaka*.
Likewise, one who, having been a man, subsequently cuts off his own male organs. [169]
A *ṣaṇḍa* may be known by the name *vātaja*, or it may be called *strīṣaṇḍa* by name;
furthermore, a *ṣaṇḍa* may be one who lacks sexual organs, while a *ṣaṇḍa* is also characterized by a flaccid penis.
A man who eats impure things, is impotent, or has lost his virility is a eunuch;
he should not be known as a *kīlaka* (a pillar-like husband) who, due to his own impotence, approaches his wife.

"Having associated with another, he later resorts to that very [person]. Those who hold such views as "there is no karma that yields fruit in another world" and "there is no deity," etc., are the *nāstikas* (atheists). Those for whom their livelihood (*vṛtti*)—that is, their means of subsistence—is dependent on such *nāstikas*, such as Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) and others, are those of "atheistic livelihood" (*nāstikavṛtti*). A *jaṭila* is a religious student (*brahmacārī*) who is "unlearned," meaning devoid of Vedic study. Now, one might object: since an unlearned *jaṭila* is already included among those who are not Vedic scholars (*aśrotriya*), his exclusion here is redundant. It is replied: "One should take care to feed even a daughter's son (*dauhitra*) at a *śrāddha*, even if he is engaged in a vow."

By this [verse], the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) and the religious student (*brahmacārī*) who remains merely under his vow (*vratamātrasthaḥ*), even if he does not study, are declared to be among those to be fed as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) among the Brāhmaṇas to be fed. In that regard, the mention of the "daughter’s son" is not intended as a restrictive rule (*atantra*); rather, it is prohibited here because it might somehow be included through error. Thus, it is not entirely redundant. Some say: "It is for the purpose of including a householder who does not study and is not a *śrotriya*. That is incorrect, for [the text states]:

"One should feed with offerings to gods and ancestors (*havya-kavya*) those householders who are *śrotriyas* and have completed their Vedic studies and vows (*vedavidyāvratasnāta*); but one should avoid those who are the opposite."

Since it is impossible for a householder—who has been specifically mentioned as one to be avoided—to be included here, the term *durvāla* refers to a rogue (*khalyāṭaka*) or one with tawny hair (*kapilakeśa*), or one who is excessively prone to anger. All of this has been stated by the author of the *Saṃgraha*: "One should not feed a foolish religious student (*brahmacārin*) who, though wearing matted locks, is accepted [as such] solely on the basis of the quality of having completed his Vedic studies."
Just as in the case of a daughter's son and others, what is obtained here through error is prohibited;
others, however, understand this to be for the purpose of obtaining such a householder.

Therefore, it is not correct [to say] that "the ignorant householder, as well as the *kalvāṭaka*, the *durvāla*, the *kapila*, or even the *caṇḍa* [are excluded]. Here, "priests for groups" (*pūgayājaka*) refers to those who perform sacrifices for many people individually. The mention of the *śrāddha* here is for the purpose of permitting [the participation of these individuals] in rites for the gods (*daiva*). If, however, its purpose were merely to indicate [their exclusion] from rites for the gods, it would be entirely redundant; for by considering the preceding and following context alone, the prohibition regarding both rites for the gods and the ancestors (*pitrya*) is already understood. For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* says:
Gautama also states in his Sūtra that the Durvāla and others [are included] specifically in the Śrāddha rite.

The phrase “as the opinion of Manu and others” is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Thus, Gautama states in the section on the examination of Brāhmaṇas: “In the case of sacrificial offerings (*havis*), one should likewise [examine] those such as Durvāla; some say this applies only to the *śrāddha*. This means that regarding sacrificial offerings, even for the gods (*daiva*), one should examine them just as for the ancestors (*pitrya*) and avoid those such as Durvāla. However, some—namely Manu and others—hold the view that one should not feed those such as Durvāla at a rite for the ancestors, but not necessarily even at a rite for the gods. Physicians are those who practice for the sake of livelihood or for the sake of dharma. For in the Taittirīya Śruti, there is seen a censure of physicians without distinction: “Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not act as a physician, for he who is a physician is impure and unholy. The nature of the temple-priest (*devalaka*) has been shown by Devala.
A Brahmin who, desiring wealth, is devoted to the worship of gods for three years is indeed called a *devalaka*; he is censured in rites for the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
"One who lives off the treasury of the gods shall be known by the name *devalaka*;
he is to be understood as one excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅkteya*) for all ritual acts at all times. Thus it is said.

*Vipaṇa* means trade; even those Brāhmaṇas who live by it during times of distress are called *vipaṇajīvins*. The repeated prohibition of one who sells meat—even though living by trade is already forbidden—is intended to demonstrate that such a person must be avoided absolutely. By this, it is understood that those who sell their Vedic learning (*śrotriya*) and so forth may be accepted as secondary options (*anukalpa*). Alternatively, those who sell meat are to be avoided even in times of distress. A *preṣya* is a servant. A *kunakhī* is one whose nails are naturally decayed. A *śyāvadanta* is one whose teeth are naturally black. The prohibition against these two is based solely on the connection to the remnants of past actions. One who opposes or rivals his teacher is a *guru-pratiroddhā*. One who has abandoned the sacred fires (*tyaktāgni*) is one who has given up the fires prescribed by the scriptures (*śrauta* and *smārta*) without a scripturally sanctioned reason. A *vārdhuṣika* is one who, having taken money at a small rate of interest, lends it to another at a higher rate; or one who buys goods for a low price and seeks to realize a high profit through their sale. Thus says the Smṛti: [text follows].
He who, having extracted wealth at a low price, gives it back at a high price,
is indeed called a usurer and is censured by those who discourse on the Veda.
He who, having taken merchandise at a low price, gives it back at a high price,
is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who speak the Veda.

A *yakṣmī* is one afflicted with consumption (*kṣayaroga*). A *paśupāla* is a Brāhmaṇa who, when not in times of distress, subsists by the profession of cattle-herding. The definitions of the *parivettṛ* (the younger brother who marries before the elder) and the *parivitti* (the elder brother so superseded) have been shown by Manu himself:

"He who enters into the bond of marriage and the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried and unestablished] is to be known as the *parivettṛ*; the elder brother is the *parivitti*. (MDh 3.172)

By the term *agnihotra*, the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) to be performed prior to the subsequent sacrifices such as the *agnihotra* is meant. And this has been stated directly by Garga: "While a full brother exists who is senior [in age], one should not perform the taking of a wife, nor the *āvasathya* [fire-consecration]; otherwise, he would become fallen."

The *āvasathya* is the establishment of the *āvasathya* fire; that is to say, the establishment of the *aupāsana* fire performed at the time of the partition of inheritance, as well as the *aupāsana* fire established at the time of marriage—both of which are excluded by the very statement, "One should not take a wife [if one has a younger brother who marries before him]. Therefore:
"One who is superseding [his younger brother] should establish the *aupāsana* fire at its proper time."

Thus, even in the statement of Brahmagarbha, it should be understood that by the term "his own time" (svakāla), the time for the partition of inheritance is meant, and not the time of marriage. "Laying of the fires" (ādhāna) refers to the establishment of the Gārhapatya and other sacred fires. "He would become fallen" means he would become guilty of a minor offense (upapātakin); this is because both the younger brother who marries before his elder (parivettṛ) and the elder brother so superseded (parivitti) are mentioned in the enumeration of minor offenses. From the mention of the "uterine" (sodarya) brother, it is understood that if the non-uterine elder brother remains unmarried, there is no fault of falling from caste even if the younger brother takes a wife or performs other rites. However, Śātātapa has explicitly stated the absence of fault regarding the case of a non-uterine brother.

"The sons of a father by different wives, as well as the sons of another man's wife, are not at fault in the act of *parivedana* (ceding the right of primogeniture) when it concerns the union with a wife and the *agnihotra* fire-sacrifice. Thus [it is said].

"Sāpatnas" are brothers born of different mothers. "Sons of another man's wife" refers to those begotten by one's own father upon the wife of another, who are thus *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas* (belonging to two lineages). The meaning is that even when elder paternal uncles and others remain without having entered into marriage or established the *agnihotra*, if a younger brother does enter into marriage and establish the *agnihotra*, there is no fault of *parivedana* (marrying before an elder). The mention of "sons of another man's wife" is intended to include by extension the *dattaputra* (given son) and others as well. For this very reason, Yama says: "Paternal uncles' sons, sons of co-wives, and likewise the sons of others..."
There is no unrighteousness for one who marries again while his wife, the sacred fires, and religious duties [are still present].

Sons born of others—those who have attained the status of being one’s own father’s sons through gift, purchase, or other means—are considered brothers. Regarding the practice of *parivedana* (marrying before an elder brother), Śātātapa states that there is no fault in certain cases while a uterine elder brother remains unmarried and uninvested with the *agnihotra*: "In the case of a brother who is impotent, residing in another country, fallen from grace, addicted to intoxicants, or devoted to the practice of *yoga*, there is no fault in marrying before him."

A mendicant, a wandering ascetic, one devoted to the science of Yoga, and one who is dispassionate— these are also [excluded], as is Kātyāyana. Likewise, those residing in another country, a eunuch, one with only one testicle, uterine brothers,
those excessively attached to prostitutes, the fallen, those equal to Śūdras, and those who are severely ill.
Those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, hunchbacked, dwarfish, or lame; those who are very old, those who are without wives, those devoted to agriculture, and the king’s [servants].
One incurs no fault by marrying those who are addicted to the increase of wealth, those who act out of lust, as well as deceivers, the insane, or thieves.

A *khoḍaka* is one whose two feet are broken. "Those without wives" refers to perpetual celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*). "Those who act out of desire" are those who have voluntarily desisted from marriage. In this context, there is no fault of superseding (*parivedana*) even without waiting for the [prescribed] time in the case of those such as eunuchs (*klība*) and others who are ineligible for marriage. However, for those who are eligible for marriage—such as those living in another country, those who are detached, those excessively attached to prostitutes, those equal to Śūdras, the very aged, those devoted to agriculture, those intent on increasing royal wealth, those who act out of desire, and deceivers or thieves—there is no fault in superseding [the elder brother] after waiting for the appropriate time. Regarding that, Vasiṣṭha states that in the case of one living in another country, a period of eight years or more must be waited: "If one does not wait for his elder brother for eight, ten, or twelve years while he has not yet married, he becomes liable to penance. The intention is that since one who has gone to another country may still have the possibility of marrying and so forth. "Not yet married" (*aniviṣṭa*) means one who has not performed the marriage ceremony. In this matter, the waiting of twelve years should be understood to apply when the elder brother has gone abroad for the sake of dharma or wealth. And thus says the Smṛti:
Indeed, it is right to wait for twelve years for an elder brother who has departed for the sake of dharma and wealth,
provided he is heard from again and again.

“Brother” means a uterine brother. The phrase “for the sake of dharma and artha” is intended to indicate *vidyā* (learning) as well. Therefore, Gautama, having introduced the topic with “When the husband has disappeared,” and having stated the period for a wife to wait for her husband—“twelve years for a Brāhmaṇa, on account of his connection to learning”—he says: “And likewise for a younger brother regarding an elder brother, in the matters of taking a bride and establishing the sacred fires. “When the husband has disappeared” means when he is gone and unknown where he is, that is to say, when he has gone to a very distant land. “Twelve years for a Brāhmaṇa, on account of his connection to learning” means that if the Brāhmaṇa husband has gone abroad for the purpose of acquiring knowledge, the wife must wait for twelve years. Regarding “for a brother”: if the elder brother has gone abroad for the purpose of learning while remaining unmarried or without having established the sacred fires, the younger brother may, after waiting twelve years, proceed to take a bride and establish the fires. However, in the case of one who has gone abroad for some other business, there are two options: eight or ten years. What is intended here is this: if a man who has gone abroad does not return even when the time is suitable for him to complete his desired task and return, and because of the uncertainty regarding his continued existence in this world, the possibility of his marriage is extinguished, then marrying [another] is not a cause of fault. In the same way, in cases such as those who are detached from worldly life or excessively attached to courtesans, since their respective dispositions persist for a long time—such as twelve years or more—and the possibility of marriage is extinguished, it should be understood that marrying [another] is not a cause of fault. With this very intention, Sumantu also said: [Sumantu’s statement follows.]
Whether the elder brother is one whose mind is addicted to vice or is an atheist,
the younger brother who desires to practice Dharma may then perform the fire-consecration ceremony (ādhāna).

The mention of *ādhāna* (the consecration of the sacred fires) is intended as an illustration for marriage as well. However, brothers who are eunuchs (*klība*) and so forth need not be waited for even for a short time, because they lack the qualification for marriage and other rites by their very nature. Thus says the Smṛti: "One who is insane, a criminal, a leper, an outcast (*patita*), a eunuch, or one afflicted with consumption (*rājayakṣman*)—it is not right to wait for such persons."
"There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] who is lame, dwarfed, humpbacked, stammering, dull-witted, born blind, deaf, or mute.
Thus, even when the eldest brother is eligible for the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires), there is no fault in superseding him with his consent. And so says Vṛddhavariṣṭha:
And when the elder brother has not established the sacred fires, how may the younger brother do so?
Having obtained the permission of the elder brother, he may perform the Agnihotra according to the prescribed rule.

The meaning is that even when the elder brother—who is eligible for the *ādhāna*—remains his entire life without having established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) by transgressing the injunctions for *ādhāna* and so forth, the younger brother may perform the *ādhāna* after obtaining his permission. This very point was also stated by Sumantu:
"As long as the elder brother remains, one should not have the *ādhāna* performed;
however, having obtained his permission, one may do so, according to the word of Śaṅkha."
The mention of the "elder brother" is intended to indicate the father as well; and thus that same [author] says:
"If a father has not performed the establishment of the sacred fires, how may his son cause them to be established?
He possesses the entitlement to the Agnihotra, according to the statement of Śaṅkha."
The mention of the "father" (pitṛ) is intended to indicate the grandfather as well. For this very reason, Uśanas states:
"If one's father, grandfather, or someone else who is senior [is alive], there is no fault in superseding [the elder] regarding asceticism, the *agnihotra*, or the sacred mantras."

This statement should also be understood as applying to the same subject matter previously mentioned, provided that permission has been granted. The word *mantra* is intended to indicate the Vedas. And so Śātātapa says: "Neither sacred fires, nor the Vedas, nor austerities, nor the *śrāddha* rite belong to the younger brother who marries before his elder; likewise, a girl who is deformed [is not to be married]."

Just as, with respect to the Vedas, austerities, and *śrāddha* rites, even if the eldest brother remains devoid of Vedic study, austerity, or the performance of *śrāddha*, the younger brother’s performance of them—even without the elder’s permission—does not constitute the cause for *parivedana* (the sin of superseding), so too the fires established by the younger brother with the permission of the elder and others do not incur such a fault. The meaning of the verse, “And the maiden who is deformed” (*yā ca kanyā virūpikā*), is this: when the eldest daughter, who is eligible for marriage, remains unmarried and deformed, a marriage performed by the younger sister—even without the elder’s permission—is not a defect, provided it is done out of fear that the proper time for marriage would otherwise pass. Thus, in cases other than those specified here, regarding daughters as well, everything stated concerning the superseding of a groom (*varaparivedana*) should be applied. However, Hārīta states that for a younger brother, there is a defect in marriage even with the permission of his elder brother.
But how can one become a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother) among all his uterine brothers?
They are superseded by means of wives, but not by the *agnihotra* fire or by sacrifice.

The statement, "But they are superseded by means of wives," refers to a case involving a uterine brother who has been authorized by the eldest brother acting as the qualified person for marriage and other rites. However, Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya states that even the eldest brother may sometimes become a *parivetta* (one who supersedes) through the performance of the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires):
"He who proceeds with the *tretā* fires while disregarding the *āvasathya* fire becomes one who has not established the sacred fires; he is likewise called a *parivetta*."

The meaning is this: just as at the time of the partition of inheritance, he for whom the establishment of the *aupāsana* fire is prescribed by his own *gṛhya-sūtra* becomes one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) if, without performing that, he performs the cooking of the *brahmaudana* with fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*) and then establishes the *gārhapatya* and other fires; because at the first establishment of the fires, the cooking of the *brahmaudana* with fire produced by friction is not the scriptural requirement, and thus the worldly consecration denoted by the terms *gārhapatya* and so forth does not arise. And likewise, because one performs the establishment of the *gārhapatya* and other fires without having first established the *aupāsana* fire which is to be established first, he is also called a "one who has superseded" (*parivettṛ*). Enough, then, with this elaborate explanation of the meanings of the words *parivettṛ* and *parivitti*.
The meaning of the term *nirākṛti* has been shown by Devala:
"A Brahmin who has forgotten the Veda after having studied it becomes a *nirākṛti*.
Kātyāyana, however, explains the meaning of the term *nirākṛti* differently.
"But he who, having established the sacred fires, fails out of laziness to offer sacrifices here to the gods and others—he who rejects the gods and so forth—is to be known as a *nirākṛti*.

A *brahmadviṭ* is one who hates Brāhmaṇas. The term *parivitti*, however, has been explained on the occasion of explaining the term *parivettṛ*. A *gaṇa* is a group of Brāhmaṇas and others who drink liquor; one who belongs to their midst is a *gaṇābhyantara*. A *kuśīlava* is a singer, dancer, and so forth. Devala speaks of the *avakīrṇin*:

"One who has concealed his marks (gūḍhaliṅgin), as well as one who has broken his vow (bhagnavrata), shall be an *avakīrṇin*. Here, "one who has concealed his marks" is one who abandons the marks of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), such as the staff and the girdle. "One who has broken his vow" is one whose celibacy has faltered through sexual intercourse with a woman;
he who, being under a vow, approaches a woman is defined as an *avakīrṇin*.
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Yama. Furthermore, the husband of a *vṛṣalī* has been shown by Devala:
"A barren woman is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*, as is one whose offspring have died;
another is to be known as a *vṛṣalī* who is a maiden that has reached puberty."
But that Brahmin who, weak in knowledge, would marry such a girl,
one should know him to be the husband of a Vṛṣalī, unworthy of receiving offerings at a Śrāddha and excluded from the row of diners.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: one should know that he who marries a girl who has become menstruating while still in the state of maidenhood is unfit for *śrāddha* rites, excluded from the row of diners (*apāṅkteya*), and is a husband of a *vṛṣalī*. Thus, it should be understood that Manu here refers specifically to the husband of a third *vṛṣalī*. A *punarbhū* is a woman married twice; the son begotten upon her by her husband in her second marriage is a *paunarbhava*. A *kāṇa* is one-eyed. Regarding the phrase "he in whose house there is a paramour," Devala has not made this explicit: "A man who, out of delusion, approaches the wife of another is called a *jāra* (paramour)."
He alone should be known as a true kinsman who always dwells in one's home.

A teacher who is hired for wages is a *bhṛtaka* (a hireling); the suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). One who is both a hireling and a teacher is a *bhṛtakādhyāpaka*. A student taught by such a hireling teacher is a *bhṛtakādhyāpita*. These two are offenders of a minor sin (*upapātakin*): the hireling teacher and the one taught by the hireling teacher.
"Both of those two Brahmins have fallen through the buying and selling of their own Vedic study."

This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Devala. "Falling away" (patitau) means those who have committed secondary sins (upapātakin), since these two are also enumerated among the secondary sins. "A Śūdra disciple" (śūdraśiṣyaḥ) refers to one whose disciple is a Śūdra; "the teacher" (guruḥ) is understood to be the one [who has such a disciple], as he is present in the mind [of the speaker]. A "corrupt speaker" (vāgduṣṭaḥ) is shown by Kātyāyana:
"One who utters the sound 'huṃ', laughs, or does anything else that is censured in the world, or who imitates or repeats [such things]—they know that man to be a corrupt speaker."
The Kuṇḍa and Golaka are defined by their own [traditional] mantra:
"Two sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from the wives of others;
the son is a Kuṇḍa if the husband is alive, and a Golaka if the husband is dead."

A son begotten by a husband and a wife who have both become Brāhmaṇas becomes a Brāhmaṇa; however, one begotten by a paramour who is a Brāhmaṇa upon a woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste who is a paramour is not so. Among all the castes, those born in the direct order (*ānulomya*) from wives of equal status whose wombs are intact are to be known as being of that same caste.

Since Manu himself has thus defined the determination of caste (*jāti*), there is no possibility whatsoever for the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*—who are non-Brāhmaṇas—to be included among those whose food should not be eaten at a *śrāddha*. Consequently, the mention of the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* in the rule "the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* are corrupt by speech" would be redundant. To this, the author of the *Saṃgraha* provides the following answer:

"The *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* produced through the practice of *niyoga* are prohibited from the *śrāddha* because they are not Brāhmaṇas; how could there be any [possibility of] their inclusion, since they are born of adultery like Śūdras?"

Although a prohibition is not possible for those born of a *kuṇḍa* and a *golaka*—since, lacking the status of a Brāhmaṇa, they have no entitlement to the *śrāddha* ceremony just like Śūdras—nevertheless, because the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* produced through *niyoga* (authorized appointment) were generated according to the scriptural path despite being born of another's wife, they possess Brāhmaṇahood; thus, the meaning is that those very *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* are prohibited from the *śrāddha* by Manu. This [position] is incorrect, because those produced through *niyoga* are not truly *kuṇḍa* or *golaka*, as they are not born of an "unmarried woman" (*ajā*), and the husband is not an "unmarried man" (*aja*) since he has been duly appointed. Thus says Devala:
"A man who approaches another's wife out of delusion is called a *jāra*.

By the word "out of delusion" (*mohāt*), it is stated that a man who approaches another's wife by legal mandate (*niyoga*) is not a *jāra*. Those born of a non-*jāra* are neither *kuṇḍas* nor *golakas*. And thus says the same author: "A *kuṇḍa* is one born of a *jāra* while the husband is alive; a *golaka* is one born when the husband is dead."

By stating "born of an adulterer" (*jāraja*), he implies that one who is not authorized [to procreate] is neither a *kuṇḍa* nor a *golaka*. However, Bṛhaspati has clearly stated that only those born of an unauthorized union are *kuṇḍas* and *golakas*: "But adultery is unrighteous; from it are born the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*. They are unworthy of invitation at *śrāddha* rites and their food is not to be eaten, as are the other sons such as the *kṣetraja*. [181]

The meaning is that those born from an unrighteous act of adultery are *kuṇḍas* and *golakas* specifically within that [unlawful] caste, and not merely from the act of adultery itself. Therefore, since adultery is not unrighteous when there is a *niyoga*, those born from it are not *kuṇḍas* and *golakas*. Rather, they are simply *kṣetrajas* (sons born of the wife). Consequently, in order to exclude them separately, it was stated: "and likewise the sons born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and so forth.
Thus, the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* produced through *niyoga* are prohibited from the *śrāddha*.

Thus, what was stated by Saṃgrahakāra is indeed incorrect. Therefore, the correct interpretation is stated otherwise: regarding the statement, “Those corrupted by speech are the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*,” the words *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* here function through metaphorical application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) to refer to the *kṣetraja* sons produced by formal appointment (*niyoga*). Among them, the word *kuṇḍa* applies to one born from the wife of another while the husband is alive, due to the commonality of being born from the wife of another during the husband’s lifetime. The word *golaka* applies to a *kṣetraja* son born after the husband has died, due to the commonality of being born from the wife of another after the husband’s death. Since such *kuṇḍas* and *golakas* as described might be considered Brāhmaṇas and thus attain eligibility for the *śrāddha*, the prohibition is meaningful. If this is so, then since the prohibition of the *kṣetraja* son is already established by the aforementioned statement of Bṛhaspati, “...and likewise the sons born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), etc.,” which declares that “adultery is unrighteous,” one must necessarily say that the phrase “the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* are ineligible for the *śrāddha*” is intended to prohibit the primary *kuṇḍas* and *golakas*. But that is incorrect; because the primary *kuṇḍas* and *golakas* are not Brāhmaṇas, they do not qualify like Śūdras, and thus a prohibition would be redundant. It is replied: Since there is no social practice of treating *kuṇḍas* and *golakas* as a distinct caste, people accept them for *śrāddhas* and other rites simply on the basis that they were fathered by a Brāhmaṇa upon a Brāhmaṇa woman, thinking, “This man is a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, for the sake of favoring the ignorant, Bṛhaspati issued a prohibition against those two, even though in reality they do not qualify. Enough with this elaborate discussion on the purpose of the prohibition of *kuṇḍas* and *golakas*.

The meaning of the phrase "one who has abandoned [parents] without cause" is as follows: even when the grounds for abandonment prescribed by the scriptures—such as "one should abandon a father who is a regicide"—are absent, he has nonetheless abandoned his mother, father, or guru. Here, the "guru" refers to the teacher (*ācārya*) and not the father, because the father is already included by the specific term "father. "Abandonment" means the failure to perform service and other duties as prescribed by the scriptures, such as "obeying the commands of those who are living.
He has entered into association with outcasts through spiritual (*brāhma*) or matrimonial (*yauna*) connections.

Thus, the prohibition would be redundant, because in the verse, “Those who are thieves, outcasts (patita), or eunuchs,” the exclusion of the five types of outcasts has already been established by the inclusion of the term *patita*. True; however, this repeated prohibition is not redundant, as its purpose is to acknowledge that one who has entered into a connection with those guilty of minor offenses (*upapātakin*) through Vedic or matrimonial relationships may, under certain circumstances, be fed when there is no other recourse. The author of the *Saṃgraha*, on the other hand, explained the meaning of the verse as prohibiting outcasts other than the five types of outcasts, thereby avoiding the charge of redundancy.

One who has entered into association with those who have fallen— those who are related by ties of Brahmanic or matrimonial kinship, including those who have killed a Brahmin and others, and those who have immediately become outcasts— is himself fallen.

"He who has fallen due to that prohibition is the third one prohibited here. This means: he who has entered into association with those who have become outcasts immediately due to their connection with the slayer of a Brahmin and others—that third person associated with such outcasts is prohibited here; for the outcast mentioned in the statement, "and the fifth is he who associates with them," has already been prohibited previously. [183] However, Devala has shown two kinds of incendiaries: "He is to be known as an incendiary who burns a corpse by means of wealth."
"And he who burns down a house out of hatred shall also be a burner of houses.
Regarding the *kuṇḍāśin*, he is one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* or a *golaka*. And so, having defined the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, Manu himself has stated:
"That twice-born man who eats their food is called a *kuṇḍāśin*."

A *somavikrayī* is a seller of the *soma* creeper. A *samudrayāyī* is one who travels by sea—the word "having boarded a ship" (*vahitram āruhya*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. A *bandī* is a reciter of praises for kings and others. A *tailaka* is one who subsists on the profession of oil-making. A *kūṭakāraka* is a maker of forgeries, such as false documents and the like. One *vivadamānaḥ pitrā* is one who disputes with his father, contending against him in a manner contrary to the traditions of the *smṛtis* and established custom. A *kekara* is one with squinting vision. A *madyapa* is a drinker of intoxicants other than *surā* (grain-liquor), since a drinker of *surā* is already excluded by the term "outcast" (*patita*). A *pāparogī* is one afflicted by any of the diseases specified by Devala as "sinful diseases" (*pāparoga*), namely: insanity, skin diseases, consumption, asthma, diabetes, fistula-in-ano, abdominal dropsy, and urinary stones. An *abhiśasta* is one who has been formally accused in court by someone for having committed a crime. A *dāmbhika* is one who practices hypocrisy in the performance of religious duties. A *rasavikrayī* is a seller of liquids such as alkaline salts and the like. A *kartā dhanuḥśarāṇām* is a maker of bows and arrows. An *agredidhiṣūpati* is the husband of an *agredidhiṣū*. If it is asked, "Who is an *agredidhiṣū*?", Devala [provides the definition]: [Devala's definition follows here.]

"If a younger sister is married while the elder sister remains unmarried, she is to be known as *agredidhiṣū*, while the former is considered *didhiṣū*. (184) *Mitradhruk* means a betrayer of friends. *Dyūtavṛttiḥ* means one who lives by gambling. A *putrācārya* is a teacher of letters for the young householders' sons in a village. Thus says the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
"He who teaches the syllables (*akṣara*) in the village is to be known as a *putrācārya*.

Alternatively, a *putrācārya* is one for whom the son himself is the teacher (*putra evācāryo yasya*). And likewise, that same author [states]: "Or, one who has obtained knowledge from his son is called a *putrācārya*."

The *bhrāmarī* (the bee-like) is one who acquires wealth solely for the sake of his own livelihood, like a bee; and thus it is said: "He who supports his dependents for the sake of his livelihood is indeed a *bhrāmarī*."

*Gaṇḍamālī* is one afflicted with the disease known as *gaṇḍamālā*. *Śvitrī* is one whose skin has become white due to the disease of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). *Piśuna* is one who, by nature or for the sake of livelihood, points out the faults of others. *Unmatta* and the others are well-known. A *poṣaka* of birds is one who keeps them bound for the purpose of sport. A *yuddhācārya* is a teacher of the science of archery (*dhanurveda*). A *bhedaka* of streams is one who leads a current in another direction; and one who is *rata* in their obstruction—that is, one who delights in blocking the path with earth and so forth for the purpose of impeding movement. A *gṛhasaṃveśaka* is one who subsists by the profession of a carpenter. A *dūta* is a messenger who carries a message. A *vṛkṣāropaka* is one who plants trees, the word "having received payment" being understood from the context, since the planting of trees for the sake of merit is prescribed by such scriptural texts as, "One who plants five mango trees does not go to hell. The terms beginning with *śvakrīḍī* (one who plays with dogs) are self-explanatory. A *vṛṣala*, however, has been defined by Manu himself.

"For the Blessed One, Dharma, is indeed a bull; those who commit a transgression against him, the gods know as *vṛṣala* (outcastes). Therefore, one should not destroy the Dharma. [185] Thus it is said.

Enough with this prohibition. Thus, among those who oversee legal proceedings (*vyavahāradraṣṭṛ*), he who causes the obstruction of Dharma is a *vṛṣala*; his son is a *vṛṣalaputra*. And since he is indeed a Brāhmaṇa, it should not be thought that this is a prohibition against one who has not [otherwise] attained [the status]. A priest for groups (*gaṇānāṃ yājakaḥ*) is one who officiates at sacrifices such as the *dvādaśāha* and others involving many sacrificers (*yajamāna*). Accordingly, the Smṛti states: "Therefore, one should not be made to sacrifice with the *dvādaśāha* for the sake of warding off evil. And thus, its non-redundancy with the phrase "and those who cause groups to sacrifice" is established. One devoid of conduct is of bad conduct (*durācāra*). A eunuch (*klība*) is one lacking enthusiasm; even if capable, he is devoid of the performance of the duties of his own stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*)—this is the meaning. And thus, its non-redundancy with the phrase "those who are thieves, outcasts, and eunuchs" is clear. One who is constantly begging is a solicitor (*yācanaka*) even while possessing wealth. A *ślīpadī* is one afflicted by the disease called *ślīpada*, that is to say, one with swollen feet. An *aurabhraka* is one for whom sheep (*urabhra*) or lambs (*avi*) are to be reared solely for the purpose of livelihood. Likewise is a *sāhiṣaka*. Alternatively, a *sāhiṣaka* is the son of an unchaste woman (*vyabhicāriṇī*). As Devala says:
"It is said that a wife who is unchaste is called a *mahiṣī*; the child born of her is indeed known as a *māhiṣaka*.

The meaning is that the son born of her to her own husband is known as a *sāhiṣaka*. A *parapūrvā* is one previously given to another; her husband is a *parapūrvāpati*. A *pretaniryātaka* is one who carries out a corpse for a price. However, [doing so] for the sake of dharma is indeed praiseworthy. When it is asked from which statement this is understood, the author of the *Saṃgraha* [proceeds].
From this it is understood that these are those of censurable conduct:
"Planting trees for the sake of merit, the funeral rites for a deceased person, and [the offering of water]—these are not seen [as obligatory for them].

(186) The meaning is that these individuals, beginning with thieves and outcasts and ending with those who perform funeral rites for such persons, are excluded from both—the *daiva* and the *pitrya* rites. Furthermore, the Brahmins who are to be avoided are also mentioned in the *Brahma Purāṇa*.
Those whose minds are afflicted by fate do not deserve to eat at ancestral rites (śrāddha):
the eunuch, the mute, the one with deformed nails, the bald man, and the one suffering from dental disease.
One with black teeth, a putrid nose, a missing limb, or an extra finger;
one suffering from throat disease, a goiter, cracked limbs, or fever.
"Those who are lame, humpbacked, or dull-witted, as well as others who are chronically ill. Thus:

one with a goitre (*gaḍumān*) is one whose chest and back possess protruding bone structures due to the influence of wind (*vāta*). A lame person (*khañja*) is one whose foot is broken. A humpbacked person (*tūpara*) is one devoid of a beard during the time of youth. A dull person (*manda*) is one who is lazy. Yama also says:
"Not [the food] of one approached by donkeys, nor that of one wearing garments stained with blood."
The ancestors partake of the sacrificial offering from one whose ears extend beyond two finger-breadths.

In the case of ear-piercing, it is forbidden to enlarge the opening by inserting palm leaves or similar objects by more than two finger-breadths (*dvyaṅgula*). Therefore, even one whose ears have been pierced more than two finger-breadths is ineligible. Śaṅkha also states: "Brāhmaṇas who study during forbidden times (*anadhyāya*), who are devoid of purity and proper conduct, and whose bodies are nourished by the food of Śūdras, are defilers of the assembly."
Śātātapa also says:
"The food of those who perform sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with small sacrificial fees must not be eaten; they are proclaimed to be unworthy of the company at a meal."
And those fools who perform that sacrifice with deficient sacrificial fees,
upon death, go to a hell that is a mire of pus and blood.

"With small sacrificial fees" means with those who, out of stinginess regarding their wealth, have accepted a small number of fees from among the various options for the number of cows mentioned in the Sūtras, such as "seven, twenty-one, sixty, one hundred, twelve thousand," and so forth. Āpastamba also says: "But one who plows with indigo and wears indigo-dyed clothes—nothing at all should be given to him, for he is like a Caṇḍāla."

The meaning is that one who has incurred the defect arising from contact with indigo (nīlī) is to be avoided. Marīci also states that such a person is to be avoided: "The son of a widow (vaidhavya), the husband of a widow," and so forth; the ellipsis is "unfit for the śrāddha. *Vaidhavya* means *vaidhaveya*, which refers to the son of a widow who has been remarried. *Vidhavāpati* means the husband of a widow who has been remarried. Devala also says:
"That which is given to those outside the four stages of life (cāturāśramya) becomes fruitless. This is also stated in the Purāṇas.
The four stages of life (āśramas) are always to be honored at rites for the gods and at ancestral offerings (śrāddhas);
one should never cause a śrāddha to be given to those who stand outside the fourfold system of life-stages.
One should not invite that person who performs ascetic penance while remaining outside the stages of life (anāśramin);
whether engaged in worldly activity or withdrawn from it, those outside the āśramas are defilers of the row.
Manu, however, speaks of those who defile the row:
"A blind man destroys the fruit of ninety [invitations], a one-eyed man that of sixty, a leper that of a hundred,
and one afflicted with a foul disease that of a thousand given by the donor."
As many Brahmins as a performer of sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his body,
for that many [Brahmins], the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the gift pertaining to the ancestors.

A blind person causes the destruction of the row (navati-nāśakatva) merely by being present in the line due to the absence of sight, not by looking. By the word "should touch" (*saṃspṛśet*), being in the same row is indicated. If the primary meaning were accepted, there would be no defilement of the row in the absence of physical contact; however, that is incorrect. A *śūdrayājaka* is either a priest at the *Sthapati-iṣṭi* sacrifice, or one who, having been deceived for his own livelihood, performs *pākayajña* and other rites for the sake of a *śūdra*. Furthermore, if the inclusion of such a defiler of the row occurs through ignorance or necessity, then Manu says:
Learn in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born who purify a row that has been defiled by one unworthy of the company— those twice-born ones by whom the row is purified.
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the scriptural teachings,
and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa sacrifice, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymns, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one who continues the lineage of a Brāhmaṇa gift, one who chants the Sāman verses, and one who sings the Jyeṣṭhasāman.
One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, an expounder, a celibate student, one who bestows a thousand gifts,
and one who lives for a hundred years— these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly.

The "succession of those given by Brahmā" refers to the son of a woman wedded according to the *brāhma* rite. "Purifiers of the row" (*paṅktipāvanas*) are those who remove the defects caused by such things as being one-eyed that may affect those seated in the row. The intention is that those who were accepted for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice without prior examination—or accepted out of necessity during times of distress—even if they are one-eyed or otherwise defective, should be employed in such a way that they are mixed with purifiers of the row, such as those who have mastered all the Vedas and their branches. For this very reason, Sumantu says:
"Those who are one-eyed, hunchbacked, lame, skinless, or hairless..."
[189] All [the invited guests] should be engaged in the śrāddha rite, mingled with those who have mastered the Vedas.

"Skinless" means those who are "śipiviṣṭas," that is to say, those who are bald (*khalvāṭa*) without hair. However, the author of the *Saṃgraha* states a prohibition regarding mixing [such persons with others]:
"One may feed those who are one-eyed and so forth at a *daiva* rite or a *śrāddha*, but one should exclude them from a gift (*dāna*)."

In the context of *śrāddha* and giving, the meaning is "the giving of a *śrāddha*. Paiṭhīnasi also mentions those who purify the row (*paṅktipāvana*): "Now, therefore, these are the purifiers of the row: one who has mastered the three *Nāciketas* fire-altars, one who knows the three *Madhu* verses, one who knows the three *Suparṇa* verses, one who has fulfilled his vows, a singer of the *Chandas* (Sāmavedin), a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, one who continues the lineage of a gift to a Brahmin, a reciter of the *Sahasra* [of Rudras], a reciter of the *Rudrādhyāya*, one who knows the four Vedas, one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), a reciter of the *Atharvaśiras*, one who maintains the five fires, and a reciter of the Veda. These are the purifiers of the row. Each one of them, when appointed at the head of the row, purifies even a row attended by thousands [of others]."
Thus concludes the determination of Brahmins to be avoided in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the ritual duties for the day preceding the *śrāddha* day;
regarding this, the *Varāhapurāṇa* states:
One who knows that "I shall perform [the rites] tomorrow" must attend to the cleansing of clothes and so forth;
having smeared the ground and prepared the site, he should invite the Brahmins.
A student of sacred knowledge should discard his tooth-stick and remain pure.

Having secured the site for the *śrāddha* and having performed the sweeping and smearing of the chosen place, one should carry out the purification of the garments and other such tasks during the day. At night, however, one should invite the Brahmins; the meaning is that one should provide them with an irrevocable request (*niyoga*) for the sake of accomplishing the rites for the gods and ancestors. An irrevocable request is known as an invitation (*nimantraṇa*). [190] There is also the statement of Madālasā:
"One should invite on the previous day the most excellent twice-born ones mentioned above."
In the same manner, one should provide them for rites dedicated to the gods and those dedicated to the ancestors.

The meaning is that it is precisely for the sake of determining the distinction: "you [are assigned] to the rite for the gods," and "you [are assigned] to the rite for the ancestors. Devala also says:
"Having resolved, 'I shall perform [the rite] tomorrow,' the donor should invite the Brahmins after everyone in the house has eaten once, having themselves eaten food free from meat."
The meaning is that one should invite [the guests] after all those people born in one's own household have finished eating. Yama also says:

"One should request the twice-born—those endowed with noble birth, proper conduct, and learning, who are self-controlled and free from greed—to eat at the end of the evening, once they have been fed and have not yet gone to sleep."

"Understanding" (*avabodha*) is the comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas and so forth. "Those who have not yet lain down" (*aśayitān*) means those for whom the act of lying down has not been performed. And as for the request—when it is asked how it should be performed—the wise one (*pracetāḥ*) says:
"Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), on the previous day he should first invite the ancestors, saying:
'May you perform our ancestral rites; please be gracious.'"
Having prostrated with the right hand for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should invite [the guests].

Having performed the *apasavya* (placing the sacred thread over the right shoulder) and become *prācīnāvītī*, he should invite [the Brahmin] with the following meaning: "Tomorrow there will be a rite for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*) for us; that should be accomplished by you through your favor by performing the duties of the *āhavanīya* fire. Thus, he should request him to be gracious for the sake of the *āhavanīya*. "With the left hand accompanied by the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) resting on the left shoulder, having prostrated, one should invite. This invitation preceded by prostration pertains to the *śrāddha* performed by a *śūdra*. As it is said: "The Brāhmaṇa should take hold of the right foot, the Kṣatriya likewise the left, the Vaiśya both feet, and the Śūdra [should do so] preceded by a prostration."
One should invite [the guests] on the day before...
This is because of such a traditional recollection (*smaraṇa*) in the Purāṇas. Regarding the grasping of the right foot, however, a specific detail is shown in the *Mātsya*:
"Having touched the right knee, [one should say] 'You have been invited by me.
The word "should say" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The rule "One should first invite the ancestors" is for the purpose of a restrictive injunction (*niyamārtha*).

"One should likewise prepare them for the rites dedicated to the gods and those dedicated to the ancestors"— since this statement by Madālāsā records that even the invitation must be preceded by the rites for the gods; therefore, "having then become one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī), [he should invite] the best of the twice-born for the sake of the deities."
But for the rite of the ancestors, one should do so with the sacred thread over the right shoulder; this may be done by oneself, or by a disciple, or by a son.

And because of this traditional teaching of Bṛhaspati, the invitation must be performed beforehand. Regarding that, Paiṭhīnasi says: "Having made the formal resolve, 'I shall perform the Śrāddha tomorrow,' one should invite seven or five Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas. The phrase "seven or five" refers to the total number of Brāhmaṇas for both the ancestors (paitṛka) and the Viśvedevas (vaiśvadeva) combined, since the latter part of this same passage states: "One should seat the Viśvedevas facing east and the ancestors to the south-east. When it is asked how the division according to the number of Brāhmaṇas is to be made here between the ancestral and the Vaiśvadeva rites, Aṅgiras [provides the answer].
In a śrāddha rite, one should feed an odd number of guests, not an even number; however, in a rite for the gods (daivika), an even number is appropriate.

The phrase "not equal" (*na samaḥ*) means that an equal number of Brahmins should not be selected for the sake of the ancestors (*pitr-arthe*). For this very reason, Manu says: [192] "Two for the rite of the gods (*daiva*), three for the ancestral rite (*pitṛ-kṛtye*). This should be understood as referring to the position of five [Brahmins]. However, in the position of seven, the division should be inferred as four for the gods and three for the ancestors. Now, one might ask: why is the division not two for the gods and five for the ancestors? For Kātyāyana, stating "an even number according to one's ability for the gods, and for the ancestors, an odd number for each individual," shows that an odd number of Brahmins is to be assigned to each of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather individually, and not to the group as a whole. Consequently, according to the maxim "it should be equal because it is not so stated," an equal distribution must be inferred by assigning an odd number to each of the five [ancestors], rather than as one wishes. Furthermore, an equal distribution of five among the three [starting from] the father is not possible, whereas it is possible among three. Therefore, the division should be made exactly as four for the gods and three for the ancestors. Regarding the Brahmins for the ancestral rite, Śaunaka also mentions a higher number: "One for each, or two for each, or three for each. The phrase "two for each" refers to the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* (prosperity rite). In the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, however, because there is a prohibition against an equal number—namely, "one should feed an odd number at a *śrāddha*, not an even number"—in the case of the position "one for each," three should be invited for the ancestral rite. With the intention of the position "three for each," Gautama also said: "One should feed at least nine. As for what was stated by Manu:
On the day before or on the day itself when the Śrāddha rite is at hand,
one should properly invite at least three Brahmins as prescribed.

Thus, in this context, the word "each" (*pratyekam*) should be understood as an ellipsis. Consequently, because it has the same meaning as the statement of Gautama, there is no contradiction with him. However, if one were to avoid supplying the word "each" and instead explain "at least three" (*tryavarān*) as referring to the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛkṛtye*), then a redundancy would result with his own statement, "two for the gods and three for the ancestral rite. Therefore, such an explanation is incorrect. Since he specifies "at least three," it should be understood that five for each is the middle course, while seven for each is the highest course. For this very reason, Gautama says: "Or an odd number, according to one's capacity. The meaning is that for the ancestors and others, one should feed an odd number of Brahmins—either five or seven for each—according to one's energy and wealth. Thus, it should be understood that the ancestral rite (*pitṛkṛtya*) should be performed by seven Brahmins each for one who is most prosperous and capable of providing hospitable treatment; by five Brahmins each for one who is more prosperous; by three Brahmins each for one who is prosperous; and by three alone for one who is merely wealthy. As for what was stated by Manu:
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each;
even if very wealthy, one should not be intent on a large number of guests.
Hospitality, the proper place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmin—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should not seek prolixity.
And as for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
"One may feed even one person, or two or three, at the rite for the gods and the rite for the ancestors;
for excellence of hospitality, the proper time, and worthy recipients cannot be fully realized in a large assembly."
Thus it is said; furthermore, in the Purāṇas:
"Due to the lack of favorable place, time, or strength, one may feed each [guest] at both [places], or the remaining ones according to one's means in another house."

[194] Because there would be a greater multitude of faults due to the abundance of Brahmins— namely, the destruction of the *śrāddha*, the destruction of silence, and the forgetting of the *śrāddha*-manual.
Contact with those who have not washed after eating, as well as reviling those who eat food,
frivolous debate, slander, and various kinds of idle chatter— these too [are obstacles].

Thus, regarding the remaining persons invited, beginning with the guests (*atithi*): this rule applies to one who, despite being very wealthy, lacks the capacity to provide hospitable treatment (*satkriyā*) and so forth due to a large number of Brahmins. However, the statement of Śaunaka and others applies to one who does possess the capacity to provide such hospitality; thus, everything is faultless. Furthermore, a distinction based on poverty is not possible here, for it is said:
"Even a very wealthy person should feed two at a rite for the gods (*daiva*), three at a rite for the ancestors (*pitṛkṛtya*), or one at each of the two."

Thus, since Manu has prescribed even a small number in the case of those who are wealthy, as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha—"Or else, one may feed a single Brāhmaṇa who purifies the row"—that refers to a situation where it is impossible to obtain several Brāhmaṇas. Having approached the Brāhmaṇas endowed with the aforementioned number while they are staying in their own homes, he should inform them. And so it has been said by Atri:
On the first day, one should invite those learned in the Vedas and others to the place of residence;
at that very time, one should inform them of their duty regarding the rites for the ancestors and the gods.

"You must be free from all exertion and devoid of desire and anger on the day after tomorrow, when our śrāddha rite takes place. Here, "on the first day" means on the previous day. [He should invite] those residing in their own dwellings. Also in the *Mātsya*:
[195] Having invited these persons, the wise man should announce the ancestral observances:
that they must be free from anger, devoted to purity, and always practicing celibacy.
You must act accordingly, and I too shall act as one who performs acts of faith.

The meaning is that while reciting the passage beginning with "akrodhanaiḥ" (by those free from anger), one should cause the invited Brahmins—who belong to the paternal line and constitute the constituent parts of the ancestral rite—to hear it. The rule regarding freedom from anger and so forth is stated so that one may say: "Just as this restraint is obligatory for me, so too it is for you. The portion "mayāpi śrāddhakāriṇā" (also by me, the performer of the śrāddha) is likewise to be recited. Atri states the duty of the invited Brahmins:
"If that night passes without obstacle in that manner, they should wait for the time of the śrāddha without weariness, according to what has been heard [in the scriptures]."

The invited Brahmins, having said to the one who extended the invitation, "So be it, provided this night passes without obstacle," should observe and maintain that collection of observances exactly as they have been heard prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras and other such texts. This refers to the time of the Śrāddha, meaning until the digestion of the food on the following day. Thus says Pracetas:
"From the consumption of the food, there shall be celibacy for both [the giver and the receiver] thereafter."

The mention of "undertaking the vow of celibacy" (*brahmacarya-grahaṇa*) is intended to indicate the observance of the rules prescribed for both types of invited guests. However, the rule regarding fasting begins from the time of the invitation and lasts until the completion of the *śrāddha* rite; thus says Āpastamba: "And once it has begun, there is no eating until its conclusion. As for that which was stated by Vṛddha-Manu:
"Having invited the Brahmins on that day, one should avoid sexual intercourse, shaving, negligence, Vedic recitation, anger, impurity, and likewise falsehood."

Thus, that [rule] refers to the subject of the *sadyaḥkāla* (immediate) *śrāddha*, because the *Purāṇa* states: "One should invite the best of the twice-born either on the preceding day or on that very day," thereby mentioning the *sadyaḥkāla* option as well. And this *sadyaḥkāla* option occurs when it is somehow impossible to perform the invitation on the preceding day.
"Or, if it is not possible, one should invite those Brāhmaṇas on the following day," according to the traditional teaching of Devala;
therefore, the wise man should first perform the act of inviting them.
On the day of attainment or even on that very day, those who are attached to women must be avoided.

This is because it has been stated even in the words of Madālasā: "The invitation (*upanimantraṇa*) should be performed on the preceding day if possible; if for some reason the invitation cannot be obtained then, it should be performed on the day of the *śrāddha*—this is the meaning. However, when the invitation is performed on that very day, then because the status of being invited is contingent upon that specific day, the observance of the restrictive rules (*niyama*) would occur on that day alone. Yama states that one may sometimes have another perform the invitation:
"One should invite the best of the twice-born for the sake of the deities with the left hand [of the invitee]."
"In the rite for the ancestors (pitrya), however, [the offering] is made with the sacred thread over the right shoulder; this may be done by oneself, or by a disciple, or by a son.
Also, regarding the one who issues the command: "One should send a trustworthy person of the same caste to invite the twice-born."

Among these alternatives, the previously mentioned rule is preferable; however, if none are available, he may send even one of a different caste, provided he is not a Śūdra, for "the food of a Brāhmaṇa invited by a Vṛṣala is unfit to be eaten."

Thus, because of the traditional legal injunction (smaraṇa) by Yama prohibiting one who has been invited by a Śūdra, it is well known that a specific prohibition is intended to permit the general case. Consequently, an invitation made by one whose food is fit to be eaten—whether prepared by oneself, by a disciple, or by someone of a different caste other than a Śūdra—is irreproachable; and for those Brāhmaṇas capable of eating, such an invitation must not be refused, provided that the invitation is irreproachable and they have given their consent.

Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Devala: when an irreproachable invitation has been made, those who have been invited should give a response—a promise—saying, "Let it be so as desired. Kātyāyana also stated: "When invited by one who is irreproachable, one should not withdraw; being capable, one should not refuse. By this, it is understood that in the case of a reproachable invitation or when one lacks the capacity to eat, a refusal must indeed be made. To indicate that once an invitation has been accepted, it is proper to withdraw even after acceptance if the capacity to eat is subsequently lacking, he himself says: "Having formally accepted the invitation (ketana), one who is capable should not withdraw. "Having accepted the invitation" means having agreed to the summons. As for that which was stated by Yama:
Having made the Brāhmaṇa their mouth, the deities together with the ancestors consume that food; therefore, one should not transgress against him.

Thus, since this refers to the case of one who is invited by an irreproachable person possessing the capacity [to perform the rite], there is no contradiction with what was stated previously. Regarding him, however, who abandons a Brāhmaṇa who has been invited, Nārāyaṇa says:
"The evil-minded man who, having caused an invitation to be made, then turns back, incurs the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa and is born into the womb of a Śūdra."
When this sin has been incurred, a Brāhmaṇa who is self-restrained and pure is liberated from that evil by performing the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa penance.

*Enaḥ* means sin. *Yaticāndrāyaṇa* is a specific type of *cāndrāyaṇa*. This [penance] is to be understood as applying when one who has accepted an invitation and is capable of eating refuses to do so. Regarding one who, having accepted an invitation, abandons the host despite being capable of eating, Manu says: "But the best of the twice-born, having been duly invited to a *havya* (offering to the gods) or *kavya* (offering to the ancestors), if he somehow transgresses that duty, becomes a sinner and goes to the state of a pig."
"In some way" means by reason of greed for fine food and abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and not, however, due to an inability to eat; this refers to the case of a wealthy Brāhmaṇa.
For it is said: "But he who, possessing wealth, is invited with food fit to be eaten and somehow transgresses [the invitation], that sinner shall go to the state of a pig."
Thus, because another Smṛti records the fault of one who possesses wealth [but does not give it], it is said by Yama: "But that foolish man who,
having been invited to a Śrāddha, should attend to the business of another,
his merit accumulated over a year perishes."
Thus it was said by Matsya:
"Even when invited by one who is virtuous but destitute,
noble twice-born men do not pass him over out of greed for the delicacies of others' food."
But those who were invited first take [the food] from him, and not from anyone else.

Thus, the intention is that others also, without bypassing the first inviter, should receive [the food] from him alone; all of this should be understood as referring to the case of a wealthy person. However, regarding one who, while receiving from that [first host], wishes to receive from another as well, Kātyāyana speaks to prohibit it: "One who has been invited should not accept other food. The meaning is: one who was previously invited by another should not accept food other than that belonging to the former—namely, the food of the later inviter—even if it is in the form of rice and so forth. As for one who nevertheless accepts it, Devala states its fault:
If one who has been previously invited by another accepts an invitation from someone else,
or eats after having already finished a meal, his merit perishes.

However, regarding one who, though invited and summoned, causes the lapse of the proper time for the *kutapa* and other elements of the *śrāddha* by failing to arrive, his fault is shown in the *Ādipurāṇa*:
"An invited Brahmin should never delay for long,
[for he is] indeed [the representative] of the deities, the ancestors, the giver, and the food."
"One who harbors malice for a long time is cooked by the fire of hell.
Regarding the fault of one who, having been invited, or being the performer of a *śrāddha*, does not observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*), Manu says:
"Even when enjoined during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*), one should never approach a woman."
Proceeding from there, one indeed obtains only an undesirable result.

By stating "during the fertile period," he indicates that there is a fault even in approaching one's own wife. By stating "being appointed," he indicates that there is a fault even when the engagement occurs out of passion. Gautama, however, states that for one performing a *śrāddha*, there is an excess of fault in approaching a *śūdrā* woman: "The performer of a *śrāddha* who goes to the bed of a *śūdrā* leads his ancestors into her excrement for a month. One who has a *śrāddha*—whether about to be performed or already performed—is called a *śrāddhin*; this refers to the donor. "Immediately" means starting from that very moment; "leads for a month" is the meaning. Manu, on the other hand, speaks of the fault for one who has been invited to a *śrāddha* in approaching the bed of a *śūdrā* woman.
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha feast, rejoices with a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī),
incurs all whatever evil deed has been committed by the donor.
Yama, however, states another fault in this regard:
"But he who, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, rejoices with a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*),
his ancestors wander for that month, subsisting on white seeds."
He states that very same fault even in the case of transgressing other rules:
"But he who, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, sets out on a journey,
his ancestors shall subsist on dust for that entire month."
But if a man who has been invited to a śrāddha engages in quarreling,
his ancestors shall subsist on tears for that entire month.
But when a twice-born man who has been invited to a śrāddha carries out the burden [of the task],
his ancestors will subsist on sweat for that entire month.
If a twice-born man, having been invited to a śrāddha, commits an act of violence,
his ancestors shall subsist on blood for that entire month.
"But if a twice-born man, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, causes distress,
his ancestors shall subsist on bile for that month," so says Uśanas.
"But if a twice-born man, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, indulges in gambling,
his ancestors consume that [food] as if it were filth.
[201] Thus, Yama says that they should remain attentive to the observances such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) in order to avoid the aforementioned faults.
But those Brahmins who have been invited when the time for the śrāddha has arrived should remain with their food restricted and devoted to celibacy.
"Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, not traveling from afar,
not carrying heavy loads, patience— these are the rules for the tranquility of one performing a *śrāddha*.
Thus ends the section on duties prior to the day of the *śrāddha* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the morning rites on the day of the *śrāddha*, Pracetas states:
"The one who is to eat at the *śrāddha*, having risen in the morning, should perform the cleansing of his teeth."
A wise performer of a śrāddha ceremony should not brush his teeth.
When it is asked what the performer of the *śrāddha* should do, Devala states:
"In that same manner, the donor, being self-restrained, having bathed in the morning and wearing fresh garments,
should begin the commencement of the food with his kinsmen using new vessels."

In the same way, the performer of the *śrāddha*, constrained and disciplined by not transgressing the aforementioned rules, should begin—that is, undertake—the commencement of food preparation for the sake of the *śrāddha*. This refers to the one who gives, the performer of the *śrāddha* and other rites, being provided with new, unblemished vessels and utensils suitable for cooking, as well as with kinsmen. Regarding what must first be done by the one authorized for the *śrāddha* during the cooking, Uśanas says: "One should perform the purification of the ground, the vessels, and the utensils with cow-dung and water.
