The meaning is that one should effect the purification of the kitchen floor by smearing it with cow-dung; and with water brought in the manner described in the section on sprinkling, one should effect the purification of the vessels intended for the addition of wheat flour and other ingredients. After the consecration of the kitchen floor, Devala says:
One should scatter sesame seeds there and tie up a goat on all sides;
everything defiled by Asuras becomes pure through sesame seeds and the goat.

After the purification of the kitchen, vessels, and utensils, one should prepare food and other items through cooking and so forth. And thus, that same [author] says: "Then, according to one's ability, one should provide food with many preparations, including various side dishes and eatables, as well as an abundance of things to be sucked and drunk."

"Abounding in preparation" (*bahusaṃskāra*) means endowed with whatever specific preparations are suitable for the king's food. "Possessing various side-dishes and edibles" (*naikavyañjanabhakṣyavat*) means provided with many kinds of side-dishes and edibles. A "side-dish" (*vyañjana*) is so called because by it the flavor of the main food is manifested; here it refers to soups, rice-puddings, and the like. That which is to be sucked (*coṣya*)—such as pieces of sugarcane—is that whose flavorful essence alone is to be consumed, not its physical substance. And that which is made by mixing molasses and other powders into the juice of uncooked fruits and the like for the purpose of drinking is "that which is to be drunk" (*peya*). Since there exist many kinds of both what is to be sucked and what is to be drunk, and they are not forbidden, it is said to be "abounding in what is to be sucked and what is to be drunk. By the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood that it is also "abounding in what is to be licked" (*lehya*). Food and the like have prescribed grains such as *vrīhi* as their primary ingredients. When it is asked what substances are prescribed, Pracetas says:
Black sesame seeds are indeed excellent, as are barley and śāli rice;
likewise, mahāyava, vrīhi-yava, and madhūlikā are also superior.
Black and white [sesame seeds] should be taken for the rite of ancestral offerings (śrāddha).

*Yava* (barley) has full awns; *śāli* and *kalamā* are varieties of rice. *Rājaśāli*, *mahāśāli*, *sugandhika*, and others are water-born [rice varieties]. *Mahāyava* and *vrīhi-yava* are specific types of barley. *Madhūlikā* is another distinct grain. *Kṛṣṇa* refers to black-colored rice grown on dry land. *Śveta* refers to white *mahāvrīhi* rice grown on dry land. *Loha* refers to red *śāli* rice grown in water, as well as *ṣāṣṭika* rice grown on dry land. Atri also says: "A *śrāddha* performed without wheat is as if it were not performed at all; a *śrāddha* performed without meat is as if it were not performed at all."
"Since the ancestors are flesh-eaters when milk-rice and other such offerings are absent. Thus it is said.

By this, it is shown through a figurative expression that food made from wheat products such as cakes (*apūpa*), as well as meat-based food, must necessarily be prepared. Regarding the method for preparing the meat-based food, Kātyāyana states: "Having slaughtered goats, sheep, and oxen, or having purchased or obtained the remainder [of other animals], or having brought those that have died of themselves, one should cook them. Here, *usrā* means a cow. "Having slaughtered" means having performed the ritual killing (*saṃjñapana*). And this refers to the Dvāpara and other ages, excluding the Kali age. Thus, in the section on the duties of the Kali age:

In such scriptural statements as, "The sacrifice of animals for guests and ancestors," we have demonstrated that the slaughter of cattle and other animals for the purpose of *śrāddha* and similar rites is prohibited. Even in the Kali age, one should not cook beef even if obtained through purchase or other means, because it is loathed by the world. Other suitable items are shown in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, whether purchased, obtained by any means whatsoever, or prepared from what is available:
"Bilva, *āmalaka*, grapes, jackfruit, *āmra-ātaka*, and pomegranate... [204]
And the fruits of *cavya*, *pāleya*, *kākṣola*, and *kharjūra*.
Kaśeru, kovidāra, tālakanda, as well as viśa,
kāleya, kālaśāka, suniṣaṇṇaka, and suvarcalā.
The *kardura*, the *koṅkaṇī* grape, the *likuca*, the *moca*,
the *karkandhū*, the *grāvaka*, the beautiful *tinduka*, and that which is called *madhu*.
The wood-apple, coconut, water chestnut, varūṣaka, pippala, black pepper, bitter gourd, and the fruit of the bṛhatī plant.

"Fish and meat should be prepared fragrant, and indeed all [other items] such as these, which are savory and sweet; furthermore, ginger and long radish should certainly be offered here. Thus it is said.

*Mṛdvīkā* is *drākṣā* (grape), as Amarasiṃha states in his lexicon: "The *mṛdvīkā*, *gostanī*, and *drākṣā* [are synonyms]. *Āmrātaka* is a yellow tree resembling the mango tree (*cūta*), as he says: "The two, *pītana* and *kapītana*, are the *āmrātaka*. *Akṣoṭa* is a tree found in the mountains. *Kaseru* is a specific type of aquatic tuber known as *bhadramustā*. *Kāleya* is *dāruharidrā* (Indian barberry). *Suniṣpaṇṇa* is a leaf-vegetable called *vitunnaka*, as Amarasiṃha states in the section on vegetables: "*Vitunna* is *suniṣaṇṇaka*. *Kardura* is a specific tree called *śrīparṇikā*, as he says: "*Śrīparṇikā*, *kumudikā*, *kumbhī*, *kaṭarya*, and *kaṭphala* [are synonyms]. *Koṅkaṇī* is grape produced in the Koṅkaṇa country. *Likuca* is a specific shrub bearing small fruits similar to the *jambīra* fruit. *Moca* is the fruit of the plantain (*kadalī*). *Karkandhū* is the *badarī* (jujube). *Tinduka* is a tree called *sitasāraka*; Amarasiṃha says: "*Tinduka*, *sphūrjaka*, *kālaskandha*, and *sitasāraka* [are synonyms]. *Śṛṅgāṭaka* is the three-pronged water plant. *Bṛhatī* is the thorny plant; Amarasiṃha says: "*Nidigdhakā*, *spṛśī*, *vyāghrī*, *bṛhatī*, and *kaṇṭakārikā* [are synonyms]"; its fruit is *bṛhatīphala*. The remaining items—*bilva*, *āmalaka*, *panasa*, *dāḍima*, *cavya*, *kharjūra*, *tālakaṇda*, *viśva*, *ekaṅkata*, *nālikera*, *pippalī*, *marica*, and *paṭola*—are well-known. The others are not well-known. "Of this kind" means belonging to such a category. *Nāgara* is *śuṇṭhī* (dry ginger). *Dīrghamūla* is *tuṇḍikerī*; its fruit is *dīrghamūlaka*. And these items, beginning with *āmrātaka*, are to be prepared only with substances for which the preparation has been prescribed. Those [substances] are shown in the Āditya Purāṇa.
Madhūka, asafoetida, camphor, black pepper,
jaggery, rock salt, and likewise salt from Lake Mānasa are commended in the performance of the Śrāddha rite.
Also in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Rock salt and likewise that which originates from Lake Mānasa—
these two are indeed supremely purifying, even though they are perceptible to the senses at all times."
Thus, Devala states that the preparation of refined food is not restricted solely to the *śrāddha* rite:

"On the occasions of *iṣṭāpūrta*, on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), during the *darśa-śrāddha*, and at the *aṣṭakā* ceremonies— at these times, one must give to worthy recipients and never provide poor-quality food."

By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that even during special occasions such as the *mahālaya* and others, inferior food (*kubhojana*) must not be given; thus, it is understood that in rites such as the daily *śrāddha* performed by those who are poor, the offering of inferior food and the like is permitted. Regarding this, Yama states:
"Whatever is eaten, chewed, or drunk, and whatever is cooked in the house—that should never be consumed without first being offered to the ancestors."
Therefore, without first offering [a portion] to the ancestors (pitṛs), one should not perform even the Vaiśvadeva and other rites from that food. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
"He who performs the Vaiśvadeva after having set aside the food intended for the ancestors—his Śrāddha becomes 'Asura' (demonic) and does not reach the ancestors."
Yama, however, states that for the sake of avoiding the defilement of cooked food, those who must be excluded from the place of cooking and so forth are as follows:

"A liquor-drinker, an unchaste woman, one whose husband has been previously superseded by another, and likewise a widow— these should never look upon the *śrāddha* at any time, starting from the pouring of the oblation."

*Āvāpa* refers to the placing of rice and other grains into a cooking pot or similar vessel to prepare them for cooking. From that point until the completion of the meal, the meaning is that the sacrificial materials (*bhojya-padārtha*) and the Brahmins eating them—whether they are staying in the kitchen, the dining area, or elsewhere—must be removed from afar so that those such as liquor-drinkers do not see them during the *śrāddha* rites. The mention of "liquor-drinkers and the like" is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all living beings who are considered unworthy. For this very reason, Manu says:
"The Caṇḍāla, the pig, and likewise the cock..."
Neither a woman in her menses nor a lame person should look at the twice-born while they are eating.
"Whatever is looked upon by these [evil beings] during the giving of a house, at a meal, or in a rite for the gods or the ancestors, that goes exactly as it was seen. Thus [it is said].

"In the home" means in the place where the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) takes place. "In the offering" means in the place where the food is abandoned. "In the eating" means in the kitchen or other places where the food is prepared. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that in any other place as well, whatever food and such is looked upon by *caṇḍālas* and others goes to its true state—that is, it becomes unfit. Therefore, the intention is that they must be removed from a great distance away from the site of the *śrāddha*. A "boar" (*varāha*) is a village pig; it is specifically mentioned because it is most unwholesome. For this very reason, Uśanas specifies: "The village pig, the cat, the cock, the mongoose, the Śūdra, a woman in her menses, and the husband of a Śūdra woman must be removed from a distance"—the phrase "at the time of the *śrāddha*" being understood. And so says Yama:
A cock, a village pig, a crow, a dog, and a cat;
the husband of a low-caste woman, the low-caste man himself, two eunuchs, and a menstruating woman.
These, indeed, must be avoided with great effort at the time of the śrāddha ceremony.
The meaning is: "at the time of the *śrāddha*, starting from the commencement of the cooking. And so Vyāsa says:
"One wearing ochre robes, one afflicted with leprosy, an outcast, even a killer of an embryo, a Brahmin of mixed birth, or one who is a relative of an outcast—"
These should be avoided by the wise when the funeral offering has been presented.

*Nivāpa* is a gift for the ancestors (*pitṛ*), according to Amarasimha’s definition: "The gift to the ancestors is called *nivāpa*. From the use of the word *samupasthita* (present/commenced), it is understood that those [persons] are to be excluded starting from the commencement of the cooking, and not only at the time of the actual offering to the ancestors. Yama also states who among men are to be removed:
"A lame man, one-eyed, a person with a withered arm, or one afflicted with leprosy shall become the servant of the giver;
likewise, one with missing limbs or redundant limbs—one should remove even him from there."
A lame person is one deficient in a foot; a one-eyed person is *kāṇa*; a one-handed person is *kuṇi*; and a leper is one afflicted with *kuṣṭha*. This also applies to a temple-priest (*devala*).

One should avoid a loathsome person, an impure person, a naked person, an intoxicated person, a rogue, a woman in her menses, one wearing blue or saffron-colored garments, and one whose ears have been cut off.
"Bībhatsa" means loathsome. Also in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Naked persons and others should never look upon this *śrāddha*;
for if it is seen by them, the fathers and grandfathers go downwards."

*Śrāddha* refers to the food and other materials intended for the *śrāddha* rite. A "naked one" (*nagna*) is one who has abandoned the Vedas; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those who have abandoned the performance of Vedic rites of that same nature are included. And thus it is said in this very [text]:
"Since the Triple Veda (*trayī*) is the covering for all beings, those who indeed abandon it out of delusion are remembered as 'naked ones' and the like."

The *trayī* is the Veda; those who abandon it are considered "naked. The meaning is that those who abandon the performance of its prescribed duties are known as "naked ones" and so forth. Also in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"A man who wears matted hair in vain, who shaves his head in vain, and who goes naked in vain—those men who are great sinners (*mahāpātakin*) are indeed the 'naked ones' and the rest."

"In vain" means without the Vedic ritual procedure. However, if it is asked what should be done if those such as the naked (nagna) should see the food and other offerings intended for the *śrāddha*, it is stated in that very same [text]: "If these should see the food during the offerings to the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*), it should be discarded for the sake of the offering; however, a purification is prescribed in times of distress."

Food seen by a naked person (*nagna*) or others of that sort must be discarded. However, in times of distress, a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is prescribed for that very food in order to remove the defect produced by the sight of such persons. When it is asked what that purificatory rite is, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"For sacrificial offerings (*havis*) that have already been prepared, discarding them first is prescribed;
then, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with water mixed with clay is enjoined."
One should also perform the scattering of white mustard seeds and black sesame seeds,
and one should diligently seek the sight of a preceptor, the sun, fire, and a goat.

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding sacrificial offerings (*havis*), whether for the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*), if one sees a naked person or others [of ill omen], the primary rule is indeed their immediate abandonment. However, in times of distress, for the sake of accomplishing the purificatory rites that remove defects, one should perform sprinkling with water touched by auspicious clay, as well as scattering white mustard seeds and black sesame seeds over the visible *havya* and *kavya*. Likewise, one should diligently ensure the sight of a teacher, the sun, fire, or a goat, by removing any intervening obstructions through clearing the space, so that the food may be successfully prepared. Alternatively, one should perform the purification of food as taught by Jamadagni.
One may remove the defects of food by means of pure water and *darbha* grass, using the *Śuddhavatī*, *Kūśmāṇḍī*, *Pāvamānī*, and *Taratsamandī* verses.

The meaning is that one should take water consecrated with the *śuddhavatī* and other mantras using *darbha* grass and perform a sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*) for the purpose of removing defects in the food arising from the sight of those who drink liquor, unchaste women, and so forth. The verses beginning with "etonvindraṃ stavāma" are the *śuddhavatī*s; those beginning with "yad devā devahelanam" are the *kūśmāṇḍya*s; those beginning with "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ" are the *pāvamānya*s; and those beginning with "taratsamandī dhāvati" are the *taratsamā*s. However, if one should remove the defect in the food arising from the sight of those who drink liquor and others by means of the aforementioned purification (either previously mentioned or to be described hereafter), such as the touching of earth, ashes, water, or gold, then that food may be eaten at a *śrāddha*. Thus says Sumantu: "Food looked upon by Caṇḍālas and others is not to be eaten, except after the touching of earth, ashes, gold, or water. The mention of the purification consisting of the touching of earth, ashes, gold, and water is intended to illustrate both types of purification previously mentioned.
Thus concludes the section on the morning rites on the day of the Śrāddha in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding substances to be avoided in the performance of the Śrāddha rite,
there is the statement of Madālasā:
Furthermore, wealth obtained through bribery and the like, that which is acquired from an outcast, and money arising from the improper dowry of a maiden— such property is here condemned.
Having said, "Give this to me for the sake of the ancestors," whatever has been acquired must be avoided by the wise in the performance of the śrāddha rite.

"By means of bribery and the like, which are causes for greed, or by theft and the like; 'improper bride-price' refers to a bride-price exceeding a pair of cattle (gomithuna), and what is obtained through that is called 'arising from improper bride-price. In this context, regarding the rite of *śrāddha*, the meaning is that such wealth is censurable and must be avoided. Vyāsa also states what is to be avoided:
'That which arises from the sale of the Vedas is not desired, nor is wealth acquired by a woman;
that which is earned from a eunuch should not be given to the ancestors or the gods.'"
The same author also states which grains and other items are to be avoided:
"Grains that are unfit for ancestral rites include *kodrava* and *pulkasa*;
likewise, among spices, *hiṅgu*, and among vegetables, *kālānala* and *śubhā*."

*Kodravas* are *koradūṣakas*, for Amarasiṃha states in his lexicon: "But *kodrava* is *koradūṣa*. *Pulakas* (or *pulākās*) are minor grains compared to *kodravas*, for he states: "The word *pulāka* may refer to a worthless grain. Thus, regarding Vyāsa’s statement that "the *pulakas* are likewise," one should understand that the absence of the long vowel in the middle syllable of the word *pulaka* is not a fault, as it is due to Vedic usage (*ārṣatvāt*). Among substances—meaning substances intended for seasoning vegetables and the like—the substance known as asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) is unfit for a *śrāddha*. Now, one might object: "Is the prohibition of asafoetida not improper?"
Madhūka, asafoetida, camphor, black pepper,
jaggery, rock salt, and likewise Mānasa salt are commended in the performance of Śrāddha rites.

This is because it is recorded as something to be accepted in the *Ādityapurāṇa*. True; since both injunctions and prohibitions are observed regarding the *hiṅgu* plant, an option (*vikalpa*) should be understood in that case. Likewise, wherever injunctions and prohibitions are seen for the same thing, an option is to be recognized there. Among vegetables (*śāka*), certain specific types known as *kālānala* and *śubha* are not to be used in a *śrāddha*. Regarding this, Devasthāmin has defined the vegetable species called *kāla* as having the appearance of *kuṭheraka*. *Kuṭheraka* is a *parṇāsa* similar to *arjaka*, according to Amarasimha’s lexicon: "Now, *parṇāsa* refers to *kaṭhiñjara* and *kuṭheraka*; here, the white variety is *arjaka*. Thus, it should be understood that the black *arjaka* is what is denoted by the word *kāla*. *Anala* is *citraka*, as Amarasimha states: "*Citraka* is known by the name *vahni*. Devasthāmin has stated that what is commonly designated in the world as the *śubha* vegetable is the very one referred to here by the word *śubha*. Bharadvāja also says: "One should give split pulses (*dvidala*), with the exception of mung beans (*mudga*), pigeon peas (*āḍhakī*), and black gram (*māṣa*). Those grains which are generally split into two by the rotation of a stone mill are *dvidala*. *Āḍhakī* is a specific type of podded grain well-known by the name *tuvarī*. *Mudga* and *māṣa* are also specific types of podded grains, well-known by their respective names. By the word *māṣa*, the *rājamāṣa* (kidney bean) is intended, and not the black *māṣa*.
Monkeys and likewise kidney beans (rājamāṣa) are to be avoided at a śrāddha ceremony.

This is because it has been specified thus in another Smṛti. *Markaṭakas* are specific types of grass-grain. Accordingly, it is stated in the section on grass-grains in the *Vaijayantī*: "Now, the wild [grass] and the *markaṭaka* are synonyms. *Rājamāṣas* generally possess pods about a span in length; in their dry state, they are pale-red in color and are well known by the name *alasāndra*. For this very reason, it is said in the *Vaijayantī*: "*Alasāndra* is the *rājamāṣa*. From the word *mudga*, neither the black nor any other variety of *mudga* is to be understood here; nor, moreover, is the black *mudga* included.
One should avoid all black grains in the rite of Śrāddha;
however, one should not avoid sesame seeds, nor likewise mung beans and māṣa beans.

Thus, because another Smṛti text provides a counter-exception for black sesame, mung beans, and black gram, among black grains, even horse-gram and others are to be avoided: "Kodrava, rāja-māṣa, horse-gram, varaka, and likewise niṣpāva— one should especially avoid these five."
The wise likewise avoid even bamboo seeds.

This is because it is stated thus in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "Kuluttha beans are well known for providing various benefits, such as soups and broths, much like mung beans (*mudga*). Both the black and non-black varieties are to be avoided, as there is no counter-exception (pratiprasava) for them, similar to the case of black mung beans and others. Varaka beans are wild mung beans; regarding wild mung beans, it is said: "Varaka, nigūḍha, kulī, and makā are [types of] wild mung beans."

This is because it is stated thus in the *Vaijayantī*: "The *niṣpāva* is the white *śimbikā*. Like the *kuluttha*, the *niṣpāvas* are well known for their utility in various preparations such as soups, and they are recognized as a type of white-podded grain (*śveta-śimbī-dhānya*). For this very reason, it is said in the *Vaijayantī*: "The *niṣpāva* is the white *śimbikā*. This prohibition of the *niṣpāva* refers specifically to the black variety, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*) which states: "One should avoid all black grains in the performance of a *śrāddha* ceremony. And so it has been stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
Barley, rice, wheat, sesame, mung beans, mustard seeds,
millet, kovidāra, and flat beans are auspicious here.

Thus, this [prohibition] should be understood as referring to [grains] other than black [gram]. *Yāvanāla* is well known in regions such as Mahārāṣṭra to the south of the Vindhya mountains by the synonym *johala*. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vaijayantī*: "The *yāvanālas*, however, are *johalas*. Marīci has also declared those things to be avoided:
"In a *śrāddha*, *kulattha* beans, chickpeas (*caṇaka*), and *kodrava* grains must not be given, nor any pungent substances, nor likewise those that are tasteless."
Chickpeas (*caṇaka*) are extremely dear to horses and are well-known everywhere except in frontier regions. In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* as well, it is stated:
"In a *śrāddha*, one should not give *pālaṅkyā*, nor *niṣpāva*, *kodrava*, *masūra*, *kṣāra*, eggplant (*vārtāka*), *kuluttha*, hemp (*śaṇa*), or *śigru*."

*Pālaṅkyā* refers to the fragrant substance called *mukunda*, because Amarasiṃha states in the section on the names of fragrant substances: "In the section on fragrant substances, *pālaṅkyā*, *mukunda*, *kunda*, and *kundaru* [are synonyms]. [214] *Masūra* is a specific type of split pulse (*dvidala*) very well known in regions other than the borderlands, having *maṅgalyaka* as another synonym. Thus says Amarasiṃha: "*Maṅgalyaka* is *masūra*. *Kṣāra* refers to alkaline salts such as *yavakṣāra* (barley-ash). *Vārtāka* is the fruit of the *bṛhatī* plant known as the small eggplant (*kṣudravārtāka*), which is slightly thicker than the fruit of the *bṛhatī* known as *kaṇṭakārikā*. The word *śaṇa* denotes a specific grain, because it is listed among the varieties of grain in the statement: "The grains have seven parts, *śaṇa*," and because this [grain] grown spontaneously is always prohibited. Although its acquisition is impossible here [in the wild], the prohibition is not meaningless because its acquisition is possible when grown through cultivation and so forth. *Śigru* is of two kinds: white-flowered and red-flowered. Since the red-flowered variety is entirely prohibited and thus cannot be acquired, the prohibition of the white-flowered variety—which can be acquired as a leaf vegetable—is meaningful. Viṣṇu also mentions those things to be avoided: "One should avoid *bhūtṛṇa*, *śigru*, mustard, *surasa*, *arjaka*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *alābukī*, eggplant (*vārtāka*), *pālaṅkyā*, *taṇḍulīyaka*, safflower (*kusumbha*), and buffalo's milk. Regarding *bhūtṛṇa*: Amarasiṃha says, "*Chatrāticchatra*, *pālaghna*, *mālātṛṇaka*, and *bhūstṛṇa* [are synonyms]. The absence of the visarga is a Vedic (archaic) usage. That specific vegetable whose nodes on the stalk are circular and serve as supports is called *bhūtṛṇa*. Here, *sarṣapa* refers specifically to the black mustard (*rājasarṣapa*), and not mustard in general, because another Smṛti specifies the prohibition: "Safflower and black mustard. A specific prohibition is intended to permit the remainder; therefore, to avoid contradiction, the general term there concludes by referring to that specific one. The prohibition is made against the inclusion of mango juice in *rājasarṣapa*, *surasa*, *nirguṇḍī*, and linctuses. *Arjaka* is the white *arjaka*. The words *kūṣmāṇḍa* and *alābukī* are well known. The words *vārtāka* and *pālaṅkyā* have already been explained. *Taṇḍulīyaka* is well known; for this reason, Amarasiṃha, in reference to *taṇḍulīyaka*, teaches: "*Taṇḍulīyaka* is *alpamāriṣa*. By the word *kusumbha* here, the thorny safflower (*kaṇṭakīkusumbha*) is meant, because the non-thorny safflower is never prohibited. The fresh leaves of both types of safflower are used as vegetables. Since their acquisition is possible as vegetables, the prohibition is meaningful. Matsya also [states]: ... [text continues] ..."
Safflower, citron, wood-apple, licorice, and linseed—
these also should not be offered to the ancestors by one who desires their satisfaction.

The prohibition of the *kapittha* (wood-apple) is because its status as a fruit makes it likely to be included [in offerings]. The prohibition of *madhuka* (licorice) is because its nature as a fragrant substance makes it likely to be included. *Atasī* (linseed) is well known as a vegetable. Sumantu also says: "One should not give *bījapūra* and *māṣa* beans at a *śrāddha*. *Bījapūraka* is the *mātuliṅga*; Amara states: "*phalapūra*, *bījapura*, *rucaka*, and *mātuliṅga* [are synonyms]. *Māṣa* refers to varieties other than the black *māṣa*. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"Those that ferment (*abhiṣava*) and *śatapuṣpā* and *gavedhukā* are always to be avoided."
The fruit produced from the *jambīra* tree should be avoided, while the *kovidāra* fruit should always be rejected.

*Abhiṣavāḥ* refers to fermented liquids, meaning those that have become sour. *Śatapuṣpā* is mentioned by Amarasiṃha in the section on vegetables. *Gavedhukā* is a medicinal plant that produces grain-like seeds from stalks; since it is not fit to be eaten, that grain is prohibited. The *jambīra* fruit is prohibited because it is used as a seasoning for vegetables such as ginger and because it is edible. *Kovidāra* is a specific tree with twin leaves; its flower or fruit is called *kovidāra*, and it is prohibited when it reaches the stage of being a tender vegetable. The same applies to *śāṭyānaya*.
"Whatever is *māriṣa*, *nālikā*, and whatever is red *kalambaka*—all this food of the Asuras does not reach the ancestors. Thus it is said.

*Māriṣa* is *jīvaśāka*. According to the *Vaijayantī*, "māriṣa may be *jīvaśāka*," and it resembles *kuṇḍalīyaka*, though it is thicker than even that. For this very reason, after stating in the *Vaijayantī* that "māriṣa may be *jīvaśāka*," it is further stated: "in this context, the small variety is *kuṇḍalīyaka*. *Nālikā* has a long stalk and bears small fruits at its tip. Since its fruit and its stalk portion would otherwise be included under the category of vegetables (*śāka*), they are here specifically excluded. *Kalambaka* grows in water, has the shape of a bamboo leaf, and is provided with sprouts. It is of two kinds: white and red. Although both would be included as vegetables, because the term "red" (*rakta*) is used as a qualifier, the prohibition does not apply to the white variety. There is also a traditional legal text (*smṛti*) to this effect: [text omitted].
"One should avoid *gāndhārikā* and *paṭola* in the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*). Thus it is said.

"Gāndhārikā is *taṇḍulīyaka*," thus explained by Devasvāmin. [The term refers to] *paṭola* fruits, but not the creeper (*latā*), because the masculine gender alone is correct for the word *latā*; for this very reason, Amarasiṃha has shown it in the masculine among the synonyms for *latā*: "the *paṭola* is *tiktaka* and *paṭu*. Hārīta also says: "One should not offer in a *śrāddha* potherbs such as *pālaṅkyā*, *potikā*, *nālikā*, safflower (*kusumbha*), *surasā*, *niṣpāva*, *caṇaka*, and so forth. *Potikā* is called *sutāhvayā*, according to the definition in the *Vaijayantī*: "The *potikā* is indeed called *sutāhvayā*. That *potikā* should be known as the one whose consumption of leaf-vegetables causes excessive sleep. The remaining terms have been explained previously. Śaṅkha also [says]:
One should avoid black cumin, long pepper, white cumin,
and likewise all types of salt, as well as rose-apple fruits.
Likewise, one should avoid food that has been sneezed upon or struck at during śrāddha ceremonies.

*Kṛṣṇajājī* is black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīraka*). *Bida* is the salt known as *bidalavaṇa*. As for what *śitapākī* is like, it remains to be considered. "Salt" refers to prepared salt, because of that very [author's] statement: "One should avoid all prepared salts and the tips of bamboo. Uśanas also says: "One should avoid *nālikā*, hemp, mushrooms, safflower, bottle-gourd, and *viḍ* salt;
and one should avoid *kumbhī*, *kañcuka*, eggplant, and *kovidāra*."
"One should avoid *gṛñjana*, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), and *piṇḍamūlaka* at a *śrāddha*,
as well as *karañja* and whatever other things have an excessively strong taste or odor."

*Chatrāka* refers to the *ślīndhra* mushroom; as stated in the *Vaijayantī*: "As for the *chatrāka*, it may be *ślīndhra*. Since the leaves and other parts of the *alābu* (bottle-gourd) fruit would also be considered vegetables (*śāka*), they are specifically prohibited here. *Kumbhī* is the *śrīparṇikā*; it is the fruit of the small *kārṣmarya* tree, according to Amarasimha’s definition: "The *śrīparṇikā*, *kumudikā*, *kumbhī*, *kaiṭarya*, and *kaṭphala* [are synonyms]. *Kañcuka* is the round-shaped *alābu* fruit, as stated in the *Vaijayantī*: "The *kuñcukā* is the round *kumbhī*. *Vṛntāka* is the fruit of the thick plant resembling the *bṛhatī*; it is well known as a vegetable along with its stalk. *Kāñjika* is *āranālaka*, which is to say fermented grain-liquid (*dhānyāmla*). *Piṇḍamūlaka* is to be investigated [as its specific identification is uncertain]. *Karañja* is the fruit of the *ciribilva*; Amarasimha states: "The *ciribilva*, *naktamāla*, *karaji*, and *carakañjaka* [are synonyms]. *Gṛñjana* is a specific type of onion. This is intended to illustrate the ten varieties of onions, beginning with garlic (*laśuna*); and those varieties are as follows: [list of varieties omitted in source].
Garlic, long-leaved garlic, picchagandha, mahauṣadha, pharaṇḍa,
palāṇḍu, latārka, and parārikā.

By stating, "The *gṛñjana* and the *yavaneṣṭa*—these are the ten species of onion (*palāṇḍu*)," [the author] demonstrates that the word *palāṇḍu* applies generally even to these ten intermediate species. For this very reason, Amarasiṃha has stated, "The onion (*palāṇḍu*), however, is the *sukandaka*," naming it as a general term. Furthermore, the word *palāṇḍu* also applies to specific intermediate species, as seen in the use of the word as a predicate in the phrase, "The *pharaṇḍa* and the *palāṇḍu*. In the Purāṇa as well, certain specific varieties have been prohibited for the purpose of illustrating the ten types.
Garlic, leeks, onions, and bulbous radishes, as well as kalambī and other such inferior plants deficient in taste and smell, [are forbidden].
Pippala, marica, paṭola, the fruit of bṛhatī, bamboo shoots,
karīra, surasa, sarjaka, and bhūstṛṇa grasses.
"Resins not mentioned in the Vedas, salts, minerals from the earth, and women who are menstruating—these are to be avoided at the time of the Śrāddha rite. Thus it is said.

*Gṛñjana* is a specific type of turmeric-colored bulb, as stated in the *Vaijayantī*: "But *gṛñjana* is that which is turmeric-colored. *Palāṇḍu* is a specific type of white bulb, as stated in the same work: "But *palāṇḍu* is the white bulb, also called *mukundaka*. The distinguishing characteristics of the variety known as garlic (*laśuna*) should be sought in medical treatises (*vaidyaka*) and similar sources. *Vaṃśakarīra* is a bamboo sprout; Amarasimha states: "*Karīra* is the bamboo sprout, not feminine. *Sarjaka* is the yellow *sāla* tree; Amarasimha states: "Now, for the yellow *sāla*, there are *sarjaka*, *asana*, *bandhūkapuṣpa*, *priyaka*, and *jīvaka*. Resins not mentioned in the Vedas means resins other than those prescribed in the Veda as acceptable; this refers to red resins produced from incisions (*vraścana*). The Śruti says: "Now, indeed, that which is red or which exudes from an incision—that must not be eaten; at will, however, [the resin] of another [tree may be eaten]. Salts are those derived from saline soil (*auṣara*), meaning salts produced from alkaline earth (*ūṣara*), i.e., artificial salts. And women who are menstruating—meaning those whose flow has not ceased even after three nights—are also to be avoided. Specific types of milk that are to be avoided are shown in the *Purāṇa*.
The milk of sheep, of camels, and all that which has a single hoof,
as well as that of buffaloes and yaks, should be avoided by one who knows the law.

*Āvikam* is the milk of sheep; *mārgam* is the milk of does; *auṣṭram* is the milk of female camels. *Aikaśapham* is the milk of single-hoofed animals such as mares and the like; *cāmaram* is the milk of the yak. Bharadvāja also says: "Water drawn at night, as well as water from a pond, very little water, the fruit of the *kūśmāṇḍa*, the *vajrakanda* root, and long pepper [should be avoided]."
The taṇḍulīyaka potherb, buffalo milk and curd, legumes,
the shoots of the bamboo, the kovidāra, and gavedhukā grass.
Likewise, horse gram, hemp, citron, and karambha,
as well as all various kinds of dry foods, both those to be chewed and those to be swallowed.
These should never be given away at any śrāddha rite whatsoever.

One should consider what kind of *vajrakanda* is; *śimbikāni* are leguminous grains such as chickpeas (*caṇaka*) and the like; *karambhaḥ* is parched barley flour mixed with curds—thus says Amara: "Karambha is curd-mixed parched barley. However, buffalo ghee should be given, because [the text] specifies "milk and curds. Although it appears from the statement "in every Śrāddha rite" that items such as the fruit of the *kūśmāṇḍa* should not be offered even in the daily Śrāddha, nevertheless, because it is extremely difficult to procure the food for a Śrāddha every single day, this should be explained as referring to all Śrāddha rites other than the daily one. For this very reason, it is stated in the Rāmāyaṇa:
"Rāma gratifies the ancestors with *iṅguda*, *badara*, and *bilva* fruits;
whatever food a man eats, his deities eat that same food. Thus it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata* as well.
The wise likewise avoid even bamboo seeds;
yet in times of distress, prudent sacrificers may even offer sesame oil.
In the event of the unavailability of bulbs, roots, and fruits, the wise have spoken thus:

In this context, the phrase "they avoid" (*varjayanti*) is also connected with the word "oil" (*tailam*). The meaning is that even though oils such as those from *yāvanāla* (a type of grain) are prohibited, the wise say that learned ritualists (*yājñika*) may offer them in the absence of unprohibited bulbs, roots, and fruits. From the negative implication (*vyatireka*), it is understood that when bulbs, roots, and fruits are available, *yāvanāla* and the like must not be given. Furthermore, by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpanaya*), it is understood that they certainly must not be given when delicious food (*mṛṣṭānna*) is available. However, another *smṛti* states that which is to be avoided: "That which is excessively fermented, pungent, salty, tasteless, or corrupted in its essence."
One should avoid that which is characterized by passion (rājasa) and that which is characterized by darkness (tāmasa) in offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).

"Excessively sour" means that, by the loss of its natural flavor due to the influence of time, it has acquired another, loathsome taste. "Pungently salty" means unbearably so due to an excess of salt. Furthermore, in the *Purāṇa*:
"Food that has been placed upon a seat, or even that which has been stepped upon by a foot;
that which is touched by those who have come from impure places, that which is sour, and that which is stale."
Food that has been cooked twice, or scorched, or likewise licked from the surface;
and that which is contaminated by sugar-candy, insects, stones, or hair.
Oil-cake, churned curd, as well as anything excessively salty,
and prepared foods that have been seasoned with salt in one's presence— these are forbidden.
"Those defiled by speech, as well as those struck down by the wicked, and garments shaken off [by others]—these are to be avoided in the rite of *śrāddha*. Thus it is said.

When food has been prepared by the process of cooking ending with the act of setting it down (*avaśrayaṇa*), and is then placed back on the fire after adding water for the sake of softening it—again ending with the act of setting it down—for the purpose of removing excessive heat, this is permitted because of the rule that "all food should be very hot," which allows placing it back on the fire for the sake of heat after cooking. However, in a case where the food was not edible at all due to the first cooking, there is no prohibition against adding water and cooking again for *śrāddha* or for daily meals, since the previous cooking has not been completed. Even in cases where, for the sake of preparing a specific dish, one first cooks with water and so forth and then performs a second cooking with oil and so forth, there is no state of being "twice-boiled" (*dviḥ-svinna*), because the single act of cooking—which results in the specific dish—is one and the same, whether performed in water or in oil. *Paridagdha* means over-burnt. *Agrāvalehita* refers to that which has been tasted by another before the intended purpose for which it was produced was fulfilled. *Śarkarā* refers to specific types of earth as hard as fine pebbles. A *kīṭa* here is a worm that frequents impure places. *Pāṣāṇa* refers to minute particles resembling mustard seeds and the like. *Piṇyāka* is the thickened sesame paste remaining in an oil-press; as Amarasimha states: "The word *piṇyāka* denotes sesame-cake and oil-cake. *Mathita* is curd stirred without the addition of water; as he says: "Buttermilk (*takra*) is curd with water added (*udaśvit*), while *mathita* is [curd] with a quarter part water, half water, or waterless. *Siddha-bhakṣyāḥ* are foods that are naturally fit for consumption, such as *āmalaka* (myrobalan) and the like. *Kṛta-bhakṣyāḥ* are foods made from things like ground black gram (*māṣa*), such as *vaṭaka* (meatballs) and the like. The term *pratyakṣa-lavaṇīkṛtāḥ* ("salted with visible salt") is an adjective qualifying both *siddha-bhakṣyāḥ* and *kṛta-bhakṛtyāḥ*. By the inclusion of the word *pratyakṣa* (visible), it is understood that those salted with salt concealed by another substance, such as curd and the like, are not to be included. Although the avoidance of stale food is already established here because it is prohibited in daily meals, the prohibition of "stale" (*paryuṣita*) must nevertheless be understood as intended to exclude even the transformation of flour products like barley and wheat, which are otherwise permitted in daily meals, from being used in *śrāddha*. Furthermore, regarding vegetables such as *kūśmāṇḍa* (pumpkin/gourd) which are very abundant, since no fault is heard of them, there would be no reason to avoid them; however, a fault is indeed shown in another *smṛti*: [The text continues: ...In the case of substances that are excessively abundant, such as *kūśmāṇḍa* and others, there is no cessation [of consumption] simply because no fault is mentioned; rather, a fault is also demonstrated in another *smṛti*.
The kūśmāṇḍa fruit, buffalo milk, āḍhakī beans, black mustard, chickpeas, and kidney beans destroy the śrāddha; of this there is no doubt.
Having offered piṇḍālūka, tuṇḍīra, karamarda, nālikā, kūśmāṇḍa,
and many-seeded fruits at a śrāddha, one goes to the lower realms.

[223] Regarding *piṇḍāluka* and *tuṇḍīra*, one should consider what they are like. *Karamarda* is the fruit that ripens black; as Amarasimha states: "In the case of the *karamardaka*, there are the *kṛṣṇapākaphala*, *āvigna*, and *suṣeṇa*. "Many-seeded" refers to the citron (*mātuluṅga*) and similar fruits. Since the prohibition of everything forbidden for human consumption does not necessarily establish its prohibition in the context of a *śrāddha*, the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* has stated this for the purpose of prohibiting them even in a *śrāddha*: "Milk and other products from buffaloes are to be avoided, as well as whatever is declared inedible."

By the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), buffalo curd is understood, based on the Smṛti of Bhṛgu: "Buffalo milk and curd... Buffalo meat is also included, as stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "...and likewise one should avoid buffalo meats at a Śrāddha. The meaning is that whatever is proclaimed in the prohibitive scriptures as unfit for consumption by virtue of being for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha) must all be avoided at a Śrāddha; that is to say, it must not be given in the rite of Śrāddha.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, regarding substances to be avoided in the rite of *śrāddha*;
now, by way of digression, some statements concerning substances to be avoided in daily meals are recorded.
Regarding this, Devala says:
"They declare food that has turned sour or has stood overnight to be unfit for consumption,
with the exception of honey, roasted flour, prepared foods, clarified butter, and molasses."
In this regard, the meaning of the word *śukta* has been shown by Bṛhaspati:
"That which is extremely sour is called *śukta*; it is censured by those who discourse on Brahman."

This is its meaning: that which is rice, soup, and so forth, naturally non-sour or slightly sour, having lost its own flavor due to being kept overnight, on the same day, or for a long period of time, and becoming excessively sour—that alone is designated as *śukta* (fermented sour) in the world. As for substances like *kāñjika* (sour gruel), they are naturally extremely sour. "Stale" (*paryuṣita*) means that which has been cooked by fire and then kept overnight; it is unfit to be eaten not only at a *śrāddha* meal but also at daily meals and the like. Honey and such things, however, may be eaten even if stale. "Edibles" refers to cakes and the like. Even in the case of honey, cooking is performed—just as with molasses—for the sake of improving its flavor; honey cooked on the day after the day of eating does not become "stale."
"A twice-born man must not eat food that is forbidden by the scriptures, such as various kinds of edible foods.
This is the meaning: "He shall not eat food from a market stall, nor what has been cooked twice, nor what is stale;
nor shall a Brahmin eat ghee or oil that has fallen on the ground due to [his] nails."
Yama declared that to be impure, equal to the eating of cow-flesh.
Oils, salt, and condiments that are given with the hand do not reach the giver; the eater consumes only sin.
One should not consume ghee, oil, salt, water, or milk-rice (pāyasa) given by a Śūdra with only one hand.

"A twice-born man shall not eat food and other items that are forbidden by such scriptural injunctions as these, nor food that is purchased from a market. Regarding this prohibition, the same author states an exception in certain cases:
"Cakes, flour-meal, parched grain, buttermilk, curd, ghee, and honey—these may be eaten when purchased in the market, provided they are not smeared with the contents of the vessel. [225]

There is also an exception to the prohibition against food cooked twice: "One should not eat anything that is cooked twice. That which is called "cooked twice" is defined as follows: even though a substance is already fit for consumption after the first cooking, it is cooked again to produce another quality, such as softness. Thus, in the case of bitter vegetables and the like, where they are not fit for consumption by the mere first cooking because they possess an unpalatable bitter taste, but become so once that bitterness is moderated, there is no state of being "cooked twice," since the first cooking was incomplete. Furthermore, it should be understood that when a specific dish is prepared by first cooking it with water and then cooking it again with oil or other substances, it is still not considered "cooked twice"; this is because the single act of cooking—performed with the purpose of achieving a specific edible result—is one and the same, regardless of whether it is carried out in water or in oil. Yama states an exception to the rule: "One should not eat stale food."
Cakes, parched grain flour, roasted grains, fried cakes and barley meal, vegetables, meat, cakes, soup, and rice cooked with sesame; these are the foods.
Barley gruel, milk-rice, and whatever else is mixed with oil or fat—
all this may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, but one should avoid anything that has turned sour.

*Apūpas* are preparations of barley and wheat flour, such as *maṇḍakas* and the like. *Karambhas* are parched grains (*saktus*) mixed with curd. *Dhānās* are roasted barley and rice grains. *Vaṭakas* are well-known small balls made from the flour of black gram (*māṣa*), fried in oil. *Śāka* (vegetables) and *māṃsa* (meat) must be cooked on the previous day; they are not permitted if merely brought on the following day, as that would constitute being stale (*paryuṣita*) by that measure alone. Thus, it should be understood that even if boiled rice (*odana*) cooked on the previous day is prepared as a specific vegetable dish by adding condiments on that very same day, it may still be eaten despite being stale. *Saktus* are the flour of roasted barley and rice grains. The mention of *apūpa* again is for the purpose of including other flour-based preparations, such as those made from chickpeas (*caṇaka*) and so forth, which are generally similar to *apūpas*. *Sūpa* is a side dish (*vyañjana*) made from green gram (*mudga*), pigeon pea (*āḍhakī*), and the like. *Kṛsara* is rice mixed with roasted sesame powder. *Yavāgū* is food in the form of a thin gruel mixed with a small amount of rice flour. *Pāyasa* is rice boiled in milk. Furthermore, whatever other food than those mentioned—such as *odana* and the rest—is mixed with fat (*sneha*) and saturated with a fatty substance such as curd or ghee, it is all edible provided it has not turned sour (*aśukta*). However, when stale *apūpas* and the like, or *odana* and the like mixed with fat, have become sour, then even that should be avoided; this is the meaning. Following the recurring term "not to be eaten," Vasiṣṭha also says: "One may eat stale food at will, provided it has been saturated with curd or ghee. In the phrase "stale food," the word "not to be eaten" (from the previous context) is connected. The meaning is: one may indeed consume or eat stale food if it has been saturated with curd or ghee. For this very reason, Manu says: [The text continues with further citations and explanations regarding the conditions under which stale food is permissible.]
Whatever food, whether hard or soft, is mixed with oil or ghee and is not otherwise censured,
may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, provided it is the remnant of an oblation.

In the context of the phrase "one should consume," Āpastamba also states: "Cooked food that has been kept overnight, having placed it in water. The meaning is that when cooked food has been placed in water and left overnight, one may then consume that food even though it is stale (*paryuṣita*). Thus, one should understand that although the liquid residue from rice-washing water—which was placed [in a vessel], left overnight, and has become stale in the process of producing *kāñjika*—is not fit for consumption, this does not apply to the *kāñjika* produced from it; indeed, such *kāñjika* is certainly not unfit for consumption. In the context of the phrase "one should eat," Śākala and Likhita also state: "One should not eat what is stale, except for products of curd, molasses, wheat, and barley flour. The word "not stale" is connected with the recurring word "one should eat. Although curd, like molasses, is not prepared by cooking and thus is not technically "stale," its exclusion might seem redundant. Nevertheless, being prepared by cooking on another day is not the defining factor for staleness; rather, it is the fact of being prepared for the purpose of eating. Since curd is also prepared for the purpose of eating, it possesses the quality of being stale, and therefore its specific exclusion is indeed meaningful. Yājñavalkya, however, says "one should avoid what is stale" in order to provide a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to his own general rule.

Food that has become stale may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat, even if it has been kept for a long time; likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk products may be eaten even if they are not mixed with oil or fat.

The word "long-standing" (*cirasaṃsthitam*) should be construed with the phrase "preparations of wheat, barley, and milk products" (*godhūmayavagorasavikriyāḥ*) by changing its form to the feminine plural, "long-standing [products]" (*cirasaṃsthitāḥ*). For this very reason, Manu says: "Even long-standing food that is not mixed with oil, as well as all products derived from barley and wheat, and indeed preparations of milk, may be eaten by the twice-born."

Preparations from wheat include *maṇḍaka* and the like; preparations from barley include roasted flour (*saktu*) and the like. Cow’s milk is *gorasa*, and its derivatives include *kūrcikā* and so forth, since Amarasimha states, "kūrcikā is a derivative of milk. Regarding derivatives of cow’s milk as well, one should observe what Yama stated: "If it has turned sour (*śukta*), one should avoid it. It was previously stated in this section that everything mentioned as fit for eating, even if stale, must be avoided at a *śrāddha*. Therefore, one should not fall into the error of thinking that because something is fit for eating, it is therefore not prohibited at a *śrāddha*. However, Śaṅkha says that among substances that have turned sour, some may still be fit for eating.
Among sour substances (*śukta*), curd is edible, as are other things derived from curd;
likewise, that which is cooked in a vessel of fermented gruel (*ṛbīṣa*) may be eaten when mixed with clarified butter—this is the established rule.

*Ūṣma* is heat without fire; that which is cooked by this is *ṛbīṣapakva*. This means, for instance, that which is cooked by the heat residing in a heap of grain and the like. And so, Dhūrtasvāmin, in explaining the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, "One should eat what is cooked without *ṛbīṣa*," stated in his commentary: "Heat without fire is *ṛbīṣa*; a prohibition is made regarding that which is cooked by it. Even *ṛbīṣapakva* food that has turned sour (*śukta*) may be eaten if it is mixed with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*); the meaning is that it is not [permissible] if it is devoid of that. That which originates from curd, such as buttermilk (*takra*), fresh butter (*navanīta*), and so forth, is "fit to be eaten" (*bhakṣya*); the meaning is that it is worthy of consumption. Yama, however, states that in times of distress, sour food becomes fit for consumption through washing.
A twice-born man should never eat foods that have turned sour;
however, if he is in a state of distress (*āpaddharma*), they become faultless once they have been washed.
Thus, when stale food is washed in an emergency, it becomes fit for consumption. For this very reason, permission for its eating was granted by that same [author]:
"That which is mixed with lentils or beans, as well as that which is stale—one should indeed eat it after having washed it and having sprinkled it [with ghee]."

Devala states that even edible items such as grain in the form of seeds should not be consumed when not in times of distress, just like food that has stood overnight, because it is utterly improper to destroy the cause of future abundant fruit:
"A wise man should not consume seeds except in cases of illness;
for by consuming them, he would destroy the infinite fruits of those seeds. [229]

The meaning is that since these seeds have infinite fruits, one who consumes them would destroy them; therefore, one should not consume seeds except in times of distress. He [the same author] says that even food that is pure by nature should be avoided if it is defiled by contact with dead flies and the like:
"One should avoid even pure food if it is defiled by flies, worms, or small creatures, or even by hair, body hair, or nails."

The phrase “in the absence of distress” (*anāpadi*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. For this very reason, Sumantu says: “Food defiled by hair, insects, sneezing, or speech; smelled by dogs; looked upon; not curd; stale; cooked again; or gazed at by a *caṇḍāla*—is unfit to be eaten, except when touched with gold and water. “Defiled by sneezing or speech” means spoiled by the sound produced through the force of a sneeze. The plural number in “by dogs” (*śvabhiḥ*) is for the purpose of including those animals mentioned in other Smṛtis—such as cows and others—whose smelling or looking causes impurity. “Not curd” means stale food, excluding curd and similar items that have been specifically exempted from the category of stale food. “Cooked again” means twice-boiled. This is what is meant: having abandoned pure food that has become defiled through contact with flies and the like, one should eat food that is not defiled. If such food is unavailable, however, one should remove the flies and the like, and after performing a sprinkling with water or touching with gold for the sake of purifying the food, one may eat it. Devala states what must necessarily be avoided even when no other non-defiled food is available:
One should not consume food that has been licked by dogs, cats, crows, cocks, or monkeys, for it is entirely impure in every respect.
"Dhvāṅkṣa" means a crow. Also in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"One should never eat what remains after a Śūdra has eaten, even if it is placed in a vessel.

By this, one should take [the food] out from the vessel, place it in another dish, and then give it. One should not eat even that which is touched by garlic and the like, just as with the leavings of a Śūdra. And so it is said in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*.
"That which has been touched by liquor, garlic, or the like, or is mixed with nectar and so forth, is said to be defiled by contact; one should treat it as the leavings of a Śūdra."

"Pīyūṣa" is the milk of a cow or other animal that has recently calved, according to Amara’s definition: "pīyūṣa is fresh milk. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), items such as mushrooms touched by [forbidden things] are included. One should not eat even vegetables and the like that are defiled by their very nature (*jātyā*), just as those defiled by contact (*saṃsarga-duṣṭa*); for Paiṭhīnasi records: "Among vegetables, the eggplant (*vṛntāka*), the *nālikā*, the *pota*, the *kusumbha*, and the *aśmantaka* are not to be eaten. The *vṛntāka* is a fruit resembling the *bṛhatī* plant, thick and growing from a stalk; it is well known as a vegetable along with its stem portion. The *nālikā* has a long stalk and bears small fruits at its tip; since both its fruit and its stalk portion would otherwise be considered edible vegetables, they are here prohibited. The *pota* is the same as *potikā*, according to the *Vaijayantī* lexicon: "the *potikā* is called *sutā*. That whose consumption of leaf-vegetables causes excessive sleep should be known as *sutāhvayā*. However, we must consider what its actual form is. Only the white variety of *vṛntāka* is forbidden to be eaten.
One should avoid the gaṇḍūla, the white-branited eggplant, and the pumpkin.

Thus, because Devala prohibits a specific variety of eggplant (*vṛntāka*), the principle that "the prohibition of a particular case implies the permission of the remainder" leads to the understanding that the eating of eggplants other than the white variety is permitted. *Gaṇḍūla* is the fruit of the *kaṇḍūlā* plant; it causes extreme itching, is covered in many hairs, and grows during the rainy season. For this very reason, Amarasimha stated: "The *kaṇḍūlā* is the *pravṛṣāyaṇī*. *Kūśmāṇḍa* is round like a jar (*kumbha*) and resembles a short gourd (*alābu*). *Kusumbha* that is devoid of thorns is inedible, because Devasvāmin has stated: "There exists a prohibition in another *Smṛti* regarding *kusumbha* characterized by the absence of thorns. Furthermore, Uśanas has pointed out the fault in eating eggplant, *nālikā*, *pota*, and *kusumbha*.

"By eating safflower, nālikā greens, eggplant, or potika, even a twice-born who has mastered the Vedānta becomes fallen. Thus it is said. In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, certain vegetables are mentioned by way of illustration among those that are "defiled by species."
Garlic, leeks, onions, mushrooms, eggplants, lotus stalks, bottle gourds, and anything corrupted by its species— one should avoid these.

The meaning is that one should know substances such as garlic (*laśuna*) to be defiled by their very nature (*jāti*), even in the absence of contact with something else. The result of knowing them to be defiled by nature is desisting from them, even when there is no contact with something actually defiled. The specific property that distinguishes the particular substance called garlic should be sought in medical treatises (*vaidyaka*) and similar works; for *laśuna*, *gṛñjana*, and *palāṇḍu* are types of onion (*palāṇḍu*). Among these, *gṛñjana* is a specific variety characterized by a yellowish-red color, as stated in the *Vaijayantī*: "The *gṛñjana* is yellowish-red. *Palāṇḍu* is a specific type of white bulb, because it is said in that same work: "In the case of *palāṇḍu*, however, the white bulb is the *mukundaka*. This, then, is the designation of the three specific types of onions beginning with garlic.
Garlic, long-leaved garlic, picchagandha, mahauṣadha,
varaṇya, onion, latārka, and parārikā.
Gṛñjana and yavaneṣṭa—these are the ten varieties of onion.

This concludes the description of the ten kinds of onions mentioned above. The distinctions among the various types of great medicinal herbs (*mahauṣadha*), forest products, and so forth, should also be consulted in medical treatises and similar works. *Kavaka* refers to the *chatrāka* mushroom. *Vārtāka* is the fruit of the large *bṛhatī* plant known as the small eggplant (*kṣudravārtāka*); it is slightly thicker than the fruit of the *bṛhatī* known as *kaṇṭakārikā*. Regarding the fault of eating mushrooms, Yama has shown:
"Those who eat *chatrāka* mushrooms, whether grown on the ground or on trees, one should know them to be slayers of Brahmins, despised among those who discourse upon the Veda."

Hārīta also states that certain items are to be avoided even in the absence of contact with impure substances: "One should not eat the fruits of the *vaṭa*, *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *dadhittha*, *nīpa*, or *mātuluṅga*. *Dadhittha* is the fruit of the *kapittha*; *nīpa* is the leaf of the *kadamba*. The remaining terms are self-evident. Manu also says: "One should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by cutting [the wood], the *śelu* fruit, and the colostrum (*pīyūṣa*) of a cow."

"Red tree-exudations" refers to lac and the like. "Exudations produced from incisions" includes those such as the exudation of the *śālmalī* tree. Because of the inclusion of the term "red," there is no prohibition against substances that are exudations but are pale-red in color, such as asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), nor against white-colored substances such as camphor. The *śelu* is the tree known as *śleṣmāntaka*. "Pīyūṣa" is fresh milk. Regarding the specific case of cow's *pīyūṣa*, a distinction is shown in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "The scum of clarified butter, the cream of clarified butter, the *pīyūṣa* of a cow while still wet with milk, or curd mixed with jaggery and sprinkled with black pepper, as well as curd that has stood overnight [are forbidden]."
The buttermilk is shattered, undrinkable, and has lost its sweetness and its froth.

The meaning is as follows: having extracted [the butter] from clarified butter (*ghṛta*), only its froth or its scum (*agra*) should not be drunk. Likewise, the colostrum (*pīyūṣa*) of a cow while she is still wet—meaning as long as the state of being moist and dusty persists in the cow at the time of birth and continues in the womb—the milk is unfit for consumption. Similarly, curd mixed with jaggery and black pepper, as well as that which has turned sour, is also unfit for consumption. Likewise, buttermilk (*takra*) that has "burst"—meaning it is devoid of the churning of a ladle, or has split on its own due to heating over fire or otherwise, or has become covered with foam after standing for many days—and which has lost its sweetness due to excessive acidity—is unfit for consumption. Yājñavalkya also states the types of milk that are to be avoided.
"One should avoid the milk of a cow that is in heat, of one whose calf has not yet passed ten days, and of one that is nursing. Thus it is said.

Regarding this, the milk of a *saṃdhinī* cow is to be avoided; this has been clearly stated by Hārīta: "A *saṃdhinī* is one longing for a bull (*vṛṣasyantī*); one should not drink her milk, for she is in her season (*ṛtumad*). *Vṛṣasyantī* means desirous, that is to say, possessing a desire for sexual intercourse. Her milk is "in season"; the meaning is that it belongs to one who is in her fertile period. By this, the following is stated: one should not drink her milk for as long as the desire for sexual intercourse persists. Therefore, it should be understood that once the desire for sexual intercourse has ceased, her milk is not prohibited. The meaning of "one should avoid the milk of a cow within ten days of calving" (*anirdaśāyāḥ*) is: one should avoid the milk of one from whom ten nights have not yet elapsed since birth. This is intended to indicate the time of the cessation of the flow of blood (*rajonivṛtti*). Consequently, if the flow of blood ceases before ten nights, there is no prohibition in that case. However, it should be understood that even after ten nights, if the flow of blood continues, the prohibition remains. For this very reason, having stated, "One should not drink the milk of a newly-calved cow because she is still in her flow of blood," Hārīta says: "Some say after seven nights, others say after ten nights; those who know the Dharma say it becomes *pīyūṣa* (colostrum) after a month. The meaning is: according to some, the milk of a newly-calved cow becomes *pīyūṣa* even after seven nights; according to others, it becomes *pīyūṣa* even after ten nights. In these views of seven nights and so forth, the rule should be understood according to the actual cessation of the flow of blood. The meaning of "one should avoid the milk of a cow without its calf" (*avatsāyāḥ*) is: *avatsā* means devoid of a calf, that is, one whose calf is dead. One should avoid her milk for as long as the grief of separation from the calf persists. For this very reason, under the recurring phrase "one should not drink [milk]," Hārīta states: "Because the one whose calf is killed is overcome by grief, and because the newly-calved cow is in her flow of blood. It should not be argued that since the phrase "because she is overcome by grief" is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) in the form of a statement of reason, one should not drink the milk of a cow whose calf is dead even when the grief has ceased. This is because of the mention of the reason "because she is in her flow of blood" (*sarajastvāt*). Therefore, "because she is overcome by grief" is indeed a reason, not an *arthavāda*. Nor should it be argued that "because she is in her flow of blood" is also merely an *arthavāda* in the form of a statement of reason and not a reason itself—how then can its status as a reason be determined by association with that? It is because the term "because she is in her flow of blood" is employed precisely with the intention of stating a reason. If it were not employed with the intention of stating a reason, then the intended meaning—that the milk of a newly-calved cow may be drunk when the flow of blood ceases either before or after ten nights—would remain unestablished. Furthermore, the immediately preceding passage by him, "Some say after seven nights, others say after ten nights; those who know the Dharma say it becomes *pīyūṣa* after a month," would be inconsistent. Therefore, the connection of "because she is in her flow of blood" is strictly as a reason, not as an *arthavāda*. Because of its association with that, "because she is overcome by grief" is also connected as a reason, not as an *arthavāda*. Enough of this excessive elaboration. The inclusion of the term "those who know the Dharma" (*dharmavidaḥ*) is intended to indicate that there is no doubt regarding the cessation of the flow of blood in that context. Therefore, when the cessation of the flow of blood is certain even after seven nights, there is no loss of merit (*dharma*) in drinking that milk. Like the *pīyūṣa* of a cow, the *pīyūṣa* of goats and buffaloes is also unfit to be drunk. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "The milk of cows, buffaloes, and goats [is forbidden] within ten days [of calving]. The ellipsis is "the milk is not to be drunk. Gautama also mentions milk to be avoided: "And [the milk] of a *saṃdhinī*, a *yamasū*, and a *syandinī*. The ellipsis is "the milk is to be avoided. A *syandinī* is one whose teats naturally leak milk. A *yamasū* is one who gives birth to twins. Bodhāyana also says: "Milk is unfit to be drunk from a cow without its calf or from one whose calf is another. Śaṅkha also says: "The milk of all two-teated animals is to be avoided as unfit for consumption. Manu also [says the same].
And of all the animals of the forest, except for the female buffalo. Thus it is said.

“Except for the buffalo” means excluding wild buffaloes. In the phrase “of deer,” there is a connection with the word *payaḥ* (milk) heard previously; thus, what is fit and unfit to be consumed is being taught. Although the use of the masculine gender in the word *mṛgāṇām* suggests male individuals, nevertheless, one should understand that because of the connection with the word *payaḥ*, the intention is merely the individual substance itself, so as to avoid the impossibility of such a connection. Consequently, since no incompatibility is perceived, its connection with the word *payaḥ* is indeed appropriate. Gautama also says: “The milk of sheep, camels, and single-hoofed animals is always unfit to be drunk”; here “always” means even in the state of being fresh. *Auṣṭram* is the milk of a female camel; * aikaśapham* is the milk of a mare or other single-hoofed animal. Thus, it should be understood that the milk of cows, buffaloes, and goats alone is drinkable, and not that of any other. For this very reason, Śaṅkha says:
One should specify that among milks, those of the buffalo, cow, and goat are fit for consumption;
however, Āpastamba states that for anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa, the milk of a tawny cow (kapilā) is to be avoided:
"Whether he be a Kṣatriya established in his duty, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra..."
The doer of unmeritorious deeds who drinks the milk of a tawny cow goes to the hells.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that one should diligently avoid the milk of a tawny cow (*kapilā*) except when it belongs to a Brāhmaṇa. Regarding even a Brāhmaṇa, the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa* demonstrates that there is a fault in drinking the milk of a tawny cow other than what remains after an oblation: "The Śūdra who drinks the milk of a tawny cow is cooked in hell; a Brāhmaṇa may drink the remnant of an oblation, otherwise he becomes a beast."

If a Brahmin drinks the remainder of an oblation (*hutaśeṣa*), he retains his status as a Brahmin even in a future birth; otherwise, if he drinks the milk of a tawny cow (*kapilā*) other than the remainder of an oblation, the meaning is that he becomes an animal in a future birth. From the very injunction to avoid [ordinary] milk, it should be inferred—just as one avoids what has been touched by nectar—that anything touched by it must also be avoided. Precisely because of the injunction to avoid milk, the avoidance of its derivatives, such as *kūrca* (curdled milk) and so forth, is established, since milk still exists within those derivatives. For this very reason, it is established in the Mīmāṃsā that when milk is to be avoided, one must also avoid preparations such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Therefore, Śaṅkha prescribes an expiation for consuming forbidden derivatives of milk, on the grounds that by eating them, one has committed a transgression of a prohibition.
"A wise person, being diligent and composed, should perform a seven-night vow with effort upon eating the derivatives of those milks which are not fit for consumption. Thus,

Yājñavalkya has stated that even the derivatives of edible grains and so forth— whether prepared according to the Vedic path or the worldly path for the purpose of offering to the deities— are unfit for consumption prior to the actual offering.
"For the sake of the deity, [one should offer] sacrificial oblation, *śigru*, and red *vraścana*. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that just as one should avoid the milk of a cow in heat (*saṃdhinī*) and so forth, so too one should avoid food intended for the gods—that is, food prepared according to worldly custom for the purpose of offering to deities—as well as the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and *śigru* (horseradish) prepared according to the Vedic path. Thus, although it appears that food for the deities and sacrificial oblations like the *puroḍāśa* should always be avoided—just like the milk of a cow in heat—the prohibition should nevertheless be understood to apply only prior to the actual offering to the deity. For this very reason, Yama has stated, citing the case of offerings made for the sake of ancestors and other deities:

"Whatever food, whether solid, soft, or liquid, is cooked in the house, none of it should ever be consumed without first being offered to the ancestors. Here, *śigru* refers to the *śobhāñjana*. Furthermore, that which has red flowers is to be avoided, not that which has white flowers; for Devasvāmin stated in another *Smṛti*: "One should avoid the red *śigru*," thereby indicating that the prohibition applies specifically to the particular [variety]. Just as things belonging to a despised genus such as the *śigru* are to be avoided, so too are things from a despised source to be avoided; and thus says Aṅgiras:
The wise have declared that food is always censurable in two ways:
that which is censurable by birth and likewise that which is censurable by its source.
"One should understand that the food of those whose food is unfit is 'condemned by reason of its source' (*āśrayagarhita*).

That food which consists of garlic and the like should be known as 'condemned by its nature' (*jātigarhita*). This means that one should recognize the food of those whose food is forbidden as being "condemned by its source. As for that edible food such as garlic (*laśuna*), *gṛñjana*, mushrooms (*chatrāka*), and so forth—which is prohibited by Manu and others solely by virtue of its nature as garlic and so on, even in the absence of contact with a defiled substance—that is to be known as "condemned by its nature. Yājñavalkya, however, states "condemned by its source" explicitly.
[The food] of misers, bound thieves, eunuchs, actors,
flute-players, those accused of crimes, usurers, courtesans, and those initiated into a guild;
[One should not study] from a physician, one who is ill, one who is angry, an unchaste woman, one who is intoxicated, or an enemy;
nor from one who is cruel, fierce, fallen, a *vrātya*, a hypocrite, or one who eats the remnants of others' food.
[The impurity lasts for one day] for those whose wives have no husbands, for goldsmiths, for those who have been conquered by their wives,
for village-priests, for sellers of weapons, for blacksmiths, for weavers, and for those who subsist by keeping dogs.
[The same applies] for those who wash clothes, dyers, leather-workers, those born together with their parents,
slanderers, liars, as well as wheelwrights and bards.
"The food of these [persons] must not be eaten, as well as that of a seller of Soma.
A miser (*kadarya*) is one who, out of greed, neither consumes nor gives away his wealth even though it exists. And so says the *Smṛti*:
"He who would cause suffering to himself, to his religious duties, and to his sons and wife..."
He who, out of greed, neglects his parents and dependents is known as a miser.

*Baddha* means one who is bound or fettered, or one who has not achieved his purpose. *Coraklība* are well-known terms for a thief and a eunuch, respectively. A *raṅgāvatārī* is a wrestler or the like. A *vaiṇa* is a lute-player. An *abhiśasta* is one accused of having committed an act that causes loss of caste (*patanīya*). *Vārdhuṣya* is living by prohibited interest; by this term, one who practices such usury is indicated. A *gaṇikā* is a prostitute. A *gaṇa* is a corporation or assembly. A *dīkṣī* is one who possesses the consecration known as *dīkṣā*, produced by the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice and other rites. Although it might appear from this Smṛti that the food of a consecrated person (*dīkṣita*) is unfit to be eaten from the performance of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice until the completion of the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice—since that consecration ceases only with the *avabhṛtha*—nevertheless, based on the Śruti text, "When the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice is concluded, one should eat in the house of the sacrificer," and so forth, it should be understood that even while the consecration called *dīkṣā* still exists, the food is unfit to be eaten prior to the completion of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice; this is what is stated by this Smṛti as well. A *cikitsaka* is a physician. An *ātura* is one afflicted by a "sinful disease" (*pāparoga*). These sinful diseases have been shown by Devala: [Devala's list follows... ...and so forth. A *kuṇḍagolaka* is one born from a woman who has conceived before marriage or after the husband's death, respectively. A *sāmudrika* is one who subsists by reading bodily marks. A *sūcaka* is a slanderer. A *kitava* is a gambler. A *śvavat* is one who keeps dogs. A *śilpa* is an artist or craftsman. A *devalaka* is one who subsists by officiating for temples. A *pākarika* is a cook. A *dhvajika* is a liquor-seller. A *māṃsika* is a butcher. A *vāgurika* is a hunter. A *kaivarta* is a fisherman. A *nāstika* is an atheist. A *maitrīka* is a spy or messenger. A *bandī* is a bard. A *rakṣaka* is a guard. A *pāradārika* is an adulterer. A *pārivindaka* is one who marries before his elder brother.
