Vātavyādhi, urinary stones, leprosy, diabetes, abdominal enlargement, fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, and dysentery—
these eight are proclaimed as the diseases of sin.

Vātavyādhi refers to paralysis (pakṣamāraka) and similar ailments. Aśmarī is urinary obstruction (mūtrakṛcchra). Meha refers to diabetes (madhumeha) and the like. Udara refers to dropsy (jalodara) and similar conditions. The others are well known. *Kruddha* is one whose anger is held within. *Puṃścalī* is an unchaste woman. *Matta* is one intoxicated with pride in wealth and so forth; one who is habitually contemptuous of others. *Vidviṣ* is an enemy. *Krūra* is merciless. *Ugra* is one intent on inflicting suffering upon others. *Patita* is one guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). *Vrātya* is one for whom the *Sāvitrī* initiation has been lost. *Ḍāmbhika* is one who practices dharma solely with the motive of gaining fame, profit, and the like. *Ucchiṣṭabhojī* is one whose habit is to eat food left over after another has eaten. *Avīrastrī* is a woman without a husband or son, according to Amarasimha’s definition: "An *avīrā* is one without a husband or son. *Svarṇakāra* is a goldsmith who fashions ornaments such as bracelets and crowns. *Strījita* is one who is subservient to his wife in all matters. *Grāmayājī* is a priest who officiates for many villages. *Śastravikrayī* is one who lives by selling weapons, such as swords. *Śvavṛtti* is one who follows the "dog's way of life," meaning a servant. *Nṛśaṃsa* is a murderer. *Rājā* is the protector of the countryside and cities. *Rajaka* is a dyer of clothes and the like. *Vadhajīvī* is one who lives by the slaughter of living beings. *Celadhāvaḥ* is a washerman. *Surājīva* is a seller of liquor. *Sahopapativeśmā* is one whose house is shared with a paramour of his wife. The meaning is that the food of these members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) who are defiled by faults such as miserliness, and the food of a member of the three castes defiled by the fault of selling *Soma* plants and the like, is food that is indirectly defiled due to its connection with a master defiled by faults such as miserliness, and must not be eaten. Even though the food of one initiated for a sacrifice (*dīkṣita*) lacks the kind of defect caused by its source, it is nonetheless unfit to be eaten solely by the force of the scriptural injunction. Paiṭhīnasi states in another manner that other food belonging to the three castes is also unfit to be eaten if it is censurable in its own source: "The food of an astrologer (*sāṃvatsarika*), a bell-ringer (*ghaṇṭika*), and a village carpenter (*grāmakūṭa*) is poison; the blood of a younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivitti*), an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him (*parivividāna*), one whose offspring is pierced (*viddha-prajanana*), the husband of a *punarbhū* (*didhiṣūpati*), and the son of a *punarbhū* is like blood. An astrologer is a *sāṃvatsarika*. A *ghāṇṭika* is defined by the author of the *Nighaṇṭu*: "A *ghāṇṭika* is an artisan of bells at the time of the awakening of kings. A *grāmakūṭa* is a carpenter in a village who is independent of others; Amarasimha says, "A *kūṭa-takṣa* is one who is not subordinate. "Poison" means it is unfit to be consumed like poison. When an elder brother remains unmarried while a younger brother takes a wife, the elder is a *parivitti*. When a younger brother performs the rites of procreation (*ādhāna*) which the elder has not performed, that younger brother is a *parivividāna*. A *viddha-prajanana* is one whose penis is pierced. A *didhiṣūpati* is the husband of a *punarbhū*. "Blood" means it is unfit to be consumed like blood. Yama also says: [The text continues with further verses from Yama.]
One who lives by the wheel, a musician, a gambler, a thief, a liquor-seller,
one who lives off his wife, and those who teach or perform sacrifices for Śūdras.

[241] “The potter, the painter, the usurer, and the seller of leather”—the phrase “whose food is not to be eaten” is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. A *cakropajīvī* is a cartwright; a *dhvajī* is a seller of liquor; a *kulāla* is one who subsists by the profession of a potter; the remaining terms are well known. Also, in another *Smṛti*:
“Likewise, the food of a king’s servant and the food of a thief, and likewise...”
Food [received] during birth-impurity or death-impurity would cause even one dwelling in heaven to fall.

"He who eats the food of one who is arrogant, foolish, of wicked conduct, evil-minded, or lacking in faith, is indeed a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā). The food of royal servants and the like is extremely censurable; the intention is that it should be avoided with great effort. "Avalipta" means proud. The food even of those such as the *sāṃvatsarika* (astrologers) and *ghāṇṭika* (bell-ringers), though included among the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), is prohibited. However, this does not apply to those belonging to the *śūdra* caste and others, because their food is prohibited by its very nature. And so it is stated in another *Smṛti*:
A Kṣatriya may always eat at the house of a Brāhmaṇa, and on the festival days (parvan) at that of a Vaiśya;
but for a Śūdra, it is never permitted.

The meaning is: "in the context of," that is, "in the great festivals such as marriages" that are under discussion. In the passage beginning with "of a Brāhmaṇa," the word "food" (*anna*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus, the food of Kṣatriyas may be eaten on the *parvan* days; however, the food of stingy (*kadarya*) and other such Kṣatriyas must not be eaten even on *parvan* days. The food of Vaiśyas may not be eaten except at great festivals such as marriages; it should be understood that the food of stingy and other such Vaiśyas must not be eaten even during marriage and other festive occasions. By the statement "never [the food] of a Śūdra," it is implied that one should especially avoid the food of those of lower status than a Śūdra, namely those born in the reverse order (*pratiloma*). Yājñavalkya [2.242], however, states that the food of certain Śūdras may also be eaten.
Among Śūdras, the food of a slave, a cowherd, a family friend,
and a sharecropper may be eaten, as well as that of a barber and one who offers himself [as a servant].

A *dāsa* is one who has been purchased and so forth. A *gopāla* is a protector of cattle. A *kulamitra* is a friend descended through the lineage of fathers and grandfathers. A *sīra* is a plough; by this, the fruit of agriculture is indicated, and thus the fruit of agriculture is expressed by the term *ardhasīra*. A *nāpita* is a Śūdra who performs work such as shaving and the like. These—the *dāsa* and the others—are those among the Śūdras whose food may be eaten. Furthermore, the meaning is that any Śūdra who offers himself like a purchased servant, surrendering [himself] saying "I am yours," his food may also be eaten. And here, only those *dāsa*s and others who belong to oneself are intended. For this very reason, Devala says:
One's own slave, a barber, a cowherd, a potter, and a farmer—
these five born of Śūdra wombs may have their food eaten even by Brāhmaṇas.

And thus, it should be understood that food belonging to the servants and others of a particular person is to be eaten by that person alone, and not by anyone else. Dakṣa states the fault in eating the food of a Śūdra who is distinct from one’s own servants and so forth:
"One whose limbs are nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food, even if constantly studying, offering oblations, or reciting prayers, does not attain the higher state."
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Even he who engages in sexual intercourse while the food of a Śūdra remains in his stomach becomes the son of the one whose food it was; for from food, semen is produced."
Hārīta also says:
"But he who dies with the food of a Śūdra still remaining in his stomach attains the state of a mule, a camel, or a Śūdra."
[243] Aṅgiras also says:
"The twice-born who eats the censured food of a Śūdra for six months becomes a Śūdra while alive and is reborn as a dog after death."
Food may be either cooked or raw. As for that which was stated by Sumantu:
"One may eat milk products, barley meal, oil, oil-cake, cakes, and whatever else is made with milk, even from a Śūdra."
Furthermore, Hārīta states:
"Manu has declared that these— food cooked on an open fire, food cooked in fat, milk-rice, curd, and parched grain— are fit to be eaten by those who do not consume the food of Śūdras."

A *kandu* is an iron vessel made circular for the purpose of baking cakes and the like; what is cooked therein is *kandupakva*. What is cooked with oil or other oily substances is *snehapakva*. Regarding the twice-born who do not eat the food of a Śūdra—there is also that which was stated by Aṅgiras:

"Food brought from a Śūdra's house, even if it has entered another vessel, may be accepted. The word "food" (*anna*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. There is also that which is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"A wise man, having sprinkled it with water, may accept the food of a Śūdra that has come to his house"—thus [it is said].
As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha:
"Especially for the sake of another, for the sake of land, and for the sake of cows..."
But Yama has declared that food from Śūdras may be eaten by one who is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).

All of this refers to times of distress (*āpad*). Likewise, even the food of one who is devoid of the sacred fires (*agnihīna*) may be eaten only in times of distress, according to the traditional teaching of Yājñavalkya: "One should not eat the food of one devoid of the sacred fires except in times of distress. Even though he possesses the qualification [to perform rites], the meaning is that one should not eat the food of one who does not maintain the Vedic and Smārta rites, nor of one who has abandoned the sacred fires, except in times of distress. By implication, it is stated that one may eat the food of one devoid of the sacred fires in times of distress. However, even in times of distress, one should not eat the food of an ascetic (*yati*) or a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). And so says Ślokāpastamba:
"Only two types of ascetics are to be fed: the student (brahmacārī) and likewise the householder (gṛhī).
The food of a sage (muni) is not to be eaten, as is the case for all those bearing sectarian marks (liṅgin).

Here, "are to be fed" means their food is edible. A "sage" refers to both the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and the renunciant (yati). "Those bearing sectarian marks" refers to those who bear marks not prescribed by the Vedas.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, the rules concerning substances to be avoided— excluding meat— in the context of daily meals have been presented.
Now, certain statements regarding meat that must be avoided in daily meals are being recorded.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Thus has been declared in its entirety what is edible and what is inedible for the twice-born;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule concerning the eating and the avoidance of meat."

The meaning is: "I shall proclaim the rule regarding both the eating and the abstaining from meat. In this regard, since the discussion of a rule for the consumption of meat is not possible without first stating a prohibition, the prohibition stated by Manu is presented first:
"Meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat."
[245] "Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the killing and binding of embodied beings, one should desist from the consumption of all meat.

The meaning is that one should desist from all meat-eating as prompted by desire so that there may be no injury to living beings, and not out of fear of transgression (*pratyavāya*). On this point, it was said by that very same author:
"There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse; this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention bears great fruit.

By this [verse], it should be understood that since there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) in eating meat and no public censure, the injunction "one should eat meat" is effectively stated for one who lacks the desire for [specific] results. Furthermore, the fact that abstention is the means to achieve great fruit has been stated by that very same [author].
"One does not obtain that fruit by eating pure fruits and roots or by consuming the food of sages which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
Thus, even for those seeking the aforementioned rewards, he [the author] states that meat must be eaten in certain circumstances.
One may eat meat that has been consecrated by sprinkling, or at the desire of a Brāhmaṇa,
or when one is enjoined by the rules, or indeed when life is in danger.

One may eat meat that has been consecrated (*prokṣita*), namely the heart and other parts of an animal used as components in a sacrifice (*kratu*); one may eat meat remaining from a ritual offering (*iṣṭi*). Furthermore, by the desire of a Brāhmaṇa, one may eat meat when invited by a Brāhmaṇa according to his wish; that is to say, the performer of a *śrāddha* may eat the meat remaining from the *śrāddha* when it is permitted by the words "let it be enjoyed together with those you love," spoken out of his own free will. And being duly appointed, one who has been invited to a *śrāddha* according to the rules may eat the meat offered for the sake of the ancestors and others. Moreover, only in the event of the failure of the vital breaths (*prāṇānām evātyaye*) may one eat meat; that is, as medicine, or during a famine and the like when food is unavailable, or in such circumstances where the maintenance of life is impossible without eating meat—one may eat meat even in such cases. Thus, it is established that apart from these four specific instances—consecrated meat and so forth—the eating of meat by those seeking merit (*phalārthin*) must be avoided; however, in the absence of the desire for merit, it need not necessarily be avoided. As for what was further stated by him:
"A Brahmin shall never eat unprepared animals with the recitation of mantras"—
this rule also pertains to one who seeks specific rewards.
"There is no fault in eating meat, nor in wine, nor in sexual intercourse."

These three statements refer to cases where there is no explicit prohibition (*prātipadyena*). When there are explicit prohibitions and injunctions, it is necessary to postulate a fault (*doṣa*) for performing what is forbidden, in order to effect the desisting of the person. Therefore, since various faults exist in approaching another's wife or a prostitute, and likewise in eating meat that is explicitly prohibited, there are indeed various faults in such acts. For this very reason, Śaṅkha has prescribed an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the explicit prohibition of eating meat: "One should drink milk for twelve nights upon eating the flesh of a village pig, a village cock, or a *kumbhika*. The explicit prohibition regarding the eating of the flesh of village pigs and so forth was shown by Manu.
One should avoid all carnivorous birds, as well as those dwelling in villages,
single-hoofed animals that are not specifically permitted, and the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird.
The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāṅga, the village cock, the sārasa, the rajjudāla, the datyūha, the parrot, and the maina;
He also ate cranes, web-footed birds, lapwings, and scratchers;
fish-eating creatures as they were sinking, and meat from a slaughterhouse as well as dried meat.
"The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, fish-eaters, village pigs, and all kinds of fish. Thus it is said.

*Kravya* means meat; one who eats that is a *kravyāda*. One should avoid those carnivorous birds such as vultures and the like. One should also avoid village-dwelling birds such as pigeons and others. Regarding those "unspecified" (*anirdiṣṭa*)—meaning unknown, whose specific sub-species are not known—the remainder of the phrase refers to wild animals and birds, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*) of Yājñavalkya: "And unknown wild animals and birds. One should avoid single-hoofed animals such as horses and the like. The *ṭiṭṭibha* is a species of bird that utters harsh sounds; thus it is said in the *Vaijayantī*: "The *ṭiṭṭibha* is the *kaṭkkāṇa*. The *kalaviṅka* is the sparrow (*caṭaka*). The *plava* is the water-fowl (*jalakukkuṭa*). The *haṃsa* is well known. The *cakrāṅga* is the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*). The *kukkuṭa* (cock) is well known. The *sārasa* is called *puṣkara*; it is a specific type of bird with a long neck and legs and dark-colored limbs. The *rajjudāla* is the tree-fowl (*vṛkṣakukkuṭa*). The *dātyūha* is the *kālakaṇṭaka*, which frequents the vicinity of water. The *śuka* (parrot) is well known; its female is the *śārikā*. Those that eat by darting forward with their beaks are the *pratyuda*s, such as hawks and others. Those with webbed feet (*jālapāda*) have feet shaped like a net. The *koyaṣṭi* is to be considered what kind of bird it is. Those that scatter [food] with their claws and eat are the *nakha-viṣkira*s, such as the *cakora* and others. And "those that eat fish while diving" (*nimajjataḥ matsyādāḥ*) refers to those that eat fish by repeatedly diving in and out. A *sūnā* is a place of slaughter; the meat of an animal killed there is *sauna*. *Vallūra* is dried meat; Amarasimha states: "Dried meat that has been roasted is *vallūra*, which is used in all three genders. The *baka* (heron) and *balākā* (crane) are well known. The *kākola* is the mountain crow (*girikāka*) or the old crow. That which ascends to the sky as far as the clouds with ease is the *khañjarīṭa*. One should avoid fish-eaters even when they are not diving. "Village-pigs" (*viḍvarāha*) are domestic swine. And one should avoid fish of every kind (*sarvaśaḥ*), meaning in every manner. He [Yājñavalkya] states an exception to what was just mentioned: He who knows the Law should avoid the flesh of animals that die of themselves, of those killed by beasts of prey, and of those killed by dogs, as well as the flesh of animals killed by carnivorous birds. One should also avoid the flesh of animals killed by poisoned weapons, by those who live by hunting, and by those who live by fishing. One should avoid the flesh of animals killed by a *sūnā*, and the meat of a cow, a horse, a camel, a donkey, a pig, a goat, a sheep, a deer, a buffalo, a boar, a rhinoceros, a bear, a monkey, a cat, a mongoose, a mouse, a rat, a hare, a porcupine, a lizard, a *śvāvidh*, a *śalyaka*, a *kapiñjala*, a *krauñca*, a *kukkuṭa*, a *sārasa*, a *cakravāka*, a *balākā*, a *haṃsa*, a *cakrāṅga*, a *khañjarīṭa*, a *koka*, a *kuliṅga*, a *dhūmyāṭa*, a *cilla*, a *bhāsa*, a *śyena*, a *vāyasa*, a *kākola*, a *vṛddhakāka*, a *khañjana*, a *matsyāda*, a *grāmakukkuṭa*, a *grāmaśūkara*, a *śāṣa*, a *śarāri*, a *cāṣa*, a *pārāvata*, a *plava*, a *krauñca*, a *madgu*, a *kaṅka*, a *kurara*, a *gṛdhra*, a *śitapuṣṭa*, a *cakra*, a *śārika*, a *kokila*, a *kapota*, a *pārāpata*, a *śuka*, a *śārikā*, a *pratudāḥ*, *jālapādāḥ*, *koyaṣṭika*s, *nakhaviṣkira*s, *matsyādāḥ*, and *viḍvarāha*s. One should avoid all kinds of fish. One should avoid the *balākā*, the *kaṅka*, the *khañjana*, the *matsyāda*s, and the *grāmakukkuṭa*. One should avoid the *śāṣa*, the *śarāri*, the *cāṣa*, the *pārāvata*, the *plava*, the *krauñca*, the *madgu*, the *kaṅka*, the *kurara*, the *gṛdhra*, the *śitapuṣṭa*, the *cakra*, the *śārika*, the *kokila*, the *kapota*, the *pārāpata*, the *śuka*, the *śārikā*, the *pratudāḥ*, the *jālapādāḥ*, the *koyaṣṭika*s, the *nakhaviṣkira*s, the *matsyādāḥ*, and the *viḍvarāha*s. One should avoid all kinds of fish. One should avoid the *balākā*, the *kaṅka*, the *khañjana*, the *matsyāda*s, and the *grāmakukkuṭa*. One should avoid the *śāṣa*, the *śarāri*, the *cāṣa*, the *pārāvata*, the *plava*, the *krauñca*, the *madgu*, the *kaṅka*, the *kurara*, the *gṛdhra*, the *śitapuṣṭa*, the *cakra*, the *śārika*, the *kokila*, the *kapota*, the *pārāpata*, the *śuka*, the *śārikā*, the *pratudāḥ*, the *jālapādāḥ*, the *koyaṣṭika*s, the *nakhaviṣkira*s, the *matsyādāḥ*, and the *viḍvarāha*s. One should avoid all kinds of fish. One should avoid the *balākā*, the *kaṅka*, the *khañjana*, the *matsyāda*s, and the *grāmakukkuṭa*. One should avoid the *śāṣa*, the *śarāri*, the *cāṣa*, the *pārāvata*, the *plava*, the *krauñca*, the *madgu*, the *kaṅka*, the *kurara*, the *gṛdhra*, the *śitapuṣṭa*, the *cakra*, the *śārika*, the *kokila*, the *kapota*, the *pārāpata*, the *śuka*, the *śārikā*, the *pratudāḥ*, the *jālapādāḥ*, the *koyaṣṭika*s, the *nakhaviṣkira*s, the *matsyādāḥ*, and the *viḍvarāha*s. One should avoid all kinds of
The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are the first two prescribed for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*);
likewise, all *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and scaled fish are permitted. (MDh 5.16)

The *pāṭhīna* is a fish with many fangs; Amara states, "the *pāṭhīna* has a thousand fangs. The *rohita* is red-colored. These two, the *pāṭhīna* and the *rohita*, when appointed—that is, offered or presented—for *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors), are to be eaten by one who has been invited; this is the meaning. The *rājīvas* are lotus-colored, or rather, marked with stripes. The *siṃhatuṇḍas* have the faces of lions. The *saśalkas* are so called because they possess scales shaped like oyster shells on their backs. Among these, the *siṃhatuṇḍas* and the others may be eaten in every respect, whether by those who are invited or those who are not. The edibility of the *saśalkas* is stated with reference to persons who are devoid of Vedic study.
"A student of the Vedas should indeed avoid all fish that have scales," according to the traditional teaching of Yama. Devala also states a categorical prohibition:
"Owls, ospreys, hawks, vultures, cocks, and crows..."
The cakora, the kokila, the rajjudālaka, the cāṣa, and the madgu;
The pigeon and the dove are also recorded as birds that are not to be eaten.

The *ulūka* is the owl. The *kurara* is that which, moving through the air like a hawk (*śyena*), swoops down and seizes fish and other creatures within the water. The *cakora* is the consumer of moonlight. The *cāṣa* is a specific type of short-bodied bird, greenish-yellow in color, which is well known for its prophetic omens. The *madgu* is the water-crow; as stated in the *Vaijayantī*: "The *madgu*, however, is the water-crow. The remaining terms are well known. Thus, wherever a prohibition is recorded by name, one should understand that the transgression incurred by eating [the meat] after violating that specific prohibitory rule does not apply to the mere act of eating meat in general. For this very reason, Śaṅkha mentioned certain birds and wild animals as examples to demonstrate that the meat of those not specifically prohibited is fit to be eaten.
Yama always declares the partridge, the peacock, the common quail, the grey partridge, the crane, and the bustard to be fit for consumption.

The *lāvaka* is a specific type of bird that quarrels with its own kind; the *kapiñjala* is the *śaru*, which has variegated-colored wings, as stated in the *Vaijayantī*: "The *śaru* and *kapiñjala* have variegated wings. The *vārdhrīṇasa* is the animal known as the rhinoceros (*khaḍga*), as stated in that same work: "The *gaṇḍaka* is called *khaḍga* or *khaḍgin*; the *vārdhrīṇasa* is the leader of the herd. The *vartika* is a specific type of bird. The remaining terms are well-known. The mention of the *vārdhrīṇasa* is intended to illustrate those domestic animals and wild beasts that are not prohibited. For this very reason, Manu says:
The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare—
these they declare to be edible among five-toed animals, as well as those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel.

The *śvāvit* is a specific type of tiger that eats carrion; it is not the porcupine (*śalya*), as that would result in redundancy. The word *śvāvit* is well-known even for this specific carnivorous tiger. For this very reason, Aparārka, having explained "the *sedhā* is the *śvāvit*," stated: "And that is a specific carnivorous tiger. The *śalyaka* is the porcupine (*śalya*); it is a specific kind of animal characterized by bristles resembling needles. The *godhā* is a hole-dweller, somewhat similar to a mongoose. The others are well-known. Regarding the phrase "and those with single rows of teeth among animals other than the camel": the connection is that they declare buffaloes, rams, and so forth—those with single rows of teeth—to be edible. The mention of the camel is intended to illustrate [the category of] cattle and the like as well. For this very reason, Devala says:
Among the species of animals, the cow, the donkey, the camel, the horse, and the elephant are not to be eaten;
likewise, the lion, the tiger, the śarabha, the snake, and the monitor lizard are not to be eaten.
"Rats, mice, cats, mongooses, domestic pigs, dogs, jackals, wolves, leopards, baboons, and monkeys. Thus it is said.

Since it was stated previously that "vyāghra" refers to a tiger, the word *dvīpin* here refers to a specific type of tiger. *Golāṅgūla* is a specific type of monkey. The mention of the "monkey" (*markaṭa*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all five-toed animals (*pañcanakha*). For this very reason, in the continuation of the rule "one should not eat," Manu stated: "likewise, all five-toed animals. It should be understood that "all" refers to those other than the dog, the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare, which were previously mentioned as being edible. Śaṅkha also speaks of meat that may be eaten: "Buffalo, goat, sheep, deer, and even the Ruru deer..."
Meat fit for consumption is specified as that which comes from the side of the animal.
And likewise, wild boars and other forest-dwelling animals fit for consumption as food.

*Urabhra* means a sheep; its meat is *aurabhra*. *Mṛga* means a deer; its meat is *mārga*. *Ruru* is a specific type of black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*), as stated in the *Vaijayantī*: "The *ruru* is a large black antelope"; its meat is *raurava*. *Pṛṣata* is a specific type of spotted deer, variegated with hundreds of circular spots formed by body hair of white color that is extremely thick in size; its meat is *pārṣata*. Thus, the grammatical connection is: "He should eat wild boars that dwell in the forest and are fit for consumption. By these aforementioned words specifying edible meats, it is understood that there is no sin (*pratyavāya*) merely from eating what is fit to be eaten; however, this does not apply even if the killing of a living being has been committed for the sake of eating, because it is possible to acquire meat without having committed the killing of a living being, and because of the prohibition against violence: "One should not harm any living beings."
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or even dead.
That man of evil conduct who slaughters animals contrary to the prescribed rules shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the animal's body.

And because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Manu and Yājñavalkya: "The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and the seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats—it is these who are the slayers. As for that which was stated by Manu:

"The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and the seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats—it is these who are the slayers."

Thus, it should be understood that the designation of "killer" applied here to the buyer, the seller, the eater, and so forth, refers to those who are in some way part of the funeral rites for the deceased, and not to a bystander; for a bystander lacks the status of being an agent of killing in any sense whatsoever. For this very reason, Devala states:
"Five five-nailed animals are proclaimed as edible according to dharma;
they are remembered as the monitor lizard, the iguana, the hare, the porcupine, and the hedgehog."

The meaning is that five-toed animals are declared to be edible when acquired through means such as sale, provided they are not obtained by violence. Although the mention of "five" here is intended for restriction, nevertheless, the statement in the *Mānava* (Manu-smṛti)—"the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and likewise the hare"—which declares the meat of the rhinoceros to be edible, is not contradictory, because the two refer to different contexts. The statement of Devala concerns the subject of daily meals, whereas the *Mānava* passage concerns the *śrāddha* rite: "With the meat of the rhinoceros, food becomes inexhaustible in the ancestral rites."
Thus, because the scriptural declaration of the fruit of offering rhinoceros meat at a *śrāddha* is observed.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, the sections concerning meat to be avoided during daily meals have been concluded.
Now, some statements regarding substances that cause an excellence of satisfaction at a *śrāddha* ceremony are being recorded.
In this regard, Manu says:
"I shall describe in its entirety that oblation which, when offered to the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, serves for many nights and even for eternity."

The meaning is as follows: I shall now declare that sacrificial offering (*havis*) which, when given according to rule to the ancestors, conduces to their satisfaction for a long duration—that is, for the sake of the ancestors' gratification persisting over a long period—and which conduces to infinity—that is, for the sake of the ancestors' gratification persisting for an extremely long time. Regarding this, he states first, in due order, that which conduces to a long duration; he himself says:
"By means of sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits, when given according to rule, the ancestors of men are pleased for one month."

The mention of the four items beginning with sesame seeds is intended as an illustration for the seven cultivated plants (*grāmyauṣadhi*). In that regard, the meaning is that they are satisfied for a month by means of cultivated plants; in the absence of those in abundance, they are satisfied for a month by water, roots, fruits, and so forth, accompanied by some food. And thus says Kātyāyana: "Satisfaction for a month is through cultivated plants; in their absence, they satisfy the ancestors for a month with roots, fruits, and water, together with some food. The meaning is that the "subsequent" items—roots, fruits, and water—satisfy them for a month when combined with some food, not by themselves alone. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
When wheat, sugarcane, mung beans, satīna beans,
and even chickpeas are offered in śrāddha rites, the ancestors remain gratified for one month.

*Satīna* refers to *kalāya*; as Amara states: "But *kalāya* is *satīnaka*. *Caṇaka* is the chickpea (*caṇaka*), round in shape, well known by that very name; it is called *harimantha*, for it is defined by that same lexicon: "*caṇaka* is *harimanthaka*. The meaning is that they are gratified for one month by other preparations of wheat and so forth offered at *śrāddhas*. For this very reason, Pracetas stated: "One should give green mung beans, black beans, *śyāmāka* millet, *priyaṅgu*, wheat, and preparations of sugarcane. The word "should give" implies [that these are given] for the satisfaction of the ancestors for the duration of a month. Thus, wheat and the like are not to be given directly, but rather their preparations such as *maṇṭakas* (wheat cakes) and so on. Viṣṇu also says: "They are gratified for a month with vegetables, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, *priyaṅgu*, and mung beans. Mārkaṇḍeya, however, elaborates upon the vegetables that produce satisfaction lasting up to a month.
With vidārī, and with tender lotus stalks, as well as śṛṅgāṭakas,
ke cukas, and tubers, and also with karkandhū and badara fruits;
With pālevatas, ārukas, and akṣoṭas, as well as panasa fruits,
kākolas, kṣīrakākolas, and auspicious piṇḍālukas;
With parched grain and grains with husks, with cucumbers, pumpkins, and bhīdas;
with mustard, royal herbs, iṅgudas, and royal jambū fruits.
[254] With priyāla, āmalaka, and other principal fruits, as well as with insignificant ones such as alābu, sprouts of vetra, stalks of tāla, cukrikā, kṣīrikā, and vacā;
"By offering *mocaka*, *samoca*, *lakuca*, and *bījapūraka* fruits,
as well as *rāga-ṣāḍava* and *coṣya* preparations combined with the three aromatics (*trijātaka*),
the ancestors of men are pleased for a month at the *śrāddha* rites. Thus it is said.

*Vidārī* is black in color; it is the fruit of the *bhūkūṣmāṇḍa*. *Bisa* is the edible part consisting of a mass of fibers situated upon the lotus-root (*padmakanda*). *Śṛṅgāṭaka* is a water-born plant with three thorns. *Kecuka* is the vegetable known as *kharjūra*. *Kanda* is the *sūraṇa*; Amarasimha states, "The *sūraṇa* tuber is a destroyer of hemorrhoids. *Badara* is the fruit of the *badarī*. *Karkandhū* is a specific variety of *badarī*, and its fruit is denoted by the word *karkandhū*. *Akṣoṭa* is a mountain-born *pīlu*. *Panasa* is well-known. *Kākolakṣīrakākolau* are well-known in the Gauḍa country. *Urvāru* is the sweet cucumber (*svādukarkaṭī*). *Bhida* is the bitter cucumber (*tiktakarkaṭī*). *Sarṣapa* is well-known; the feminine designation *sarṣapī* is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). *Rājaśāka* is the vegetable called *rājavṛkṣa*, which is to say black mustard (*kṛṣṇasarṣapa*). *Iṅguda* is the tree of ascetics (*tāpasataru*). *Rājajambū* is a specific type of *jambū*. *Priyāla* is the tree called *rājādana*; Amarasimha states, "The *priyāla* is the *rājādana*. *Mukhyāni āmalakāni* are large myrobalans; *phalgūni* are small myrobalans. *Vetrāṅkura* is well-known. *Tālakanda* is a root originating from a palm buried underground, shaped like the fruit of the *āragvadha*, and famous as an edible item in regions such as Pāṇḍya. *Cukrikā* is *āmlikā*, *tiṃtriṇī*, or *ciñcā*. [255] Regarding *kṣīrikāphalādhyakṣa*, Amarasimha states, "In the *kṣīrakā* there is the *adhyakṣa* of the *rājādana* fruit. *Mocā* is the plantain (*kadalī*), for he [Amarasimha] himself says, "The *kadalī*, *vāraṇabusā*, *rambhā*, *mocā*, and *aṃśumatphalā* [are synonyms]. *Lakuca* is *likuca*; Amarasimha says, "The *lakuca* is the *likuca* and the *ḍahu*. It is a specific shrub possessing short fruits similar to those of the citron (*jambīra*). *Bījapūra* is the *mātuluṅga*; Amarasimha says, "The *phalapūra*, *bījapūra*, *rucaka*, and *mātuluṅgaka* [are synonyms]. *Padmaphala* is the seed-vessel of the lotus, that is, the *karṇikā*. *Rāgaṣāḍavas* are specific types of syrups (*pānaka*). *Trijātaka* is a collection of the three: cloves, cardamom, and cinnamon leaves. The remaining items are extremely well-known. This is also mentioned in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.

"Food together with curd and milk, cow-ghee mixed with sugar, satisfies all the ancestors for a month; so said Keśava. Thus [it is stated]. Manu has declared those things which serve as the means for satisfaction lasting from two months up to a year.
For two months with fish-meat, for three months with the meat of the deer,
for four months with the meat of sheep, and for five months here with the meat of birds.
With the meat of a goat, one [attains this] for six months; with that of the spotted deer (pārṣata), indeed for seven;
with the meat of the black antelope (aiṇeya), for eight; and with the meat of the Ruru deer, for nine.
They remain satisfied for ten months with the flesh of boar and buffalo;
however, with the flesh of rabbit and tortoise, they are satisfied for exactly eleven months.
"But for one year [he should subsist] on cow's milk and milk-rice. Thus it is said.

The *hariṇa* is the deer; its meat is *hāriṇa*. The *urabhra* is the sheep; its meat is *aurabhra*. The *śakuni* is the bird; its meat is *śākuna*. The *pṛṣata* is the spotted deer; its meat is *pārṣata*. The *eṇī* is the doe; its meat is *aiṇeya*. The *ruru* is the large black antelope; its meat is *raurava*. The mention of milk (*payas*) is an indicative term for products derived from milk. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "For one year, however, with milk or its derivatives. Although no specific type of milk is mentioned in the phrase "with milk-rice (*pāyasena*)," nevertheless, because cow's milk is proximate, it is understood that the milk-rice is prepared with that milk. As for the statement by Paiṭīnasi—"for six months with milk-rice"—while the word "pleases" (*prīṇāti*) is understood to follow, that refers to milk-rice prepared with the milk of animals other than cows. "By the meat of a *vārdhrāṇasa*, there is satisfaction for twelve years"—this is the [text]. The word "for the ancestors" (*pitṝṇām*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Here, the *vārdhrāṇasa* should be understood in its technical sense, and not as the rhinoceros (*khaḍgamṛga*), because that animal will be mentioned by Manu himself among the substances that provide satisfaction for an exceedingly long period of time. When it is asked what this technical *vārdhrāṇasa* is, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states:
"One who drinks from three [parts of the body], whose senses are decayed, and likewise one who goes at the head of the herd..."
"O King of kings, they know the red-colored goat to be the *vārdhrāṇasa*.

[This is] because of the etymological derivation "one who drinks with three"—namely, with the mouth and the two ears; thus, he is one whose ears are extremely long. Although he does not actually drink with his ears, nevertheless, at the time of drinking water from ponds and the like, both his hanging ears come into contact with the water just like the mouth; therefore, the figurative term "three-drinker" (*tripiba*) is appropriate. "With senses decayed" means incapable of sexual enjoyment. The mention of the "red color" is intended to indicate the white color as well.
But that which drinks from three vessels, being white, aged, lord of goats, and with its senses diminished—
that they call a *vārdhrīṇasa* in the ritual for the ancestors.
Because it is stated thus in the concluding summary (*nigamana*): "The *vārdhrāṇasa* is a specific kind of bird. And so it is said in that very same place:
'The bird with a black neck, a red head, and white wings—he is indeed called the *vārdhrāṇasa*; such is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*')."
That substance which conduces to infinity has also been shown by Manu:
"Kālaśāka, mahāśalka, the flesh of the rhinoceros and the red goat, honey,
and all kinds of food fit for ascetics (munyanna) lead indeed to infinity."

We do not know what *kālaśāka* is like. *Mahāśalka* is a fish whose back is covered with many bone-fragments resembling very thick oyster-shells. *Khaḍga* is the animal known as the rhinoceros. *Loha* is a red-colored goat; for among substances that provide satisfaction for an exceedingly long time, Yama has explicitly stated: "The goat and likewise the *loha*. The term *āmiṣa* (flesh) is connected to each of these, beginning with *mahāśalka*. Consequently, this is the meaning of the sentence: *kālaśāka*, the flesh of the *mahāśalka*, the flesh of the *khaḍga*, the flesh of the red goat, honey, and the seven kinds of food produced from wild grains such as *nīvāra*, serve to bring about the satisfaction of the ancestors for an extremely long period of time. Thus, one should understand that the intended meaning extends up to this point: that according to the respective degrees of satisfaction for an exceedingly long duration mentioned in the Smṛtis, there is also a corresponding gradation in the fruit obtained by the performer of the Śrāddha. For this very reason, Hārīta, having cited one example, stated: *“Kālaśāka, mahāśalka, khaḍga, lohachāga, honey, and the seven kinds of wild grains—these, O best of Brahmins, are said to be inexhaustible.”* In this regard, the following should be understood: the word *atyanta* (extremely) is used to indicate a degree of satisfaction exceeding even that which lasts for a hundred years, as seen in the passage: “Satisfaction lasting for a hundred years is attained through the offering of sesame. Therefore, it is established that the fruits of Śrāddha performed with various materials are indeed graded according to the specific nature of those materials. Furthermore, the word *atyanta* is used here to exclude the possibility of a single substance providing satisfaction for all times; for if that were the case, there would be no need for the mention of other substances. Thus, the meaning is that while the satisfaction provided by *kālaśāka* and the rest is indeed long-lasting, it does not extend to eternity. This is because the Smṛtis state: “Whatever is offered with devotion, that becomes inexhaustible,” and “Whatever is given with faith, that is called inexhaustible. Moreover, since the word *atyanta* is used in connection with the phrase “satisfaction for a hundred years,” it follows that the satisfaction resulting from the aforementioned substances is greater than that of a hundred years, but not eternal. This is because the Smṛti says: “Whatever is offered with devotion, that becomes inexhaustible”; and since the word *devotion* (*bhakti*) implies a mental state characterized by the absence of greed and the like, it follows that the satisfaction is not eternal. "Those rhinoceroses that are devoid of horns—those we eat as long as the sun remains.

having concluded the discussion concerning substances that cause an excellence of satisfaction for the ancestors— both directly relevant and those following by way of incidental connection— we now turn to the subject at hand.
Regarding the remainder of the morning duties, Mārkaṇḍeya says therein:
"When six muhūrtas of the day have passed, [he should approach] those twice-born ones."
He should dispatch messengers one by one, providing them with water infused with *āmalaka* fruit.

The meaning is that after twelve *ghaṭikās* have passed, one should send messengers to those invited Brahmins with the instruction, "Let *āmalaka* paste be given to each of the invited Brahmins for the purpose of bathing," having placed the *āmalaka* paste in the hands of the attendants. This offering of *āmalaka* paste is to be understood as applying to those lunar days (*tithis*) on which the use of oil is prohibited. Even among those, it should be given on all except the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), because of the prohibition against bathing even with *āmalaka* water on the new moon day, stating: "One should not bathe with *dhātrī* fruits on the new moon day. However, on lunar days from the second onwards when the use of oil is not prohibited, Kātyāyana states that oil and such should be provided for the purpose of bathing.
Oil for massage, a bath, and the cleaning of the teeth—
one should give these to them on the following day, once their hair and nails have been clipped.

The meaning is that on the following day, in the forenoon, one should give oil and other requisites for bathing, as well as wood and other materials for cleaning the teeth, to those who have been invited and have had their hair and nails clipped. As for that which was stated by Pracetas: "One should provide oil, unguents, and a bath to the guests of the *śrāddha* in the forenoon itself; however, one should not cause them to have their nails or hair cut."

In that regard, the prohibition against cutting nails and so forth refers specifically to occasions when shaving is forbidden due to the lunar day (*tithi*). Devala states the specific rule concerning the offering of oil and other items:
"One should offer oil, body-unguents, bathing water, and various articles for bathing using vessels made of *udumbara* wood, preceded by offerings to the Viśvedevas."

*Udumbara* means copper. However, Vṛddha-Śātātapa states another requirement: "One should fetch *darbha* grass together with its roots. The phrase "for the sake of rites for the ancestors" (*pitṛkarmārtham*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. For this very reason, Yama says:
"But for the ancestral *śrāddha* rite, the *darbha* grass should be provided with its roots."

*Darbha* is *kuśa*. It alone is the primary [grass] for the *śrāddha* rite. In its absence, *kāśa* and the like should be brought, because of the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "In the absence of *kuśa*, one should offer *kāśa* or *dūrvā* in the place of *kuśa*. However, in the absence of *kāśa* and the rest, Gobhila has stated: "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is cut near its roots for the ancestors; in its absence, all other grasses are used, excluding *śūka-tṛṇa*, *śara*, and *balvaja*. Although the word *barhis* refers to grass in general, it nevertheless applies specifically to *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and *dūrvā*, which are prescribed as particular types of grass. Therefore, the phrase "in its absence" (tadalābhe) should be understood to mean "in the absence of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and *dūrvā*. "Cut near the root" means cut in the vicinity of the root. *Śūka-tṛṇa* is a grass with awns, such as awned grain. *Śara* is *puṇḍra*, meaning fragrant grass. *Balvajas* are grasses resembling *muñja*. An option should be understood between this rule—"the sacrificial grass is cut near the root"—and the statement of Yama: "But *darbha* should have its roots. Just as the fetching of sacrificial grass is to be performed, so too is the fetching of barley and other items; for this very reason, it is stated in the Purāṇa.
There he should prepare kuśa grass with its roots cut off near the base,
as well as barley, sesame seeds, seats, a bronze vessel, and water collected for the sake of purification.

"The vessels should be made of leaves, silver, or copper; there should be sacrificial fuel, honey, flowers, incense, fragrant substances, and so forth, as well as a linen thread and a stirring-ladle."

In this context, the meaning is "the place for the *śrāddha*. *Brusī*s are seats for the purpose of seating the invited Brahmins; Amarasimha states: "The seat of those observing vows is called a *brusī*. Although they are invited, they are termed "vow-observers" (*vratinaḥ*) because they have undertaken vows such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*); thus, the term is used in its primary sense even for their seats. *Kāṃsya* is a vessel made of bell-metal. *Pārṇa* means made of leaves. *Kṣaumasūtra* is silk thread. A *mekṣaṇa* is a wooden ladle. The preparation of vessels made of bell-metal, leaves, silver, or copper should be done according to one's capacity. The provision of a *brusī* and a vessel should be made for each individual Brahmin. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "fragrant substances, etc.," unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), lamps, covers, and so forth are included. As for the sesame seeds (*tila*), if available, only wild varieties should be prepared.

"Jartilas are said to be black-colored sesame seeds growing in the wild," according to the statement of Satyavrata. The meaning is that sesame seeds of such a kind are prescribed as acceptable for the *śrāddha* rite. Jartilas are sesame seeds produced in unplowed ground; they are to be known as those which have been produced in unplowed soil.

This is because it has been stated by that very [author]. However, in the event that *jartila* (wild sesame) seeds are unavailable, other types of sesame seeds should be procured; for when those of superior quality cannot be obtained, seeds possessing the mere genus (*jāti*) are to be accepted according to the principle of the omission of the qualifier (*guṇilopanyāya*). As for what was stated by Āpastamba:
"Those sesame seeds which grow in the forest, produced without being ploughed, they alone are pure for the *śrāddha*; they are sesame, not [ordinary] sesame."

Thus, one should consider that the statement "not sesame seeds" is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory or figurative remark), similar to such passages as "others than cows and horses are indeed not cattle" or "that which lacks the *chandomas* is indeed not a *sattra* sacrifice. However, Aparārka has explained "not sesame seeds, [they are] sesame seeds" differently: "The domestic sesame seeds are 'not sesame seeds,' meaning they do not perform the function of sesame seeds. That is incorrect, because even those [domestic varieties] perform the function of sesame seeds when true sesame (*jartila*) is unavailable for the *śrāddha*. For this very reason, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states: "A mendicant [should carry] a triple staff, a water-pot, and a silver vessel..."
A daughter's son, the Kutapa period, a goat, and likewise a black antelope skin.

"White, black, and likewise wild—these three kinds of sesame seeds were created by Brahmā himself for the satisfaction of the ancestors. Here, "tridaṇḍī" is an epithet of the ascetic (*yati*); "rājatam" refers to the vessel; and "kutapa" refers to the time. White sesame, black sesame, and wild sesame are three distinct items distinguished by their qualities and forms. In this way, the number ten is accounted for. Furthermore, the term *dauhitra* has been explained by Vṛddha-Śātātapa.
That which is called the "rhinoceros horn" (khaḍgaśṛṅga) is located on the forehead;
the vessel belonging to that horn is celebrated as the "daughter's son" (dauhitra).
The term *kutapa* has been explained in another Smṛti:
"There are always fifteen well-known muhūrtas in a day;
the eighth muhūrta among them is remembered as the time of *kutapa*."

The subject at hand is now stated; Manu speaks of a specific distinction regarding seats: "One should provide a *kutapa* for the seat. The various meanings of the word *kutapa* are shown in another *smṛti*:
"Midday, a sword, a vessel, as well as a Nepalese woolen blanket (*nepālakambala*), silver, *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter's son is recorded as the eighth."

"They say that evil is contemptible; since these eight cause torment for one who has committed it, they are therefore renowned as *kutapa*s. Regarding the meanings of the word *kutapa*, among the eight [listed], Manu has specified that the *kutapa* is a woolen blanket (*kambala*) made from the hair of sheep produced in the country of Nepal, because it is most suitable for its designated purpose. In the absence of that, even a simple blanket is recommended over a mere seat (*pīṭha*) and so forth. The preparation of seats should be done at the places where they will sit down for the meal. And upon the prepared seats, a layering of *darbha* grass should also be performed.

"One should have them sit on separate seats provided with *darbha* grass," because this prescribes sitting on seats prepared beforehand. The qualification of the water as "brought by pure carriers" is for the purpose of making known the prohibition against preparing water that is forbidden. By this, [it is understood]:
"Water from a stagnant pool, which is foul-smelling and frothy, must likewise be avoided."
Where a cow cannot find satisfaction, and that which is taken at night; [these are not to be accepted].
O dear one, that water which has not been offered to all, and that which comes from an unfit vessel or source, must always be avoided during rites for the ancestors.

One should not prepare water that is prohibited by such statements as these. Furthermore, one must avoid water that has not been released for all beings—that is, water which the makers of wells and other reservoirs have not set free for the sustenance of all living creatures. A *nipāna* is a reservoir constructed near a well for the purpose of watering cattle and other animals. All vessels made of bell-metal, wood, silver, and copper should be prepared for holding the water of the *arghya* offering. Large vessels should also be prepared for the purpose of eating. Regarding wooden vessels, those made from leaves other than the *palāśa* leaf should not be prepared for eating.
One should not use vessels made of clay for meals offered to the gods or the ancestors;
nor should there be vessels made of other leaves for such meals, except for those made of *palāśa*.

Because of this prohibition here, and because [the prohibition] is specified as being "in regard to eating," this prohibition does not apply to the *arghya* vessel. For this very reason, it was stated by Vaijavāpa:
"In the rite of *śrāddha*, the *arghya* vessels may be made of *khadira* or *udumbara* wood;
they may also be made of stone or clay, or likewise of leaf-cups."
The flowers suitable for ritual preparation are shown in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"White *sumanas* flowers are best, as are *padma* and *utpala* lotuses, and whatever other [flowers] there may be that are endowed with fragrance and beauty in their entirety."
*Sumanas* flowers. Also in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Jāti flowers, *sallikās*, and white *yūdhikās* should always be offered, as well as all water-born flowers and the *campaka*."

The *jāti* flowers are *mālatī*s; as Amarasimha states: "The *sumanā*, *mālatī*, and *jāti* [are synonyms]. *Śvetayūdhikā* refers to *yūdhikā* other than the *hemapuṣpikā*, for that same author’s lexicon says: "The *yūdhikā* is called *ambaṣṭhā*; when yellow, it is the *hemapuṣpikā*. Flowers to be avoided are also shown in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"The *japā* flower, *bhaṇḍī*, *rūpikā*, and *kuraṇṭaka*—these flowers are always to be avoided in the performance of *śrāddha* rites."

*Japā* is the *rudrapuṣpa*. As Amara states: "The *rudrapuṣpa* is the *japā*. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the avoidance of flowers such as the *karavīra* and others that are red like the *japā* flower is indicated. *Bhaṇḍī* is *mañjiṣṭhā*. [As stated: "Mañjiṣṭhā, vikasā, jiṅgī, samaṅgā, kālameṣikā, maṇḍūkaparṇī, bhaṇḍīrī, bhaṇḍī, and also yojanavallī."
Thus says Amara. *Rūpikā* is well known. *Kuraṇṭaka* is a yellow-flowered, unfading plant. *Almāna*, however, is *mahāsahā*.
Among them, when red it is *kuravaka*, and when yellow it is *kuraṇṭaka*.
Thus says Amara. Flowers from plants such as the *bhaṇḍī* and others are to be avoided. Śaṅkha also states which flowers are to be avoided:
"Flowers that have a pungent odor, those that are odorless, those growing on sacred trees (*caityavṛkṣa*), and those that are red in color—these flowers are to be avoided."

A *caityavṛkṣa* is a tree from a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). An exception regarding red flowers has been shown by that very [author]: "Water-born flowers should be offered, especially those that are red. Thus it is said.

Viṣṇu also, by way of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), has stated what is to be avoided: "One should not give that which is thorny; even if it is thorny, one should give it if it is white and fragrant. As for that which was stated by Aṅgiras: "Neither *jāti* flowers nor plantain leaves," here the plantain leaf is prohibited because it is [otherwise] obtained as a vessel for food. The prohibition of *jāti* flowers is not absolute; if it were an absolute prohibition, Mārkaṇḍeya’s statement—"All *jāti* flowers should be given"—would be rendered purposeless. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Kratu:
"Born into the lineage of the Asuras, this birth was acquired in a former existence; by the mere sight of it, the ancestors have departed, rendered hopeless. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the phrase "in the previous acquisition," which refers to the occasion of taking up a body in a previous birth: although in the sentence, "There are indeed three bellies of the sacrifice—the Gāyatrī, the Bṛhatī, and the Anuṣṭubh; for in these they insert [verses], and from these they extract them"—which is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the form of a statement of present fact, a rule for insertion and extraction is inferred in order to justify its status as an *arthavāda*; likewise, here too, within this sentence in the form of a condemnatory *arthavāda*, a prohibitive injunction is inferred. Nevertheless, since this prohibition is merely optional (*pākṣika*), the statement of Mārkaṇḍeya is not rendered purposeless; rather, it concerns cases where other unprohibited flowers are unavailable. It should be understood that the two prohibitory statements, however, concern cases where such [other flowers] are available. Matsya also mentions those [flowers] to be avoided.
The pāṭala, bilva, arka, dhattūra, pāribhadra,
and aṭarūpaka should not be given in rites for the ancestors, nor should the milk of a sheep.

*Duttūra* is called *kanaka*. *Pāribhadra* is *mandāra*, characterized by clusters of red flowers. *Aṭarūpa* is *siṃhāsya*; for Amarasimha states in his lexicon: "The bull (*vṛṣa*), *aṭarūpa*, *siṃhāsya*, *vāsaka*, and *vājidantaka* [are synonyms]. However, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, it is stated that even *tulasī* should be avoided; the basis for this must be investigated, as a prohibition against *tulasī* is not observed in the well-known compendia of *smṛti* texts. Regarding the materials to be prepared for incense, those shown in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* are: "Among incenses, *guggulu* should be given, as well as the essence of sandalwood."
Then there are aloe-wood, camphor, turuṣka, and likewise cinnamon bark.
*Turuṣka* is an incense substance prepared from the bark and other parts of the *sallakī* tree. *Tvak* is an incense substance known as *lavaṅga*. Marīci also mentions incense substances:
"Both sandalwood and agallochum, as well as *tamāla*, *uśīra*, and *padmaka*."

*Uśīra* is the root of the fragrant grass known as *vīraṇa*. As Amarasimha states: "It is called *vīraṇa* or *vīratara*; its root is *uśīra*, which is not feminine. *Tamāla* and *padmaka* are well-known by their own names. However, Viṣṇu has stated that certain incense materials are to be avoided: "And everything produced from living beings is not for the purpose of incense. This means that substances derived from living creatures—such as musk obtained from specific types of animals—should not be taken for the purpose of incense. Regarding the fragrant substances to be prepared for the purpose of unguents (*anulepana*), those prescribed by Marīci are as follows: "Fragrant *haricandana* mixed with camphor and saffron."
Furthermore, the offering of fragrance is praised whether it pertains to the divine or to the ancestral rites.

Viṣṇu also states: "Sandalwood, saffron, camphor, agallochum, and padmaka are for the purpose of unguents. Regarding the oily substances to be prepared for the purpose of lamps, Marīci says: "The lamp [should be lit] with ghee or sesame oil, but not from any other substance. Here, "other substance" is intended to mean substances such as fat or marrow; it does not refer to oily substances derived from castor seeds, safflower, or linseed, etc. Therefore, Śaṅkha says:
A lamp should be offered with ghee, or else with the juices of medicinal herbs;
one should carefully avoid a lamp produced from fat or marrow.

Fat (*vasā*) is the oil of the flesh, distinguished by cooking and other processes. Fat (*medas*) is a specific type of flesh that covers the heart-lotus; here, its oil—distinguished by cooking and other processes—is indicated by the word *medas*. There is also a form of the word *medas* ending in *-a*, as seen in such terms as *medinī*. Regarding coverings, those to be prepared for the sake of specific results have been shown in another *Smṛti*:
"He who gives an unwashed (*ahata*) garment at a *śrāddha* rite obtains long life, the power to fulfill desires, sovereignty, and auspicious beauty."
"He who gives these—silk, linen, cotton, *dukūla*, and likewise unwashed cloth—at *śrāddha* ceremonies, obtains abundant fulfillment of his desires.

Silk (*kauśeya*) is that produced from threads originating in the cocoon of a silkworm. Linen (*kṣauma*) is made from threads derived from the bark of the flax plant (*atasī*). *Dukūla* is well known as an extremely fine woven garment. "Unwashed" (*ahata*) has been defined by Kāśyapa.
"That garment which is unwashed and not yet released was declared by the Self-Existent One.
However, this [garment] must not be given at a *śrāddha*, because that same author immediately thereafter says:
"It is recommended for auspicious rites, but only for that duration, not at all times."
Auspicious rites include marriage and the like. Regarding what should be given at a *śrāddha*, it has been stated by Pracetas:
"That which is slightly washed, new, white, with its fringes intact, and never previously worn—one should know that as 'unwashed' (*ahata*), and it is purifying for all ritual acts."
"Slightly washed by oneself"—this is the implied meaning. For this very reason, Vriddha-Manu says:
"Ritual acts pertaining to dharma should be performed by a wise man using [garments] washed by himself, but not those washed by a washerman... and so forth.

The washerman is the *nejaka*. Although the exclusion of the washerman is already established by the very mention of "himself" (*svayaṃ*), the prohibition of the washerman is repeated again for the purpose of making known that the rite may be performed even with cloth washed by another, such as a Brāhmaṇa. It should be understood that the preparation of the linen thread (*kṣauma-sūtra*) is intended for giving in place of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) in the event that no cloth is available. As for the stirring-stick (*mekṣaṇa*), it is mentioned as something to be prepared because it serves as an instrument for the oblation (*homa*); therefore, one should take one made from a tree suitable for sacrifice (*yajñiya-vṛkṣa*). Having thus prepared everything from the *darbha* grass down to the stirring-stick, and having performed the ritual bath (*karmāṅga-snāna*) in common (*tantra*), he should put on a white garment.
One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors;
the performer of a śrāddha should wear white garments.
Because of this traditional teaching (smṛti).
Thus concludes the section on the remaining duties of the forenoon on the day of the Śrāddha in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the duty for the afternoon of the day of the Śrāddha;
regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"Having bathed, he should honor those who have bathed and been invited individually with a welcome."

The meaning is that when twice-born men who have bathed have been summoned by servants and arrive at one's own house in the afternoon, one should honor them individually with a welcome; rising up and joining one’s palms, one should say "Welcome" to each of them separately. And so Śaṅkha says: "Being self-restrained, pure, dressed in white garments, and holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should say 'Welcome'. The two words "self-restrained" (*prayata*) and "pure" (*śuci*) are intended to ensure that he possesses the two kinds of purification, both external and internal. Here, the term "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*) refers to the portion of the day following the meridian (*āvartana*), as the day is divided into two parts; for it has already been established in the determination of the afternoon that it is precisely such an afternoon that is to be understood in the context of the *śrāddha*. In this case as well, the afternoon to be taken is that which is distinct from the time of the *śayāhna* (the period of rest).
The four muhūrtas that follow the Kutapa muhūrta—
this group of five muhūrtas is indeed desired as the abode of Svadhā.
This is in accordance with another traditional text (*smṛti*). The Brahmins should respond, "A very warm welcome," because an answer is required for the question. Yama also says:
"Then, having bathed and returned, one should rise up with palms joined in reverence and offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) in due order."

The meaning is that, having risen with palms joined in reverence and said "Welcome," one should sequentially offer water for washing the feet and water for sipping (ācamana) in order to purify any defilement incurred on the road. Thereafter, whatever ancestral rite (*pitrya*) is performed must be done without the sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*), with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), until the conclusion of the *śrāddha*, and it should be performed according to rule with *darbha* grass in hand. Thus says Manu: "With the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the *darbha* in hand, and without sloth, the entire ancestral rite should be performed according to rule until its completion."

"Counter-clockwise" means not to the right, from the beginning until the conclusion, that is, until the completion of the *śrāddha*. By the mention of "pertaining to the ancestors" (*pitrya*), it is indicated that in rites pertaining to the gods (*vaiśvadevika*), one should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*) and perform everything clockwise. However, in matters such as welcoming or rising to greet [guests], it must be done wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder; this is merely a general rule (*sāmānyadharma*), because those acts are forms of superior hospitality and do not constitute integral parts (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*. A distinction between rites for the gods and rites for the ancestors is also stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "Facing north for the gods, but facing south for the ancestors."
"One should offer [the food] in the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha according to the rule, beginning with the deities.
Kātyāyana also states a specific rule:
"One should always keep the right knee bent while attending to the deities."
One should always keep the other knee on the ground while attending upon the ancestors.
Bodhāyana also says:
"For the gods it is clockwise, but for the ancestors it is counter-clockwise;
for the gods the darbha grass-blades are straight, and for the ancestors they are likewise doubled."

"Dviguṇāḥ" means having doubled them by folding them in the middle. And so says Śaunaka: "One should cause [the guest] to be given a seat of formidable *darbha* grass, doubled. The mention of the "seat" (*āsana*) is intended to indicate all rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkarma*) that are accomplished with *darbha*. The common rules (*sādhāraṇadharma*) for both the rites for the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*) are shown in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"In rites for the gods and likewise in those for the ancestors, one should not touch anything that has not been sprinkled with water.
The various duties of the *śrāddha* are proclaimed here as being common to both."

High and low, of many kinds, are the rites such as the preparation of the site for the *śrāddha*, the smearing with cow-dung, and the enclosure. Regarding what must be done after the water for rinsing the mouths (*ācamana*) has been offered to the assembled Brahmins, Śaṅkha says:
"One should draw a mandala at the door on a place that has been swept and smeared.
By "at the door" is meant near the entrance, specifically the courtyard area of the house; thus it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.
[271] "...on the ground in front of this meditation hall, a mandala should be made with cow dung and cow urine," so it is said.

The word "should be made" (*kartavyam*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. It is with cow urine together with cow dung; for it is impossible to achieve the requirements mentioned below, such as sloping toward the north, by means of cow urine alone. When it is asked how it should be made with cow dung and cow urine together, Śaṅkha says:
"The northern [circle] should have its slope toward the north (*udakplava*), and the southern [circle] should have its slope toward the south (*dakṣiṇaplava*).

This means that the northern circle should be sloped toward the north (*udakpravaṇa*) and the southern circle should be sloped toward the south (*dakṣiṇāpravaṇa*); it should be constructed in the manner described so that this is the case. He states what must be done immediately after the drawing of the circles:
"To the north, one should place *kuśa* grass together with unbroken grains, with their tips pointing eastward."
"A twice-born man should place [the grains] with their tips pointing southward on the south side, together with sesame seeds.

Here too, it should be performed according to the stated sequence. The mention of "unbroken grains" (*akṣata*) is intended to indicate flowers as well. For this very reason, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states:
"Having worshipped that [deity] with unbroken grains and flowers while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*)."
Having saluted him again and again, he should wash the feet of the Brahmins.

"Pradakṣiṇa" means counter-clockwise (aprasavya). In the northern mandala (*udīcyamaṇḍala*), worship with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*puṣpākṣata*) is performed first, and subsequently in the southern mandala (*dakṣiṇamaṇḍala*). The preparation of the mandalas, the placement of *kuśa* grass and other items, and the washing of the feet should be performed according to the method of "succession by object" (*padārthānusamaya*), and not by the method of "succession by group" (*kāṇḍānusamaya*). For in the case of succession by object, all constituent acts maintain their proximity to the primary rite without inequality, whereas this is not the case in succession by group. Therefore, performance according to succession by object is established as the general rule. However, due to the force of specific scriptural injunctions, performance by succession by group will be discussed later in certain instances. A specific detail regarding the washing of the feet is shown in the *Brahmasiddhāntanirukti*.

One should first offer the water for the feet (pādya) and likewise the water for the guest-offering (arghya) to the deities; one should cause the water for the feet to be presented with the mantra "śaṃ no devī."

The statement that the *pādya* (water for washing the feet) and *arghya* (offering of respect) are preceded by the rites for the gods (*daiva*) is intended to indicate that all procedures to be performed, beginning with the invitation (*nimantraṇa*), follow this same order. At the conclusion of the mantra "śaṃ no devī," one should say, "O Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, this is your *pādya*," and having poured the *pādya* water upon the feet of the Brahmins representing the gods, one should wash their feet. The washing of the feet of the Brahmins representing the ancestors (*pitṛs*) is similar, with this distinction: at the conclusion of the mantra "śaṃ no devī," one should say, "O Father, [Name] Devadatta Śarman, descendant of [Gotra], this is your *pādya*; O Grandfather, [Name] Yajñadatta Śarman, descendant of [Gotra], this is your *pādya*; O Great-grandfather, [Name] Viṣṇumitra Śarman, descendant of [Gotra], this is your *pādya*. In the offering of the *pādya* and other items, the *gotra* and the name of the ancestors must be uttered.

"For the name and lineage [of the ancestors] are what convey the *havya* and *kavya* offerings"—thus it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*. The mention of *havya* and *kavya* is intended to indicate by extension other items to be offered, such as water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth. For this very reason, in the ritual offering of the *arghya*, Aśvalāyana has said: "O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*; O Great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*. In this manner, one should personally perform the washing of the feet;
one should perform the washing of the feet personally and with humility.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Yama. Regarding what must be performed immediately after washing the feet, Kratu says:
"With darbha grass in hand, having sipped water twice, wearing light clothing, with senses subdued, in a secluded and pure place smeared with cow dung..."
"On ground sloping toward the south, one should cause those who have properly sipped water, who are self-restrained and pure, to sit on separate seats provided with *darbha* grass. [273]

In secluded places where [the guests] do not touch one another, Viṣṇu states the order for seating: "One should seat the invited Brahmins, who have performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), upon seats covered with kuśa grass, according to their respective degrees of learning. This means that on seats such as woolen rugs or mats, which are already covered with kuśa grass placed on top, one should seat them according to their relative knowledge—that is, in accordance with the hierarchy of learning—and also in the Vaiśvadeva row of Brahmins, following the sequence of the first and second [rows]. Regarding the case where the previously prepared seats are unavailable, it is stated in another Smṛti:
"In that [rite], seats should be provided, as well as sesame seeds together with *kuśa* grass;
on each individual seat, lamps should be placed with sesame oil.

The word "should be placed" (*sthāpanīyāḥ*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. There, in that place for the *śrāddha*, after the lamps have been established, one should fashion square mandalas out of the flour of wild rice (*nīvāra*) and other grains at the locations where the eating vessels are to be set. And likewise, in that same [text]:
The mandalas should be prepared with wild rice (nīvāra), auspicious chickpeas (caṇaka),
white clay, or refined ashes.

The mandalas should be fashioned with excellent, auspicious powders; however, mandalas must not be made with stone powder. One should avoid that which is brought forth mixed with stone powder, because it is stated in that very same [text]: "āhṛtam" means "produced. Immediately after the construction of the mandala, one should seat the Brahmins on their seats in the manner previously described. This too is stated immediately thereafter in that same [text].
With hands, feet, and faces moistened, having sipped water for purification, and being well-composed,
those Brahmins should be seated upon those seats in that specific order.

The meaning is: "in that order" refers to the sequence by which, when seating is performed, there is no transgression of those worthy of respect. For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi says: "For those who are superior in learning and austerity, the first seat is prescribed;
however, for those seated in a single row, eating and so forth are traditionally held to be equal."
Hārīta also says:
"If worthy ones are present, he who is unworthy should not occupy the seat of honor;
he takes on the impurity of the row and is deprived of his lifespan."

Therefore, the intention is that one should resort to a specific seat only by not overstepping those worthy of honor. However, if the Brahmins are to sit on seats prepared beforehand, then once they have sat down, the placing of the lamps and the drawing of the mandala should be performed according to the previously described method. Regarding the manner of seating them upon the seats, Yama says: "Touching the seat with his right hand, which is not used for sacred rites (*apasavya*), and having grasped the Brahmin [by the feet], he should cause him to sit, saying, 'Be seated'. Or, he may cause them to sit after saying, "Please be seated"; indeed, he should say to them, "Be seated," even while touching the seat.

For it is stated thus in another Smṛti: "In place of the formal salutation (upasaṃgrahaṇa), there is the touching of the knees; and Dharma declares the mantra for the seating of the Brahmins invited for the ancestors:
'Then, having touched the knees, having seated the gods, and then the ancestors, one should cause them to sit upon their seats with all the Vyāhṛtis.'"

Having touched the knees of the Brahmins invited for the gods (*daivika*) and seated them on their seats with the words, "Please be seated here," and having likewise touched the knees of the Brahmins invited for the ancestors (*paitṛka*) while reciting "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and saying, "Please be seated here"—this is the meaning. Regarding this, there is a Purāṇa:
"One should first seat two Brahmins facing east for the gods;
and one should always seat three Brahmins facing north for the ancestors."

One should always seat two Brahmins facing east for the sake of the gods; the meaning is that one should always seat the Brahmins intended for the ancestors facing north. The mention of "two or three" is intended as an illustration of the number of Brahmins prescribed in other Smṛtis. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"Two for the gods facing east, three for the ancestors facing north, or even one for each;
the same applies to the maternal grandfathers, or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single unit."

The [guests] for the ancestors should be seated facing east; those for the gods should be seated facing north. Regarding the statement "the same applies to the maternal grandfathers," this meaning should be understood as follows: the option regarding the number of Brahmins for the maternal grandfather’s rites—just as previously stated—is to be known as established by the instructions that will be set forth hereafter. Furthermore, the meaning of the word *vā* (or) in the phrase "or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single common procedure (*tantra*)" has been clarified by Marīci through the presentation of an alternative view: "Likewise, the Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather should be accompanied by the Vaiśvadeva rite."
"Or, endowed with devotion, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva ritual according to the Tantra. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that one endowed with devotion should perform the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* together with the *vaiśvadeva*, repeating the procedure (*āvṛtta*). Here, by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not, it is stated that one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* repeatedly. For while the repetition of the principal rite—accompanied by its other subsidiary parts—is established by logic alone, the repetition of the *tantra* (common procedure) regarding the *vaiśvadeva* was previously unestablished and must now be explained. Furthermore, this sentence must be interpreted in this way; otherwise, the mention of an alternative view—that "the *vaiśvadeva* may be performed as a *tantra*"—would be incoherent. This is because, if the alternative of repetition had not been mentioned in the preceding statement, it would be improper to introduce *tantra* as a different option. The meaning of "the *vaiśvadeva* may be performed as a *tantra*" is that the performance of the *vaiśvadeva* rite for the sake of both the paternal and maternal grandfather *śrāddhas* should be done either by *tantra* (simultaneously) or performed only once. However, this *tantra*-performance option can only apply when the paternal and maternal grandfather *śrāddhas*, along with their subsidiaries, are governed by a single procedural injunction (*ekaprayogavidhi*), and not when they are governed by separate procedural injunctions. This is because it is established in the chapter on *Tantra-cintā* that "there is no *tantra* among ritual elements governed by separate procedural injunctions. Consequently, by the very mention of the *tantra* option, it is implied that the paternal and maternal grandfather *śrāddhas* are governed by a single procedural injunction.
