And being governed by a single procedural injunction occurs only when they accomplish a single *adhikārāpūrva* (the transcendental result of the qualified obligation); thus, the fact that these two accomplish a single *adhikārāpūrva* is known from this very sentence. Moreover, the word "or" (*vā*) indicates that accomplishing a single *adhikārāpūrva* is optional for these two. From that same word "or," it should be understood that there is also the possibility of them accomplishing separate *adhikārāpūrvas*. Therefore, it is known from this very sentence that first the paternal *śrāddha* should be performed, beginning from the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) up to the dismissal of the Brahmins. Nor should it be argued that because of the phrase "endowed with devotion," the maternal grandfather *śrāddha* need not be performed in the absence of devotion.

Wherever the ancestors (pitaras) are worshipped, there the maternal grandfathers (mātāmahas) must certainly be worshipped as well; it should be performed without distinction, for by failing to do so, one goes to hell.

Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. For this very reason, in both types of Śrāddha, the number of Brāhmaṇas and so forth is shown in the Purāṇa according to one's capacity and without partiality: "The two Śrāddhas may be performed with five Brāhmaṇas each, or with two each, or with three each, or even with one each."

Regarding the view that the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the principal rite (*pradhāna*) are to be performed separately: when, at the *pitrya* Śrāddha, one seats two Brahmins for the gods (*daiva*) and three Brahmins for the ancestors (*pitrya*), then one should seat them in the same manner at the Mātāmaha Śrāddha. However, when at the *pitrya* Śrāddha one seats one Brahmin for the gods and one Brahmin for the ancestors, then one should seat them in the same manner at the Mātāmaha Śrāddha. But when there is the option of performing both Śrāddhas simultaneously, then, in the event that a second Vaiśvadeva Brahmin cannot be obtained, one should seat only a single Brahmin for the Vaiśvadeva portion of both Śrāddhas; the remaining food intended for that purpose should be offered once, dedicating it to the Viśvedevas. Furthermore, when only one Brahmin is available for the purpose of both Śrāddhas, one should seat him for the sake of both groups (*varga*); having set aside food in a vessel for the Vaiśvadeva portion belonging to both Śrāddhas and having placed him in the position of the Vaiśvadeva Brahmin, it should be offered as before. It should be understood that the purport of the statement is that one must by no means create a disparity in the number of Brahmins and so forth between the *pitrya* Śrāddha and the Mātāmaha Śrāddha. Thus, at the time of invitation, the invitation of Brahmins should be made according to the very numbers prescribed for seating in the two Śrāddhas; and likewise says Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:

"One intending to perform two *śrāddhas* should invite ten, or four, or three Brahmins; or two, or even one who is a knower of the Veda. Thus [it is said]. Yama speaks to the Brahmins who have been prepared for their seating:
“They should sit with their faces turned toward the south, not touching one another.

Regarding this phrase “facing south” (*dakṣiṇāsaṃsthā*), it should be understood that it does not refer to facing the southern direction, but rather refers to facing the east (*prāksaṃsthā*). Although the intention was to express facing the east, the use of the term “facing south” was made to indicate that this rule pertains specifically to the Brahmins invited for the ancestral rite (*pitṛyajña*). For this very reason, another Smṛti states:
“Having begun from the western half, let the conclusion take place in the east.”
"For this [direction] ending toward the south indeed belongs to the ancestors in the *śrāddha* rite.

Here, *niṣṭhā* means completion. Regarding the Brahmins for the *vaiśvadeva* portion, Bodhāyana says: "But for the deities, it is clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*). The meaning is that the Brahmins for the deities should sit so as to proceed from the south toward the north, moving clockwise. Concerning the Brahmins who serve both purposes, it is stated in another *smṛti*:
"All of them, with *pavitra* grass in their hands and observing a vow of silence..."
"Mutually avoiding contact with the remnants of one another's food.

This means that all those Brahmins—intended for the gods and intended for the ancestors—with *pavitra* grass in hand and observing the vow of silence, should conduct themselves until the conclusion of the meal, avoiding mutual contact with the remnants of food arising from their own gracious acceptance. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that the performer of the *śrāddha* should also observe the vow of silence. Regarding an exception to the observance of silence, Yama says: "They should engage in dialogues concerning the Veda (*brahmodya*); this is desired by the ancestors."

Paiṭhīnasi also says, with reference to those Brāhmaṇas who are prepared to sit down: "One who is not appointed should not go to the foremost seat; he takes away the evil deeds of the row. Here, "not appointed" refers to one who has not been invited by the performer of the Śrāddha with the words, "Please be seated. "Foremost seat" means the first seat. Gautama states that even while they have not yet sat down, one should behave in such a way that there is no mutual physical contact.
"Sin would arise from mutual contact due to being seated in the same row;
however, it is appropriate [to sit] in a row with those of low conduct and so forth. Therefore, one should maintain a double distance. On this point, Yama says:
"A mendicant or a celibate student who has arrived seeking food should be fed at will, even if he arrives after others have already sat down.
Here, "mendicant" refers to an ascetic (*yati*). And so says Chāgaleya:
One should also honor an ascetic who is a fellow student during the time of a śrāddha;
such an act delivers the brāhmaṇas, as well as one's ancestors and the host of maternal forefathers, from sin.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa also says:
"Those learned twice-born who eat at a śrāddha that lacks hospitality for guests,
they go to the womb of a crow through that useless preparation of food and drink."

Even when a Brahmin who possesses the characteristics of a guest arrives at a place devoid of hospitality (*ātithya*), if he is not honored, [the following applies]: therefore, when there is space, a mendicant, a student (*brahmacārī*), or a guest should be fed near the seated Brahmins by being included among those invited for the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Thus, after prescribing the feeding of the invited Brahmins, it is stated in the *Purāṇa*:
"One should feed the remaining [guests] in another house according to one's means."

The term *śeṣān* refers to those other than those invited, such as guests (*atithi*) and so forth. This feeding of guests should be understood as occurring when one who possesses the characteristics of a guest has arrived; however, one must not treat someone as a guest merely by imagining them to be so, because of the scriptural warning of the fault: "They go to the womb of a crow. Regarding one who lacks the characteristics of a guest and creates an obstacle to the *śrāddha* by begging for food and the like, Hārīta states the following concerning his fault: "A Brāhmaṇa who causes an obstacle takes away the sin of four: of the Lord of Food (the deity), of the row of guests, and likewise of those desiring to eat."
"Those desiring food at the *śrāddha* for those desiring food" means the relatives of the performer of the *śrāddha*.
Thus ends the section on the seating of the invited Brahmins in the *Smṛticandrikā*; now follows the intermediate ritual acts such as the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
In that regard, the Purāṇa states:
"Having meditated upon Gayā as the site of the śrāddha, and having meditated upon the Lord Gadādhara,
and having paid obeisance to both of them, one should then perform the śrāddha."

The meaning is that one should make an intermediate resolve (*avāntara-saṃkalpa*) for the Śrāddha. In this context, the intermediate resolve is for the purpose of obtaining the permission of the seated Brahmins; and thus it is stated in that very same [text]:
"Having placed both hands level, situated between the knees, and being humble, one should question all those best of the twice-born who are seated."

The grammatical construction is as follows: having placed both hands together in a gesture of salutation (namaskārāñjali) so that they remain level between the knees, being humble and endowed with the discipline of bowing and joining the palms in salutation, he should inquire of all the invited, seated, best of the twice-born. To the question of how he should inquire and how the answer should be given by them, it is stated in that very same work:
"Concentrated in mind, he should ask the Brahmins, 'I shall perform the Śrāddha.
And when told by them, 'Do so,' he should then offer the seats of Darbha grass."
Prior to the offering of the *darbha* seats, the mantra "To the deities and to the ancestors... should be recited three times. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"To the deities and to the ancestors, and likewise to the yogis;
let there always be obeisance, to *svadhā* and to *svāhā*."
At the beginning of the rite, one should always recite this three times while seated;
having heard this being recited when the time for the *śrāddha* has arrived.
The ancestors arrive quickly, and the Rākṣasas flee.

By the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that the *asuras* and *piśācas* flee. Regarding the removal of *rākṣasas* and others, the *Nigama* states another ritual act to be performed: "One should scatter sesame seeds with the words 'The *asuras*, *rakṣasas*, and *piśācas* who dwell upon the earth are struck down; let them go elsewhere, wherever their minds have gone. *Apahatā asurā rakṣāṃsi piśācā ye kṣayanti pṛthivīm anu | anyatreto gacchantu yatraitad eṣāṃ gataṃ manaḥ ||*

From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of this mantra, it is understood that one should scatter sesame seeds with this mantra for the purpose of driving away the Asuras and others. Kratu states that in a *śrāddha* ceremony, every ritual act must be performed preceded by the deities (*daivapūrvaka*) in order to ward off the Rākṣasas and other obstructors: "One should always perform the *śrāddha* in this manner and proceed with the rites preceded by those [deities]. For otherwise, the Asuras and Rākṣasas will always snatch it away."
"Always"—that is, at all times—this *śrāddha* is accompanied by the ritual for the Viśvedevas. Manu also says:
"For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*) is superior to the rite for the gods (*devakārya*);
yet the rite for the gods is traditionally held to be the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors."
"One should first appoint a deity as their protector;
for the *rakṣas* plunder a *śrāddha* that is devoid of protection. Thus it is said.

The ancestral rite (*pitṛkārya*) is superior to the rite for the gods (*devakārya*), because the rite for the ancestors is the primary act while the rite for the gods is its subsidiary; this is the intended meaning. "Filling" (*pūra*) refers to the nourishing rite for the gods, which is to be performed first as an auxiliary that supports and benefits the ancestral rite—it is, in other words, its subsidiary. Thus, after giving permission with the words "Do so," one should recite the mantra "To the deities and to the ancestors," scatter sesame seeds on the ground of the *śrāddha* with the mantra "Driven away" (*apahatāḥ*), and then offer a seat of *darbha* grass for the Brahmins invited to the Vaiśvadeva portion; such is the sequence of performance to be understood. Furthermore, the offering of the *darbha* seat should be performed by pouring water into the hand of the Brahmin.
Having given water for washing the hands and also *kuśa* grass for the seats, he should, being authorized, invoke [the ancestors] with the verse beginning "O Viśvedevas... (*viśve devāsaḥ*).

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Yājñavalkya: "The *viṣṭara* kuśas" means the kuśas intended for the seat. Although it might appear from the force of the words that one should invite [the ancestors] after giving water for washing the hands into the Brāhmaṇa’s hand and giving the *viṣṭara* kuśas there as well, nevertheless, the meaning must be understood through the functional power (*sāmarthya*) of the term "*viṣṭarārthān*" (for the sake of the *viṣṭara*), namely: "having given the *viṣṭara* kuśas upon the seat. For this very reason, Pracetas says:
"One should give *darbha* grass upon the seat, but never into the hand.
As for what was stated by him:
"Straight darbha grasses should be offered separately to each of the gods;
then, with the mantra 'Thou art Dharma,' they should take up those kuśa blades. [283] Thus it is said.

This is its meaning: seated upon the previously prepared seats, even if they desire other seats, they should utter the mantra "You are Dharma" and mentally accept those *kuśa* grasses for the purpose of seating, but not with their hands. Therefore, there is no contradiction between the earlier and later statements. Deva Svāmin also stated this very point for the sake of avoiding contradiction: "The prohibition against giving *dharma* in the hand refers to the *darbha* grass intended for spreading over the seat; because of the force of the injunction to take them up with a mantra and because of the statement of Yājñavalkya, the *darbha* grass intended for the *viṣṭara* (seat-mat) should indeed be given in the hand. That is incorrect, because since the *darbha* grass intended for spreading over the seat is to be thrown onto the seat, there is no possibility of it being given in the hand, and thus the prohibition has no scope there.

Furthermore, it contradicts the injunctions found in the Ādipurāṇa and other texts which prescribe the placement of *darbha* grass for the purpose of a seat on the left or even on the right: "One should offer a seat upon a seat. Here, the term "left" refers to the offering of a seat for the Brāhmaṇas intended for the ancestors (*pitṛ*), while "right" refers to the offering of a seat for the Brāhmaṇas intended for the gods (*deva*). Thus, it is stated immediately thereafter in that very same source:
"In rites for the ancestors, [it is] indeed on the left; in rites for the gods, on the right."

On the left, on the left side of the seat; on the right, on the right side. In the rite for the two ancestors (dvau-pitṛ), one should provide a seat of *darbha* grass mixed with barley, because it is stated in the *Kāṭhaka*: "For the gods, *darbha* grass is accompanied by barley. On the right side of the seat, one should offer a *darbha* seat with the words, "This is the seat for the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava. And so says the author of the *Ślokasaṃgraha*: "The genitive case is prescribed for the inexhaustible water (*akṣayya*) and the seat (*āsana*); the accusative is remembered for the invocation (*āvāhana*); the dative should be used for the offering of food (*annadāna*); and the remaining cases are remembered as vocatives. [284]

After the offering of the *darbha* seats, the author of the *Gadyasaṃgraha* states: "Then, having again offered water, the performer should say, 'May the moment be granted for the gods' (*daive kṣaṇaḥ kriyatām*); the Brahmin should reply, 'Om, so be it' (*oṃ tathā*). The performer should speak again, 'May you accept [the invitation]' (*prāpnotu bhavān*); the Brahmin should respond again, 'I accept' (*prāpnavāni*). This invitation, however, must be performed by grasping the hand of the Brahmin with the exception of the thumb; but by grasping [the hand] excluding the thumb, one should invoke the Viśvedevas."

This is because it is so stated in the Purāṇa. The meaning is that after taking [the food] without using the thumb and having performed the invitation (*nimantraṇa*), one should subsequently invoke the Viśvedevas. Yama describes the method of invocation:
"Then, with barley in hand, having informed the gods regarding the invocation, one should, being authorized, invoke them with the verse beginning 'O Viśvedevas... (*viśvedevāsa*).
"O Viśvedevas, hear this mantra! Having recited this, one should then scatter unbroken grains (akṣata) clockwise while reciting the mantra beginning with "oṣadhayaḥ. Thus it is said.

The performer of the *śrāddha*, holding barley, should inform the Vaiśvadeva Brahmins, saying, "I shall invoke the Viśvedevas by their specific and general names. Being authorized by them with the words, "Invoke them," he should invoke the Viśvedevas into the Brahmins with the verse, "O Viśvedevas, come hither" (*viśvedevāsa āgata*). Having placed the barley upon the Brahmins' right foot, left foot, right knee, left knee, right shoulder, left shoulder, and head, and having meditated upon the Viśvedevas as having arrived within the Brahmins, he should mutter the mantra, "O Viśvedevas, listen" (*viśve devāḥ śṛṇuta*). Then, moving clockwise from the right foot to the head, he should scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) while reciting the mantra, "O plants, rejoice" (*oṣadhayaḥ pratimodadhvam*); the meaning is that he should place them. This method for placing barley and unbroken rice has been shown by Pracetas after citing the placement of flowers.
"The worship of the gods with flowers [is performed] from the feet up to the head. Thus it is said.

The manner of requesting permission and granting permission has been shown by Kātyāyana using general names: "He asks, 'I shall invoke the Viśvedevas,' and [the other] grants permission, saying, 'Invoke them. However, the manner of requesting permission using specific names—such as "those known as Purūravas and Ārdrava"—must be inferred by oneself.
[The Viśvedevas are: Kratu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāla, and likewise Kāma.
Dhuri, Rocana, and likewise Purūravas.
And Ārdrā—these ten are proclaimed as the Viśvedevas.
The phrase "having divided among the *śrāddhas*" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. And so says Śaṅkha:
"In the *iṣṭi-śrāddha*, Kratu and Dakṣa are to be invoked in the *vaiśvadevika* portion;
in the *nāndīmukha*, Satyavasu; but in the *kāmya*, Dhuri and Ulocana."
"Purūravas and Ārdrava are declared for the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha];
for the *naimittika*, Kāla and Kāma—thus one should recite them in all cases.

The *iṣṭi-śrāddha* is a subsidiary part of rituals such as sacrifices; that is to say, it is the śrāddha performed at the beginning of Vedic and Smārta rites, such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the Soma sacrifice, the *puṃsavana*, and the *sīmanta*.
At the time of the impregnation rite (niṣeka), during the Soma sacrifice, and likewise at the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana),

as well as at the rite for ensuring a male child (puṃsavana), the Śrāddha should be understood as a constituent part of the ritual, performed with the same formalities as a rite of prosperity (vṛddhi).

By Pāraskara himself, while defining the *śrāddha* as an auxiliary part of a ritual (*karmāṅga-śrāddha*), stating that "it is performed like the *vṛddhi* [śrāddha]," it is shown that the *karmāṅga-śrāddha* is distinct from the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. The *nāndīmukha* is the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* which has the ancestors known as the *nāndīmukhas* as its deities;
thus: "Having circumambulated clockwise, one should worship the *nāndīmukha* ancestors at the *vṛddhi* [rite]... [etc.]
Thus, because Yājñavalkya prescribes those known as the Nāndīmukha ancestors as the deities for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* has been defined by Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:
"The *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is prescribed on occasions such as the birth of a son and marriage."

The meaning is that the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* performed on occasions such as the birth of a son or a marriage is designated as the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of the sacramental rites (*saṃskārakarma*) other than *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, and *sīmantonnayana*, such as *annaprāśana*, *cūḍākaraṇa*, and others; for the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* performed during *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, and *sīmantonnayana* falls within the category of *karmāṅga-śrāddha* (rites ancillary to a primary ritual). A *kāmya-śrāddha* is one to be performed with a desire for a specific fruit, such as the *mahālaya-śrāddha* and others: "Sons, long life, health, and likewise incomparable sovereignty..."
By giving a śrāddha on the fifth day, one obtains abundant fulfillment of desires.

Thus, according to the fifth position, since it is recorded that the *śrāddha* known as Mahālaya—performed when the sun has entered Virgo (*kanyā*)—accomplishes desired fruits such as [the birth of] sons; and since the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, which is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of all *śrāddhas*, is the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*. Accordingly, Śātātapa states: "That which is declared as the *darśa-śrāddha* is celebrated as the *pārvaṇa*;
however, that *śrāddha* which is performed for a single ancestor (*ekoddiṣṭa*) is called occasional (*naimittika*)."

Although it may appear from this statement that the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha is indicated here by the term *naimittika*, nevertheless, in the second half of that same verse, it says: "That too should be performed without [invoking] the gods; one should feed an odd number of twice-born."

Thus, because the Vaiśvadevika rite is prohibited in the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha mentioned in the first half [of the verse], it would be impossible to enjoin that the Viśvedevas be designated there by the names Kāla and Kāma; therefore, setting aside the *ekoddiṣṭa* understood through its conventional (*rūḍhi*) meaning, one must understand that the term *naimittika*—derived from the etymological (*yoga*) sense of "that which occurs on a specific occasion" (*nimitte bhavam*)—refers to the śrāddha performed out of devotion to the ancestors when an occasion such as the acquisition of new grain arises. Alternatively, the term *naimittika*, which denotes the *ekoddiṣṭa*, indicates the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since the *ekoddiṣṭa* is also present within the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Consequently, in the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the invocation of the Viśvedevas should be performed using the names Kāla and Kāma. The phrase "one should recite thus everywhere" means that one should recite the names in place of the formal mention in all śrāddhas according to the method described. Specific names are shown in the Ādipurāṇa.
Viśvedevas are Kratu and Dakṣa, as proclaimed in all sacrificial rites; Vasu and Satya are always [the deities] in the Nāndīmukha śrāddha, and likewise in the ancestral (paitṛka) rite.
Indeed, at the time of obtaining new grain, the two gods Kāla and Kāma are always to be worshipped;
even when the sun has entered Virgo, Dhuri and Locana are to be honored at the Śrāddha ceremony.
"And Purūravas and Ārdrava, as well as the Viśvedevas, [are worshipped] at the Pārvaṇa [śrāddha]. [288] Thus it is said.

In all *iṣṭi* sacrifices, in all *karmāṅga-śrāddhas*, and upon the acquisition of new grain—when the occasion for obtaining new grain arises—one should perform a *śrāddha* with new grain out of devotion to the ancestors prior to beginning the consumption of that new grain, just like a *śrāddha* performed with new grain. This is intended as an illustration of those *śrāddhas* performed under specific occasional injunctions (*nimittādhikāra*) which include the Viśvedevas. The meaning is that when the Sun is in Virgo, there is the *śrāddha* known as the *Mahālaya*, performed with the desire for fruits such as sons; thus, this serves as an illustration of all optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddhas*. Furthermore, regarding the *Pārvaṇa*—the *Pārvaṇa-śrāddha* performed on the new moon day—one should also perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) after knowing their origin, namely that the birth of Kratu, Dakṣa, Satya, and the others occurred in the world-renowned daughter of Prajāpati Dakṣa named Viśvā. For this very reason, their origin is described in the Purāṇas.
The virtuous daughter of Dakṣa, renowned by the name Viśvā,
had high-souled sons known as the Viśvedevas.

The intention is that the origin [of the goddess] mentioned in this way is to be understood at the time of invocation. For this very reason, Śaṅkha has stated an alternative procedure for those twice-born who do not know the names such as Kratu, Dakṣa, and so forth, nor the birth of the daughter of Dakṣa: "Those twice-born who do not know her name and likewise her origin should recite this verse while standing in the presence of the Brāhmaṇas."
"May the illustrious and mighty Viśvedevas come;
may they who are appointed here at this Śrāddha be attentive.

The meaning is that those standing near the Brāhmaṇa invited to the Vaiśvadeva rite should mutter the mantra beginning with "āgacchantu mahābhāgāḥ" after reciting the mantra "viśve devāḥ śṛṇutemam. And so says the Purāṇa:
[289] Thus, remaining silent, one should mutter the mantra: "O Viśvedevas, come hither!
and immediately after that, the second: "O Viśvedevas, listen!"
But for the third [time], one should recite the mantra beginning with "May they come" (āgacchantu) and so forth. Thus it is said.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having first invoked [the deities] with this *ṛc*, "O Viśvedevas," one should thereafter mutter the mantra, "O Viśvedevas, hear this. Although the Smṛtis and Purāṇas nowhere state that ten Viśvedevas exist as deities in rites such as the *śrāddha* that forms part of a larger ritual, rather they specify two deities for each individual *śrāddha*, nevertheless, during the invocation and other rites, the formula must be used in the plural form, such as, "I shall invoke the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava. This is because the plural form is seen in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas, such as: "Saying, 'I shall invoke the Viśvedevas,' one should invoke the Viśvedevas while taking hold of [the Brahmins'] ring fingers. Just as when there is only one father, grandfather, or great-grandfather, the use of the plural—such as "Fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, here is your seat"—is not improper for the sake of honor, so too the use of the plural for the sake of honoring both [deities] is entirely appropriate. Even though the Brahmins representing the Vaiśvadeva deities may be only one, the invocation is not repeated for each Brahmin, since the superimposition of the deity upon multiple Brahmins is possible through a single invocation. However, after the invocation, because the deity is superimposed upon each Brahmin individually, when there is a plurality of Brahmins, the deity also becomes distinct due to those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Therefore, whatever worship of the deity is performed after the invocation—such as the scattering of barley, which is a directly contributing auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*)—must be repeated for each Brahmin, just like the offering of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), because in the case of directly contributing auxiliaries, the purpose is not accomplished for another Brahmin without repetition. As for the muttering of the mantra, "O Viśvedevas, hear this," although it is performed after the invocation, it is not repeated; for the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) to be achieved by the muttering is accomplished by the muttering once alone.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, the intermediate rites beginning with the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and ending with the invocation for the Vaiśvadeva have been described.
Now follows the procedure for the worship of the Vaiśvadeva;
regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:

"Then, having scattered barley grains over [the vessels], and having poured water into the two vessels containing the *pavitra* grasses with the verse *śaṃ no devīr*, one should likewise place barley grains with the formula *yavo 'si*.

This is the meaning: having placed barley grains on the feet and other limbs of the two Brahmins representing the Viśvedevas, and having muttered the hymn beginning with "O Viśvedevas, listen," one should place two vessels for the *arghya* offering face upwards. Then, having placed a single *pavitra* made of two blades of *darbha* grass—either pointing eastward or northward—in each vessel, one should pour water into each vessel with the verse "May the divine waters be for our well-being."
You are barley, the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are joined with honey.
You are the cleansing of all sins, a vessel fashioned by the seers.

With this mantra, one should place barley grains into each vessel; likewise, one should also place other items such as fragrances and so forth. Here, the meaning of the first quarter-verse is clearly stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having worshipped the Viśvedevas with barley and flowers, preceded by the offering of a seat, one should fill the pair of vessels while placing *darbha* grass purifiers upon them."
But Pracetas has clearly stated the meaning of the final three quarters [of the verse]:
"One should pour the *arghya* water into the vessel for each individual Brahmin;
having thrown barley grains with the mantra 'You are barley' (*yavo 'si*), it should be well-honored with perfumes and flowers."

*Arghya* is water intended for the *arghya* offering; one should pour that into a separate vessel for each individual Brahmin, repeating the mantra for each, and at that very moment, having cast *yava* grains into them, one should make them well-adorned with perfumes and flowers—this is the meaning. Regarding the specific vessels for the *arghya*, Kātyāyana says: "In any one of the following: those made of gold, silver, copper (*audumbara*), rhinoceros horn, or gems, or in leaf-cups and the like, whichever are available. Vaijavāpa also states: "Silver vessels are recommended for the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), and golden ones for the divine rite (*daivika*);
or alternatively, copper vessels may be used for both the divine and ancestral *arghya* rites."

In the latter half [of the verse] as well, the word "praiseworthy" (*praśastāni*) is to be supplied. However, silver vessels are censured in rites for the gods; thus, regarding the silver vessel, Matsya has stated:
"Since it was produced from the eye of Śiva, it is therefore dear to the ancestors;
being inauspicious, it should be carefully avoided in rites for the gods."

It originated from Śiva’s eye and was produced from the water of Śiva’s eye; thus says the Śruti: "He wept. Because he wept, that is the Rudra-nature of Rudra. That which was his tear became silver and gold. Regarding the statement that it is inauspicious, the intended meaning should be understood as its being produced from tears. As stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "Having placed two blades of grass each in the vessels for the gods, one should pour milk into them. These two purifiers (*pavitra*) used to cover the *arghya* vessels must be prepared separately for each vessel.

The word *śalākā* (splinter) refers to tips of *darbha* grass and similar materials that have their points intact. By the repetition "two by two," it is shown that two splinters each are to be placed in every vessel. Yājñavalkya describes the method for preparing the *pavitra* (purifiers): "With the mantra 'You two are purifiers,' one should prepare two purifiers made of *kuśa* grass, cut from a *kauśa* plant, without internal nodes, and measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length."

Having placed a blade of *kuśa* grass between [the thumb and forefinger] when cutting the *kuśa*, one should cut the two *pavitra* strainers made of *kuśa* with the mantra: "You two are *pavitra* strainers belonging to Viṣṇu; may Vāyu purify you both with his mind. Yajñapārśva also says: "Placing a blade of herb between the thumb and forefinger, one should cut the *pavitra*—which has Viṣṇu as its deity—to the measure of a span (*prādeśa*)."
Not with a fingernail, nor with wood, nor with iron, nor from an earthen vessel;
for by using a fingernail there may arise disease, and with wood one's purpose is not accomplished.

"Death would occur through an iron [vessel], and in one made of clay, strife is certain. Thus [it is said]. Gārgya states that after performing the worship with perfumes and flowers, one should utter "svāhā" during the fire-offering (homa) for the gods.

The word *homa* here is used in the sense of giving (*dāna*), due to the commonality of the presence of relinquishment (*tyāga*). Consequently, the meaning is as follows: when the rite of offering the *arghya* to the gods is about to be performed, one should utter "Svāhā" in order to present the *arghya* to the gods. The meaning is that, having pronounced "Svāhā-arghya," one should place the *arghya* vessel near the Brahmins. After placing it, Yājñavalkya says: "[293] With the mantra beginning 'yā divyā,' one should pour the *arghya* into their hands."

With the mantra, "May the divine waters be easy to invoke," at the end of the mantra, having said, "O Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, this is your *arghya*," one should pour all the water contained in a single vessel into the right hand of the single Brāhmaṇa representing the Viśvedevas, which is covered by the *arghya-pavitra*; this is the meaning.
Having given [the water], one should place the *pavitra* in the hand and then distribute the *arghya* among the hands.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Gārgya. Although a contradiction appears here between the statements in the opening and the conclusion, nevertheless, following the maxim that "the conclusion must be explained in accordance with the opening because the former has not yet encountered any contradiction," one should understand that the plural number used here is employed for the sake of completing the verse. Likewise, in the statement of Yājñavalkya—"one should pour the *arghya* water into the hands"—the plural "hands" (*hasteṣu*) is used for the sake of completing the verse; however, it should be understood that the intended meaning lies merely in establishing the hand as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). After pouring the *arghya* water into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas, Yājñavalkya says:

"Having given water, fragrance, garlands, the offering of incense, and a lamp. This means that the offerings of fragrance, garlands, incense, and lamps should each be performed after first giving water. And so says Gautama: "The giving of alms is preceded by water; and it is the same among those who give" (GDh 5.18–19). That from which water is first given in the act of giving is "water-preceded" (*appūrva*); thus, among those who give—meaning even when giving other things besides alms—it is the same: the gift must be preceded by water. Regarding the mantras to be employed for the purpose of dedication in gifts made to the Viśvedevas, they are shown in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
"O Viśvedevas, this water for the feet, this respectful offering (arghya), these flowers, ointments, this light of a lamp, and so forth are now presented to you. Thus it is said.

The offering of water for the feet (*pādya*) and other items is presented using the neuter gender designation: "O Viśvedevas, this is your *pādya*; O Viśvedevas, this is your *arghya*. Incense and other items are offered using the masculine gender designation: "O Viśvedevas, this is your incense; O Viśvedevas, this is your light of the lamp. The meaning is that these are to be offered to the Viśvedevas. The application [of the formula] is as follows when offering perfume and the rest: having poured water into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa, one should place the perfume in the Brāhmaṇa’s hand, saying, "O Viśvedevas known by the names Purūravas and Ārdrava, this is your perfume. Having poured water as before, one should give the garland, saying, "O Viśvedevas known by the names Purūravas and Ārdrava, this is your garland (*mālya*). Having poured water as before and having uttered their names as previously, one offers the incense, saying, "This is your smoke (*dhūma*). Having poured water as before and having uttered the name of the deity, one offers the lamp, saying, "This is your lamp (*dīpa*). Again, having given water and having uttered the name, one should offer—according to availability—one of the following: clothing, its price, or a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), saying, "This is your covering (*ācchadana*). The performer should say, "May the entire worship be complete. The Brāhmaṇa should say, "May it be complete. The performer should say, "May you all say, 'May there be the fulfillment of the resolve (*saṃkalpasiddhiḥ*).'"; the Brāhmaṇas should say, "May there be the fulfillment of the resolve. Regarding the seat and all other items, the Brāhmaṇa should say, "A good seat for you, a good *arghya*, good perfume, a good garland, good incense, a good lamp, a good covering. All of this has been stated by the author of the *Gadyasaṃgraha*. Those perfumes, flowers, incenses, lamps, and coverings which are to be accepted or rejected for the worship of the gods and ancestors have not been mentioned here, as they were already discussed during the occasion of describing the materials to be prepared. Therefore, those [items] mentioned at the time of describing the preparatory materials should be understood as what is to be offered here.
Thus ends the procedure for the worship of the Viśvedevas in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the procedure for the worship of the ancestors.
Regarding this, Devala says:
"The twice-born, being self-restrained, should face the north as prescribed;
the sacrificer, however, should worship according to the rule while facing the south."
Yājñavalkya also says: "Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), one should perform the circumambulation of the ancestors in a counter-clockwise direction."

The meaning is as follows: having placed the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) in the *upavīta* position for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* rite, and then, after the worship of the *vaiśvadeva* deities, having made it *apasavya*—that is, *prācīnāvīta*—one should perform the offerings such as the seat (*āsana*) and so forth for the ancestors in a non-circumambulatory (leftward) manner. Although the offering of seats for the ancestors should follow that for the *vaiśvadeva* deities, and the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the ancestors should follow that of the *vaiśvadeva* deities—in this way, the items consisting of the seat, invocation, water-offering (*arghya*), scent (*gandha*), flower (*puṣpa*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamp (*dīpa*), and clothing (*ācchādana*) should be performed according to the sequence of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*) for both the *vaiśvadeva* and the ancestral rites, rather than performing all items from the *vaiśvadeva* section (from the seat to the clothing) first and only thereafter performing the items for the ancestors according to the sequence of individual items; nevertheless, because the performance of the *vaiśvadeva* items according to the sequence of sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) is expressly enjoined here, one must perform it exactly in that way. This express injunction is established by the statement beginning with "having then made it *apasavya*," which prescribes the ancestral worship after the section of *vaiśvadeva* worship. When it is asked how the ancestral worship is to be performed, he says the following:
Having offered double-folded *kuśa* grasses while reciting the verse "uśantas tvā," he should invoke the ancestors; then, permitted by them, he should recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ."

[296] Having given double the quantity of sesame seeds—because of the traditional law (smṛti) stating, "For the ancestors, double the quantity with sesame seeds"—and having given *kuśa* grasses in odd numbers such as three, five, and so on—because of the traditional law stating, "Likewise, in rites for the ancestors, [offer] uneven numbers"—one should place them on the left side of the seat.
One should offer *darbha* grasses upon the seat, but never into the hand;
in ancestral rites (*pitṛkarman*), they should be on the left.

This is because of the traditional injunction (*smaraṇa*). Before and after giving the seat, water should be poured into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa, according to the Smṛti of Śaunaka: "Having offered water and having given a seat with double-folded *darbha* grass, one should offer water again. Regarding the phrase "one should invoke the ancestors" (*pitṝn āvāhayet*), the word "ancestors" (*pitṛ*) refers to the deceased male forefathers of the performer—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—because they are to be invoked as deities (*devatā*) since they are the intended recipients of the sacrificial offering (*havis*) in the Śrāddha rite. Thus says Āpastamba: "Now Manu has declared this rite called 'Śrāddha' for the sake of the ultimate welfare of progeny; therein the ancestors are the deities, while the Brāhmaṇas serve the purpose of the *Āhavanīya* fire. The "rite called Śrāddha" means the rite named Śrāddha. "For the sake of the ultimate welfare of progeny" means for the purpose of attaining the excellence of the lineage consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth. "Therein"—that is, in the rite named Śrāddha—"the ancestors are the deities": the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of the performer of the Śrāddha who have gone to another world are the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) and the intended objects of the offering; however, the Brāhmaṇas are not the recipients or the intended objects of the offering. Rather, they exist solely for the purpose of the *Āhavanīya*, meaning for the function of the *Āhavanīya* fire, which consists in receiving the offering that has been relinquished to a deity and is about to be cast into it. And their functioning for that purpose does not occur through the medium of the hand—as in the rule "it should be offered into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa"—because there is no such statement here; rather, [they function] in the following manner: [The text continues: ...and the pouring of water is to be done by the right hand, as indicated by the rule "water should be poured with the right hand," and because of the Smṛti: "One should pour water with the right hand. The pouring of water is performed before and after the giving of the seat, as stated in the Smṛti: "Having offered water and having given a seat with double-folded *darbha* grass, one should offer water again. Because of the scriptural statement, "One should feed two at a rite for the gods, three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each," it is understood that this refers to the act of feeding by means of the food offered [to the deities]. "At a rite for the ancestors" (*pitṛkṛtye*) means the act of feeding with the food offered in honor of the sacrificer’s father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"I shall worship the fathers,
the grandfathers, and all the great-grandfathers, as well as their fathers, in due order with food."

The meaning is: "At the time of offering the rice-balls (piṇḍas), I shall worship [the ancestors] with the ointment held in my hand—namely, the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of that great-grandfather. Vaijavāpin also, having stated that the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of the sacrificer are the deities of the Śrāddha, very clearly prescribed their invocation alone: "Standing, having addressed [them] saying, 'I shall invoke the ancestors,' one should invoke the sacrificer’s father, grandfather, and great-grandfather by name with the verse, 'uśantas tvā'. In the Purāṇa as well, intending that the ancestors of the performer of the Śrāddha alone are the deities of the Śrāddha, it very clearly states that they alone are the recipients of the *kavya* offerings.
As for the act of forming the funeral ball (piṇḍa) there, it becomes the food of the Brahmins;
that indeed goes to the sacrificer and his ancestors, and not otherwise.

In that context, regarding the *śrāddha* rite, the performance of the *piṇḍa* offerings—the initial *piṇḍa* offering connected to the ancestors—and the feeding of the Brahmins with the words, “Enjoy at your pleasure,” such that whatever food is offered for the Brahmins’ meal, that twofold food goes for the enjoyment of the sacrificer’s ancestors—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—and not otherwise; it does not go for the enjoyment of others. However, one might ask: how can food and other substances, which are insentient and lack a leading agent, go to provide enjoyment for all those individuals who, by virtue of their own respective good and evil karma, have gone to realms such as heaven or hell and are thus devoid of the capacity to consume *kavya* (offerings) from afar? To resolve this apparent impossibility, it is stated in that very same text: [The passage continues: "Just as a cowherd leads his cattle to pasture, so too do the ancestors, being summoned by the power of the mantras, come to the place where the *śrāddha* is performed. Having arrived, they partake of the food. Thus, through the power of the mantras and the mental intention (*saṃkalpa*) of the performer, the ancestors are brought to the vicinity of the offering, where they experience the results. It is not that the food travels to them, but rather that they descend to the site of the rite to enjoy it. This is the intended meaning.
Just as a calf finds its mother when the cows have been lost,
so does the mantra direct the food intended for the Śrāddha to the ancestors.

The mantra and the efficacy of the mantra. Furthermore, to refute the logical inconsistency as to how the efficacy of the mantra can cause food that has been destroyed to reach [the ancestors] through such acts as feeding Brahmins, it was stated by Matsya:
"The name and the lineage of the ancestors are the means of reaching them for the offerings to gods (havya) and ancestors (kavya);
likewise, names, mantras, and directions [lead] even those who have gone to other births."
These [beings] satisfy living creatures that have become their food,
even if a deity has been born as a father due to the force of auspicious karma.
His food, having become nectar, follows him even into divine existence;
in the state of a god it takes the form of objects of enjoyment, but in the state of an animal it becomes grass.
The food of a śrāddha rite follows one even in the state of a nāga in the form of wind;
it becomes drink in the state of a yakṣa, and likewise meat in the state of a vulture.
Likewise, in the state of a Danuja, there is flesh; in the state of a Preta, blood and water;
and in the human state, food, drink, and so forth, which provide various enjoyments.
The power of pleasure is a beloved woman; the power of enjoyment is the capacity for eating;
the power of giving is accompanied by wealth; and beauty as well as health [are likewise powers].
"This is declared to be the flower of the ancestral rite (śrāddha); its fruit is union with Brahman. Thus it is said.

*Names* are those such as Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and so forth. *Mantras* are those beginning with "The earth is your vessel" (*pṛthivī te pātram*). *Instructions* (*ādeśāḥ*) are designations such as "Let this food and so forth belong to such-and-such a person. "Having attained that state of being food" means having reached the state of being food appropriate for each respective class [of beings]. That food—food offered with the intent for that specific recipient—becomes nectar (*amṛta*) and, by the power of the mantra, becomes another substance suitable for their particular enjoyment; thus it follows them and serves as the means of enjoyment at the place where they reside. "In the state of divinity" (*divyatve*) means in the state of being a deity residing in heaven. "In the form of objects of enjoyment" means while existing in another world other than heaven, established in a divine state, in the form of enjoyments appropriate for a god. This capacity of the *śrāddha* rite to serve as a means of enjoyment—in the form of food and so forth appropriate for a body according to one's own karma—is the "flower," the intermediate fruit. The "meeting with Brahman" (*brahmasamāgama*), meaning the attainment of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), is declared to be the supreme fruit. Here, the attainment of the intermediate fruit occurs upon obtaining specific conditions such as time and so forth. And so says Hārīta:
"Food that has been acquired by righteous means and offered according to the rule into a worthy recipient at the proper time reaches the person who has given it, wherever that being may reside.
Furthermore, the attainment of the supreme fruit occurs upon reaching specific locations such as Gayā.
By reciting whose name one should cast the rice-ball, that person shall be led to the eternal Brahman.

Thus, because it is heard as a scriptural teaching that the fruit belongs to the *śrāddha* performed at specific locations such as Gayā, [the phrase] "he should lead [them] to eternal Brahman" means he should lead them to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), which effects the attainment of Brahman along with Brahmā himself. In this way, by the statements of Āpastamba and others, it is established that in the rite of *śrāddha*, the Brāhmaṇas are not the intended recipients; rather, the intended recipients are the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of the performer of the *śrāddha* who have gone to another world. Regarding those intended recipients—the father and so forth—it is said by Śātātapa that one should apply the mental conception of Vasu and the other [ancestors] to them in due order for the purpose of the dedication.
The Vasus are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras are to be known as the grandfathers, and the Ādityas likewise as the great-grandfathers;
such is the Vedic revelation.

Having understood this, Paiṭhīnasi states that when a *śrāddha* is performed, there is satisfaction even for the Vasus and others: "The Vasus are the fathers, the Rudras are the grandfathers, and the Ādityas are the great-grandfathers; he who, knowing thus, worships the ancestors—the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas become pleased with him. The meaning is as follows: by performing a *śrāddha* while identifying the fathers and others specifically with the forms of the Vasus and so forth, the Vasus and others become pleased. Being characterized by the pleasure generated by the *śrāddha*, they—acting as the deities of the *śrāddha* and equivalent to the fathers and others—satisfy the ancestors of those humans who, through the power of the names, lineages, mantras, and substances employed, cause the ancestors to obtain everything from food such as *amṛta* down to ordinary food and drink, which is the result of the offerings given by sons and others. These ancestors have entered into other bodies initiated by their own auspicious and inauspicious *karma*. Therefore, sons and others must necessarily meditate upon the fathers and others in the form of the Vasus and so forth, just as they recite the names, lineages, and mantras. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the śrāddha;
when satisfied by the śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of human beings.

The Ādityas are the sons of Aditi. Thus, there is no mutual contradiction between the statements of Āpastamba and others and those of Śātātapa and others. Therefore, it is established that for the performer of the *śrāddha*, the ancestors who have departed to the other world are themselves the deities of the *śrāddha*. As for that which was stated by Devala: "The Vasus are to be known as the fathers; the Rudras are to be known as the grandfathers;
and the Ādityas likewise as the great-grandfathers—this is the eternal Vedic revelation."
Whatever rite is performed here by humans with reference to the *pretas*, the ancestors (*pitṛs*) are satisfied by that, for the *pitṛs* are not remembered as being *pretas*. [301]

The meaning is as follows: when humans, by means of their sons and others, perform here in the world of men that rite called *śrāddha* intended for the deceased ancestors—such as fathers and so forth—who have gone to the other world and are meditated upon in the form of the Vasus and other deities during the *śrāddha*, then by that rite performed in such a manner, the ancestors—the fathers and so forth—who were designated while being meditated upon in the form of the Vasus and others, are satisfied; however, they are not satisfied when designated in their own actual forms. This is because the deceased who have gone to the other world are not remembered in the Smṛtis as being the ancestors who constitute the deities of the *śrāddha* merely by virtue of their own individual forms. Therefore, there is no contradiction between this [view] and the statements of Āpastamba and others. Having thus established that the status of being the deity for the performer of the *śrāddha* belongs to the ancestors along with the mother, paternal grandmother, and so forth, and not to them alone, Śātātapa says:
When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed, she attains oneness of form;
the wife indeed becomes a sharer in the respective portions of her husband’s ancestors.

This statement indicates that in a *śrāddha* dedicated to the ancestors and other deities, the wives of those ancestors possess the status of deities by virtue of their association (*sahabhāva*). Consequently, the meaning expressed is that the ancestors together with their wives (*sapatnīkāḥ*) are the deities. Thus, it should be understood that in the *pārvaṇa* and other types of *śrāddha*, satisfaction is attained by the ancestors along with their wives, and not by them alone. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"In the *śrāddha*, the mother partakes of nectar together with her own husband;
likewise the paternal grandmother and the great-grandmother, each with her own [husband]."

In the same way, it should be understood that the maternal grandfathers and others also possess the status of *śrāddha* deities in the form of Vasu and the rest, and their wives likewise possess the status of deities by virtue of accompanying them; for this is stated by Yājñavalkya and others: "In this manner, for the maternal grandfathers. Thus, the specific procedure for the invocation of the *śrāddha* deities as thus defined is shown in the Purāṇa:
"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*) and taking up sesame seeds while self-controlled, one should ask the Brahmins facing north, 'I shall invoke the Pitṛs.'"
Being thus authorized with the word "Invoke," he should invoke the ancestors with the verse "uśantas tvā.
Then, having cast [the water] while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apavīta), he should remain concentrated, meditating upon the ancestors.

"One should recite the mantra 'āyantu naḥ' completely and correctly. Regarding the verse beginning with "uśantas tvā," the meaning of the passage starting with "pitṝn" is as follows: having invoked the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather with the verse "uśantas tvā," one should immediately scatter the previously taken sesame seeds in a counter-clockwise direction from the head down to the feet with the mantra "namo vaḥ pitaraḥ," while meditating upon the ancestors, and then recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ. Thus says Pracetas: "In rites for the ancestors, [one scatters] from the head down to the feet with the mantra 'namo vaḥ'."

In the rite for the ancestors (*paitṛka-karma*), the meaning is that one should perform worship with flowers, sesame seeds, and so forth—beginning from the head down to the feet, moving counter-clockwise—using the mantra "Obeisance to you, O ancestors" (*namo vaḥ pitaraḥ*). A specific detail regarding the invocation (*āvāhana*) has also been shown by Vaijavāpa: "Standing and having addressed [the ancestors] with the words 'I shall invoke the ancestors,' he should invoke the sacrificer’s father, grandfather, and great-grandfather by their names using the verse 'May they come to us' (*uśantas tvā*); then, having recited 'May our ancestors come' (*āyantu naḥ pitaraḥ*). By "by their names" is meant [names] ending in the second case (accusative) and other such inflections. And so says the author of the *Ślokasaṅgraha*:

"The sixth case-ending is used for the imperishable seats (akṣayya-āsana) and likewise for the second case in the invitation; the fourth case is used in the giving of food, while the remaining cases are traditionally taught as vocatives. [303]

In all these cases of the sixth and other case endings, there is an option between the singular and plural numbers, because in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, *Gṛhyasūtras*, and other texts, the words for father (*pitṛ*), grandfather (*pitāmaha*), great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), and so on, are seen used in various places with either a singular ending or a plural ending. Thus, the ritual procedure for offering the seat (*āsana*) and the invocation (*āvāhana*) is as follows: Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), facing north, and having first seated himself, he should pour water into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa. Then, taking pairs of *kuśa* grass seats—folding them double by breaking them in the middle—and adding sesame seeds, he should sit facing south and say: "This is the seat for our father, who is of such-and-such a lineage (*gotra*) and such-and-such a name, together with his wife. Having placed the previously taken *kuśa* grass with sesame seeds on the left side of the Brāhmaṇa’s seat, he should again pour water into the Brāhmaṇa’s hand. He should perform the same sequence—from pouring water into the hand of the next seated Brāhmaṇa to the final pouring of water—for the hands of the Brāhmaṇas seated in subsequent order. The distinction is that for the grandfather one says "who is of the form of Rudra," and for the great-grandfather "who is of the form of Āditya. In the same manner, he should perform the offering of water and so forth into the hands of the three Brāhmaṇas occupying the place of the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*). The distinction here is: "for our maternal grandfather, who is of the form of Vasu; for our mother’s grandfather, who is of the form of Rudra; for our mother’s great-grandfather, who is of the form of Āditya. Having thus offered the seats to the six Brāhmaṇas according to the method of sequential performance (*padārthānusamaya*), he should thereafter perform the invitation (*nimantraṇa*) for each Brāhmaṇa according to the method described in the previous section. In the formula "May the moment be made for the gods" (*daive kṣaṇaḥ kriyatām*), the word "for the gods" (*daiva*) should be replaced by the locative form "in the Śrāddha" (*śrāddhe*) when addressing the six Brāhmaṇas. However, the response "Om, so be it" (*oṃ tathā*) and so forth should be performed exactly as described in the previous section. Having invited the sixth Brāhmaṇa, he should take sesame seeds, wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), and stand facing south. He should ask the Brāhmaṇas, who are seated facing north: "I shall invoke our father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, who are of the forms of Vasu, Rudra, and Āditya. Being permitted with the reply "Invoke them" (*āvāhaya*), he recites the verse "We call you, longing" (*uśantas tvā havāmahe*). At the end of the verse, he should invoke the father into the first Brāhmaṇa, saying: "I invoke our father, who is of the form of Vasu, of such-and-such a lineage and such-and-such a name, together with his wife"; the grandfather into the second, saying: "I invoke our grandfather, who is of the form of Rudra..."; and the great-grandfather into the third, saying: "I invoke our great-grandfather, who is of the form of Āditya...". Then, while reciting the mantra "Salutation to you, O fathers" (*namo vaḥ pitaraḥ*), he should place sesame seeds upon the head, the left shoulder, the right shoulder, the left knee, the right knee, the left foot, and the right foot of each Brāhmaṇa. Meditating upon the father of the first Brāhmaṇa as Vasu with his wife, the grandfather as Rudra with his wife, and the great-grandfather as Āditya with his wife, he should mutter once the verse beginning with "May our fathers come" (*āyantu naḥ pitaraḥ*). He should perform the invocation of the maternal grandfathers and others in the same way. The specific difference there is that he should ask the Brāhmaṇas occupying the place of the maternal grandfathers: "I shall invoke our maternal grandfather, mother’s grandfather, and mother’s great-grandfather, who are of the forms of Vasu, Rudra, and Āditya. At the end of the mantra "We call you, longing," he should invoke the maternal grandfather into the first Brāhmaṇa, saying: "I invoke our maternal grandfather, of such-and-such a lineage and such-and-such a name, together with his wife"; likewise the mother’s grandfather with his wife as Rudra, and the mother’s great-grandfather with his wife as Āditya. Invoking them into the first, second, and third Brāhmaṇas respectively, he should mutter "May they come" (*āyantu naḥ*) while meditating on each one individually. The word "grandfather" (*pitāmaha*) should not be substituted for the word "maternal grandfather" (*mātāmaha*) in the two mantras "We call you, longing" and "May they come," because the scripture states: "The father does not increase" (*na pitā vardhate*), which prohibits the substitution of the word "father" except when it refers exclusively to the biological progenitor. Following the muttering of "May our fathers come," what must be done next is stated in the *Purāṇa*.
For the sake of protecting the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛsatra), one should properly recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ" three times in its entirety toward every direction.
One should scatter sesame seeds while reciting the mantra beginning with "apahatāḥ."

Having recited the mantra: “Struck down are the Asuras, the Rakṣasas, and the Piśācas who dwell upon the earth; let them go elsewhere, wherever their minds have gone,” one should scatter sesame seeds three times in all directions around the Brāhmaṇas, moving counter-clockwise (apradakṣiṇa). This is the meaning. *Pitṛsatra* is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyāga*), that is to say, the *Śrāddha*.
Thus ends the procedure for the ritual services up to the invocation (*āvāhana*) in the section on the rules for ancestral worship (*paitṛkārcana*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for the ritual services beginning with the water-offering (*arghya*); regarding this, there is a Purāṇa:
He prepares vessels for the *argha* offering made of gold, silver, lotuses, or jewels, or even a cup fashioned from auspicious leaves and the like.

The meaning is that for the sake of the *arghya*—for the purpose of placing the *arghya* water—one should indeed consecrate vessels made of gold or other materials, whichever are available, by means of placing them upon *darbha* grass and sprinkling [water over them]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "leaf-cups and so forth," items such as *camasa* bowls are included. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: [306] "Upon *darbha* grass with tips pointing south, in three *camasa* bowls arranged ending toward the south and containing *pavitra* strainers, one should pour water with the mantra, 'May the divine waters be auspicious to us' (*śaṃ no devīḥ*). The meaning is that upon three *camasa* or similar *arghya* vessels placed upon *darbha* grass with tips pointing south and arranged ending toward the south, one should pour water into each vessel individually with the mantra "May the divine waters... Pracetā also says: "In *camasa* bowls made of sacrificial wood, containing *pavitra* strainers, one should pour water into each one. Śaunaka also says: "In vessels made of metal, stone, or clay—whether consisting of a single material or multiple materials—having placed water upon *darbha* (or *pavitra*) strainers, he pours sesame seeds over the water consecrated with the mantra 'For our welfare, may the divine waters... (*saṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaye*). He pours [sesame] with the mantra: 'Thou art sesame, whose deity is the Pitṛs; thou art produced from the cow-sacrifice (*gosava*), fashioned by the gods. Mixed with the *patnīvats*, through the *svadhā* offering, do thou gratify these Pitṛs and these worlds for us; *svadhā*! Obeisance! *Metallic* (*taijasa*) means made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and the like. *Stone-made* (*aśmamaya*) means made of gems such as emerald (*marakata*) and the like. "Consisting of a single material" refers to those made of any one of bell-metal, silver, copper, etc. "Consisting of multiple materials" refers to those made of various materials such as bell-metal and others. "Containing *darbha*" means containing *pavitra* strainers. The meaning is that having poured water with the mantra "May the divine waters...", and once the water has been poured and consecrated with the previously mentioned mantra, one should throw sesame seeds into it with the mantra "Thou art sesame... The plural number in "in the vessels" (*pātreṣu*) is restricted to exactly three, because it refers to the rule of one vessel per deity in a *śrāddha* centered on the three primary deities. For this very reason, Pracetas stated: "There are only three water-vessels. The meaning is that even when there is the appointment of multiple Brahmins for each of the three ancestors (father, grandfather, great-grandfather), or even when all are appointed to a single Brahmin, since the *śrāddha* remains centered on the three deities, there are only three water-vessels and they are not numbered according to the number of Brahmins.
