"Having brought [the sesame], the knower of dharma should prepare three vessels for the ancestors, either upon one Brāhmaṇa or upon many, according to the rule.

The meaning is that having brought [them] with sesame seeds, he should cast the sesame seeds into the water for the *arghya* offerings. He [the same author] states the method for making the *pavitra* blades for the purpose of consecrating the *arghya* water:

"Two blades of *kuśa* grass, equal, with unfrayed tips, and without internal nodes—cutting them with *kuśa* grass, that shall always be the *pavitra* in the rite of *śrāddha*. Here, the number "two" (*kuśau*) refers to the *pavitra* for the *arghya* vessels dedicated to the Viśvedevas, because it is inappropriate for the *pavitra* of the *arghya* vessels dedicated to the ancestors (*paitṛka*). For this very reason, an odd number is shown in the *Caturviṃśatimata* for the *pavitra* of the ancestral *arghya*.

"In the *pārvaṇa* rite, three blades of grass (*śalākā*) are placed in each of the vessels for the ancestors. Here, "blades of grass" refers to *darbha* grass resembling blades, meaning those with uncut tips. Following the addition of sesame seeds into the *arghya* vessels, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states what must be performed:
"The *arghya* offerings, along with flowers and perfumes, should be worshipped according to the scriptures."

The water intended for the *arghya* offering, mixed with sesame seeds, should be honored with perfumes (*gandha*) and flowers; the meaning is that one should cast the perfumes and flowers into that water. After the casting of the perfumes and other items, Śaunaka says: "And intending to cause them to accept those, [one offers] the *svadhā-arghya*s. The meaning is that, intending to have the Brahmins accept that water intended for the *arghya*, one should place it before the Brahmins while reciting the mantra *svadhā-arghya*. After placing it, Paiṭhīnasi says: "Then, having first given *darbha* grass into the hands of the Brahmins with water, he gives the *arghya* water with water first, reciting the verse *yā divyā āpaḥ*; 'This is your *arghya* water,' and he should touch water [afterward]. In the same way for the other two. The meaning is: after placing the *arghya*, having first poured water into the hands of the Brahmins and thrown the *darbha* strainers used for the *arghya* with their tips pointing south, and having again poured water, he recites the mantra *yā divyā āpaḥ*. At the end of the mantra, saying, "O our father, of such-and-such *gotra*, named so-and-so, in the form of Vasu, together with your wife—this is your *arghya* water," he offers the *arghya* into the right hand using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) and touches water. "In the same way for the other two"—the meaning is that he should offer the *arghya* into the hands of the Brahmins for the grandfather and great-grandfather as well. The specific difference is: "O our grandfather, of such-and-such *gotra*, named so-and-so, in the form of Rudra, together with your wife" (or "O our great-grandfather, in the form of Āditya"). Kātyāyana prescribes the offering of the *arghya* after reciting the entire mantra *yā divyā āpaḥ*: "Into hands containing the *darbha* strainers, [he recites]: 'May the divine waters which have come together with milk, those of the atmosphere and those of the earth, golden-hued and worthy of sacrifice—may those waters be auspicious, pleasant, and easy to invoke for us. Having poured the vessels of water into the hands of the Brahmins, saying 'O Fathers, this is your *arghya*; O grandfather, this is your *arghya*; O great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*', he causes the remainder to flow onto the *darbha* grass with the words 'May there be inexhaustibility for the ancestors. "Vessels" means the water contained in the vessels. It is stated by Dharmasūtra that the mention of the *gotra* must be performed: "Having lifted the vessel with both hands while reciting *yā divyā āpaḥ*, and having taken the name and *gotra*, he should give the *arghya* into the hand containing the *darbha* strainer. It is understood that he should give it with the vessel lifted by both hands. Pracetas also [says the same].

One should perform the circumambulation for each of these [ancestors] individually, starting from the left according to the paternal order; having addressed them by their lineage and names, one should say, "This is your *arghya*."

[309] The meaning is that one should address each of these—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—in their paternal order (the sequence beginning with the father), by means of their respective lineage names (*gotra*) and personal names, saying, "This is your *arghya*," and thus worship each Brāhmaṇa with a single *arghya*. Thus says Gautama: "As before, one should worship them separately, one by one, in order, with each [offering]. This was stated with reference to the view regarding the number of Brāhmaṇas mentioned as "three for the ancestral rite" (*trīn pitrye*). However, in the view regarding the number of Brāhmaṇas mentioned as "three for each" (*trīn trīn*), one should worship three Brāhmaṇas with each *arghya*. For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi stated, "In the hands," and so forth. It should not be argued that the phrase "in the hands" is appropriate only in the case of the view "three for the ancestral rite," because the three right hands exist only among the three Brāhmaṇas representing the group of ancestors. This is because he, having stated "in the hands" specifically regarding the worship of the Brāhmaṇas standing in the place of the ancestors, subsequently said, "The same for the other two. Therefore, in the view "three for each in the ancestral rite," one should perform the actions from the pouring of water into the right hands of the Brāhmaṇas standing in the place of the ancestors up to the offering of the *arghya*, all at once. Likewise, one should pour [the *arghya*] into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas standing in the place of the grandfather, because of the statement, "The same for the other two. In this manner, for the maternal grandfathers and others, one should perform the rites from the preparation of the *arghya* vessels up to the giving of the *arghya* into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas, accompanied by the names and lineages, according to the method of sequential performance (*padārthānusamaya*), because of the traditional rule of extension (*atideśa*): "The same for the maternal grandfathers. After the giving of the *arghya* into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas representing the father and others, Yājñavalkya [says]:
Having offered the arghya water and having placed their remnants in a vessel according to the rule,
he turns the vessel face down below with the mantra, "Thou art the station of the ancestors."

Having collected the *saṃsravas*—the remnants of the *arghya* water offered to each of those Brahmins that have flowed from their hands into other vessels—into the vessel for the ancestors (*pitṛpātra*), one should place that vessel face down as a lower offering (*adhobali*) upon the ground with the mantra, “Thou art the seat for the ancestors” (*pitṛbhyaḥ sthānam asi*). The meaning is that it should be placed on the ground, not on top of another vessel or similar object. Thus says Pracetas:
“Having collected all the *saṃsravas* into the first vessel, which is for the ancestors, and having said, ‘Thou art the seat for the ancestors,’ one should place it face down upon the ground.”

Regarding this, a specific rule has been stated by Gobhila: "One should place [the vessel] face down, like a *pavitra*. The meaning is that, having taken the *pavitras* placed in the hands of the Brahmins and having set them in the vessel for the ancestors (*pitṛpātra*), one should place [that vessel] face down on the ground together with them. A specific rule on this point has also been stated by Kātyāyana: "On the ground strewn with *kuśa* grass, one should place [it] face down, and *kuśa* grass upon it. The word "should place" (*nidadhyāt*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Matsya also says: "Having first offered the remnants of the oblation (*saṃsrava*), and then having placed them in the vessel for the ancestors, one should set it down face down to the north."

The meaning is as follows: having first offered the *arghya* water and having placed the residue (*saṃsrava*) into the vessel for the ancestors (*pitṛpātra*), one should set that vessel face down at a short distance to the north of the place where the Brahmins are seated. Atri also stated a specific rule regarding the vessel for the ancestors: "Having honored it with perfumes and so forth. By the word "and so forth," flowers are included, according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Śaunaka: "Having honored it with perfumes and garlands. Thus, turning [the vessel] face down is not mandatory; for it is said: "Then, having performed the *apasavya* (sacred thread over the right shoulder), being composed, [one should place it] beside the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*)."
Having cast away the darbha-strainers, he should then pour out the remnants of the oblation.

Thus, because the retention of the *saṃsrava* water until the time of the *svadhā*-invocation is observed in this statement of Atri, and because such retention occurs when the paternal vessel (*pitṛpātra*) is placed face-up (*uttāna*) and not when it is placed face-down (*nyubja*), the position of placing it face-up is also understood. In this view, the paternal vessel must be covered by the vessel of the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) and so forth. And so says Kātyāyana:
"One should place the vessel of the grandfather upon that paternal vessel;
then, having placed the vessel of the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), one should neither lift it up nor move it."

The meaning is that one should cover the vessel of the father with the vessel of the grandfather, and then cover that with the vessel of the great-grandfather. (In the absence of the great-grandfather’s vessel, one should cover it with some other vessel. Kātyāyana has pointed out the fault in altering the position of a vessel that has been placed either face-down or face-up: "Upon seeing a vessel that has been touched, lifted, moved elsewhere, or opened, the ancestors depart quickly and their [offerings] flow away."
"Opened" (udghāṭita) means uncovered by the removal of the vessel of the grandfather and the others; this is the meaning. For this very reason, Uśanas says:
"When the vessel of the ancestors is turned face-up or opened, that food shall not be eaten, as the hosts of ancestors have departed in anger."

The meaning of the first half-verse is as follows: when the vessel for the ancestors has been turned face-down (*nyubja*), it should be turned face-up (*uttāna*); or when the ancestral vessel has been placed face-up and covered with another vessel, it should be opened. Having turned the vessel face-down, Vaijavāpa said:
"Having placed *kuśa* grass upon it, one should present [the offerings] beginning with the gods—namely, perfumes, flowers, incense, a lamp, clothing, and the sacred thread."

The meaning is that, having placed *kuśa* grass upon that [surface], and having placed *kuśa*, perfumes, and flowers upon the overturned paternal vessel (*pitṛpātra*), one should offer the perfumes and other items beginning with the Vaiśvadevika Brahmins. By this, it is stated that after performing the offering of perfumes to the Vaiśvadevika Brahmins, it should be done for the paternal Brahmins; the same applies to the offering of flowers and so forth. Thus, by way of expression, it is indicated that the worship of the Vaiśvadevika Brahmins must be performed simultaneously with the sequential performance of the ritual items (*padārthānusamaya*). In this regard, Yājñavalkya has prescribed a sequence based on the order of sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) for the Vaiśvadeva rite; it should be understood that there is an option between that and the sequence of the aforementioned performance of ritual items. Nor should it be said that this option applies only from the offering of perfumes onwards and not before; for that would result in an inconsistency of meaning, and because Paiṭhīnasi records simultaneous performance even prior to the offering of perfumes and other items, stating: "Having requested permission, saying, 'I shall invoke the gods and the ancestors... and so forth. Viṣṇu also mentions the offering of perfumes and other items: "Having honored the Brahmins according to one's ability with ointments, garments, ornaments, flowers, and incense. The meaning is that one should give the ointments and other items to the Brahmins, designating them for the deities of the ancestors and others. For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi says: "Having taken perfumes and having uttered the name and lineage of the father, one should touch water; the same applies to the other two; likewise for incense, lamps, garlands, and coverings. Having poured water into the hand of the Brahmin intended for the father, and taking perfumes such as sandalwood, saffron, and camphor, one should say, "O our fathers, belonging to such-and-such lineage, named such-and-such, in the form of Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, together with your wives, here are your perfumes," and having given the perfumes into the very hands of the Brahmins, one should touch water. In the same way, the offering of perfumes is to be made for the grandfather and great-grandfather; the distinction is that for the grandfather one says "in the form of Rudra," and for the great-grandfather, "in the form of Āditya. The offering of flowers, incense, lamps, garlands, coverings, and so forth, should be performed in the same manner as the offering of perfumes. And so says the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
Having said, "This is your flower," one should offer flowers;
having said, "This is your incense," one should offer gentle incense.
"Having said, 'This garland is for you,' one should offer a very beautiful garland.

Thus, in this manner, having said, "This light is for you," one should present the lamp. Having said, "This garment is for you," one should present the cloth; in this way, the two [substitutions] are to be inferred. For this very reason, Devala has stated for the purpose of demonstrating the method of such inference: "Having said, 'This light is for you,' and also, 'O well-lighted ones, this light is for you.'"

One should present the light with the words, "This is your light. The meaning is that the Brahmins should say, "A good light. Regarding the phrase "And they [should say] 'A good light,'" the word "and" (ca) indicates that one should understand that the Brahmins should offer responses corresponding to the gender of each item for the seat and so forth—such as "May the seat be auspicious," "Excellent fragrance," "Fine flowers," "Good incense," "A fine lamp," and "An excellent covering. For this very reason, these responses were stated by the author of the *Gṛhyasaṃgraha*. When the question arises as to what kind of fragrances should be offered, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:

"One should provide white sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and other auspicious substances for the purpose of anointing, as well as whatever else is dear to the ancestors. Regarding this anointing, the Brahmins may perform it themselves, or the performer of the *śrāddha* may do so. In that regard, Vyāsa states a specific rule concerning the case where the performer of the *śrāddha* performs the anointing:
One should worship with perfumes using the mantra "gandhadvārām" while performing the purification of the vessel. Thus it is said.

With the mantra "gandhadvārā," preceded by the mention of their names and lineages, and having said "These perfumes are for you" while placing the perfumes into the hands of the Brahmins, one should worship with those perfumes. The meaning is that, with the *pavitra* grass in hand, one should smear the perfume upon the foreheads of the Brahmins. Even in the case where one smears it oneself, the mantra "gandhadvārā" is still used, as it is the instrumental mantra for the offering of perfume. However, the specific rule of having the *pavitra* in hand does not apply here. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Śātātapa pointed out a fault when the performer of the *śrāddha*, while in the act of smearing, applies the perfume with the *pavitra* still in his hand.
If one who has placed the sacred grass (pavitra) in his hand touches the twice-born, that śrāddha becomes for the Rākṣasas; the ancestors depart with their hopes frustrated.
Anointing is the smearing with fragrant substances. Devala has pointed out a fault common to both fortnights:
one should never remove the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) from the shoulders during rites for the gods or the ancestors, for the sake of accomplishing worship with perfumes and other offerings.

The meaning is that for the sake of successfully applying perfumes and other unguents, the *vipras* should not remove their sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Śaṅkha has stated a fault regarding the application of unguents after removing [the thread] from the shoulder: "If one should apply unguents to the limbs having placed the sacred thread around the waist, or if one should eat while wearing only a single garment, the ancestors depart disappointed."
However, it is stated that there is a fault if the *puṇḍra* on the forehead is made circular by means of a ritual act (*kratu*).
"Upon seeing the *puṇḍra* on the forehead and likewise a garland on the shoulder,
the ancestors depart in despair, having seen the husband of a *vṛṣalī*."

Thus, because this prohibition—which must be inferred by the force of the recollection of a fault—is overridden by the established injunction for the vertical *puṇḍra*, it refers specifically to the circular *puṇḍra*. Since the wearing of a garland on the shoulder is remembered as being faulty, a Brahmin should wear a garland only on his head; even there, only on the crest-lock (*śikhā*), for it is not enjoined that he should wrap a garland around his head excluding the crest-lock.

Thus, according to the recollection of Vṛddha-Manu: "A Brahmin who has been invited (*niyukta*) to a *śrāddha* [should not wear] garlands; however, a garland made of prescribed flowers should be given. When it is asked what flowers are prescribed, the *Brahma-purāṇa* states:
"Flowers from the *śulka* tree are best, as are lotuses and water-lilies (*utpala*), along with all other [flowers] that are endowed with fragrance and incense."

Viṣṇu, however, states the mantra for the offering of flowers: "With the words 'puṣpāvatīḥ,' [one offers] the flower. The word "should give" (dadyāt), heard in the preceding sentence, is supplied here as well. "O plants, rejoice; you who possess flowers and are rich in fruit—this seasonal embryo has taken its seat in your ancient dwelling place."

This phrase "puṣpāvatīḥ" is the citation of the middle portion of the mantra. At the end of the mantra, one should offer a flower preceded by the mention of the [recipient's] name and lineage, saying, "This flower is for you. Regarding the specific substance for incense, it has been stated by Śaṅkha:
"For the purpose of incense, one should offer guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter and pungent substances."

Vyāsa, however, states the mantra for the offering of incense: "Having said 'dhūpaṃ ca dhūr asi'... The meaning is that one should offer incense after reciting the Yajurveda mantra: "dhūr asi dhūr va dhūrvantam. In the Purāṇa, however, another mantra is stated: "This divine incense, the essence of the forest tree, rich in fragrance and most enchanting, fit to be offered to all the gods—may it be accepted. [316]

It should be understood that this [offering] is optional with the mantra "dhūr asi. Here too, at the end of the mantra, preceded by the mention of the name and lineage, one should offer incense, saying, "This incense is for you. Incense wafted by the breath from the hand must not be used by a Brahmin, because it is prohibited. Śātātapa says:
"The best of the twice-born who inhale incense struck by the breath from the hand—by that, the *śrāddha* becomes fruitless; therefore, one should avoid it."
Regarding the lamp, Marīci states the specific rule:
"The lamp should be made from ghee or sesame oil, but not from any other substance."

Regarding the mantra for the garment and its substitute in the absence of a garment, Śātātapa says: "One should give a cloth with the mantra 'yuvā suvāsāḥ'; in its absence, a sacred thread (yajñopavīta). Here too, at the end of the mantra, one should say, "This is a garment for you," or "This is a sacred thread for you," after first pronouncing the name and lineage (*gotra*), and then give either the garment or the sacred thread. There are also other statements from other *Smṛtis* concerning acceptable and avoidable perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and garments; these have been written by us in the section on the preparation of materials for the *śrāddha* and should be consulted here as well. In this manner, the offering of perfumes, flowers, and so forth for the maternal grandfather and others must also be performed according to the sequence of items (*padārthānusamaya*), accompanied by their names and lineages, because of the traditional rule of extension (*atideśa*): "The same applies to the maternal grandfathers. After the offering of the garment to the maternal great-grandfather, the performer should say, "May the worship be complete. The Brahmins should say, "Let it be. The performer should say, "May you all say, 'May there be the fulfillment of the resolve' (*saṃkalpasiddhi*). The Brahmins should say, "May there be the fulfillment of the resolve."
Thus ends the procedure for the offerings of water and other honors in the *Smṛticandrikā* [317].
Now follows the procedure for the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*).
Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
Having offered perfumes and seasonal flowers to Brahmā,
one should thereafter offer incense into the fire in the proper sequence.

"Seasonal flowers" (*ṛtubhavāni puṣpāṇi*) refers to those produced in well-known seasons such as spring and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include items not explicitly mentioned. Thus, the meaning is this: having prepared perfumes, flowers, ornaments, incense, and garments for the sake of the Brahmins, one should immediately thereafter perform the rite called *agnaukaraṇa*. When the question arises as to how one should perform it, Hārīta says: "Then, after the food has been set aside, he asks everyone at the head of the row: 'I shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa*. The *Nigama* also states: "Having set aside the food and sprinkled it with clarified butter, he asks: 'I shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa*. This is also stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
Having said, "I shall perform [the offering] in the fire," and being told by them,
"Do so," he should offer oblations according to the very procedure prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* and cause [the portions] to be placed in the vessels.

The meaning is that, having offered [the oblation], one should give the remains of the offering (*hutaśeṣa*) into the vessels of the ancestors and the Brahmins. The restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only by that which is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*" is not intended to exclude the procedures stated in the *Dharma-śāstras* and other such texts, because the procedures stated in the *Dharma-śāstras* and those stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* are mutually dependent. Therefore, the *eva* here is intended to exclude the procedure stated in the *Purāṇas*. For this very reason, after stating that the fire-offering (*agnaukaraṇa*) must be performed according to the rite prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, that same *Purāṇa* demonstrates a procedure not mentioned in the *Gṛhyas*:
"Then a man should offer food, excluding condiments and salt."

"O bull of the Bharatas, having been permitted three times by those twice-born ones... (318). Thus, "food fit for an oblation" (*haviṣyam annam*) means food excluding condiments and salt. As for that which is stated in another Purāṇa:
"Of flowers, fruits, and edible items, with great care..."
Having extracted the best portion from all of them, one should offer it into the Jātavedas fire.

Thus, the Smṛti rule regarding the performance of oblations (*homa*) of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) that has been touched by salt, condiments, and so forth—prepared for the sake of the ancestors—is intended for those whose *Gṛhya-sūtra* prescribes that after the *agnaukaraṇa-homa*, another oblation of non-sacrificial food (*ahaviṣya*) must be performed without mantras. Therefore, there is no contradiction with what was stated previously. "In *jātavedas*" means in the fire consisting of hot ashes; and thus Āpastamba, as part of the *agnaukaraṇa* rite, has said: "There is no oblation of alkaline or salty substances, nor of non-sacrificial food mixed with inferior food. Having pushed aside the hot ashes toward the north, one should offer therein; that becomes both offered and unoffered in the fire. Pāraskara also describes the *agnaukaraṇa*.

"Having offered perfumes and the like, as well as incense, one should take up the oblation mixed with clarified butter; permitted by the paternal [Brāhmaṇas], one offers it according to the rite for the ancestors. The word "by the paternal" refers to the Brāhmaṇas; this is the ellipsis.
Authorized by the Brahmins, a Brahmin should perform [the rite] in the fire together with the Brahmins.

This is because of the *Manusmṛti*. The meaning is that he is authorized simultaneously by all the paternal Brāhmaṇas. The meaning of the injunction “he offers the *pitṛyajña* oblation” has been elaborated upon by Hārīta: “Being authorized with the words ‘Do so,’ having scattered [the grass] once with *sakṛd-ācchinna* blades—cut near the roots—over the fire previously kindled, and having offered two oblations with the *mekṣaṇa* while facing east using a single fuel-stick (*samit*) according to the *tantra* rule, he should dispose of the *mekṣaṇa* into the very fire. The phrase “in the fire previously kindled” means in the fire that was awakened even before the scattering of grass; “scattered with *sakṛd-ācchinna* blades” means strewn with *darbha* grass cut in one effort near the root; “using a single fuel-stick according to the *tantra* rule” means facing east, taking only one fuel-stick for the purpose of both oblations, and having offered the two oblations with the *mekṣaṇa* made of sacrificial wood, he should throw the *mekṣaṇa* into the fire. By the phrase “using a single fuel-stick according to the *tantra* rule,” the specific ritual duty (*dharma*) of the *pitṛyajña* is not being stated, because there is no placing of a fuel-stick in the *pitṛyajña*. Rather, a different ritual duty is taught here. Therefore, Suyajña also states the extended duties (*atideśa-dharma*) along with the two taught duties: “Having swept around, sprinkled water, scattered [grass], bent the right knee, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), sitting facing east, he offers with the *mekṣaṇa*. Here, sweeping and sprinkling are taught. The two mantras for the oblation, obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) from the rule “he should offer like the *pitṛyajña*,” have been shown by Madālasā.
"To Agni Kavyavāhana, svāhā!"—this is the first oblation;
"To Soma Pitṛmat, svāhā!"—thus should the other be performed.

The word *vai* is for the purpose of filling out the meter; therefore, it should not be employed at the time of recitation. However, Gobhila has stated, in reverse order, two *svāhā*-utterance *mantras* for the *agnaukaraṇa* offering prior [to the main offerings]: "One should offer by scooping with a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*): first, 'Svāhā to Soma accompanied by the ancestors'; second, 'Svāhā to Agni, the carrier of the *kavyas*'; after this, one should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*). Since he specifies that one should wear the thread over the right shoulder after the oblation, it is understood by implication that during the oblation itself one wears it over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*). "Scooping with a stirring-spoon" means that one offers after having taken a portion with the stirring-spoon. In the *Purāṇa*, however, the view of three oblations is set forth with *mantras* ending in *svadhā* and *namaḥ*.
Having placed a fuel-stick inside, one should offer it into the Jātavedas while saying:
"To Agni Kavyavāhana, svadhā! Homage!"
Reciting "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā!
Homage!"—these are the oblation mantras for the three [ancestors] in their proper order.

"To the north, one should always offer to Agni, and to Soma in the south; between these two, one should always offer to Vivasvat. Regarding this, it is stated in that very same place for the purpose of determining whether the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) to be placed therein are acceptable or unacceptable: "Fuel-sticks that have fallen from a tree, those that have been broken by wind, those that are hollow, those that are burnt at the tip, those that are black, those that are gnawed by insects, those that are split, and those that are crooked—these are not fit for sacrifice. "However, those that are straight, unblemished, and of the same length, and which have grown on the eastern or northern side of the tree, are fit for sacrifice. "One should offer with fuel-sticks that are fresh, not dried up, and of the same size; one should avoid those that are old, dried up, or of different sizes. "One should offer with fuel-sticks that are as long as an arm, or as long as a span, or as long as a thumb; one should never offer with those that are shorter than that. "One should offer with fuel-sticks that have leaves, that are not leafless, and that have not lost their bark; one should avoid those that are leafless, stripped of bark, or scorched. "One should offer with fuel-sticks that are not split, that are not cracked, and that are not worm-eaten; one should avoid those that are split, cracked, or worm-eaten. "One should offer with fuel-sticks that are not curved, that are not bent, and that are not twisted; one should avoid those that are curved, bent, or twisted. "One should offer with fuel-sticks that are not too broad
The palāśa, phalguna, nyagrodha, plakṣa, aśvattha, vikaṅkata, udumbara, śamī, bilva, candana, and those trees which are fit for sacrifice;
The jackfruit tree, the deodar, the sal tree, and likewise the khadira—
these trees are especially recommended for the purpose of sacrificial fuel.
Those that are thorny, those suitable for sacrifice,
as well as the *śleṣmātaka*, the *naktamāla*, the *kapittha*, and the *śālmali*— these are to be taken.
The nīpa, the vibhītaka, the ciribilva, the ṭaṅka, the tinduka, and the āmrātaka are likewise censured for use in the performance of śrāddha rites.
The *tilvaka* and the *kovidāra*—these are censured for use in *śrāddha* rites.

*Phalgu* is the *kākodumbarikā* tree. The option regarding the number of *emasūktāhuti* offerings is established by the very mention [in the texts]. In the archetype, the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, both alternatives have been stated. Thus, Āpastamba, concerning the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, says: "The Adhvaryu, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), bending his right knee, having made an under-layer (*upastīrya*) on the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), having taken a portion with it and sprinkled it with clarified butter, offers it into the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) with the mantra: *svadhā namaḥ* to Soma, who drinks the libations of the ancestors. [321] He offers a second [oblation] with: *svadhā namaḥ* to Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors; a third with: *svadhā namaḥ* to Agni Kavyavāhana. Having offered those rice grains which were in the stirring-spoon, he silently places the spoon [into the fire]; some say he does not offer to Yama. The option between mantras ending in *svadhā namaḥ* and mantras ending in *svāhā* is also established, as before, through extended application (*atideśa*), because two types of mantras are prescribed in the archetype. Among these, the mantras ending in *svadhā namaḥ* have been shown as stated by Āpastamba. However, the mantras ending in *svāhā* for the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* are stated by Sāṅkhyāyana: "Bending his right knee, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), sitting facing east, he offers with the stirring-spoon: *svāhā* to Agni Kavyavāhana; *svāhā* to Soma; *svāhā* to Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors. The phrase *pitṛmate svāhā* is to be supplied here after *somāya*. Therefore, although the two specific mantras "to Agni, *svāhā*" and "to Soma, *svāhā*" are prescribed [elsewhere], they apply to the fire-offering (*agnaukaraṇa*) by extended application, because such mantras are taught even in the archetype. Likewise, Vaijavāpa, concerning the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, says: "Having poured clarified butter and moved it [to the side], wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, he offers two oblations with the stirring-spoon on the *Anvāhāryapacana* fire: the first with *agnaye*, the latter with *somāya*. The *Anvāhāryapacana* is the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*). Thus, regarding the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* offering, the authors of the ritual manuals (*kalpasūtra*)—Āpastamba, Sāṅkhyāyana, and Vaijavāpa—who state that wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder is understood from scripture (*śruti*) as a duty belonging exclusively to the gods (*daiva*), consider the primary act consisting of the offering to be of a divine nature (*daivika*). Kātyāyana also thinks in this very way, as he says: [The original Sanskrit text follows here.]
"The offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇahoma), however, must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī);
for there is a Vedic revelation stating, 'One offers to the gods facing eastward. Thus it is said.

The meaning is as follows: In the *śruti* that prescribes the *piṇḍapitṛyajña-homa*, which serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for the *agnaukaraṇa-homa*, it is heard: "Having lifted [the food], he offers two oblations into the fire for the gods. By the force of this, since the *agnaukaraṇa-homa*—which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of that—is like its archetype in possessing divine characteristics, it must be performed with divine characteristics such as wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītitva*). In this context, regarding the two oblations prescribed by the injunction "he offers two oblations," there arises a doubt: since Soma and Agni are understood from the wording of the mantras—"Svāhā to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs" and "Svāhā to Agni, the bearer of the *kavyas*"—to be the deities, and because in the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the *Pitṛyajña* within the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices they are seen designated sometimes as Pitṛs and sometimes as gods, are they here deities in their form as Pitṛs or in their form as gods? With the intention that the deityhood here belongs only to those in their form as gods—based on observing an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*) saying "for the gods"—it is stated: "because of the hearing of the *śruti* 'he offers to the gods'. However, it should not be understood as intending that deityhood is explicitly heard in the *śruti* as belonging only to those in their form as gods. For this very reason, immediately thereafter, that same author stated another alternative view (*pakṣāntara*) due to dissatisfaction [with the first].
"It should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder or facing south;
for once the sacrificial oblation has been set aside for one [deity], it is not offered to another."

The meaning of this is as follows: In the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the offering (*nirvāpa*) for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*) and for the sake of the ancestral deities (*pitṛ-devatā*) is performed only once with the mantra, "I offer what is pleasing to the ancestors. Consequently, by the power of the mantra of the offering, it is understood that Soma and Agni, in their capacity as ancestors, alone are the deities of the oblation. However, if one were to rely on the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), "To the gods," to establish them as deities in their divine form, it would be improper to say that what was offered for one [set of deities] is then offered to another. Therefore, they must be deities only in their capacity as ancestors; thus, the model oblation (*prakṛtibhūto homaḥ*) is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) and facing south. Accordingly, the modified oblation (*vikṛtibhūta*) of the *agnaukaraṇa* should also be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder and facing south. Considering this very position to be superior, Āśvalāyana states—regarding the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* oblation—that according to his own view it possesses ancestral characteristics (*paitṛka-dharma*), while according to the view of others it possesses divine characteristics (*daivika-dharma*): "Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), having added fuel to the fire, and having taken portions with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) in accordance with the rules of portioning, he should offer [saying]: 'Svadhā! Adoration to Soma accompanied by the ancestors! Svadhā! Adoration to Agni, the bearer of the offerings to the ancestors! Or, with the utterance of 'Svāhā,' he may offer first to Agni [then to Soma], wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*). Thus, because the model *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* has two forms and its ritual characteristics are optional, the modified *agnaukaraṇa* oblation, by extension (*atideśa*), also possesses optional characteristics and may be performed either with the sacred thread over the left shoulder or over the right. Among these, those who follow the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-sūtra* should perform it with ancestral characteristics. And so it is stated by him himself in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "Having set aside food smeared with ghee, he asks for permission, saying: 'I shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa*'; or 'I will do it'; or 'I am doing it. The response is: 'Do it'; or 'Perform it'; or 'Go ahead. Then he offers into the fire as previously described. In the *Kātyāyana-gṛhya-sūtra*, however, it is said: "Having set aside food smeared with ghee, he asks, 'Shall I perform the *agnaukaraṇa*? Being permitted with the words 'Do so,' he offers into the fire like the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Although it appears from the etymology—"the *Pitṛyajña* accomplished by means of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*)"—that the name *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* applies only to the *Pitṛyajña* consisting of the offering of rice-balls and not to the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* consisting of the oblation, nevertheless, the name is applied to both the rice-ball *Pitṛyajña* and the oblation *Pitṛyajña* through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just as the term "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) refers to both the staff and the person carrying it, or as the name *Vaiśvadeva* applies to the seven sacrifices beginning with the *Āgneya* performed during the first seasonal festival (*parvan*) of the *Cāturmāsya*. Thus, both the rice-ball offering and the oblation are primary here; it is not the case that only the rice-ball offering is primary and the oblation is merely a subordinate part (*aṅga*). Precisely because the oblation is also primary, Āpastamba has stated: "If the father is living, having performed [the rites] up to the oblation, he should desist. If the oblation were merely a subordinate part, then upon the cessation of the primary rite called the rice-ball offering, the subordinate oblation would also cease due to the absence of its motivating cause; in that case, the sūtra "having performed up to the oblation, he should desist" would be utterly inconsistent. Therefore, it is known that the *Pitṛyajña* consisting of the oblation is also a primary rite. And thus, the meaning of the phrase "having offered like the *Pitṛyajña*" is: "one should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* like the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* consisting of the oblation. This is what he intends when speaking in his own Smṛti.
"One offers to the gods facing east," so says the Vedic revelation; for once the sacrificial oblation has been set aside for one [deity], it is certainly not offered to another.

Thus, by these two [verses], the intention should be understood to be that [the rite] is like the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* among the previously mentioned divine (*daivika*) and ancestral (*paitṛka*) duties, because no specific sūtra prescribing the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* has been stated here. This is clear from the *Baijavāpagṛhya*, which states: "Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), having addressed the fire with the words 'O Agni, eat the oblations' (*akravāṇi*), one performs the *agnaukaraṇa*"; thus, the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* possesses the divine characteristics just like the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* prescribed in one's own sūtra. As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya without even mentioning the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*: "Having been authorized with 'Om, do so,' and having offered into the fire according to the *pitṛyajña*... [325]
Thus, as stated by Pāraskara:
"Permitted by his paternal relatives, he offers oblations like the Pitṛyajña."

Thus, in all these instances, the meaning to be understood is "like the *pitṛyajña* characterized by divine (*daivika*) ritual rules," because this has been stated by many authors of the *sūtras*. Nor should it be argued that being stated by many is irrelevant; for Jaimini has declared its relevance in the rule: "The property of the majority should prevail. Now, one might object: even the opinion of the majority is irrelevant because it contradicts the principle, "Having set aside the oblation for one, it is not offered to another. This is not so. Indeed, Āpastamba and others also think as follows: when rice grains are to be sprinkled with water—having been set aside through the *darśa* sacrifice, connected to a single deity, and placed together in a single vessel, namely a winnowing basket—the sprinkling mantra, "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni," contains the word "you" (*vaḥ*), which refers to some of them but does not apply to all. And likewise, regarding those same rice grains, the sprinkling mantra, "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Indra and Agni," contains the word "you" (*vaḥ*), which refers to some but does not apply to all. Similarly, regarding the rice grains placed in a single vessel, the setting-aside mantra, "I set you aside, acceptable to the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*)," contains the word "you" (*vaḥ*), which refers to some of the rice but does not apply to all the rice in the vessel. Thus, not everything in the vessel is set aside for the ancestors, but only half of it; that portion set aside for the ancestors is offered to Pitṛmat Soma and the others. Therefore, the opinion of the majority is not contrary to logic, and everything is faultless. Furthermore, in the view where the entire setting aside is done silently (*tūṣṇīm*), there is no conflict with logic at all. That position too was stated by Āpastamba: "He sets it aside in an earthen vessel with the mantra, 'I set you aside, acceptable to the ancestors,' or silently. In the case of setting aside separately, the conflict with logic is cast far away. This position, however, was stated by Vatsa: "Having placed the strainers inside, he sets aside the sacrificial porridge (*caru*). Three times with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*yajñopavītī*) using the right hand, and three times with the thread over the left shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) using the left hand, he should offer it with a ladle while wearing the thread over the right shoulder, saying: 'Svadhā, obeisance to Soma accompanied by the ancestors; Svadhā, obeisance to Yama, son of Aṅgiras, accompanied by the ancestors; Svadhā, obeisance to Agni, the bearer of offerings to the ancestors (*kavyavāhana*). Therefore, it is correct that in the *smṛtis*, the term *pitṛyajña* denotes the *pitṛyajña* characterized by divine ritual rules. As for what was stated by Manu..."
"Having performed everything, including the circumambulation, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) toward the fire—
this refers specifically to the domain of the Āśvalāyana Śākhā;
for [the rule] 'svāhā, svadhā, namaḥ, with the thread over the left (savya) or likewise over the right (apasavya)' applies to that."
As for the number of oblations, however, that should be understood from one's own ritual manual (sūtra).

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Kātyāyana. Thus, it should be understood that the number thirteen of oblations mentioned by Āpastamba applies specifically to those who follow the *Āpastamba-sūtra*. In the *Dharma-sūtra*, Āpastamba prescribes the method for making offerings into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*): "He addresses [the invited guests]: ‘Let [food] be set aside; let it be offered into the fire. Having been granted permission—[by the reply] ‘Let it be set aside as you wish; let it be offered into the fire as you wish’—he should set it aside and offer it. Although the number of oblations ought to be stated here in connection with this injunction for the fire-offering, one must understand that while the number thirteen is effectively shown there through the restatement of the mantras prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, the specific number is not explicitly mentioned in that [Dharma-sūtra] passage. “Having been granted permission” (*atisṛṣṭaḥ*) means being authorized. Thus, having performed the inquiry regarding the setting aside of the food and so forth, he should set the food aside and perform the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the *ājyabhāga* (butter-portions), following the sequence prescribed in the *Āpastamba-gṛhya-sūtra*. This is because the collection of preliminary rites (*prācyāṅgakalāpa*) is ordained as common to all the principal oblations (*pradhānahoma*) which will be described later. At the end of the *ājyabhāga*, he should offer oblations with the mantras beginning with "yan me mātā" (RV 10.38.1–4). Accordingly, the *Āpastamba-gṛhya-sūtra* states: "He offers [portions] of the food with the subsequent [verses], and the subsequent [verses] are butter-oblations. Taking small portions of the set-aside food according to the rules for sacrificial cutting (*avadāna*), and placing them on the *darvī* ladle, he offers two oblations with the two verses "yan me mātā pralulobha carati" and "yās tiṣṭhanti," ending each with "amuṣmai svāhā," while pronouncing the father’s name in the dative case (*amuṣmā*) in place of "amuṣmai. In the same manner, with the two verses "yan me pitāmahī pralulobha carati" and "antardadhe parvataiḥ," ending with "amuṣmai svāhā," he offers two oblations, pronouncing the grandfather’s name in the dative case (*amuṣmā*). Likewise, with the two verses "yan me prapitāmahī pralulobha carati" and "antardadha ṛtubhiḥ," ending with "amuṣmai svāhā," he offers two oblations, pronouncing the great-grandfather’s name in the dative case (*amuṣmā*). With the two verses "yan me mātāmahī pralulobha carati" and "yās tiṣṭhanti," he offers two oblations to the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*). With the two verses "yan me mātuḥpitāmahī pralulobha carati" and "antardadhe parvataiḥ," he offers two oblations to the maternal great-grandfather (*mātuḥpitāmaha*). With the two verses "yan me mātuḥprapitāmahī pralulobha carati" and "antardadha ṛtubhiḥ," he offers two oblations to the maternal great-great-grandfather (*mātuḥprapitāmaha*). Regarding these, in the first mantra, the modification (*ūha*) should be made: "yan me mātāmahī pralulobha carati... tan me reto mātāmaho vṛṅktām. In the second mantra, the modification is: "antar anyaṃ mātāmahād vadhaḥ. In both mantras, the name of the maternal grandfather should be pronounced in the dative case (*amuṣmā*) in place of "amuṣmai. In the third mantra, the modification is: "yan me mātuḥpitāmahī pralulobha carati... tan me mātuḥ pitāmaho vṛṅktām. In the fourth mantra, the modification is: "antar anyaṃ mātuḥpitāmahād vadhaḥ. In both mantras, the name of the maternal great-grandfather should be pronounced in the dative case (*amuṣmā*) in place of "amuṣmai. In the fifth mantra, the modification is: "yan me mātuḥprapitāmahī pralulobha carati... tan me mātuḥ prapitāmaho vṛṅktām. In the sixth mantra, the modification is: "antar anyaṃ mātuḥprapitāmahād vadhaḥ. In both mantras, the name of the maternal great-great-grandfather should be pronounced in the dative case (*amuṣmā*) in place of "amuṣmai."
In place of the words "father" and so forth, the terms "maternal grandfather" and so forth should be applied during the food-oblation,
the ritual touching, and the offering of water, rice-balls, and other items.
The passage beginning with "yan me mātāmahī" would serve as an illustration in that regard.

This is because it has been stated by the author of the *Gṛhyabhāṣyārthasaṃgraha*: Regarding the touching [of the food]: when touching the food intended for the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas, one uses the three mantras beginning with, "O Father, this honeyed wave of thine is refreshing; svāhā. Then, having taken portions as before, he offers one oblation (*āhuti*) with the verse, "And those fathers who are here... Having thus offered the oblations of food, he offers six oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*). Among these, he first offers an oblation with *svāhā* to the father. He offers the second with the word *svāhā* at the end. Having offered the third and fourth oblations with these same two mantras, he offers the fifth with *svadhā svāhā*, and the sixth with *agnaye kavyavāhanāya svāhā*. Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, he takes a little from all kinds of edible foods—both solid and soft—and having pushed the ashes aside toward the north, he offers it silently into those hot ashes. Then, having silently smeared the two [spots on the ladle] and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) like the *prastara* and cast them into the fire, and so forth, having performed the subsequent set of rites ending with the sprinkling of water as prescribed for the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice to Agni, he should place the remains of the oblation into the bowls of the Brāhmaṇas for their meal. All of this has been stated by the author of that *bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha*.
Having prepared the fire and fuel and performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings,
they should then take portions of the food and perform seven oblations of food into the fire with the respective mantras beginning with "yan me."

"Homages with clarified butter should be performed even with mantras beginning with *svāhā*; then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and removed the ashes, there should be the oblation of the food-offering (*haviḥ-anna-homa*) and the smearing of the two ladles (*darvī*) upon the smearings (*lepa*). Having completed the remainder of the rites up to the final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), one should place the remnants of the offered food into the vessels. Thus it is said.

The statement "with seven offerings of food" (*annahomāḥ*) is said with the intention that the mantras are not modified (*anūhita*); for if the mantras were modified (*ūhita*), the number would become thirteen, making the expression "with seven" inappropriate. Thus, this *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), because it pertains to the ancestors (*paitṛka*). Accordingly, Āpastamba has stated in his own Gṛhyaśāstra and other works: "In the dark fortnight, the rites for the ancestors are performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, moving counter-clockwise, and ending on the south. Even in that context, whatever does not pertain to the ancestors—such as the pouring of the *āghāra* libation and the kindling of the fire—must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*); for this very reason, it was stated by the author of the *Bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha*.
The same applies during the pouring of the libations (āghāra), the offering of wood, the portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), the circumambulation, and the following after [the fire].
For the one with matted hair (kapardin), the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) is prescribed for the two libations and for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
Thus concludes the procedure for the *agnaukaraṇa* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination of the fire intended for both types of *agnaukaraṇa*.

In this regard, Yājñavalkya says: "A householder should perform the *smārta* rites daily in the marriage fire, or in the fire brought at the time of inheritance; he should perform the *śrauta* rites in the *vaitānika* fires."

*Smārta* ritual action refers to the *aupāsana-homa*, the *vaiśvadeva*, the *agnaukaraṇa*, and so forth. It should be performed in the *vivāha-agni*—the *aupāsana* fire produced at the time of marriage—or in the *aupāsana* fire brought at the time of inheritance, having been fetched from the household of a Vaiśya or others at the time of receiving the inheritance; this is the meaning. In the case of a total consecration (*sarvādhāna*) where the *aupāsana* fire is unavailable, there is an omission of the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* prescribed by Āpastamba, but not its performance in the *vaitānika* (śrauta) fires, because of the statement: "The śrauta [rites] are in the *vaitānika* fires. Nor is it to be done in a common (*laukika*) fire, because, unlike the deities and so forth, there is no substitute for the fire. For this very reason, Dhūrtasvāmin has stated regarding the impossibility of the *aupāsana* due to a total consecration: "The Śrāddha should be performed after the *homa*; however, the Brāhmaṇa [invited] serves the purpose of the *āhavanīya*, because that [fire] is also primary. This means that even for the Śrāddha characterized by the offering of food, which is performed after the *homa*, [this applies]. As for the *agnaukaraṇa* which follows the rites of the *pitṛyajña*, there is no cessation even when the *aupāsana* fire is absent due to a total consecration. Although the *aupāsana* fire taught by the rule "the *smārta* rite in the *vivāha-agni*" etc. is absent, the performance takes place in the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire) because of the possibility of its presence through the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "like the *pitṛyajña*. With this very intention, Mārkaṇḍeya has stated:
"But one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), being composed, should offer oblations in the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni).

Regarding the *agnaukaraṇa* rite mentioned by Āpastamba, since there is no extension (*atideśa*) from the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the southern fire is not obtained; therefore, it is logical that in the case of a total establishment of the fires (*sarvādhāna*), there is an absence of *agnaukaraṇa* as stated by Dhūrtasvāmin. Or rather, according to the intention expressed previously, it is also stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "Having diligently brought the southern fire for the purpose of the oblation..."
"Or one may offer oblations even with a worldly fire for the sake of the fire, for the accomplishment of the rite."

The meaning of this is as follows: for the purpose of the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation, in the absence of the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*), one should fetch and take possession of either the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) or the common fire (*laukikāgni*), and offer the oblation for the successful completion of the ritual act. By the phrase "for the sake of the fire," it is implied that when the domestic fire is present, there is no taking of another fire. In that regard, if the option of the southern fire is impossible due to travel abroad or other reasons, the option of the common fire applies; because that [common fire], which is understood through two means of knowledge—direct instruction and extended application—is the primary fire in the absence of the southern fire, it must be resorted to out of necessity. For this very reason, it is stated: "having fetched the southern fire with effort. As for the other Smṛti text:
"One who possesses a sacred fire [should perform the rite] in the fire; one without a sacred fire, however, [should do so] in the hand of a twice-born man or in water.
One should always perform the rite in the fire; it is certain that this does not apply to the common (laukika) fire."

This is its meaning: a man possessing the sacred fires (agnimān) should perform the *agnaukaraṇa*—the offering into the fire—in the *aupāsana* fire, or in the *dakṣiṇāgni*, or in the fire previously mentioned for the *vyasthā* rite. However, one who has not established the *aupāsana* fire before partitioning the inheritance, or who is "one whose fire is severed" (*chinnāgni*), or who is separated from his wife, should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* either in the hand of a twice-born (*dvija*) or in water; he must never do so in an ordinary worldly fire (*laukikāgni*). Consequently, there is no contradiction with the statement in the *Vāyupurāṇa*. Even for one who possesses the *śrauta* fires, in certain circumstances, the *agnaukaraṇa* should be performed in the hand of a twice-born, just as for one who does not possess the fires. And so it is stated in another *Smṛti*:
"A twice-born man who maintains a sacred fire should perform the offering into the fire either in his hand or in the fire itself. [332] Thus it is said.

Here, by the word "fire" (*agni*), the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) is not meant, because while that is present, there would be no room for the [other] options such as the hand. Therefore, either the Śrauta fire or the common worldly fire (*laukikāgni*) is meant. By the term "one who possesses the fire" (*sāgnika*), all types of consecrated fires (*sarvādhāna*) are intended. Consequently, the meaning is this: when the *aupāsana* fire is absent due to a *sarvādhāna*, one should perform the *agnaukaraṇa*—which shares the characteristics of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*—in the *dakṣiṇāgni*; in its absence, in a common worldly fire or in the hand of a twice-born (*dvija*). Even in that case, if the *dakṣiṇāgni* is absent due to travel abroad and so forth, the options of the common worldly fire or the hand should be understood according to the logic previously stated. Since no such specific distinction is known regarding the common worldly fire, it stands in equal option with the hand. Although, according to logical principle (*nyāya*), there can be no substitute (*pratinidhi*) for the fire, nevertheless, the *dakṣiṇāgni* and others are not taken here on the basis of the rule for substitutes. Rather, since the performance of the rite achievable by that fire would otherwise be impossible due to the absence of the *gṛhya* fire, the text prescribes that the rite achievable by the *gṛhya* fire may be performed even in a non-*gṛhya* fire and so forth; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. In this way, for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* is like the *aupāsana*; likewise, for one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*) but has performed only a partial consecration (*ardhādhānin*), the *agnaukaraṇa* is in the *aupāsana* fire itself. For an *āhitāgni* who has performed a *sarvādhāna* and is devoid of the *aupāsana*, there is simply an absence of the *agnaukaraṇa* mentioned by Āpastamba. However, the *agnaukaraṇa* characterized by the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is performed in the *dakṣiṇāgni*; in its absence, in a common worldly fire or in the hand of a twice-born. It is established that for one without fire, the two kinds of *agnaukaraṇa* are performed in the hand of a twice-born or in water. For one who has not established the fires, it is like the *aupāsana*; for one who has established the fires but possesses the *aupāsana* through *ardhādhāna*, if the *aupāsana* is somehow absent due to travel abroad and so forth, the *agnaukaraṇa* must be performed in the hand of a twice-born or in water. "And one who has not established the sacred fires [should perform the offering] in the *aupāsana* fire; in the absence of fire, in a twice-born man, or in water" (333). The *aupāsada* is the domestic (*gṛhya*) fire. In the phrase "one who has not established the sacred fires," the word "and" (*ca*) serves to include those who have established the fires. Consequently, the meaning is as follows: both one who has not established the sacred fires and one who has established them by means of the *ardhādhāna* rite and possesses the *aupāsana* fire should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* offering in the presence of that domestic fire, or in that very fire itself. In the absence of fire—that is, when the domestic fire is not present—one should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* in water or in the hand of a twice-born man. Regarding this alternative of performing it in water, Kātyāyana has specified the particular scope of its application.
Regarding the view that one should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation in water:
when the *śrāddha* takes place near water, that is to be understood as the prescribed rule.

Thus, when the *śrāddha* is performed elsewhere than near water, the position that the offering should be made into the hand of the twice-born (*dvija*) must be accepted. Furthermore, this distinction of subject matter is to be seen even in the verse, "But one without fire [should offer] into the hand of a twice-born or into water," because there is no reason to assume that this refers to another *smṛti*—such as the statement by Mārkaṇḍeya in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*—rather than the present text itself. As for what was stated by Manu:
"In the absence of fire, however, one should place [the offering] directly into the hand of a Brahmin."
Thus, this refers to the domain of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) *śrāddha* rites to be performed prior to taking a wife. This very subject has been clarified by Jātūkarṇa:
"In the absence of the sacred fire, however, one should give [the offering] into the right hand of a Brahmin;
the absence of the fire is said to persist as long as one has not found a wife."

One should place food in the right hand; the remainder of the sentence is "for the purpose of the two kinds of *agnaukaraṇa* oblations. As for that which was stated by the author of the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "The *anvaṣṭakya*, the [rite] on the previous day, the monthly [rite], the *pārvaṇa*, the optional [rite], the [rite] on the occasion of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), the eighth [rite], and the *ekoddiṣṭa* as the eighth."
[334] For those who maintain the sacred fires, the oblation is prescribed to be offered into the fire during the first four [rites];
for the latter four as well, it should be placed into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors.

Thus, the *aṣṭakā* śrāddhas are those prescribed by the rule: "The *aṣṭakās* [are performed] on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the winter and cool seasons. Among these, the śrāddha performed on the ninth day (*navamī*) following the day of the *aṣṭakā* śrāddha is the *anvaṣṭakya*; the śrāddha performed on the preceding day, the seventh (*saptamī*), is indicated by the term *pūrvedyuḥ* (on the previous day). The monthly śrāddha performed during the dark fortnight is expressed by the phrase "month after month. The *pārvaṇa* is the *darśa* śrāddha, which serves as the archetype for all śrāddhas. The *kāmya* is the śrāddha performed with a desire for sons and other benefits. The *ābhyudayika* śrāddha is indicated by the word *abhyudaya* (prosperity). The śrāddha known as *aṣṭakā* is indicated by the phrase "on the eighth day. By the term *ekoddiṣṭa*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is indicated through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*), because the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is also present within the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Regarding these, in the first four, for those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* (the oblation into the fire) is performed only in the fire; however, in the latter rites, for those with fires, it is performed in the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors (*pitrya*). This is the meaning. This rule establishes the procedure only for those whose *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* it is; it does not apply to everyone. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the previously mentioned arrangement, and everything is faultless. When, however, the option of performing the oblation in the hand (*pāṇi-homa*) is chosen, Kātyāyana states that the oblation is offered into the hand of only one Brahmin, not into the hands of all the Brahmins.

"In the rite for the ancestors, having offered into the hand of him who is the head of the row according to the mantra, one who does not maintain a sacred fire should silently deposit [the offering] into the vessels of the others.
This oblation into the hand of the first Brahmin of the paternal rite is not mandatory.

"During an impediment caused by fate, the twice-born who does not maintain the sacred fire shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa* offering into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the Viśvedevas," because of this injunction by Yama for performing the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa for the Viśvedevas. And thus, an option (*vikalpa*) between the hands of the Brāhmaṇas for the ancestors and those for the Viśvedevas should be understood as being like that between rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*). Even in the case of the alternative of performing the *homa* into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the gods, one should deposit the remnants of the oblation only into the eating vessels of the Brāhmaṇas representing the ancestors. And so says the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Having offered into the hand of the deity, one who does not maintain the sacred fire should present the remainder to those representing the ancestors."
For the Viśvedevas are not remembered by those who follow the Purāṇas as partakers of the remnants.

Except in the case of a failure of fate (*daivaviparyaya*), the Viśvedevas do not become partakers of the remnants even when an oblation is made into the fire from the hands of the ancestors or Brahmins; this is indicated by the general statement, "The Viśvedevas are not remembered as partakers of the remnants. Precisely because the Viśvedevas do not generally become partakers of the remnants, for that very reason the offering of remnants is specifically prohibited in another Purāṇa:
"One should not give the remnant of the *agnaukaraṇa* [oblation] in the rite dedicated to the Viśvedevas."

Even when performing the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* in the hand of a Brāhmaṇa belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* group, one should perform it in the hand of only a single Brāhmaṇa; for the principal act is not to be repeated merely for the sake of a subordinate detail, and since the fire-nature is identical, the rite must be performed in the hand of just one priest. This very point is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "If there should be two or more twice-born men at the *vaiśvadeva* [offering], then the oblation should be offered in the hand of only one; such is the prescribed rule."

When, in a single ritual act of feeding Brahmins for the Viśvedevas, two, four, six, or such like even numbers of Brahmins are present as the recipients for the deities (*daivika*), then the offering is to be made into the hand of the first seated Brahmin; this means that the rule for the oblation (*āhuti*) is prescribed and performed there. Thus, Śaunaka states that the request for permission from the Brahmins should be made with the words, “I shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation in the hand of the Brahmin,” or “I will perform it,” or “I am performing it”; and the response from the Brahmins should be, “So be it. Regarding the statement in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*: “In the *pāṇihoma*, there is no fuel-stick (*idhma*), no stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*), and no permission from the Brahmins,” the claim that there is no permission from the Brahmins is to be disregarded, as it is based on a failure to see this very text. The claim regarding the absence of the stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*) is also to be questioned, since no injunction for its function is observed here. Furthermore, the statement in that same work, “The sweeping around (*parimārjana*) and the sprinkling around (*paryukṣaṇa*) exist,” is also to be questioned, because their visible purpose—such as the removal of dust—is absent here, and a mere unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is not a sufficient motive. However, the unseen refinement (*saṃskāra*) which is the purpose of the spreading of grass (*paristaraṇa*) does exist here. And so says Yama: [336] “I shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation in the hand of the Brahmin” — whether one says “I will do it” (*karavai*) or “I am doing it” (*karavāṇi*). Likewise, the Brahmins’ reply should be “So be it” (*tathāstu*). Śaunaka says: “If one is without fire (*anagnika*), having taken the first portion, he should indeed perform the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation in the hand [of the Brahmin]. ‘The first’ refers to the food smeared with ghee. The rest is the request for permission from the Brahmins as before; the rest is the Brahmins’ reply, ‘So be it. As for what is stated in that same work: “In the *pāṇihoma*, however, there is no fuel-stick, no stirring-ladle, and no permission from the Brahmins,” the mention of the absence of permission from the Brahmins is based on not seeing this [present] text and is thus to be ignored. The mention of the absence of the stirring-ladle is also to be reflected upon, because no injunction for its function is seen here. And as for what is stated in that same place, “The sweeping around and the sprinkling around exist,” that too is to be questioned, because their visible purpose, such as the removal of dust, is absent here, and a mere unseen merit resulting from a restrictive rule is not a motive. But the unseen refinement (*saṃskāra*), which is the purpose of the spreading of grass (*paristaraṇa*), exists here. "In that case, the oblation in the hand of the one representing the gods (daivakara) should be performed like the *agnaukaraṇa* rite; having spread the *paryasta-darbhas*, for he is indeed equal to the fire. Here, "hand of the one representing the gods" refers to the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the Vaiśvadeva deities. "*Paryasta-darbhas*" means darbha grasses placed all around, that is to say, the *paristaraṇa* (encircling) darbhas. The mention of the "hand of the one representing the gods" is intended to include by implication the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the ancestors (*pitrya*). That which is offered into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa must not be consumed by the Brāhmaṇa at that very moment, but rather at the time of the meal. Thus says the *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa*:
[337] In the past, the unintelligent ate food given directly into the palm of the hand;
by that, their ancestors were satisfied, yet they did not receive the remaining food.
That which is placed in the palm of the hand and that which is otherwise prepared should be enjoyed as one; no distinction exists between them.

The *śeṣānna* is the food prepared for the purpose of feeding the Brahmins. Except for the palm of the hand of the Brahmin invited to the ancestral rite (*pitryabrāhmaṇa*), the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) is performed as in the *pitṛyajña*. In both the *pitṛka-śrāddha* and the *mātāmaha-śrāddha*, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the Vaiśvadeva deities is common, because there is agreement regarding the unity of the substratum (*adhikaraṇa-kāraka*), just as there is regarding the material and the deity. However, that which is performed in the palm of the hand of the Brahmin invited to the ancestral rite must also be performed repeatedly in the palm of the hand of the Brahmin invited to the maternal grandfather’s rite, because there is no agreement regarding the unity of the substratum-kāraka. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"Even when there is a distinction regarding the maternal grandfather, one who maintains the sacred fire (sāgnika) should perform [the rite] according to the *tantra* method.

This is the meaning: one should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) separately in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the maternal grandfather. And this applies equally to both the view that there is a distinction for the Vaiśvadeva deities and the *tantra* view. This statement is to be understood as applying to that specific case where it has been stated that the *agnaukaraṇa* for one who maintains the sacred fire takes place in the hand.
Thus concludes the determination of the fire for the two types of *agnaukaraṇa* in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the procedure for serving the food (*pariveṣaṇavidhi*).

In that regard, first, vessels (*amatra*) should be procured as excellent as possible, provided they are available. For the rite for the gods (*daiva*), golden vessels are best; for the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*), silver ones. Thus, Atri states, following the term "excellent": [The text continues: ... [as cited by Atri].

"At the meal for the gods and the ancestors, vessels of gold and silver should be used respectively. Regarding the absence of these, Viṣṇu states: "One should provide vessels made of metal. "Metallic" refers to bell-metal, copper, and so forth. In their absence, vessels made from *pālāśa* leaves may be used;
however, apart from *pālāśa* leaves, there should be no leaf-vessels for eating.

Thus it is stated by Atri. Even in the case of using leaf-vessels (*parṇapātra*), metallic vessels should be prepared if possible for the purpose of holding substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), because of the traditional law (*smaraṇa*) of Viṣṇu: "For the offering of clarified butter and other substances, metallic vessels [are to be used]. In their absence, leaf-cups made from *palāśa* leaves serve for holding clarified butter and the like, but never earthen vessels; for it is said: "One should never use earthen vessels for meals offered to the gods or the ancestors."

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Atri, these vessels obtained as far as possible should be washed twice. In that regard, first one should pour out water, wipe [the vessel] with the hand, and then wash it; subsequently, it should be washed with water alone. And so says the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "Having washed the hands, the vessels, and so forth, one should afterwards pour out the washing-water according to the rule, mixed with *darbha* grass and sesame seeds, into pure [water]."

The compound *hastapātrādi* is a *madhyamapadalopī* (elliptical) compound; it means "having washed the vessels and so forth wiped with the hand. By the word *pātra* (vessel), the base [of the vessel] is meant, while by the word *ādi* (and so forth), those items used for holding clarified butter and the like are included. Following the washing of the vessels, Yājñavalkya says:
"With a concentrated mind, he should offer the remnants of the oblation into the vessels, especially into those made of silver, as they may be available."

"In vessels" means in those vessels intended for the ancestors and the Brahmins; "especially in silver ones" is because of the mention of highly praised silver in connection with the ancestral rite (*pitryakarman*). Śaunaka has stated this clearly:
"Having offered into the fire, one should immediately place the remainder in the vessels of the ancestors;
having thus presented it, one should perform the serving with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*)."

The term "apasavyena" (with the sacred thread over the right shoulder) connects only with the preceding [statement], and not with the subsequent one: "The ancestral rite (pitrya-kṛtya) must specifically be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
everything except the offering of food is likewise so for the maternal grandfathers as well."

Thus, because of the traditional teaching of Kārṣṇājini; "the giving of food" means the placing of food, that is to say, its serving. And in this way, it is stated by implication that the performer of the *śrāddha* must perform the serving. This has also been explicitly stated by Manu:
"Holding the vessel of food with both hands himself, while meditating on the ancestors in the presence of the Brahmins, he should slowly pour [food] over [them]."

The "kinsman of food" refers to the serving vessel filled with food; having grasped it with both hands, one should place it gently into the Brahmins' eating vessels. The phrase "meditating on the ancestors" refers specifically to the Brahmins representing the ancestors (*pitrya*), because the word "food" was already mentioned in relation to the Brahmins representing the gods (*daiva*). As for what is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "Serving [the food] by a wife is recommended for the satisfaction of the ancestors, since the assistance of women is traditionally prescribed for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings."

Thus, regarding the term "praiseworthy" (*praśasta*) therein, the ellipsis should be understood as "because of serving by an attendant. This is because praise is impossible in comparison with serving performed by oneself. For this very reason, it is stated immediately thereafter in that same work:
"The fruit is said to be infinite when one serves by oneself.

In this way, it should be understood that the wife herself, or others who are restricted and distinct from Śūdras, are fit to perform the service. Even the wife, if she is of a different caste (*asavarṇā*), is not fit for the service. Therefore, it was stated by Nārāyaṇa:
"Whatever is an offering for the gods, whatever is a purificatory rite, whatever pertains to the ancestors, and whatever brings happiness—
these are given by the hand of a woman of the same caste as the twice-born.
Here, "by the hand" means by both hands.

"One should serve the food having taken it with both hands," because it has been stated thus by Matsya. Even with both hands, however, one should not give directly; rather, it should be given by means of a ladle or similar utensil, for those fats, salts, condiments, and so forth which are given directly by hand [are forbidden].
They do not attend upon the giver; the eater shall consume the guilt.

Thus, because Vṛddha-Śātātapa explicitly records that what is given by one who has killed is a cause of fault; furthermore, when possible, the ladle and other implements should be made of gold or similar materials: "What is given with a golden or silver [ladle], or with one of khadira, udumbara, or even phalgu wood, attains imperishability."

Thus it is from the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Hārīta. "With a rhinoceros" means with a ladle or similar utensil made from the horn of a rhinoceros deer. "With a *phalgu* vessel" means with a ladle or similar utensil made from the wood of the tree known as *kākodumbarikā*. However, in the *Purāṇa*, prohibited implements for serving food are shown:
"One should not serve at a *śrāddha* with an impure hand, nor with only one hand, nor without *kuśa* grass; nor should one serve with iron, nor indeed upon iron. [341]

"By what is impure" means by that which is rendered impure through contact with foul smears and the like. "By iron" means by a ladle or similar utensil made of iron. One should not serve food even in an iron vessel (*āyasa*). Even when unprohibited ladles and such are unavailable, it is stated in that very same [text]:
"Therefore, it should be given separated [from the hand] by means of a leaf or a blade of grass.
