Since giving directly from the hand after picking up [the food] is prohibited, the meaning is that when unprohibited ladles and such are unavailable, one should give it after having interposed a leaf or similar object. Vasiṣṭha speaks with reference to the twice-born recipient:
The food released from both hands and offered to the ancestors—
that food is seized by the evil-minded Asuras.

"Therefore, the twice-born should make the food that has been presented non-empty with his hand; having touched the vessel, he should remain [seated] until the remnants are removed. The intended meaning is that from the beginning of the serving until the removal of the leftovers from the vessel, he should act without ever letting go of the vessel with his left hand. When the left hand is occupied for the purpose of scratching, he should continue by touching the vessel with his right hand. Śaunaka describes the manner of commencing the serving:
"Having brought all the cooked food forward and having made it known individually to each [guest],
one should perform the serving according to the prescribed rule, beginning with the deities.
Here, "having made it known" (*saṃvedya*) means having caused it to be perceived by the eaters.

"Having described the qualities of the various kinds of food and drink, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas slowly," according to the traditional teaching of Bṛhaspati. The meaning of the phrase "all the cooked food" has been elaborated upon by Manu:
"Various kinds of food and drink, as well as roots and fruits..."
And delicious meats, as well as fragrant drinks.
Having brought all that, being composed and self-restrained, he should serve it slowly while praising all its qualities.

"Driving forward" means "making known. An explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the injunction that one should serve [the food] preceded by the gods is shown in the *Purāṇa*: "The Viśvedevas, being urged by the command of Brahmā, always exert themselves with intense austerity for the sake of protection at the sacrifices to the ancestors."
"Therefore, food should first be given to them in the rite for the ancestors.

The term "should be given" (pradātavyam) means it should be placed into the vessels. By stating that "one should perform the serving starting with the gods," he shows that for the purpose of serving, one should first perform the under-layering (*upastaraṇa*) with clarified butter (*ājya*) beginning with the deities, then give the rice, and likewise serve everything else, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*), individually and separately. Manu also mentions other items to be served:

The meaning is that one should place the *guṇas*—those items such as soup, vegetables, honey, and so forth, which directly facilitate the act of eating and are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) rather than being the primary objects of perception—into small vessels set upon the ground, and not into the large vessel containing the principal food (*pradhānānna*). Thus says Hārīta: "One should place them on the ground itself, not one vessel above another. The meaning of this is: those small vessels which are to be placed above the large vessel—that is, those serving as receptacles for ghee and other substances—should be placed here on the ground itself, and not atop the large vessel. Furthermore, having placed the large vessel upon the aforementioned square circular mandala called *paritaka*, made of flour and other materials, one should pour various foods such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and cakes (*apūpa*) into it; however, it should not be placed atop a *yantrikā* (a stand or tray), as this is understood from such injunctions as "one should not lift the vessel from the ground. Whatever has been prepared for the sake of the *śrāddha* by means of cooking and so forth, all of that must necessarily be served, taking portions little by little. For this very reason, Pracetas stated: "Having given everything that was prepared and having touched the vessel, one should recite [the mantra]. Paiṭhīnasi states the mantra to be recited: "The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer [this] into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa; *svadhā*! Following the recitation, Kātyāyana says: "With the Vaiṣṇava verse and the *yajus* formula, one should seize the thumb [of the guest] in the food. When it is asked what the Vaiṣṇava *ṛc* is here, or whose thumb it refers to, Yājñavalkya [provides the answer].
"One should place the thumb of the twice-born into the food with the mantra 'idaṃ viṣṇuḥ'. Thus [it is said].
Yama, however, while stating the rule for placing the thumb along with its explanatory context (*arthavāda*), describes the nature of the *yajus* mantra employed here:
"The blessed Viṣṇu, the size of a thumb, wanders over the earth."
Who, being weak, would strike for the sake of slaying the Rākṣasas?
Therefore, in all śrāddhas, the grasping of the thumb is prescribed;
one should say "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering to the gods and the offering to the ancestors," respectively.

One should speak regarding the food (*anna*) in the rites for the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*). Here, regarding the food for the gods, before placing the thumb [into the vessel], one should recite the *yajus* mantra: "O Viṣṇu, protect the sacrificial offering (*havya*). Regarding the food for the ancestors, however, one should recite the *yajus* mantra: "O Viṣṇu, protect the ancestral offering (*kavya*). In this regard, the practice following the tradition of the elders (*vṛddhācāra*) is as follows: Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), having bent the right knee, and facing north, one should first sprinkle the food served for the deities with water, touch the vessel, and perform the sequence beginning with the silent recitation (*japa*) of "The earth is your vessel" up to the placement of the thumb. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), having bent the left knee, and facing south, one should sprinkle the food served for the ancestors with water, touch the vessel, and perform the sequence beginning with the silent recitation up to the placement of the thumb. In the same manner, at the places of the vessels for the maternal grandfather and others, the actions from sprinkling and washing up to the placement of the thumb must be performed. Whether in the rite for the gods or the rite for the ancestors, if there is only one Brahmin, these actions—from sprinkling and washing up to the placement of the thumb—must be performed for each individual Brahmin's vessel.

"Then, having respectfully taken the thumb of each Brahmin [one by one]," as stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*. After placing the thumbs into all the food contained in the vessels, it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"The twice-born man should touch the vessel while saying, 'This food is for you.'"

The meaning is as follows: having touched with the left hand the vessel that serves as the support for the served food, one should perform the renunciation of the food (*annatyāga*) while not releasing the vessel, uttering the words, “O Viśvedevas, this food is for you. However, Viṣṇu states that Viṣṇu should be remembered prior to the renunciation of the food: “Saying ‘Salutation to the Viśvedevas,’ one should first offer the food to those facing east; to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, by name and lineage, to those facing north. By the word *ca* (“and”), he indicates that one should also offer it to the great-grandfather. By using the dative case in “to the Viśvedevas” and “to the father and grandfather,” it is shown that the Viśvedevas and the ancestors (father, etc. function as the deities (*devatā*). This is for the purpose of offering while recollecting, “The Viśvedevas are the deities; the ancestors are the deities. By the locative case in “to those facing east” and “to those facing north,” it is shown that the Brahmins serve the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire. This is for the purpose of offering while recollecting, “The Brahmin serves the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire. What is meant is this: before the renunciation of the served food, one should offer the food preceded by the utterance of the word *namaḥ*, while recollecting, “The Viśvedevas named so-and-so are the deities; this food is the oblation (*havis*); the Brahmin serves the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire,” and so forth. Likewise, one should offer it preceded by the utterance of the word *namaḥ*, while recollecting, “The deity named so-and-so, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, this food is the oblation; the Brahmin serves the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire,” and “The grandfather, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, is the deity; this food is the oblation; the Brahmin serves the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire,” and so forth. Thus, it is understood that the rite called *śrāddha* consists essentially of a *homa* (fire-offering). Consequently, by the expression “one should offer,” it is indicated through a figurative turn of speech that one should perform the rite consisting of a *homa*. For this very reason, the rite called *śrāddha* consists of a *homa*. Therefore, it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: “Having said, ‘This food is for you,’ one should sacrifice to the Viśvedevas. Because there is very little difference between *homa* and *yajña* (sacrifice), the statement “one should sacrifice” is appropriate even when the *śrāddha* consists of a *homa*, provided one does not insist on a strict distinction. But if it did not consist of a *homa*, the statement “one should sacrifice” would be utterly inconsistent. Therefore, it is understood here that the rite called *śrāddha* consists of a *homa*, because of the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) that “the Brahmin serves the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire. Immediately thereafter, one should offer the food after meditating upon the ground occupied by the Brahmins as being the form of Gayā, and meditating upon the Brahmin as being the form of Gadādhara (Viṣṇu).
Having meditated upon Gayā as the ground of the śrāddha rite and having meditated upon the Lord Gadādhara,
and having paid obeisance to both of them, one should then proceed with the śrāddha.

Thus it is stated in the Purāṇa. Atri describes the manner of offering the Vaiśvadeva food: "One should utter over the food released by hand, 'This is food'; then one should say 'Svāhā' and thereby effect the withdrawal of one's own ownership."

The meaning is as follows: one should utter the words "this food" (*idam annam*) immediately after pronouncing the name of the deity who is the recipient of the offering, for the purpose of designating the food placed before one—which has been released from the hand of the server—as the sacrificial oblation to be given. Then, immediately after uttering "this food," one should utter the word *svāhā*, which indicates the giving of the oblation. Thereafter, immediately after uttering the word *svāhā*, one should effect the withdrawal of one's own ownership. Here, the word *sva* denotes ownership; the existence of ownership is "one's own possession" (*svasattā*). The withdrawal of that—namely, the mental act consisting of the thought "it is not mine"—which is called the renunciation of ownership, is what one should perform. He explains the manner of renouncing food to the ancestors and others as well:
Having uttered the names connected with the lineage, saying "This food is for [him], svadhā," one should then recite the ancestral rites and withdraw one's own sense of self-identity.

The meaning is as follows: One should designate each ancestor in the sequence beginning with the father and grandfather as a deity. Having uttered the names along with their lineage (*gotra*) and relationship, ending in the dative case—such as "to the father, *amuka-gotra*, *amuka-śarman*; to the grandfather, *amuka-gotra*, *amuka-śarman*" and so forth—and then having uttered the words "this food" (*idam annam*) to indicate the substance of the offering to be given, one should then utter the word "svadhā," which makes manifest the act of giving, and thereby relinquish one's own ownership. One should perform the mental act consisting of the thought "not mine," which effects the destruction of one's own property-rights. This very method of renouncing the food as prescribed by Viṣṇu and the Tri-vacanā is stated again in detail for the sake of clarification and for the ease of practical application. After placing the thumb into the food intended for the maternal great-grandfather, one should sit facing north in the presence of the Brāhmaṇa representing the Vaiśvadeva deities. Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), bending the right knee, and taking water mixed with barley in the right hand while touching the vessel with the left hand, one should say: "The Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava are the deities; this food is the oblation (*havis*). This Brāhmaṇa is the *āhavanīya* fire. This earth is Gayā. This eater is the Brāhmaṇa Gadādhara. To the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava, this served food and that which is yet to be served until satiety—*svāhā*, obeisance, not mine. Having said this, one should pour the water mixed with barley near the vessel and perform a prostration with devotion. If there are multiple Brāhmaṇas representing the Vaiśvadeva deities, one should renounce the food served in each respective vessel in this same manner. Then, sitting facing south in the presence of the Brāhmaṇa representing the paternal ancestors, bending the left knee, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), and taking sesame seeds and water in the hand while touching the vessel with the left hand, one should say—as before, from "our father, *amuka-gotra*, *amuka-śarman*, in the form of a Vasu, together with his wife" down to "this Brāhmaṇa is Gadādhara"—and then say: "To our father, *amuka-gotra*, *amuka-śarman*, in the form of a Vasu, together with his wife, this served food and that which is yet to be served until satiety—*svadhā*, obeisance, not mine. Having said this, one should pour water mixed with sesame seeds near the vessel and perform a prostration with devotion. If there are multiple Brāhmaṇas, one should renounce the food served in each respective Brāhmaṇa’s vessel in this same manner. The renunciation of food for the grandfather and others is exactly the same. However, for the renunciation of food for the grandfather, the specific formula is: "Our grandfather, *amuka-gotra*, *amuka-śarman*, in the form of Rudra, together with his wife... and "to our grandfather, *amuka-gotra*, *amuka-śarman*, in the form of Rudra. For the renunciation of food for the great-grandfather, the specific formula is: "Our great-grandfather, *amuka-gotra*, *amuka-śarman*, in the form of Āditya, together with his wife... and "to our great-grandfather, *amuka-gotra*, *amuka-śarman*, in the form of Āditya. For the maternal grandfather, the specific formula is: "Our maternal grandfather, *amuka-gotra*, *amuka-śarman*, in the form of a Vasu, together with his wife... and "to our maternal grandfather, *amuka-gotra*, *amuka-śarman*, in the form of a Vasu," and so forth. The specific formulas for the renunciation of food for the maternal grandmother and the maternal great-grandmother are to be inferred by oneself. Even when there are multiple Brāhmaṇas in the place of the maternal grandfather and others, the repetition of the renunciation of food follows the previously mentioned method. When, however, there is only one Brāhmaṇa for the father and other ancestors, one should mentally divide the food and other items served in a single vessel into as many portions as there are intended recipients, and then renounce each portion individually, designating each for the father and the others. When a guest is seated for the purpose of eating, one should honor him with perfumes, flowers, and so on, and after the renunciation of food for the ancestors, one should renounce the served food for him with the formula: "To this Brāhmaṇa, who is in the form of Viṣṇu or Śiva, this food and that which is yet to be served until satiety—obeisance, not mine. On this point, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states: *(Note: The source text ends here with the citation of the Viṣṇupurāṇa.)*
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through this which has been offered here by me with devotion.
May his maternal grandfather attain satisfaction, as well as his father and his father’s father or whoever else;
may the Viśvedevas reach supreme satisfaction, and may the malevolent spirits (yātudhānas) perish.
Lord Hari, the Lord of Sacrifice, the imperishable Self who partakes of all sacrificial offerings and ancestral oblations, is the Sovereign here;
by His presence, may all demons and all Asuras immediately depart.
[349] After reciting the aforementioned ancient verses, the *Laghuyama* states:
"Whatever may be deficient in food, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in mantra, one should say,
'May all be without flaw,' and then feed them with diligence."

The sentence for the declaration of the absence of defects (*acchidrabhāṣaṇa*) must be completed by supplying the words "let [it] be without defect" (*acchidraṃ jāyatām*), because the statement is otherwise incomplete. However, Bodhāyana stated only: "let [it] be without defect. Although, according to the *Laghuyama* statement, it appears that the declaration of the absence of defects should be performed immediately after the declaration of the absence of defects—since the understanding arises that eating occurs right after that—nevertheless, it must be performed *before* the *āpośana* (sipping of water), not after. Thus says Pracetas:
"Because of the declaration of the absence of defects [made] by those who have already performed the *āpośana*..."
The ancestors depart disappointed along with the gods; of this there is no doubt.
When it was asked, "What, then, should be done immediately after giving the *āpośana* water?", he himself replied:
"Having given the *āpośana*, one should then recite the *Sāvitrī* three times;
likewise, the three-verse hymn beginning with 'madhu vātā' and the triad beginning with 'madhu'."

The meaning of the fourth quarter [of the verse] is that the word *madhu* (honey) is to be repeated three times. Having recited the *vyāhṛtis*, one should recite the *Sāvitrī*, because of the traditional teaching of Yājñavalkya: "The *Gāyatrī* together with the *vyāhṛtis*. Since the rule for offering *āpośana* water is prescribed, it is understood that the obligatory rules pertaining to eating—beginning with the sprinkling of water (*paryukṣaṇa*) and ending with the *prāṇāhutis*—apply to those who eat here as well. For this very reason, Bharadvāja states the fault in performing such [other] observances in order to prohibit certain eating rules in this context:
"But he who, having taken food for the ancestors, offers the *bali*..."
By that theft, a slayer of a Brahmin becomes a stealer of gold.

[350] Food for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) refers to the food served for the sake of the gods and ancestors. For this very reason, it was stated generally by Atri: "Whether it has been offered or not yet offered, if one should place the *bali* offering on the ground, that food goes forth fruitlessly, as the ancestors depart disappointed."
Having first performed the ritual of the daily meal-restriction, one should offer the *bali*— a portion of the first-fruits of the food— to Dharmarāja as a *bali*, and then, being self-controlled,

one should recite this for Citragupta: "Having given a *bali* consisting of a small portion of the first-fruits of the food to Dharmarāja, one should then, being restrained, utter this for Citragupta."

This means that it has been thus prescribed. After the recitation of the *vyāhṛtis* and so forth, Yājñavalkya states: "Having performed the recitation, one should speak according to one's pleasure. The word "according to one's pleasure" (*yathāsukham*), because it is incomplete and requires a verbal connection (*anvitābhidhāna*), necessitates another word. Therefore, the word "juṣadhvam" (enjoy) must be supplied. For this very reason:
"Thus addressed with the words 'juṣadhvam,' they, having properly steadied their vessels and observed silence, should eat immediately after the *āpośana* rite."

Thus it was stated by Vyāsa. The meaning is that immediately after the *āpośana* (the ritual sipping of water), one should drink water with the mantra, "Thou art the spreading of nectar" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*). Since the *prāṇāhutis* (the offerings to the vital breaths) are included within the act of eating, there is no contradiction in saying that they should eat together even when performing those offerings, provided it is immediately after the *āpośana*. Kātyāyana states what must be done by the performer of the *śrāddha* while the Brahmins have begun to eat: "While they are eating, he should recite the *Gāyatrī* preceded by the *vyāhṛtis*, accompanied by the *praṇava*, either once or thrice; [he should also recite] the *rakṣoghnī* verses, the *pitrya* mantras, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Apratiratha*, and other purificatory hymns. The *rakṣoghnīs* are the verses beginning with "Make thy strength wide-spreading like a net" (*kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ prasitiṃ na pṛthvīm*). The *pitrya* mantras are those beginning with "May the lower ones rise up" (*udīratām avare*). The *Apratiratha* is the hymn beginning with "The swift one, sharpening his weapons" (*āśuḥ śiśānaḥ*). Manu also says:
At a rite for the ancestors, one should indeed cause [the guests] to hear the Vedic recitation, the treatises on Dharma,
as well as narratives, histories, and all the Purāṇas.
The remainder [of the rule] is that he should cause [the Brahmins] to hear [the recitation] while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī).
All of the śrāddha must be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) according to the prescribed rules,
except for the recitation of hymns and praises, the muttering of prayers, and the dismissal of the Brahmins.

Thus, because of the *jamadagni-smaraṇa*. The mention of "hymns and praises" (*sūktastotra*) is for the purpose of indicating all that is to be muttered (*japya*) while the Brahmins are eating. Bṛhaspati, however, states that other acts besides the muttering of mantras and so forth must also be performed:
"Having described the qualities of the food to be eaten and consumed, one should feed the Brahmins slowly. Vṛddha-Śātātapa speaks with regard to both the eater and the host:
Whatever is required for the sake of the *śrāddha* should be requested from what has been prepared;
if a twice-born man does not request it, he is a fool and becomes a slayer of his ancestors.
He who does not give what is requested when it has been prepared for the sake of a śrāddha—
being both miserly and dull-witted— he shall obtain the fruit of his faith.
Not only is there no attainment of the fruit of the *śrāddha*, but one also incurs a most miserable birth. Thus says the *Nigama*:
"He who does not give what was required and prepared for the sake of the *śrāddha* is born thereafter in the terrible wombs of animals. [352]
As for that which is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"If a Brahmin devoid of knowledge begs from a donor, his ancestors become angry with him, as well as with the donor and the eater; of this there is no doubt."
"And that from which those who perform ritual actions are liberated by Yama through a twelve-night penance (kṛcchra)—
therefore, a wise man should neither give, nor beg, nor cause [others] to give. Thus it is said.

This refers to items not specifically prepared for the sake of the *śrāddha*, because it is stated in general terms. Even regarding food and other items prepared for the *śrāddha*, the giver should not give what is excessively large, and the recipient should not accept it. Thus, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not give nor accept what is excessive. To avoid accepting an excessive amount of food, the recipient should not say, "There is already plenty served here; what is the use of more?", but rather should indicate this by means of a gesture of the hand. Accordingly, those same two authorities state: "They should not say that the food, drink, and so forth are not sufficient, except by means of a gesture of the hand. The *Nigama* also says the same.

One should never verbally prohibit food, drink, or other offerings at a *śrāddha* ceremony; whether because of their unpalatability or their abundance, such prohibition should be made only by means of a hand gesture.

Likewise, one should not make a request verbally, as that would result in breaking one’s vow of silence; therefore, even that should be done by means of a hand gesture. Similarly, when it is time for the donor to give again, he should not say aloud, "I am giving only a little," in order to indicate that there will be no excessive giving. Rather, remaining silent, he should show something slightly and, in the absence of a hand signal indicating prohibition, give when there is a hand signal indicating permission. As Yama said: "As much as there is of the sacrificial food, and as much as is desired, so much is given."
"The ancestors eat as long as I have not said, 'I give.

When the food has been served, one should infer that whatever is eaten without leaving a remainder and whatever is taken again and again for the purpose of eating is what is desired by them; having brought such food and shown it, it should be given provided there is no indication of refusal. And so says that same [author]: "Whatever may please the Brahmins, that one should give without envy."
The mention of "envy" (matsara) is intended as an illustration for other faults as well; for this very reason, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states:
"One should never shed tears, nor utter harsh speech;
one should not stare at another while they are eating, nor should one harbor envy."
"A wise man should always perform the *śrāddha* with his mind focused one-pointedly, neither dejected, nor angry, nor distracted. Thus [it is said].
"Harsh" means bitter. Kārṣṇājini also [says]:
"One should perform [the rite] without weariness, free from hypocrisy and egoism;
one should avoid anger, greed, and delusion during the performance of the *śrāddha* ceremony.
Thus he says that, among similar offerings, one should give the most excellent foods and edibles in order to achieve preeminence for oneself.
He who gives all the most excellent kinds of food— whether chewed, eaten, sucked, drunk, or licked— shall become the most excellent of men.

Regarding the foods and other items served, one should not leave anything remaining at will until one is fully satiated. Thus says Sumantu: "Free from anger, one should properly eat the flavors if they please him; eating until satiety, there should be no leaving of food out of desire."
Thus ends the section on the rules for serving food in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, certain other statements concerning the invited Brahmins are recorded here.
And so says Pracetas:
"Having sipped the *āpośana* water, one should eat what is placed on the vessel, provided it is not forbidden;
one should not allow any restlessness of the senses, nor of the hands and feet."

Fickleness regarding the sense organs and so forth refers to an activity exceeding that required for the purpose of eating. Regarding this, Hārīta says: "If one eats at the time of a *śrāddha* while lifting [the food] with both hands, laughing, angry, or filled with wonder, that indeed does not please the ancestors."
Bodhāyana also says:
"The twice-born man who, when not in distress, eats while placing one foot upon another, is not to be fed at a śrāddha; his ancestors depart disappointed."

Not even any verbal activity should be performed. As the *Nigama* says: "They should eat in silence, without looking around, and without lifting the vessel. The phrase "without looking" implies "without looking in the directions. Manu also says: "All food should be very hot; they should eat while restraining their speech.
And the twice-born should not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering when questioned by the giver."

By the word "even" (*eva*) in the phrase "and even while eating," he states that when Brāhmaṇas seated in a single row are eating, there should be no cessation of the meal even if they somehow touch one another. For this very reason, Śaṅkha says: "If a Brāhmaṇa eating in a funeral feast row (*śrāddha-paṅkti*) should touch another Brāhmaṇa, he should eat that food without discarding it and recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times."

Since the prohibition against speaking of the qualities of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is already established by the rule for restraining speech, this further prohibition is intended to prevent its indication even by means of hand gestures. Therefore, Atri states that there is a fault in describing the qualities of the *havis* even with a hand gesture:
"If one should speak [of the qualities] even with a grunt (*huṅkāra*), or describe the qualities with the hand, or lift the vessel from the ground, or release it with the hand."
One who eats with his feet raised, with his garment tucked outside, or with his hands outside his knees;
or one who eats without using the thumb, or makes a noise with the mouth.
Or, having drawn out again the water and other liquids remaining after being drunk, one may drink them;
or for the purpose of eating, one may eat again sweetmeats or fruits.
If one blows upon the food with the mouth, or spits into the vessel,
a twice-born man eating in this manner destroys the śrāddha and goes to a low rebirth.

*Prāuḍhapādaḥ* means one who has placed his feet upon a seat. *Bahiḥkaṣaḥ* means one whose two armpits are exposed by the upper garment. Regarding the fault of lifting a vessel from the ground, this refers to a large vessel used for holding food and the like; for regarding a small vessel used for drinks and the like, permission to lift it is understood from the rule: "Or, having lifted it again, he may drink" (356). As for that which was stated by Devala:
"While being watched by those giving food, drink, or cold water, he should eat with his hand, making a sign when something needs to be said."

The meaning of this should be understood as follows: when the giver of food, drink, cool water, and so forth, observes him in order to ascertain his needs, and when the cause of those needs—such as hunger, thirst, and the like—is to be expressed, he should eat while making a gesture with his hand, a sign (*saṃjñā*) or convention (*saṅketa*), that indicates his need and so on. It does not mean, however, that he makes a sign regarding the cause of need in the form of the qualities of the sacrificial offering (*havirguṇa*), such as its deliciousness; for if one were to adopt such an interpretation, it would result in a contradiction with the previously cited statement. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says that the giver of food and drink must by no means ask about the qualities of the sacrificial offering, as doing so is an extreme fault.
One should not inquire about salt and other such items while those engaged in the *śrāddha* are eating;
for if one does so inquire, the ancestors depart as if defiled—of this there is no doubt.
"The arm of the giver indeed falls, and the tongue of the enjoyer is split asunder. Thus it is said.

Regarding salt and other such items, because there is no possibility of deficiency or excess, one should not ask again for the sake of ensuring the excellence of the sacrificial offering (*havis*). Nor, having asked, should one give a report of its perfection, because of the scriptural flow of fault stating, "The arm of the giver falls [off]. Furthermore, based on the force of the censure, "The tongue of the eater is split," it is understood that this is a prohibitive injunction: "The eater should not indicate the excellence of the offering even by means of a sign. Viṣṇu says: "The invited Brāhmaṇas should eat neither wearing sandals nor with their feet placed upon a seat. Regarding the fault of one who eats while transgressing this second prohibition, Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
O best of the twice-born, he who eats while placing his foot upon a seat destroys the offerings for the gods and the ancestors, as well as that food, his progeny, and his cattle.
Pracetas states another prohibition:
"While eating food, one should never touch it with the left hand;
nor should one touch one's feet, head, bladder, or the vessel with the foot."
The *Nigama* also says:
One should not eat meat, cakes, fruits, sugarcane, and the like by biting with the teeth;
one should not place the remnants of a mouthful back into the bowl, nor should one drink what remains after having drunk.

One should not eat by biting with the teeth; having taken meat and other food with the hand, one should not eat it by cutting off very small pieces with the teeth. One should not put back into the vessel the remnants of a morsel that have been placed in the mouth. Uśanas also says: "A wise man should never leave a vessel entirely empty, except in the case of curd, milk, honey, or roasted flour."

Thus, as for what was stated by Jamadagni—"They should neither criticize [the food] nor leave any remainder"—that refers to the case of excessive leftovers. For immediately thereafter he himself says: "However, a small amount should be left over, because it is the portion of those who died before receiving the sacraments. Pracetas also mentions what is to be avoided: "One should avoid biting with the teeth, drinking from the hand, and overeating. "Drinking from the hand" means one should avoid drinking liquids and the like directly from the hand; rather, one should do so using a small vessel (*lughupātra*). "Overeating" refers to eating even when one is already satisfied.
Thus ends the section concerning those invited to eat in the *Smṛticandrikā* [358].
Now follows the procedure for the scattering of the fire and other rites (*agnivikiraṇādividhi*).
Having perceived that they are satisfied, one should take food mixed with sesame seeds and mutter [the mantra] as before.
One should ask, "Are you satisfied? ... Thus.

The meaning of the phrase "one should mutter as before" and so forth has been explained by Kātyāyana: "Having muttered the Gāyatrī and 'madhu madhu,' he asks, 'Are you satisfied? When asked thus, those Brahmins should say, "We are satisfied."
When asked, "Are you satisfied? they should reply, "We are satisfied.
This is according to the Smṛti of Vyāsa. After they have said, "We are satisfied," the Brāhmaṇḍa Purāṇa states:
"Then, having sprinkled the ground with water, one who is devoted to the ancestors [should act] upon the ground..."
Then one should perform the scattering rite according to the ritual procedure as prescribed by the rules.
When it is asked, "What, then, is the rite prescribed by rule? Manu says:
Having gathered together food fit for all castes and having sprinkled it with water, he should scatter it on the ground in front of those who have eaten, while reciting the *samutkṣepa* mantra.

The meaning is as follows: having collected all kinds of food and side dishes (*annādya*) in which the colors of the foods consumed by all the Brahmins are present—that is, taking portions from each respective dish that was eaten by the Brahmins and combining them into a single vessel—the *Matsyapurāṇa* states:
"O King, when they have finished eating, one should collect the food of all castes (*sārvavarṇika*) from the vessels near [the guests] and drench it with water."
One should cast it away and scatter it upon the ground in front of those who have finished eating.

"Having bathed" means having sprinkled. One should "discard," that is, cast it down, because Pracetas has stated: "One should cast [the remains] on the ground with the mantra beginning 'Those who in fire... The mantra beginning with "Those who in fire... was shown by Kātyāyana as follows:

"Those who were cremated by fire and those who were not cremated by fire, or those who were born in my family—may they, satisfied by this rice-ball (piṇḍa) offered upon the earth, attain the supreme goal."

Although it might appear from the wording of the mantra, "having given on the ground," and from the mention of "on the ground" (*bhuvī*) in all prescriptive statements that there is no spreading of *darbha* grass, nevertheless, because the statement of Manu, "the scattering which is upon the *darbhas*," is seen as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the presence of *darbha*, the injunction is inferred that one should scatter [the food] there after having spread *darbha* grass. Therefore, it should be understood that the scattering is to be performed on ground covered with *darbha*, not on bare ground alone. All acts, such as the removal of food from all castes, must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), since the status of being *prācīnāvītī* is prescribed for the Śrāddha rite except for the recitation of hymns (*sūkta*) and similar acts. At the place where the scattering is to take place, one should silently pour water mixed with sesame seeds before the scattering, and again pour water mixed with sesame seeds over the scattered food.
Then, with devotion, one should scatter food along with water before the Brahmins who are facing north.

Since it has been stated thus by Mārkaṇḍeya: "Immediately after scattering the food, one should become *upavītī* (wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder) and perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water), for there is a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) regarding the fault in failing to sip water. And so says Marīci:
"In śrāddha rites, if one who has offered the scattered food (*vikira*) does not perform *ācamana* due to a lapse of intellect, his ancestors shall remain eaters of leftovers for six months."
Immediately thereafter, one should cause the Brahmins to perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Thus says Madālasā:
"...having scattered [flowers] all over the ground, one should then give water once for each [Brahmin] for the purpose of sipping."

Following that, after the scattering of food (annavikiraṇa), for the purpose of sipping water (ācamana), regarding the rule for regular meals (*nityabhojana*), it is stated: "With the mantra *amṛtāpidhānam asi*, one should pour water once for each Brahmin, beginning with those invited on behalf of the Viśvedevas, for the sake of the mouthfuls (*gaṇḍūṣa*). The meaning is as follows: the instruction to "eat [the water] once for each" is intended to indicate that the Brahmins must perform the rinsing of the mouth (*gaṇḍūṣa*) without having yet washed their hands. Thus, just as in a regular meal, if one rinses the mouth after washing the hands, there is a personal fault due to the transgression of a rule pertaining to the person; likewise here, by transgressing the rule pertaining to the Śrāddha rite, a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) arises in the Śrāddha itself. So says Marīci: [Marīci’s verse omitted in source] The meaning is: "One should eat [the water] once for each [Brahmin]. This is said to indicate that the rinsing of the mouth must be performed by the Brahmins even before they have washed the smears from their hands. And so, just as in the case of a regular meal, if one performs the rinsing of the mouth after washing the hands, there is a personal fault because of the violation of a rule concerning the person; similarly, in this case, by violating the rule concerning the Śrāddha, a deficiency occurs in the Śrāddha. Thus says Marīci.
"If an ignorant person, having washed his hands, should drink a mouthful of water [before the rite], that śrāddha becomes demonic; it does not reach the ancestors. Thus [it is said].

"He who drinks the *gaṇḍūṣa* when the meal has ended" means that he who should drink water with the mantra, "Thou art the covering of nectar" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*). Regarding the giving of water for the purpose of rinsing the mouth (*gaṇḍūṣa*), Viṣṇu states: "One should first give water for sipping (*ācamana*) to those facing north, and thereafter perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) for those facing east; having sprinkled the remainder of the *śrāddha*, one should perform everything while holding *darbha* grass in the hand. This means that after first giving water for the purpose of sipping—preceded by the washing of hands—to the Brahmins invited for the ancestors (*paitṛka*), and then giving it to the Brahmins invited for the gods (*vaiśvadaivika*), one should sprinkle the place of the *śrāddha* with the mantra "Well-sprinkled" (*suprokṣitam*), and then, holding *darbha* grass in the hand, perform all the subsequent rites. Śātātapa explains this procedure for the sequence of washing the hands and sipping water, along with its underlying reasons and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), as follows: [The text continues with the citation of Śātātapa's verses.]
"For those [deities] assigned to the Viśvedevas, the final washing of the hands and the dismissal (visarjana) are prescribed, since protection remains firm among them.
Thus ends the section on the rules for scattering food and so forth in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, regarding the procedure for the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa), Manu states:
"Some perform the offering of the rice-balls even beforehand."

The meaning is that some perform the offering of the *piṇḍas* either before the feeding of the Brahmins, after their worship, or after the *agnaukaraṇa* rite; for in other *smṛtis*, two such timings for the offering of the *piṇḍas* prior to the feeding are observed. From the expression "some," it is understood that others perform the offering of the *piṇḍas* after the feeding of the Brahmins, but before the sipping of water (*ācamana*), or after it (or even before the dismissal of the Brahmins); for in other *smṛtis*, two such timings for the offering of the *piṇḍas* subsequent to the feeding are observed. In this matter, the arrangement is according to one's own *śākhā*. And so says another *smṛti*:
Regarding the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) prescribed by the sages for times when [one's own lineage] is divided,
a wise man should perform it according to his own Vedic school (śākhā), wherever that may be.

That *piṇḍadāna* (offering of rice balls) is prescribed for different times; the meaning is that one should perform it at whatever time is approved and accepted in one's own *śākhā*. Regarding the two positions—whether before or after the feeding of the Brahmins—Lokākṣi states the settled rule:
"In unholy sacrifices, the washing of the *piṇḍas* comes first;
but in a holy sacrifice, one should arrange it only after the meal."

In the case of *apraśasta-yāgas* (inauspicious sacrifices), namely those *śrāddhas* prescribed prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *avanejana* (the pouring of water) is performed with the hand facing downwards. Regarding the *bhojana* (feeding)—that is, the feeding of the invited Brahmins—it is prescribed that in *praśasta-śrāddhas* such as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and others, one should prepare the food at the proper time only after the feeding has taken place. Thus, in a *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, one should offer the *piṇḍas* (rice balls) only after the feeding, at a time permitted by one's own *śākhā*. In this regard, for followers of the Āśvalāyana school, the time for offering the *piṇḍas* is after the Brahmins have eaten and have rinsed their mouths (*ācānta*). Accordingly, Āśvalāyana states: "One should place the *piṇḍa* after they have eaten and rinsed; some say before they have rinsed. Between these two options, the latter—namely "some say before they have rinsed"—should be adopted even by those whose specific timing is not mentioned in their own *gṛhya-sūtra*, because it is more convenient. Yājñavalkya, however, describes the procedure for offering the *piṇḍas*.
Taking all the food together with sesame seeds, facing south,
one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) near the remains of the meal, as in the Pitṛyajña.

The meaning is as follows: having set aside small portions of every kind of food prepared for the *śrāddha*, and having gathered them together in a certain vessel, one should offer rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) made from that food near the remains of the meal (*ucchiṣṭa*), according to the procedure for the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* prescribed in one’s own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*), accompanied by the specific requirements taught by the authors of the *Smṛtis*, such as the inclusion of sesame seeds and facing the south. Now, one might object: "Since the place near the remains of the meal is an impure location, how can the offering of rice-balls be prescribed there? Anticipating this doubt, Atri says: "On three *aratnis* (cubits) from the seat of the ancestors, on the ground... [363]
The placing of leavings [should be done] there, not in the vicinity of the seat for the leavings.

The phrase "in three *aratnis*" is stated for the purpose of indicating a location close to [the fire] that is free from contact with food-leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*). Therefore, there is no restrictive rule of exactly three *aratnis* here. For this very reason, Jātūkarṇya says:
"Having left a space of one fathom (*vyāyāma*), one should cause the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) to be offered there.
Pāraskara also says:
"The offering of the *piṇḍas* is prescribed at a distance of one cubit from the vessels.

This means that, like those who eat the remnants, the vessels are not to be moved from their supporting place; "at a distance of one cubit" means one should cast [the offering] to a distance of one cubit. Vyāsa also says:
"Having left a space of one *aratni*, one should cause the *piṇḍas* to be offered there."
"Where even drops do not reach those who are performing the ritual ablution.
Kārṣṇājini also states a specific rule regarding the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) when it is performed according to the procedure for the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*:
"Having taken up food from all that has been prepared into a vessel..."
"But one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in sequence, preceded by the question regarding the remaining food. Thus it is said.

The phrase "the remaining food" (*śeṣam annam*) refers to all the food that remains after setting aside the portion for the *piṇḍas*. One should offer the *piṇḍas* preceded by an inquiry regarding that food of such a nature. That is to say, having made an inquiry such as, "Let there be something left over," and having heard the response from the Brahmins accordingly, one should thereafter perform the ritual for offering the *piṇḍas*. When it is asked what kind of response the Brahmins should give accordingly, Uśanas has stated for the sake of indicating this: "Permitted by them, one should give the remainder to those who are dear, or one should eat it oneself. The meaning is: "one should give to those who are dear" means one should feed those who are dear, or "one should eat it oneself. Here, the word "or" (*vā*) should be understood in the sense of "and" (*ca*), because Yājñavalkya prescribes eating as a constant duty (*nitya*) in the words, "One should eat what was consumed by the ancestors. Precisely because eating the remainder of what was consumed by the ancestors is a constant duty, a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) is prescribed in the Smṛtis for the purpose of achieving a fast on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) in place of eating the remainder consumed by the ancestors.
"When fasting is obligatory and a Śrāddha occurs on that same occasion,
one should perform the fast after first smelling the food consumed by the ancestors."

Furthermore, regarding the fact that Devasvāmin stated that the word *vā* in the statement of Auśanas has its well-known meaning—namely, "The rule 'one should eat what was eaten by the ancestors' is not mandatory"—and thus, since the word *vā* in the Auśanas statement "he himself should eat" indicates that eating the remnants of what was eaten by the ancestors is merely optional, his book's meaning is that this injunction of Yājñavalkya, "one should eat what was eaten by the ancestors," is not mandatory (*naiyamikam*) and not obligatory (*nityam*)—this must be considered. For the statement of Yājñavalkya is indeed obligatory, as has been shown by the presence of a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) statement.
If a Brahmin, having performed a Śrāddha, never eats [the remains],
the gods do not accept the sacrificial offerings (havir), nor do the ancestors accept the ancestral oblations (kavya).

This is because Devala also records the fault in not eating the remnants of what was served to the ancestors. Thus, it should be understood that Uśanas has indicated that Brahmins should give a reply in the form of permission, such as, "Let it be eaten together with those who desire it. Devala also states a specific rule regarding the offering of the *piṇḍas* according to the procedure for the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*):
"Then, having taken all the food into a vessel himself according to the rules, he should pour it from that vessel into the place where their leavings were set."
When those Brahmins have finished eating, "in the place of the remnants" means in the vicinity of the leavings; the rule that the offering must be made with a vessel is not mandatory. As Marīci says:
"The offering of the *piṇḍas* is prescribed to be made with a vessel, specifically a sword-shaped vessel, or with one of silver or Udumbara wood, or else with the hand itself."

The particle *eva* has been used for the purpose of indicating that the position [of performing the rite] on the right side is superior; it does not, however, serve the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). If it were so, there would be a contradiction with what precedes and follows, as well as a contradiction with the words of the gods. That which must first be performed at the place where the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) are offered is shown in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"A twice-born man, being unwearied in the performance of the *śrāddha* rite, should perform the scraping with his left and right hands, and thereafter he should perform the rubbing."
The breaking [of the vessel], the sending [of the remains],
and likewise the act of scraping should be performed only once for the ancestors, but it is said to be done three times for the gods.

*Khaṇḍana* is the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and so forth; *peṣaṇa* is the grinding by rubbing against the ground and so forth; the action of *ullekhana* is the drawing of lines for the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). In response to the expectation of what instrument should be used for the drawing, it is stated in that very same source:
"A twice-born man should scratch the earth with either a *vajra* or with *kuśa* grass.
By *vajra*, the meaning is "with a wooden sword" (*sphya*), according to the Vedic scripture: "The *sphya* is indeed the *vajra*. However, Pāraskara has expressed this using the word *sphya* itself.
"A twice-born man should scratch the earth with his two hands, or with a wooden sword, or even with kusha grass. [366] Thus it is said.

The meaning is that one should scratch the earth with a *sphya* (wooden sacrificial sword) held in both hands, or with *kuśa* grass held in the hands. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the mantra: "Having scratched [the ground] with *apahatāḥ*... The syntactical connection is: "Having scratched with the mantra, 'The Asuras, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas who sit upon the altar are struck down'. By this mantra, the scratching with the *sphya* is established by the rule: "As in the Pitṛyajña. Immediately after scratching, one should sprinkle water on the scratched spot, because Āśvalāyana, in describing the ritual rules for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, states: "One should scratch them with the *sphya* with the mantra, 'The Asuras, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas who sit upon the altar are struck down,' and having sprinkled that [spot]... One should scratch the line directed toward the south and east, because he himself stated in the *Paribhāṣā*: "In all rites, [one faces] that direction. On the sprinkled spot, one should spread *kuśa* grass, because the *Purāṇa* states: "And one should cast *kuśa* grass there with their tips pointing south. This too is obtained by the very rule "as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña," since it is prescribed in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña that one should "strew [grass] cut once. Thus, the only specific distinction from the *Purāṇa* is the southward orientation of the tips. In the event of the unavailability of *kuśa*, it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
The offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) should be performed by the wise when kuśa grass is unavailable; in such cases, kāśa grass and royal dūrvā grass are remembered as the supreme purifiers.
Regarding *rājadūrvā* (royal *dūrvā*), this refers to very long *dūrvā* grass. A specific rule for the spreading of *kuśa* grass is shown in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"One should spread the *darbha* grass only once for the sake of the *piṇḍas*, facing south, with the tips directed toward the east and south, remaining self-controlled. [367] Thus it is said.

In this manner, it should be understood that there is an option between having the tips pointing south and having the tips pointing south-east. Immediately after the spreading of the *darbha* grass, Sumantu says: "O [Name], bend down!"—addressing each person individually—and one should perform the ritual washing three times for each with one hand.

In this context, regarding the phrase "asau" (so-and-so), one should utter the name of the father and others together with their *gotra* in the form of a vocative, followed by the words "avanenikṣva" (wash yourself).
However, the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and water should be performed even in obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites;
for indeed, at all times, the act must be performed after touching [the object] while pronouncing the name and *gotra*.

This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Vyāsa. The meaning is that one should sprinkle [water] while addressing the ancestors and others. The phrase "with one hand" is stated for the purpose of excluding the use of both hands joined in the añjali gesture. And so Sumantu says:
"At the time of pouring water during a śrāddha, it is given with one hand;
however, in the rite of libation (tarpaṇa), one should use both hands—this is always the rule."
"One should pour water on the ground with one hand— the right hand,
not the left"— so states the traditional teaching of Manu. Regarding the specific part of the right hand for this act, Madalasa has described it as follows:
And with a concentrated mind, one should offer water to them using the *pitṛtīrtha*. Thus it is said.

"To those ancestors"—by the word *ca* ("and"), water mixed with sesame seeds (*tila*) is to be understood. Thus it has been stated by Uśanas: "Having sprinkled with water mixed with sesame seeds, one should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) upon ground strewn with *darbha* grass. Kātyāyana, however, states that the pouring of water (*avanejana*) must be performed with a water-vessel: "He pours water for the three ancestors of the sacrificer, beginning with the father, saying, 'O So-and-so, come down! Āśvalāyana, on the other hand, prescribes a different mantra for the pouring of water: "Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he should lead the line three times with water, saying: 'May the fathers be purified; may the grandfathers be purified; may the great-grandfathers be purified. Kātyāyana, moreover, states that the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) should be done immediately after the pouring of water: "Having placed once-cut grass, including its roots, upon the line, he offers the rice-balls according to how they were poured. Regarding the option of sequence between the pouring of water and the spreading of the grass, the arrangement is determined by one's own *śākhā* (Vedic school). In the same way, there is an arrangement according to one's own *śākhā* regarding the mantras such as "come down" (*avaneniṅkṣva*) and "may the fathers be purified" (*śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*). Likewise, there is an arrangement regarding the hand and the water-vessel used as the instruments for the pouring of water. Regarding the offering of the rice-balls according to how they were poured, Kātyāyana states the mantras: "'O So-and-so, this is for you,' and some say, 'And those who follow you. In the word *asau*, one should mention the name of the father and others together with their *gotra* in the form of an address, and then say, "this is for you" (*etat te*).
The offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and water, however, should always be performed— even during obligatory and occasional rites—
after touching [the recipient] by their name and lineage.

Thus, according to the *Smṛti* of Vyāsa. And so, the mantra for the offering of the *piṇḍa* should be inferred as: "O you of such-and-such lineage, named such-and-such, this is for you. Regarding the alternative view expressed in the verse, "And those who follow you," in all three mantras, the remainder of the mantra—"and those who follow you"—should be understood as following immediately after the words "this is for you. Āśvalāyana, however, states the mantras for the offering of the *piṇḍa*s differently: "This is for you, O [Name], and those who follow you. Here too, in the place of the word "O [Name]" (*asau*), one must utter the name of the father and the others together with their lineage (*gotra*). Now, one might ask: why is there a neuter gender reference in the word "this" (*etad*) in the phrase "this is for you" (*etat te*), given that the *piṇḍa* is denoted by the word *etad*, and that [the word *piṇḍa*] is masculine? For this very reason, Gobhila said: "O [Name], this *piṇḍa* is for you, and those who follow you. On this point, some say that an ellipsis must be supplied, namely, "this food in the form of a *piṇḍa* is for you. That is incorrect; an ellipsis should only be resorted to when there is no other way. But here there is another way: because we see the usage of elders in such expressions as "the *piṇḍa* of the angry man falls. Furthermore, the word *piṇḍa* exists as a neuter gender, established by extensive usage. Therefore, even in the mantra for the offering of the *piṇḍa*, the meaning should be understood without supplying the words "this *piṇḍa* is for you. The acts such as the sprinkling of water (*avanejana*) and so forth are already established by the rule: "Everything is like the *Pitṛyajña*. The only distinction is the inclusion of sesame seeds (*tila*). Regarding the *piṇḍa* as well, the specific detail of containing sesame seeds has been stated by Madālasā.
Then, O son, the son should offer three morsels of food mixed with sesame seeds upon *darbha* grass near the remains of the meal, dedicating them to the ancestors.
The meaning is "the ancestors of the sacrificer," such as his father and others. And so says Kārṣṇājini:

"For those [ancestors] residing in other worlds, three rice-balls (piṇḍas) should indeed be offered by their kinsmen upon blades of darbha grass, using their names and lineages (gotra), with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya)."

Of those [ancestors], namely the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—with the right hand, while the sacred thread is over the right shoulder (apasavya). Regarding the phrase "residing in other worlds," he himself stated this in order to indicate "those who have died":
"But here, among various species within the wombs of animals and other births, these [ancestors] become partakers of the rice-balls in those respective wombs."

"Here" means in this world. By this, it is understood that even in the *śrāddha* consisting of the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), the ancestors of the sacrificer alone are the deities, and not the Vasus and others. And thus, what is stated in another *smṛti* is appropriate:
"The first deity is Varuṇa, and Prajāpati is the next;
the third is remembered as Agni; indeed, the ritual of the rice-ball is remembered as being the rice-ball itself."

Thus, this [passage] is not intended to establish that Varuṇa and others are the presiding deities (*devatā*); rather, it should be understood as being intended to show that—just as Yājñavalkya stated that the ancestors (*pitṛ*) in the form of Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas are the deities of the *śrāddha*, and thus the ancestors and others are to be meditated upon in the forms of Vasu and so forth during the offering of food and other rites—likewise, during the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), the ancestors and others are to be meditated upon in the forms of Varuṇa and so forth. Therefore, just as the offering of food is performed by designating the ancestors and others, together with their wives, in the forms of Vasu and so forth, using the word "to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ*) in the dative case along with the lineage name (*gotra*) and the name (*nāman*), so too, after reciting the mantra "This is for you" (*etat te*), the offering of the rice-ball should be made by designating the ancestors and others, together with their wives, in the forms of Varuṇa and so forth. Alternatively, from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of food, and at every stage including the presentation of the rice-balls, one should perform the invocation and so on while meditating upon oneself as Aniruddha, and upon the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather respectively in the forms of Pradyumna, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Vasudeva. And so it is said in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
The god Aniruddha is himself [the source], while Pradyumna is remembered as his father;
Saṅkarṣaṇa is his progenitor, and Vāsudeva is his father.

The performer of the *śrāddha* himself is the deity Aniruddha. The father of the performer of the *śrāddha* is remembered as Pradyumna. His progenitor—the progenitor of the father of the performer of the *śrāddha*—is remembered as Saṅkarṣaṇa. His father—the father of the progenitor of the father of the performer of the *śrāddha*—is remembered as Vasudeva; such is the meaning. Regarding the giver of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), it is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "At the time of offering the rice-balls, the giver of the rice-balls should perform the offering while bending his left knee.
[371] "The wise man, devoted to the ancestors, should offer three rice-balls mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, having likewise placed his left knee upon the ground."

"Having placed the left knee on the ground" means having bent the left knee; this is already established by the rule "as in the Pitṛyajña. By stating "three piṇḍas," he shows that there is no separate offering of piṇḍas for the mother and others. Therefore, one piṇḍa each should be offered for the father and the rest, together with their wives. Vyāsa states the measurement of the piṇḍas: "The size of the piṇḍas, as spoken by Vyāsa, should be made such that they fit comfortably in the mouth of a two-year-old calf, or even twenty [times that]."
A "two-year-old" is a calf two years of age. Aṅgiras states other measurements:

"One should offer balls of food according to the prescribed rule, either the size of a wood-apple (kapittha) or a bilva fruit, or the size of a hen's egg, or equal in size to myrobalan (āmalaka) fruits."
"Or one endowed with the śrāddha rite may offer [the pindas] equal in size to jujube fruits.
Regarding the *āmalaka* fruit, Marīci states a specific rule:
"In the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, one should fashion the pindas to the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit."
On the full-moon day known as *amāvāsyā*, following the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*:
"Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should perform the monthly *śrāddha* called *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* when the moon has waned."

That which is prescribed by this statement is designated by the term *pārvaṇa*—either through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or through a connection (*yoga*) characterized by its application to the occasion (*parvan*) consisting of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Thus says Śātātapa:
"That which is proclaimed as the *darśa-śrāddha* is celebrated as the *pārvaṇa*."

In this regard, since all dharmas beginning with the invitation of the Brahmins are prescribed therein, it should be understood that this [Pārvaṇa Śrāddha] is the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all other Śrāddhas, while other Śrāddhas such as the *ekoddiṣṭa* are its modifications (*vikṛti*). Thus, although the purpose of the Pārvaṇa is already established by the context even without the explicit mention of "Pārvaṇa" regarding the size of the *ārdrāmalaka*, the inclusion of the term "Pārvaṇa" is for the sake of clarity. An arrangement among these measurements should be devised according to one's capacity. Another measurement is also shown through a figurative expression in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
"Three balls [of rice], in succession, from the fist-closure including the thumb.

This means they are slightly larger than the measure that can be grasped by a fist including the thumb. "In succession" refers to a sequence that avoids contradictions such as ending toward the south or ending toward the southeast; for, by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the term "ancestral sacrifice" (*pitṛyajña*), it is established that the balls should end toward the south or end toward the southeast. After the offering of the balls, Manu says:
"Having offered the balls to the ancestors, being self-restrained, according to the rule..."
Upon those Darbha grasses, he should wipe that hand for the sake of those who partake in the remnants of the food.

The great-grandfather, the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather are the *lepabhāginaḥ* (those who partake of the smearing). This is because Matsya states: "The fourth and those following are the *lepabhājaḥ*. Viṣṇu states the mantra for the wiping away of the smearing: "At this place, O ancestors, rejoice; thus one rubs the hands at the roots of the *darbha* grass. Rubbing the hands (*karāvagharṣaṇa*) means wiping away the smearing from the hands. After rubbing the hands, Kātyāyana says: "Having said, 'O ancestors, here,' he sits facing north until he is satiated; having turned himself around, he mutters, 'These [ancestors] rejoice' (*amī madantaḥ*). Having turned his body toward the south, he should sit facing north until he is satiated—that is, until the pressure on the breath is relieved through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Then, without breathing out as much as possible, having turned back and muttered "these [ancestors] rejoice," he should release his breaths. A specific rule is stated in the *Karmapradīpa*.
Some declare that the turning [of the hand] should be counter-clockwise, ending toward the north;
having turned [the vessel] and restrained the breaths, one should meditate upon the ancestors as is appropriate.
Having performed the recitation and returned by that same path, he should then release the vital breaths.

Turning to the left means turning counter-clockwise; turning to the right means turning clockwise. Munis other than Gautama and others declare that one should turn only as long as it takes to face north by turning toward the north, and no more than that; however, Gautama, Śāṇḍilya, and Śāṇḍilyāyana maintain that the entire [turning] should be performed.

Because it is stated in that very same [text]: "Reciting *amī madanta*, he should turn back by that same path, and having turned back toward the south facing west, he should release his breaths"—the meaning being that he should exhale. Viṣṇu, however, following the *Pitṛyajña* prescribed by Āśvalāyana from the consecration of the offered rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) up to the taking of the water-sipping (*ācamana*), says: "Having given the rice-balls, he should consecrate them while they are withdrawn [from the fire], saying: *O fathers, rejoice; partake according to your respective portions*. Then, turning back to the left, facing north, and having performed the retention of breath for as long as he is able, he turns around, consecrates [the balls] with *amī madanta*, smells the remnants, pours out water as before with *śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*, and then gives the ointment over the rice-balls with *asāv abhyaṅkṣva*, the collyrium with *aṅkṣva*, and then the garment—or in its absence, a fringe or wool—with *etad vaḥ pitaro vāsaḥ... mā no 'nyat pitaro yuṅgdhvam*. Having offered the rice-balls, he smells the remnants, smells the remnants remaining in the vessel, pours out water as before, and then after the pouring of water, he should give the ointment over each individual rice-ball with the mantra *asāv abhyaṅkṣva*; here, in the form of a vocative, he should utter the names of the father and others. With the mantra *asāv aṅkṣva*, he should give the collyrium over each individual rice-ball. With the mantra *etad*, he should give a fringe or the like, according to availability, over each rice-ball. As for what was stated by Śaṅkha:
"A thread of *kṣumā* or new cotton (*kārpāsa*) should be provided;

a wise person should avoid the fringe (*daśā*), even if it is from unwashed cloth. Here, *kṣumā* refers to flax (*atasī*). Although in this [text] the prohibition of the fringe appears to be mandatory, nevertheless, because the fringe is prescribed in the previously cited *smṛti*, an option should be understood, similar to the case of whether or not to take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. Regarding the absence of cloth, it is also stated in the *Purāṇa*:
"He should cause wool, fringe, or even a garment's border to be given as hair. Thus it is said.

The husband is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Regarding the practice of offering hair, this does not occur in the first stage of life; thus says Kātyāyana: "‘This for you, O ancestors’—having uttered these *sūtra*-verses, [he offers] either the balls of rice (*piṇḍa*) or, in the latter stage of life, the sacrificer’s own hairs. "In the latter stage of life" means after the age of fifty. Because of the word "or" (*vā*), in the latter stage of life there is the option of the hair-offering, as well as other alternatives. All of this is obtained by the rule "as in the *Pitṛyajña*. However, regarding the ritual washing (*avanejana*), Vyāghra states a distinction from the *Pitṛyajña*.

"Having washed that vessel with water, one should perform the *avanejana* (sprinkling) for each *piṇḍa* as before, making the *piṇḍa*-vessel face downwards. The phrase "as before" means as was prescribed previously during the *avanejana* performed before the offering of the *piṇḍas*. Thus, the second *avanejana* should also be performed with the water used for washing the *piṇḍa*-vessel, and not with other water as in the *Pitṛyajña*. For this very reason:

"One should perform the rinsing again with the very water used for washing the vessel"—thus the particle *eva* (only) is employed in the *Purāṇa*. Vyāghra states that after the taking of the fringe (*daśā*), there is a distinction from the *pitṛyajña* regarding the mantra *etad vaḥ*:
"One should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, and indeed a lamp."
O ancestors, having given this garment to each of you individually, [be pleased].

The meaning is that, having attached a fringe of the cloth to each *piṇḍa* with the mantra "etad vaḥ," one should also offer the fragrant substances (*gandha*) and so forth to each *piṇḍa*. As for what was stated by Viṣṇu—"Having performed the offering of the *piṇḍas*, one should present the *arghya*, flowers, incense, ointments, food, edibles, and delicacies, as well as a water-pot joined with honey, clarified butter, and curds"—that is intended to specify the particular items such as the *arghya* to be offered after the offering of the *piṇḍas*. Otherwise, [it would contradict the following]:
"Having offered the *piṇḍas* to the ancestors, being self-restrained and according to the rule..."
Upon those darbha grasses, he should wipe that hand for the sake of those who partake of the ritual smears.

For otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with the more logical sequence taught by Manu. Therefore, the statement of Viṣṇu is intended merely to indicate the offering of *argha* and so forth, and not for the purpose of establishing that it must immediately follow the offering of the *piṇḍas*; thus, it should be understood that this does not conflict with the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) asserted by Vyāghra. As for what is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"One should offer perfumes, incense, and so forth, after having performed the *pratyavanejana* (the second rinsing of the hands)."

Thus, this [statement] intends only that the offering of fragrance (*gandha*) and other items does not occur prior to the *pratyavanejana* (the ritual rinsing); it does not intend that the offering of fragrance and other items must be performed immediately after the *pratyavanejana*. For if it were so intended, it would contradict the previously cited statement of Vyāghra—which prescribes the sequence based on the underlying principle that "what is not mentioned in the archetype (*prakṛti*) should be placed at the end"—which establishes the order: the offering of ointment (*abhyañjana*) and so forth after the *avanejana*, and the offering of fragrance and so forth after that. Therefore, this [interpretation] also does not obstruct the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) stated by Vyāghra. Precisely because the Matsya Purāṇa statement does not concern the mutual sequence between the *pratyavanejana* and the offering of fragrance and so forth, Viṣṇu has here stated only the sequence of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* as it exists in the archetype: "With the words 'May the ancestors be purified,' one pours water over the *piṇḍas* as before; then one should offer the ointment with the words 'O [Name], be anointed. Therefore, it is established that, according to the sequence understood from the statement of Vyāghra, one should worship the *piṇḍas* with fragrance and other items immediately after giving the *daśā* (fringe-cloth). Regarding the worship of the *piṇḍas*, it is said in the Purāṇa: [text continues].
Whatever food, whether hard or soft, that is cooked in the house and is not forbidden,
one must never eat it at the base of the *piṇḍa* without first offering it.

The intention is that, having taken [all these items] from everything, an offering (upahāra) should be presented during the worship of the rice-balls (piṇḍārcana). Bṛhaspati states what is to be done after the worship of the rice-balls: "Then, having worshipped them equally with incense, lamps, garlands, perfumes, as well as garments, collyrium, and so forth, one should place a vessel of water upon them."

The sequence of recitation beginning with incense and lamps (*dhūpadīpa*) is not intended here, because the order is established by the verses themselves. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: having worshipped the *piṇḍas* with ointments, collyrium, garments, perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and offerings of food of all kinds, one should pour out water filling a vessel over those *piṇḍas* using that very same vessel. After the pouring of the water-vessel, Viṣṇu states: "Then he pays homage to them with the mantra beginning 'Homage to you, O Fathers' (*namo vaḥ pitaraḥ*) and ending with the verse 'We call the mind back' (*mano 'nvāhuvāmahe*). Then he should move these *piṇḍas*, saying: 'Go back to us, O gentle Fathers, by the deep, ancient paths; having given to yourselves the auspicious wealth here, bestow upon us riches and sons endowed with all heroes. The phrase "with the mantra beginning 'Homage to you, O Fathers'" implies it is the mantra recited by Āśvalāyana, since the *Viṣṇusmṛti* follows the ritual manual (*kalpa*) for the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*) taught by Āśvalāyana. The mantra beginning with "Homage to you, O Fathers" is that which has the three-verse hymn "We call the mind back" at its end; thus it is called "ending with the three-verse hymn. Consequently, in this case, one should perform the homage by joining the palms in reverence (*añjali*), in accordance with the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra. For this very reason, relying on the gesture of reverential salutation, a mere rule is stated in the *Brāhmaṇapurāṇa*.
With his right and left hands, he should always recite this mantra properly and without weariness: "Homage to you, O fathers, for food... and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: while reciting "namo vaḥ pitaraḥ" correctly, one should place the right hand palm upwards with both hands—the left being uppermost—and, having formed a reverential *añjali* over it with the downward-facing left hand, one should recite this mantra stated by Āśvalāyana: "namo vaḥ pitara iṣe. Immediately after the scattering of the rice-grains (*piṇḍavālanā*), one should approach the fire used for the *agnaukaraṇa* offering with the verse beginning "agne tad adya. One should approach the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse beginning "yad antarikṣam. Accordingly, it is stated by Āśvalāyana in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña-kalpa*: "One should go toward the fire with [the verse]: 'Agni, today... like a horse with hymns. And regarding the *gārhapatya*: "Whatever [sin] I have committed against the atmosphere, the earth, or the sky, or against my mother or father—may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin; may he make me free from evil, whatever misdeeds we have done. This prescribed procedure for the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*), starting from the drawing of lines (*ullekhana*) and ending with the approach to the fire, should be understood to apply equally to the offering of rice-balls intended for the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and others.
"Likewise, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) to the maternal grandfathers.

This is because Yājñavalkya has stated this. The meaning is that just as the ritual procedure for the Śrāddha for the fathers and others—beginning with the invitation of the Brahmins and ending with their dismissal—is prescribed, so too should the entire Śrāddha procedure for the maternal grandfathers and others, beginning with the invitation of the Brahmins, be understood. Thus, one should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas) for the maternal grandfathers and others in the same manner as for the fathers and others. And so says Madālasā:
"In the same way, one should offer the rice-balls to the maternal grandfathers according to the rule."

The meaning is "in that manner," that is, "like unto the fathers. Although in this passage, after stating the rule for offering rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to the group of paternal ancestors, the phrase "in that manner" refers to the offering of rice-balls to the group of maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*), it might appear that the offering of rice-balls for the group of maternal grandfathers should be performed as a separate ritual procedure (*bhinnatantra*) once the rule for the rice-ball offering for the paternal group has been completed. Nevertheless, because it has been stated in the very same context—namely, under the rule "or the *vaiśvadeva* [portion] is common"—that the performance of the entire *śrāddha* for both groups is by way of a common ritual procedure (*samānatantra*), the offering of rice-balls for both groups must likewise be performed as a common ritual procedure. For this very reason, the performance by way of a common ritual procedure is declared in the Purāṇas.
Having spread darbha grass from the base of the roots near the remains of the food,
