and having performed the ritual sprinkling (avanejana), one should offer three rice-balls (piṇḍas) for each [ancestor] in due order.

"From the base," meaning from near the root; "three" is used distributively (vīpsayā) to indicate that the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa) for the two groups is performed according to the same procedure.
Thus ends the rule for the offering of rice-balls in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the procedure for the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍadāna) according to the ritual rules of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).

Now, the procedure for offering the *piṇḍas* (rice balls), established through the synthesis of direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*), is described. From all the cooked food prepared for the *śrāddha*, one should set aside a portion sufficient for six *piṇḍas* plus a little extra into another vessel. Having asked, "Is there any remainder? What shall be done with it? and having heard the response from the Brahmins in the form of permission, "Let it be enjoyed together with those you love," he should immediately thereafter, using either a wooden sword (*sphya*) or *darbha* grass, draw a single line toward the south-east at the place of the *piṇḍas* with his left hand uppermost, reciting the mantra: "The Asuras, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas who sit upon the altar are driven away. Then, to the south of that, he should draw a second line in the same manner as the first. Next, having dug up the ground near the two lines and sprinkled water on them twice silently, he should spread *sakṛdācchinna* grass—cut near the roots—with its tips pointing south-east or south, separately upon each of the two lines. With his right hand, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors), he should pour water mixed with sesame seeds onto the grass at the place of the first *piṇḍa* on the first line, reciting the three mantras: "May the fathers be purified; may the grandfathers be purified; may the great-grandfathers be purified. Then, onto the grass at the places of the *piṇḍas* on the second line, he should pour water mixed with sesame seeds while reciting: "May the maternal grandfathers be purified; may the maternal great-grandfathers be purified; may the maternal great-great-grandfathers be purified. Alternatively, on the first line, he should pour water with the mantras: "O Father, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, descend; O Grandfather, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, descend; O Great-grandfather, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, descend. On the second line, he should pour water with the mantras: "O Maternal grandfather, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, descend; O Maternal great-grandfather, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, descend; O Maternal great-great-grandfather, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, descend. Then, facing south and bending his left knee, he should make a *piṇḍa* of food mixed with ghee, honey, and sesame, of the size prescribed in the previous section (such as a fresh *āmalaka* fruit). Having said, "This is for you, Father, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, and for those who follow you," and having declared, "This food is for Father, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, in the form of Vasu, together with his wife; it is not mine," he should place the first *piṇḍa* at the first spot with his hand turned downwards. Having said, "This is for you, Grandfather, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, and for those who follow you," and having declared, "This food is for Grandfather, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, in the form of Prajāpati, together with his wife; it is not mine," he should place the second *piṇḍa* at the second spot. Likewise, having said, "This is for you, Great-grandfather, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, and for those who follow you," and having declared, "This food is for Great-grandfather, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, in the form of Agni, together with his wife; it is not mine," he should place the third *piṇḍa* at the third spot. These *piṇḍas* should be placed so that they end toward the south or the south-east, following the direction of the grass-strewing. Then, in the same manner, he should place *piṇḍas* at the spots on the second line. The specific difference for the first *piṇḍa* is: "This is for you, Maternal grandfather, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, and for those who follow you; this food is for Maternal grandfather, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, in the form of Varuṇa, together with his wife; it is not mine. For the maternal great-grandfather and great-great-grandfather, he should place the *piṇḍas* with the formulas "in the form of Prajāpati" and "in the form of Agni," respectively, saying "it is not mine. These *piṇḍas* should also be placed ending toward the south or the south-east, following the grass-strewing. Thus have the mantras for offering the *piṇḍas* according to the school of Āśvalāyana been shown. The mantras for offering the *piṇḍas* according to the schools of Kātyāyana and others were already shown in the previous section; those following their views should apply them here as well. Having thus offered the *piṇḍas*, he should perform the wiping of the hand-leavings on the grass strewn over the lines, simply by saying, "O Fathers, rejoice here. Then, saying, "O Fathers, rejoice here; enjoy yourselves according to your portions," he should turn away from the right (counter-clockwise) and face north. Sitting without exhaling as much as possible, and then turning back, he should consecrate all six *piṇḍas* at once with the mantra: "Those Fathers have rejoiced; they have enjoyed themselves according to their portions. Then he should exhale. Next, having silently smelled the remains in the *piṇḍa*-vessel, he should perform the second libation (*avanejana*) on the six *piṇḍas* as before, using the six mantras beginning with "May the fathers be purified" and the six mantras beginning with "O Father, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, descend. He should then turn the *piṇḍa*-vessel upside down. Then, having applied oil to the six *piṇḍas* according to their names, saying "O [Name], of such-and-such gotra, be anointed," and having applied collyrium to the six *piṇḍas* according to their names, saying "O [Name], of such-and-such name, be anointed," he should give a piece of cloth or similar item to the six *piṇḍas* with the mantra: "This is your garment, O Fathers; do not take anything else, O Fathers. Then, he should silently worship each *piṇḍa* with offerings of *arghya*, perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and various kinds of food, along with a vessel of water containing honey, ghee, and sesame. Then, he should pour the water filling the vessel over all the *piṇḍas* using that same vessel. Making his right hand palm-upward and forming a salutation-gesture (*añjali*) with his left hand turned downward over it, he should worship all the *piṇḍas* at once with the three verses: "Salutation to you, O Fathers, for food; salutation to you, O Fathers, for strength; salutation to you, O Fathers, for vigor; salutation to you, O Fathers, for the terrible; salutation to you, O Fathers, for life; salutation to you, O Fathers, for sap; *svadhā* to you, O Fathers; salutation to you, O Fathers; salutation! These are yours, O Fathers; may we, being living here, belong to you. We invoke the mind with the *Nārāśaṃsa Soma* and with the hymns of the Fathers. Then, he should move the *piṇḍas* with the mantra: "Return, O Fathers, who are worthy of Soma, by the deep, ancient paths; having given us here auspicious wealth and a son endowed with all heroes, depart. Then, he should go toward the fire used for the *agnaukaraṇa* rite with the verse: "O Agni, today [accept] this with our hymns, like a horse, like a noble sacrifice, touching the
Thus concludes the procedure for the offering of the *piṇḍas* according to the *Pitṛyajña-dharmaka* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some other statements concerning the offering of the *piṇḍas* are also recorded;
among them, Bṛhaspati says:
From all the food prepared, one should offer rice-balls mixed with honey and sesame seeds to the fathers, maternal grandfathers, and others, according to the rules of the Gṛhya-sūtras.

This is what is meant: In the *Gṛhyasūtras* of Āpastamba and others, where the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍadāna*) is prescribed by a rule other than the injunction for the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, those who follow that particular *Gṛhya* must perform the offering of rice balls to the paternal ancestors (*pitṛs*) and the maternal ancestors (*mātāmahas*) according to that specific rule alone. However, for one whose *Gṛhya* does not prescribe a different rule, or where the injunction for the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is specifically mentioned, it should be understood that the offering of rice balls must be performed according to that very ritual procedure of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, and not otherwise. To illustrate the various rules mentioned in the *Gṛhyas*, the alternative procedure stated in the *Āpastamba-gṛhya* is shown here, for it is stated therein: "Having followed [the guests] after they have eaten and having circumambulated them, he should spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south in two rows; having poured water on them with the subsequent [mantras], and having offered the rice balls ending toward the south with the subsequent [mantras], having again poured water as before with the subsequent [mantras], having worshipped with the subsequent [mantras], having sprinkled around three times counter-clockwise with a water-pot, having turned the vessels upside down, having recited the subsequent *Yajus* formula without pausing for at least three [breaths], and having sprinkled the vessels, he should bring them back in pairs. The meaning of this is analyzed as follows: By the phrase "having followed [them] after they have eaten and having circumambulated them," it is indicated that the primary rite consisting of the feeding of the Brahmins—accompanied by its concluding subsidiary elements such as following and circumambulation—must first be completed. It is not said that the primary rite of feeding the Brahmins is to be finished immediately thereafter [without the conclusion]. Therefore, the offering of the rice balls (*piṇḍanirvāpaṇa*) should be performed once the Brahmins have returned to their own places; it is not to be understood as occurring while the Brahmins remain standing, whether they have already rinsed their mouths (*ācānta*) or not. "Having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south in two rows" means having spread the *darbha* grass with tips pointing south separately in the front and back parts of the unpolluted ground so that there are two rows. Having poured water on them with the subsequent [mantras]—that is, on those *darbhas* spread in two rows—one should pour water with each of the subsequent mantras, such as "May my fathers purify themselves" (*mārjayantāṃ mama pitaraḥ*), at each individual place for a rice ball. On the *darbhas* in the front part, one should pour water with the mantra "May the fathers purify themselves" (*mārjayantām pitaraḥ*) at the place for the first rice ball; at the places for the second and third rice balls, one should pour water with the two mantras "May the grandfathers purify themselves" and "May the great-grandfathers purify themselves" (*mārjayantāṃ pitāmahāḥ* and *prapitāmahāḥ*). On the *darbhas* in the back part, one should pour water with the mantra "May the mothers purify themselves" (*mārjayantāṃ mātaraḥ*) at the place for the first rice ball; at the places for the second and third rice balls, one should pour water with "May the grandmothers purify themselves" and "May the great-grandmothers purify themselves" (*mārjayantāṃ pitāmahyaḥ* and *prapitāmahyaḥ*). "Having offered the rice balls ending toward the south with the subsequent [mantras]" means that at each individual place for a rice ball, one should offer one rice ball dedicated to the paternal ancestors and others, preceded by the renunciation (*tyāga*), using each of the subsequent mantras such as "This is for you, O father, N.N., and those who follow you" (*etat te tatāsau ye ca tvām anu*). In that regard, following the sequence of pouring water on the *darbhas* in the front part, the offering of the first rice ball is performed with the mantra "This is for you, O father, N.N., and those who follow you. The offering of the rice balls for the grandfather and great-grandfather is done in the same way. On the *darbhas* in the back part, the offering of the first rice ball is performed with the mantra "This is for you, O mother, N.N., and those who follow you" (*etat te mātar asau yāś ca tvām anu*). The offering of the rice balls for the grandmother and great-grandmother is done in the same way. Since the author of the *Gṛhyabhāṣyārthasaṃgraha* states, "And the rice balls for the women should be here in the west," it should be understood that the offering of rice balls for the female ancestors takes place on the *darbhas* in the back part. In all six rice-ball mantras, at the word "N.N. (*asau*), one must utter the name of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, or the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother, in the vocative case.
In the offering of the *arghya*, in the formal declaration (*saṃkalpa*), and likewise in the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and the inexhaustible water,
one should correctly provide the lineage, the relationship, and the names.

Thus, because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Pāraskara, the *piṇḍas* should not be made from all kinds of food remaining after the feeding of the Brahmins, mixed with honey and sesame seeds. Some say that the offering of *piṇḍas* should be performed with rice alone, because Āpastamba has not prescribed [the use of other foods] in the passage beginning with "from all the prepared food. As before, having offered water with the subsequent [mantras], one should pour out water near the *darbha* grass close to the *piṇḍas*—just as in the previous pouring of water—with the six mantras beginning with "May the ancestors purify themselves" (*mārjayantāṃ pitaraḥ*), which are recited after the mantras beginning with "This for you, O father, N.N. Some say that in both the previously mentioned pouring of water and the subsequently mentioned pouring of water, water mixed with sesame seeds should be used. Having worshipped with the subsequent [mantras], meaning having worshipped with the mantras beginning with "And those who are here among you," etc.; by these mantras—"And those who are here among you, and those who hope for us from us, may they carry [this] to you; may you be satisfied, may you be satisfied, may you be satisfied"—the worship of the *piṇḍas* intended for the paternal lineage is performed. By these mantras—"And those women who are here among you, and those who hope for us from us, may they carry [this] to you; may you [women] be satisfied, may you be satisfied, may you be satisfied"—the worship of the *piṇḍas* intended for the maternal lineage should be performed; this is to be understood from the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantras. Having sprinkled around three times to the left with the subsequent [mantra] using a water-vessel, meaning having sprinkled around all the *piṇḍas* of both [lineages] with the verse "Sons and grandsons," etc. Having turned the vessels face down, meaning having placed them with their openings downward. Having repeated the subsequent Yajus formula without pausing for half a *āvarta*, meaning having muttered the single Yajus "Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied" three times while leaning on another side and without breathing in. Having sprinkled the vessels and having lifted the two pairs of vessels, meaning having sprinkled the vessels that were turned face down and having lifted two vessels simultaneously, he should place them elsewhere. Thus, according to the rule of the *Āpastamba-gṛhya-sūtra* mentioned above, or according to the rule stated in another *Gṛhya-sūtra*, one should offer the *piṇḍas* according to one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. Even in the rule stated in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, the offering of *piṇḍas* for the maternal grandfather and others must be performed.

"One should offer [the piṇḍas] for the fathers, maternal grandfathers, and others according to the rules of the Gṛhya-sūtra," because this has been shown by the statement of Bṛhaspati within this very context. In that regard, the offering of separate piṇḍas for the maternal grandfathers and others must be performed according to the rules of the Āpastamba-Gṛhya, since a modification (vikṛti) must be performed in accordance with its archetype (prakṛti). And the status of the Śrāddha for maternal grandfathers and others as a modification has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha:
"One should likewise perform the Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather and others with diligence."

Consequently, for those who follow that specific domestic manual (*gṛhya*), the procedure for offering the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for the sake of the maternal grandfather and others is as follows: Having prepared the layering of *darbha* grass for the group of the mother, one should then prepare a layering of *darbha* grass for the group of the maternal grandfather behind that, and then prepare a layering of *darbha* grass for the group of the maternal grandmother behind that. Having offered water for the group of the mother, one should offer water for the group of the maternal grandfather; the mantras beginning with "May the maternal grandfathers purify themselves" (*mārjayantāṃ mātāmahāḥ*) are to be modified accordingly. Having offered water for the group of the maternal grandfather, one should offer water for the group of the maternal grandmother; the mantra "May the maternal grandmothers purify themselves" (*mārjayantāṃ mātāmahyaḥ*) is to be modified accordingly. Having offered the rice-balls for the group of the mother, one should offer the rice-balls for the group of the maternal grandfather; the mantras for the offering of the rice-balls, such as "This is for you, O maternal grandfather, of such-and-such lineage, named such-and-such, and those who follow you," are to be modified accordingly. Having offered the rice-balls for the group of the maternal grandfather, one should offer the rice-balls for the group of the maternal grandmother; the mantras for the offering of the rice-balls, such as "This is for you, O maternal grandmother, of such-and-such lineage, named such-and-such, and those who follow you," are to be modified accordingly. Having again offered water near the rice-balls for the group of the mother, one should again offer water near the rice-balls for the group of the maternal grandfather, and immediately thereafter, pour water near the rice-balls for the group of the maternal grandmother. The modification of the pouring mantras should be performed exactly as before. After performing the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) for the rice-balls for the group of the mother, the ritual attendance for the rice-balls for the group of the maternal grandfather should be performed using the very same mantras used for the ritual attendance of the rice-balls for the group of the father. Then, the ritual attendance for the rice-balls for the group of the maternal grandmother should be performed using the very same mantras used for the ritual attendance of the rice-balls for the group of the mother. With the verse beginning "Sons and grandsons" (*putrān pautrān*), one should simultaneously perform the threefold circumambulation from right to left (*prasavya*) around all twelve rice-balls; the remaining rites, such as the repetition of the *yajus*, should be performed only once as common to all. The commentator on the *Bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha* has indicated that the modification of the mantra "May the maternal grandfathers purify themselves" (*mārjayantāṃ mātāmahāḥ*) is to be applied here.
In place of the words "father" and so forth, the terms "maternal grandfather" and so forth should be applied during the food-oblation (annahoma),
as well as during the ritual touching and the offering of water-balls (piṇḍa) and other such rites.
"‘My maternal grandmother,’ and so forth, would serve as an illustration in that regard. Thus [it is said].

In the *annahoma* (food-oblation), one uses the mantras beginning with "yan me mātā pralulobha caranty ananuvratā" during the oblation of food into the fire. In the *sparśa* (touching) rite for the purpose of feeding Brāhmaṇas, one uses the mantras beginning with "eṣa te tata madhumāṃ ūrmiḥ sarasvān. Regarding the offering of water and rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), the meaning is that in place of words such as "father" (*pitṛ*) found in the water-offering mantra "marjayantāṃ pitaraḥ" and in the rice-ball offering mantra "etat te tatāsau ye ca tvām anu," words such as "maternal grandfather" (*mātāmaha*) should be substituted and employed. The phrase "yan me mātāmahītyādi" serves as an illustration; its meaning is as follows: there, in place of the word "father" and so on, the word "maternal grandfather" and so on are to be inserted. For instance, when performing the *annahoma* for the sake of the maternal grandfather using the mantra "yan me mātā pralulobha caraty ananuvratā tan me retaḥ pitā vṛṅktām," by substituting the word "maternal grandmother" (*mātāmahī*) for the word "mother" (*mātṛ*) occurring in the mantra, the resulting modification (*ūha*) becomes "yan me mātāmahī. Similarly, by substituting the word "maternal grandfather" (*mātāmaha*) for the word "father" (*pitṛ*) occurring in that same mantra, the resulting modification becomes "tan me reto mātāmaho vṛṅktām. This is the illustration. Regarding the offering of rice balls when names are unknown, another *Gṛhya* text states: "If one does not know the names, one should offer the first rice ball with the formula, 'Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth'; the second with 'Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in the intermediate space'; and the third with 'Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in heaven. These mantras are to be employed even in the context of the rice-ball offering for the maternal grandfathers and others when their names are unknown. Regarding the loss of the lineage name (*gotra*), Vyāghrapāt says: "But in the case of the loss of the *gotra*, [one uses] Kaśyapa. When the *gotra* is unknown, one should employ the Kaśyapa *gotra*, because the Kaśyapa *gotra* is common to all. Thus the Śruti says: "Therefore they say, 'All progeny are Kaśyapa. Accordingly, even when the *gotra* of the maternal grandfather and others is unknown, one should employ the Kaśyapa *gotra*.

Thus ends the section concerning the offering of the *piṇḍas* in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follow the matters concerning the subsidiary rite that follows the principal act, namely the feeding of the Brahmins; regarding this, the *Matsya Purāṇa* states:
Then, after they have sipped water, he himself should sip water and offer water once to each. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that when the Brahmins have sipped water (ācānta), he himself should also sip water, and having eaten, he should pour water once into each of the right hands of the Brahmins. This should be understood as applying to the case where the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) is performed while the Brahmins have not yet sipped water. In the case where the offering of rice balls is performed after they have sipped water, he should first sip water and then offer the rice ball; thereafter, he should pour water once into each of the Brahmins' hands. Darbha grass should also be given so that their hands may be purified (*pavitrapāṇi*), because the purifiers used at the time of eating have been discarded as being defiled by food remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*). Thus it is also stated in the *Padmapurāṇa*.
"When they have sipped water, one should offer water, flowers, and barley."

The phrase "in the hands of the Vaiśvadeva Brāhmaṇas" is to be understood as the ellipsis, because of the mention of "along with barley. However, in the hands of the Paitṛka Brāhmaṇas, sesame seeds (tila) should be offered in place of barley, as that is seen to be the case in the *arghya* offering and other rites. By the word "ca" (and) in the expression "along with barley," it is indicated that water should be offered once again. Since there is no purpose for holding the barley and other items placed in their hands—just as there is none for the *darbha* grass—the Brāhmaṇas should discard them somewhere in a clean place once their function has been fulfilled. After the discarding, they should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) once more.
Once they have sipped water, the wise man should again offer water, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata);
having offered these, he should receive blessings from the twice-born while facing the east.

By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), it is indicated that water with barley and flowers, as stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*, should be offered first. The meaning is: one should offer water, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*); having first offered water, one should offer water again after having presented the unbroken rice and flowers. Regarding the phrase "one should accept the blessings" (*āśīḥ pratigṛhṇīyāt*), the meaning is that one should receive the benedictions. When it is asked: what are these blessings, how are they to be accepted, and what should be done after accepting them?—it has been stated immediately thereafter by that same [author]: "When the twice-born have said, 'May the ancestors be non-terrible (*aghorāḥ*),' [the host should reply] 'So be it. (*aghorāḥ pitaraḥ santu santv ity ukte punar dvijaiḥ*)
"May our lineage likewise increase," they said to him in return.
May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.
And having been told by them, "May these true blessings be fulfilled, may they be fulfilled," one should perform the recitation of auspicious benedictions (*svastivācanaka*)... [thus].

The performer of the *śrāddha* should say, "May the ancestors be non-terrible (*aghora*). The meaning of this is, "May the ancestors be auspicious (*śiva*). When [the ancestors] have said "May they be," and the twice-born have replied, "May the ancestors be non-terrible," the performer should say, "May our lineage increase. When they have said "So be it," and the twice-born have again said, "May the lineage increase," the performer, having recited the verse beginning with "May our givers [of gifts] increase," should say, "May these blessings be true. When they have said "May they be," he should then perform the *svastivācana*. When the performer has been told by those twice-born, "May these blessings be true," he should receive with his head the unbroken rice and flowers offered by the twice-born and perform the *svastivācana*. In the *Kātyāyana-gṛhya-sūtra*, however, the passage beginning with "May our givers" is not mentioned; when it says "May the ancestors be non-terrible," it states only, "May our lineage increase. Although it might appear from the statement of the *Matsya-purāṇa* alone that the *svastivācana* should be performed immediately after receiving the blessing, nevertheless, one should perform the *svastivācana* after receiving the blessing and moving the eating vessels, because otherwise a fault is heard [to be incurred]. And so says Nārāyaṇa:
Those twice-born ones who pronounce a blessing without moving that vessel leave their ancestors disappointed; having uttered a curse, they depart as they came.
Bṛhaspati also said: "If those twice-born ones offer blessings while the vessels still remain [full], that which was given is consumed by the Asuras, and the ancestors depart disappointed. [391]

Therefore, the intention is that the shifting of the vessels (*pātracālana*) must necessarily be performed prior to the recitation of the *svastivācana*. Regarding the person who performs the shifting of the vessels, Jātūkarṇya has shown both a rule and a prohibition: "In a *śrāddha*, one should shift the vessels oneself, or else a disciple or a son;
never by women, nor by a child, nor by one of a different caste under any circumstances."

The method for the recitation of the *svasti* (benediction) has been shown by Pāraskara: "O Blessed One, say ‘Svasti’—this is the recitation. A specific detail stated by Kātyāyana is that the *svastivācana* follows the offering of water with sesame seeds (*akrodaka*). The procedure here is as follows: wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), the performer, having offered water into the hands of the Brahmins representing the Viśvedevas, should say: "O Blessed One, say ‘Svasti’ to the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava. And the Brahmin should say, "Svasti to them. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), the performer, having offered water into the hands of the Brahmins representing the ancestors, should say: "O Blessed One, say ‘Svasti’ to the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*) and such-and-such name (*śarman*). And the Brahmin should say, "Svasti to them. In the same manner, having offered water into the hands of the Brahmins representing the maternal ancestors, the performer should say: "O Blessed One, say ‘Svasti’ to the maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name. And the Brahmin should say, "Svasti to them. After the *svastivācana*, Yājñavalkya states: "Then one should perform the *akṣayyodaka* (the rite for inexhaustibility). This means that immediately after the *svastivācana*, one should perform the *akṣayyodaka*. Having said, "May it be inexhaustible," one should pour water into the hand of the Brahmin; this is the meaning. However, into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors, one should pour water mixed with sesame seeds, because Kātyāyana has stated that one should offer "sesame-water" while saying, "May it be inexhaustible. The Brahmins should respond, "May it be inexhaustible. Thus says the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Immediately thereafter, water should be offered to the ancestors by their name and lineage;
the twice-born should then say to the Brahmins, "May this be inexhaustible."

The phrase "in the hands of the Brāhmaṇas" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Herein is the ritual procedure: wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), one should pour pure water into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas representing the Viśvedevas, saying: "May there be inexhaustibility for the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), one should pour water mixed with sesame seeds into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas representing the ancestors, saying: "May there be inexhaustibility for [the names of] the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*) and such-and-such name (*śarman*), together with their wives. In the same manner, one should pour water mixed with sesame seeds into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas representing the maternal grandfathers and others, saying: "May there be inexhaustibility for [the names of] the maternal grandfather and others, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, together with their wives. After the twice-born have received the offerings for the Viśvedevas and the others, they should say: "May this be inexhaustible. Immediately after the offering of the inexhaustible water (*akṣayyodaka*), one should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Thus says Mātsya:
"And [he should offer] inexhaustible water with sesame seeds, giving a monetary gift (dakṣiṇā) according to his ability, mentioning the name and lineage.

This means that one should offer the inexhaustible water with sesame seeds while reciting the names and lineages of the ancestors and others; immediately after that, one should give a monetary gift according to one's capacity—this is the meaning. Having specified the items to be given here, Vyāsa says:
One should give cows, land, gold, garments, new beds,
and whatever else is desired by the Brahmins, as well as for oneself and one's father.

"Free from stinginess regarding wealth, he should act so as to bring pleasure to the ancestors. This means that, free from stinginess regarding wealth, he should give cows and other such items to the ancestors; the syntactical connection is that he should do so while acting for their pleasure. Pāraskara also says: "Gold for the Viśvedevas, silver for the ancestors, and other things such as cows, black antelope skins, and so forth, as much as one is able. In the Vāyupurāṇa: "Whatever is most excellent in the world and whatever is dear to oneself..."
Everything should be given to the ancestors by one who desires that their merit remain inexhaustible.
"Of the ancestors" means "to the ancestors. Jamadagni describes the manner of giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the ancestors:
"One should give, according to one's ability, a sacrificial fee consisting of sesame seeds along with [the mention of] the name and lineage, as well as gold, jewels, garments, mansions, and beds."

The meaning is that, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"I offer this substance, such as gold and so forth, together with sesame seeds, to the ancestors [named] along with their lineage names"—one should present it to the paternal Brahmins who have finished eating; for it has been stated: "Having fed the Brahmins, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability. As for what is declared in the *Vāyu-prāṇa*:

"Whatever is most beloved in the world, and whatever else exists in the house—that very thing should be given to a virtuous person by one who desires that [the gift] be inexhaustible at that very moment."

Thus, that which is intended for the gods and the ancestors is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) material, not food such as *bhakṣya* and *bhojya*. However, *bhakṣya* and *bhojya* food should be given equally to the Brahmins who are the eaters. It should be understood that even the sacrificial fee and other materials are to be given unequally according to the qualities of the Brahmin eaters; it does not mean that they are to be given specifically with reference to a Brahmin who possesses [extraordinary] qualities. As Pāraskara says: "In the Śrāddha rite, to the Brahmins seated in a single row, *bhakṣya* and *bhojya* food should be given equally, but the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to their [respective] merit."

The meaning is that the gift should be given equally, setting aside any inequality based on the relative degree of merit (*guṇatāratamya*). There is no fault even if inequality based on the relative degree of merit is applied in the case of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth. "According to the capacity" (*anusārataḥ*) means according to the merits of the invited Brahmins. The procedure for giving the sacrificial fee is as follows: Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I offer gold and other items as a sacrificial fee to the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava," one should place it into the hand of the Brahmin representing the Vaiśvadeva portion. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), having made the resolve: "I offer silver and other items as a sacrificial fee to my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, named so-and-so, belonging to such-and-such lineage, together with their wives," one should place it into the hand of the Brahmin representing the paternal ancestors. One should offer in the same manner to the maternal grandfathers and others. Now, if the renunciation of the substance is made with the ancestors and others as the intended recipients, and not with the Brahmins as the recipients, how then can the Brahmins have ownership (*svāmya*) over the gift-substance? It is said in reply: Just as in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, when the sacrificial fee is given, the sacrificer says, "O Brahmins, this is your rice," and having offered the rice, although there is no renunciation of the rice with the Brahmins as the intended recipients, the ownership of the rice arises for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) solely by virtue of their being the performers of the ritual action (*karmakartṛtva*). Likewise here, upon the offering of gold, silver, and so forth, the ownership of the Brahmins is established solely by virtue of their being the performers of the ritual action. Or, for example, in the case of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and similar rites, the ownership of the preceptor (*ācārya*) over the garments, ornaments, and so forth dedicated to the deity being installed arises solely through his role as the instrumental agent (*karaka*), supported by the scriptural statement: "At the conclusion of the installation, the preceptor takes all the implements. Similarly here, the ownership of the Brahmins over the silver and other items dedicated with the ancestors and others as the intended recipients is accomplished by virtue of their being the instrumental agents, as supported by the rule: "Having fed the Brahmins, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's capacity. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Alternatively, the ownership of the Brahmins will arise here simply because the renunciation is made with them as the intended recipients.
"Then one should present the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born who have sipped water. Thus it is said.
Devala has stated that the sacrificial fee should be given with reference to the twice-born:
"One should give the sacrificial fee first to the Brahmins representing the ancestors, and then to the two [representing the gods]."

"To two" means to the two Brāhmaṇas belonging to the Vaiśvadeva rite. The word "to two," though in the genitive case (*dvayoḥ*), should be understood as having the sense of the dative case, due to its proximity to the dative phrase "to the Brāhmaṇas of the ancestors" (*pitṛviprebhyaḥ*). Thus, the meaning is this: having first given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brāhmaṇas of the ancestors, one should afterwards give it to the two Brāhmaṇas of the Vaiśvadeva rite. According to this view, since the giving of the fee belongs to the ancestral rite, one should give it even to the Brāhmaṇas of the ancestors while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*). For this very reason, Jamadagni says: "All ritual action is performed with the thread over the right shoulder (*apasavyena*), except for the giving of the sacrificial fee.
As for that which was further stated by him:
"The Lord Matsya indeed considered that even in that case [the gift] should be made with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (aprasavya).

This is to be understood as referring to the occasion when a gift is given to the ancestors (dakṣiṇādāna). Bṛhaspati, however, states that a gift may be given even to Brahmins who have not been formally invited:
"Relatives, kinsmen, those who are destitute, and likewise other guests."
"One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to all of them in accordance with their merit.
Here, "kinsmen" (*jñātayaḥ*) are those related through the father; "relatives" (*bāndhavāḥ*) are those related through the mother. Following the giving of the sacrificial fee, Yājñavalkya says:
"But having given the sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should utter the word *svadhā*."

The meaning is that immediately after the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should request permission from the Brahmins by saying, "I shall cause the *svadhā* to be uttered. Atri also states: "One should thus pose the question, 'I shall cause the *svadhā* to be uttered,' among the twice-born.
The meaning is that one should pose this question regarding the *svadhā* while the twice-born are still seated. Thereupon, the twice-born should grant permission, saying, "Let it be uttered."
"Let it be recited"—thus they, being pleased and composed, should grant permission;
for this was stated by that very same author immediately thereafter. When it is asked what one who has been thus permitted should do, Yājñavalkya says:
"Being permitted with the words 'Let it be recited,' let the *svadhā* be uttered for the ancestors."

By this, the following is stated: the performer (*kartṛ*) should say, “Let the *svadhā* be spoken for the fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers, together with their wives. The Brahmins should reply, “Let there be *svadhā*. Thereafter, the performer should sprinkle water on the ground near the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) using a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). However, Kātyāyana states that after spreading *darbha* grass on that ground, the sprinkling should be performed with a mantra: “Having spread *kuśa* grass along with the *pavitra* strainers, he asks, ‘I shall cause the *svadhā* to be recited. When [the Brahmins] have said, ‘Let it be recited,’ he says, ‘Let the *svadhā* be spoken for the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers. While [the response] ‘Let there be *svadhā*’ is being uttered, he should pour water with the mantra ‘ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ’ onto the *kuśa* grasses upon which the *pavitra* strainers are placed. The phrase “upon those with *pavitra*” means upon those accompanied by the *pavitra* used for the consecration of the *arghya* water. By saying “upon those with *pavitra*,” he indicates that at this time, one should turn the *arghya* vessel—which had been turned face down—face up and take the *pavitra* strainers from it. For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* says:
Yājñavalkya desires the vessel to be turned face-up before the dismissal;
Yama, as well as Śaunaka the author of the Gṛhya-sūtra, [desire it] after having performed the dismissal.

"But before the inquiry regarding the satisfaction of the gods, Kātyāyana and others [state that the Viśvedevas are to be dismissed]. [397] This means: prior to the dismissal of the Brahmins (*vipravisarjana*), prior to the inquiry regarding the satisfaction of the gods—that is, prior to the utterance, "May the Viśvedevas be satisfied"—at the time of the *svadhā* recitation. In this matter, the arrangement follows one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*; for all these positions, however, the specific rule is taken from one's own respective *Gṛhya-sūtra*.

Thus it is from the *Smṛti*. However, in the absence of the specific option prescribed by one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, one’s own preference alone is the regulating factor for choosing a particular option; for it is also stated in the *Smṛti*: "In the absence of what is prescribed by one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, the selection may be made according to one’s own wish. Then, on ground provided with *kuśa* grass and *pavitra* blades, after the sprinkling of a stream of water, the performer (*kartṛ*) should say: "May the *svadhā* be accomplished. And the Brahmins should utter the benediction (*āśis*) of the ancestors consisting of the word *svadhā*: "May the *svadhā* be accomplished. Thus says Atri.
When they have replied, "Let there be *svadhā*," he should sprinkle [water] and utter the eternal formula;
for the self-existent Brahmā has declared that the utterance of *svadhā* is the supreme blessing for the ancestors.
"For the sake of longevity, progeny, wealth, health, and peace, one should cause the twice-born to recite [the scriptures]. Thus it is said.

When those Brahmins have said, "Let there be *svadhā*," the performer should recite the mantra beginning with "For the Ṛk, for splendor, for you; together they flow like rivers... and ending with "...milking the *svadhā*, the stream of immortality. This mantra is applicable here precisely because of its indicative power (*liṅga*) as a form of efficacy. Having poured down a stream of water, he should cause the twice-born to recite that supreme and excellent blessing (*āśis*), consisting of the utterance of *svadhā* by the self-existent Brahmā, for the sake of attaining fruits such as longevity. After the recitation of *svadhā*, Yājñavalkya says:
"And when this has been uttered by the Brahmins, let the Viśvedevas be pleased. [398] Thus:

first the performer of the *śrāddha* says, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," and afterwards, when the Brahmins presiding over the Vaiśvadeva rite say, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased"—and because of the word "ca" (and), first the performer says, "May the ancestors be pleased," and afterwards, when the Brahmins presiding over the ancestral rites say, "May the ancestors be pleased"—the performer should mutter this which is about to be stated. The meaning is that the performer should recite the collection of benedictory prayers beginning with "May our donors increase," and so forth. On this point, the author of the *Saṃgraha* [states]:
By the sacrificial formula "O giver," the purpose of the feet is traditionally held to be a prayer;
however, those who possess higher consciousness consider that prayer to consist of inquiries for the pleasure of the gods.
Pāraskara stated that the recitation of benedictions (*svastivācana*) should be performed for the reception of blessings;
Manu, however, declared this to be done once the Brahmins have been dismissed and are standing outside.
Regarding those rites which the sages have proclaimed here for different times,
an option among them is appropriate according to the specific requirements of one's own *gṛhya* [sūtra].
However, this does not apply to those for whom no *gṛhya* or other *smṛti* text is found available regarding the *śrāddha* and similar rites.
They are capable of performing all this for whichever sage it may be.

The meaning is that, regarding optional rites (*vaikalpika*), if the specific procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* or other texts is absent, one may adopt the procedure of whichever sage one prefers according to one's own inclination. Having said, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," and having offered water into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas representing the Vaiśvadeva deities; and having said, "May the Pitṛs be pleased," and having offered water into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas representing the ancestors; immediately thereafter, one should offer water along with flowers and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) into the hands of all the Brāhmaṇas. Thus says Atri: "Then, having offered water along with flowers and unbroken grains into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa... [399]
"One should give water"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"Having uttered 'vāje vāje,' one should dismiss those Brāhmaṇas;
having circumambulated the Brahmins clockwise, one should request boons from the ancestors."
One should release those flowers and unbroken grains held in the hands; one should cause them to rise from their seats for the purpose of returning to their own places.

Having caused them to rise with the mantra "vāje vāje" and having performed a circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa) of them, this is because of the traditional teaching of Mārkaṇḍeya. Furthermore, in the act of causing them to rise, one should not grasp the Brahmins directly by the hand, but rather through the medium of Darbha grass held in the hand.
Reciting "vāje vāje," one should dismiss [the deity] with the tip of a *kuśa* blade.

This is because it is stated thus by Matsya. The meaning is that one should touch the hands with the tip of a *kuśa* blade. For if the touching of the hands were performed with the very tip [alone], there would be contact with only one hand at a time, not with many. Consequently, the plural form in the mantra “*tṛptā yāta*” (Be satisfied and go) would be unintended, just as in the case of “*aditiḥ pāśān*” (Aditi, the fetters). Thus, the mantra is to be recited once for as many hands as can be touched simultaneously with the *kuśa* blade, since the purpose—namely, the dismissal of the many Brahmins—is accomplished by the single utterance due to the plural verb “*yāta*. If this is impossible, the mantra is to be repeated. Since the rising and departing of the Brahmins occur together, it follows by implication that the command “*uttiṣṭhata*” (Arise) is also expressed by the word “*yāta*” itself. In the *Smṛtis*, the rising of the ancestors and the invoked deities is not mentioned separately, as it is accomplished simply by the rising of the Brahmins. Nevertheless, for the sake of clear mental coordination, one should say, “Arise, O Pitṛs, together with all the Viśvedevas,” before touching them with the *darbha* grass, and then perform the dismissal of the Brahmins. In this way, the dismissal of the ancestors and others—which occurs concurrently with the dismissal of the twice-born (*dvija*)—need not be performed independently; therefore, one should not wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) during the dismissal. For this very reason, Śaunaka has stated: “The dismissal is performed while wearing the thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*). The sequence for the dismissal of the Brahmins is shown in the *Purāṇa*.
Afterwards, one should dismiss the gods, and first the twice-born ancestors;
for the maternal grandfathers as well, this same sequence with the gods is prescribed.

One should [invite] the gods, the twice-born who represent the Vaiśvadeva deities; and the ancestors, those representing the Pitṛs and others, seated in their respective places. After the Brahmins have been raised from their seats, Kātyāyana says: "Having followed them with the mantra *Āmā vājasya* and having circumambulated them. After the circumambulation, one should request boons from the presence of the ancestors using the two verses beginning with "O Givers" (*dātāraḥ*). And so says the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Having dismissed those Brahmins and performed circumambulation around them, a man, looking toward the southern direction, should entreat the ancestors for boons."
May our donors increase, as well as our Vedic knowledge and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.

"May we have abundant food, may we receive guests, may there be those who ask of us, and may we not have to ask anything from anyone. Looking toward the southern direction and facing south, he should request the desired boons indicated by the two verses, while addressing the ancestors with one quarter-verse of the two; the meaning is that he does not address the Brahmins. Bṛhaspati also says:
"Having circumambulated the Brahmins, one should request boons from the ancestors. Thus it is said. Regarding the period after the request for boons, Vṛddha-Śātātapa states:
"They should say, 'So be it,' and that [request] should be accepted by him with a bow of the head. [401]

By those Brahmins who have previously served as the representatives of the ancestors, it should be said, "So be it," since it is impossible for the ancestors themselves to say, "So be it. Having said, "So be it," they should offer flowers and consecrated rice (akṣata) held in their own hands. That performer of the śrāddha should then receive those flowers and rice upon his head. Regarding this, he himself has stated immediately after the acceptance of the blessing:
"Then, having performed a circumambulation and again joining his palms in reverence toward them, and having spoken pleasant words, he should prostrate and seek their favor."

He should speak pleasant words such as: "Blessed are we, for through your favor we have become free from our debt to the ancestors. Bṛhaspati has stated what should be said for the purpose of propitiation:
"Today my birth has become fruitful through the salutation of your feet;
today, by your grace, all those born in my lineage have gone to heaven."
"You have been distressed by such things as the gift of leafy vegetables;
you ought to forgive this, having forgotten that distress in your hearts.
Having thus propitiated them, the Brahmins should then be requested: "May everything be complete. And so says Viṣṇu:
"O best of the twice-born, may this Śrāddha— though deficient in mantras, deficient in ritual acts, and deficient in devotion— reach completion through your grace. Having said,
"May everything be complete," the Brahmins should also perform the praise of the qualities of the sacrificial oblation (havirguṇastuti).

"At the conclusion of the *śrāddha*, the twice-born should offer praise for the qualities of the food," according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Vṛddhavasiṣṭha. Thereafter, one should dismiss the Brahmins so that they may return to their own places. And thus says the Purāṇa:
"Then, having honored and worshipped them, one should dismiss them with affection."
Mārkaṇḍeya also says: "Having gone to the ground on his knees and prostrated, he should bid farewell.
There is also the statement of Madālasā:
"One should dismiss [the guest] after speaking pleasant words and bowing with devotion;
one should follow him as far as the door, and return once he has expressed his approval. The phrase "having been approved" implies "approved by the Brahmins."

Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, the sections concerning the subsidiary parts following the principal rite consisting of the feeding of Brahmins have been presented; now follow those concerning the disposal of the *piṇḍas* and so forth.
In this regard, Devala says:
Then, once the ritual action has been completed, immediately thereafter,
a Brāhmaṇa, fire, a goat, or a cow should consume those rice-balls, or he should cast them into water.

"When the rite is completed" means when the śrāddha rite—consisting of the performance of the *piṇḍas* along with the other constituent parts—is finished. This refers to the case where there is no desire for a son. If there is a desire for a son, the wife should eat the middle *piṇḍa*. Thus says Manu:
"A devoted wife, the lawful consort, intent on the worship of the ancestors, and desiring a son, should properly eat the middle *piṇḍa* from that [offering]."
"One shall obtain a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence, wealthy, possessed of progeny, righteous, and likewise virtuous. Thus [it is said]. Yama also says:
When the wife, restraining her speech and desiring a son, eats that middle ball of food,
the great-grandfathers make her possessed of a son.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa* as well, it is stated:
"A wife desiring offspring should eat the middle [portion] preceded by the mantra.
The mantra from the Purāṇa is also shown here by way of its opening words.
He should then cause his disciplined wife to eat the middle piṇḍa;
with the mantra that increases progeny, "The ancestors have taken up the embryo," [he offers it].

The mantra beginning with “ādatta pitaro garbham” (O ancestors, take up the embryo) is for the purpose of increasing progeny. This is what is meant: “The wife should consume the middle *piṇḍa* with this mantra: ‘O ancestors, take up the embryo—a boy adorned with a lotus-wreath—so that he may become one who protects from the enemies. However, a specific rule regarding the wife is shown by Śaṅkha and Likhita: “Or the wife, having bathed after her menses, should eat the middle *piṇḍa*.”

A woman who has not conceived is said to be "one who has bathed after her menses. Consequently, a wife who is pregnant should not eat [the middle piṇḍa]. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati prescribes an alternative mode of disposal for the middle piṇḍa in such a case: "If the wife is in another country, or is ill, or likewise pregnant, then a worn-out bull or a goat should be fit to eat it."
That is the middle *piṇḍa*. [The goat] is aged and its semen has departed. For this very reason, the *Vāyupurāṇa* states:
"But that goat whose vigor has departed, and likewise the ox of that same description—for those two, the *piṇḍa* should be offered, for in whom vigor does not grow."
Āpastamba also says:
"If the wife is in a foreign land, or if she is impure, or if she is dead, or if she is wicked or unfriendly— what becomes of her share of that funeral cake?"
"One standing in water, facing south, should cause the *piṇḍas* to go into the sky;

for the sky is the place of the ancestors, as is the southern direction. Thus, regarding old bulls and the like, the optional disposal (*pratipatti*) should be understood as being according to what is available. However, in the case of a *tīrtha-śrāddha*, the disposal of all *piṇḍas* is to be made in the water alone. And so it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:

At a śrāddha performed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should always cast the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) into the water with a concentrated mind, facing the south; for that direction is proclaimed to be the quarter of the ancestors (pitryā dik).

A *tīrtha-śrāddha* is a *śrāddha* performed near water. "One should cast [the remains] at the sacred site" means one should cast them into the water near the place where the *śrāddha* was performed. Yājñavalkya states, using a particular turn of phrase to show that the cleaning of the Brahmins' leftovers must be done immediately after the disposal of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*):
"But one should give the rice balls to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or else throw them into fire or water. While Brahmins are present, one should not clean up the leftovers of the twice-born."

Because of the plural number in the word *piṇḍān* ("pindas"), this rule also applies to the case where there is no desire for a son; that is, as long as the Brahmins are present, one should not clear away the leavings before their dismissal. Rather, the meaning is that one should clear them away once the Brahmins have been dismissed and the ritual disposal of the pindas has been performed. As for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha:
"In a Śrāddha, the leavings should not be removed until the end of the day;
for the offerings of *svadhā* continue to drip, and those who have not yet offered water for the ancestors drink them."

For those deceased for whom the offering of water is forbidden, the water-offering has not been performed; therefore, since they have a share in the pouring out of the remnants of the food, one should not remove the remnants until sunset—this is the meaning. As for that which was stated by Vyāsa:

"One should not wipe away the remnants until the sun has set," that refers to a situation involving multiple households, because in such cases it is possible for relatives and others to eat the remains of what was served to the ancestors in other houses as well. On this very point, Pracetas says:
Surrounded by his circle of servants and kinsmen, he eats the remnants of the *kavya* offerings;
until evening, one must not sweep away the leavings of the twice-born from the hall of the *śrāddha*.

He eats the *kavya-śeṣa*—the remnant of the food offered to the ancestors together with those kinsmen who share the same lineage (*sagotra*). The phrase "having completed the remainder of the midday rites" is the implied sense. Thus says Mārkaṇḍeya: "Then one should perform the daily rites and likewise feed the guests;
thereafter, the man should eat that food together with his servants and others."

The daily rites (*nityakriyā*) refers to those such as the worship of the deities (*devatārcana*) and the *vaiśvadeva* offering that have not been performed prior to the commencement of the *śrāddha*. One should perform them. As it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "O mighty-armed lord of men, having performed the *śrāddha* and having dismissed the Brahmins, one should thereafter perform the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites."

Thus—referring to the *vaiśvadeva* and so forth, namely the *vaiśvadeva-balikarma* and other rites—this [procedure] pertains to the case where the worship of the deities has not been performed at the time following the morning fire-oblation (*prātar-homa*). Furthermore, that which is stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
"Having gratified the ancestors according to the rule, one should offer the *bali* according to the injunction;
thereafter one should perform the *vaiśvadeva*, and afterwards the recitation for the Brahmins (*brāhmaṇavācana*)."

Thus, this is its meaning: having gratified the ancestors by feeding the Brāhmaṇas and having offered the *bali* oblation in the form of scattered food (*vikira*) consisting of all the remaining food, one should thereafter perform the *vaiśvadeva* rite; afterwards, one should perform the recitation of the *svasti* formula and so forth, following the dismissal of the Brāhmaṇas. To clarify this very point, it is stated immediately thereafter in that same [text]: "O Hero, know that which a wise man should place upon the ground with the mantra 'ye agnidagdhāḥ' is always the *bali* in the performance of the *śrāddha* rite."

"Always" means at all times. And thus, it should be understood that the performance of the Vaiśvadeva rite must be carried out either immediately after the conclusion of the Śrāddha or during the course of the Śrāddha, following the offering of the *vikira* and the *bali*. Wherever the Vaiśvadeva is performed—either at the end or in the middle of the Śrāddha—the offering of the *bali* must be performed immediately thereafter;
for one should perform the Vaiśvadeva as well as the regular (*nityaka*) *bali*.

Thus, because the two are mentioned consecutively in the *Matsyapurāṇa*, for this very reason, another *smṛti* records that the *bhūtayajña* and other rites must be performed at the conclusion of the *śrāddha*: "One should offer the *vaiśvadeva* oblations into the fire before the feeding of the Brahmins; it is recorded in tradition that one should perform the *bhūtayajña* and so forth after having completed the *śrāddha*."

By the statement "before the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas," it is indicated that one should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblations immediately after the *agnaukaraṇa* rite. By the statement "having performed the Śrāddha, the *bhūtayajña* and so forth are prescribed," it is shown by implication that the *baliharaṇa* (offering of food to beings) must be performed immediately after the Vaiśvadeva oblations. As for what is stated in the Purāṇa:
"When a man desires to give a Śrāddha to the ancestors, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva at the conclusion of the Śrāddha rite."

Thus, this [statement] intends to prohibit the *vaiśvadeva* offering prior to the *śrāddha*, but not even during its course; for if it were so [prohibited throughout], it would result in a contradiction with the previously cited texts. For this very reason, the fault of performing the *vaiśvadeva* at the very beginning of the *śrāddha* is stated immediately thereafter in that same source: "If the daily *homa* is performed at the start of the *śrāddha*, the gods will not accept the *havya* and likewise the ancestors will not accept the *kavya*."
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it is performed by taking [food] out from the food intended for the ancestors. For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi says:
"He who performs the Vaiśvadeva rite after taking [food] out from the ancestral cooking—that Śrāddha becomes 'demonic' (āsura); it does not reach the ancestors."

Thus, there is no fault in performing the *vaiśvadeva* offering from a separate cooking [of food] at the beginning of a *śrāddha*. However, because of the consequence of the previously mentioned fault if one were to perform the *vaiśvadeva* by taking [food] out from the *pitṛ-pāka* (the food cooked for the ancestors) in the middle of the *śrāddha*, the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites should be performed immediately after the *agnaukaraṇa* using food from a separate cooking. At the end of the *śrāddha*, however, one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* and so forth by taking [food] out from the *pitṛ-pāka*. Accordingly, it was stated by that same author immediately thereafter:
"Having completed the *śrāddha* according to the rules, one should then perform the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites; thereafter, one should give alms (*bhikṣā*) as well as the *hantakāra* and so forth."

The meaning is that one should not eat food taken from the cooking intended for the ancestors (*pitṛpāka*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), all daily rites (*naityaka*) accomplished with cooked food are included. Therefore, even the obligatory ancestral rite (*nityaśrāddha*) must be performed using food taken from the cooking intended for the ancestors. Alternatively, the *nityaśrāddha* should be performed with a separate cooking; for since it is of the nature of a *śrāddha*, the cooking that constitutes a duty of the *śrāddha* applies to it as well. For this very reason, regarding the *nityaśrāddha*, Mārkaṇḍeya stated: "Others say 'not with a separate cooking'. This means: the *nityaśrāddha* should be performed with a separate cooking; "others say no," meaning others believe it should not be performed with a separate cooking, but rather with the remnants of the [other] *śrāddha* alone. Furthermore, this *nityaśrāddha* is optional when another *śrāddha* has already been performed. As he himself says:
Some men desire the daily rite for the ancestors, while others likewise [desire] that for the ancestors; in such cases, one should perform the remainder as previously described.

The *nityakriyā* for the ancestors is the daily *śrāddha*. The remainder, such as the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites, one should perform as before; the meaning is that one should carry them out according to the established rules. As for what Lokākṣi stated:
"One should prepare cooked food for the sake of the ancestors and likewise for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*;
the *vaiśvadeva* is not for the sake of the ancestors, nor is the *darśa* [new-moon] offering for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*."

*Dārśa* means the *darśa-śrāddha*, that is to say, the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*. The meaning is that food set aside for that purpose does not become available for the *vaiśvadeva* even after the *śrāddha* has been performed. This refers specifically to the *darśa-śrāddha* involving one who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimad-darśa-śrāddha*). Because the *vaiśvadeva* is prescribed for him prior to the *darśa-śrāddha* itself, it is impossible to perform the *vaiśvadeva* at the conclusion of the *śrāddha* using the remnants of the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, the rule that the *vaiśvadeva* must be performed precisely before the *darśa-śrāddha* is demonstrated by that very [text] for one who possesses the sacred fires: "Having completed the rites up to the end of the fortnight, the one who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *vaiśvadeva*."
"Then the wise man should perform the piṇḍayajña, and after that, the anvāhāryaka. [409] Thus it is said.

The ritual at the end of the fortnight (*pakṣānta-karma*) consists of the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyanvādhāna*). The *anvāhāryaka* is the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*. Thus, for one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), it should be understood that the cooking for the *vaiśvadeva* must be performed separately and prior to the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*; however, in other cases, there is no rule requiring separate cooking. For those whose own *gṛhya-sūtra* states that the *śrāddha* is to be performed after having first performed the *vaiśvadeva*, even for them, the cooking for the *vaiśvadeva* must indeed be separate. Even when the cooking for the *vaiśvadeva* has been performed separately, the meal is taken from the cooking intended for the ancestors (*pitṛ*) alone.

"Having circumambulated [the place] clockwise, he should eat what was consumed by the ancestors," according to the traditional teaching (smṛti) of Yājñavalkya. By this, it is restricted that he should eat only what was consumed by the ancestors and nothing else; likewise, it is also restricted that he must indeed eat what was consumed by the ancestors and not fast. For this very reason, Devala states the fault in not eating:
"But that brahmin who, having performed a śrāddha, does not eat at all..."
The gods do not accept the oblations, nor do the ancestors accept the offerings to the manes.
And this food to be consumed by the ancestors should be prepared by taking small portions from each and every kind of food served to the ancestors. Thus says the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Then, at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* rite, one should eat everything that was served to the ancestors, together with servants, sons, kinsmen, and guests."

Even if one is not hungry, nevertheless, because it is necessary to consume the remainder of the food, one should eat at least a small portion of the entire offering served to the ancestors. For this very reason, Āpastamba says:
"Having taken portions from all [the food], one should eat a portion of the remainder that is no smaller than a mouthful, with the subsequent Yajus formula."

“‘I offer the immortal into the breath; may that Self enter into Brahman for the sake of immortality’—this is the subsequent *yajus*. With this *yajus*, one should eat from all kinds of food according to one’s capacity, taking portions until satisfaction. The meaning is that if one lacks such capacity, one should consume at least a mouthful (*grāsa*). This aforementioned necessity of eating the remnants should be understood to apply when the invited *brāhmaṇas* have been told, “Let the food remaining from the *śrāddha* be eaten together with those you hold dear. However, if the *brāhmaṇas* themselves take the food remaining from the *śrāddha*, then other food must be prepared and eaten [by the host].”

For there is a traditional legal text (*smṛti*) stating: "When the *śrāddha* has been performed, the daughter should not fast at home. Since it has been said that "the food remaining from the *śrāddha* should be eaten together with loved ones," this rule regarding the consumption of the remnants applies only when permission has been granted; for this very reason, Śātātapa states the rule for consuming the remnants specifically in the case where permission is given:
"One should eat the remaining food after it has been permitted, immediately thereafter."
But together with those dear to him, the wise man, being well-composed, should perform [the rite] according to the rule.

By stating "one who is wise," he shows that one must determine what is fit to be eaten and what is not by investigating the relative strength of the scriptures that prohibit the eating of meat, and then perform engagement or abstention accordingly. Therefore, even though beans, meat, and so forth were consumed by his ancestors, one who has performed the *anvādhāna* on the day of the sacrifice must not eat them, because of the scriptural prohibition: "One should observe the vow without beans or meat. However, for one who has not performed the *anvādhāna* or one who is without the sacred fire (*anagni*), meat consumed by ancestors may indeed be eaten on the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*), since it is enjoined by such statements as "one should eat what was consumed by the ancestors. This is because, in the context of the continuation [of the rule], "It destroys the family up to the seventh generation," the statement prohibiting meat-eating on the fifteenth day—"Meat-eating on the fifteenth day"—applies only to meat-eating prompted by worldly desire (*rāga*), and does not prohibit meat-eating that is prescribed by Vedic law (*vaidha*). Furthermore, a person observing a vow (*vratin*) who has made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) such as "I shall not eat honey, meat, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and so forth during the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha" and is intent on maintaining that vow, must nevertheless eat the honey, meat, milk-rice, and so forth consumed by his ancestors; for even if he eats them, there is no breach of the vow because it is [regarded as] being done according to Vedic injunction.
