"One appointed to a rite for the gods or a *śrāddha* must not abandon the restrictive observances (*niyama*). Fault accrues to those who perform what is forbidden, and likewise to those who fail to perform what is prescribed by law.
Since the consumption of meat may be prescribed by law, there is no lapse from one's vow for those who eat it [when so authorized]. Thus it is said.

The rule stated in the Smṛti is: “They should eat what has been served, remaining restrained in speech. The mention of those who are “appointed” (niyukta) is intended to include the performer of the Śrāddha as well, because the reason for the fault is the same in both cases for those who fail to perform the Vedic rites. As for another Smṛti text:
“For those who abstain from honey and meat while performing the Śrāddha rite, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors merely by smelling the fragrance of the food placed in the vessel.”

Thus, because it lacks acceptance by the great majority of people (*mahājana*), it cannot be inferred to have a valid source and should be disregarded. Even if it were to have a source based on the acceptance of some individuals, there would be no contradiction with the statement of Bṛhaspati, as that [statement] pertains specifically to forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), ascetics (*yati*), and students (*brahmacārin*). For Devasvāmin has established the resolution of the contradiction in both ways. In the same manner, even in the case of animal sacrifices and the like, there is no violation of the vow regarding the eating of meat. As Bṛhaspati said:
"In a sacrifice or a *śrāddha*, because it is an integral part of those rites, [the vow is suspended] due to the violation of the Brahmins' command."
Even when questioned about its edibility, the one observing the vow eats even meats.

"One afflicted by disease, one who has performed the *dhuta* observances according to rule, and likewise one invited by a Brahmin—these four are proclaimed as those for whom the eating of meat is permitted. Here, "invited" (*vṛta*) refers to being invited for the *madhuparka* offering and so forth; "invited by a Brahmin" (*vipravṛta*) means the same. "Afflicted by disease" means tormented by a chronic illness. The *Nigama* also supports this permissive view regarding the rule of consuming food traditionally served to ancestors, stating: "Having been authorized, he should eat after satisfying his household dependents, children, and the elderly. "Household dependents" (*gṛhyān*) refers to those living in the house under his own authority. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include sisters and others. For this very reason, the *Ādi-purāṇa* states:
Sisters and kinsmen are indeed always to be honored at śrāddha ceremonies,
even if they are stricken by poverty, miserable, deformed in limb, or possess an extra finger.
The elderly, those born with a natural aversion to worldly life, and those oppressed by the burden of disease—
these are always and everywhere worthy of receiving food from a host.
Furthermore, panegyrists, bards, and genealogists, as well as those skilled in the triple symphony of music, dance, and song,
destroy great fame when they fail to obtain rewards at the ancestral rites.

"Therefore, they too must be divided; let the wife also be divided. The phrase "in the house of the prosperous enjoyer" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The mention of the "wife" (*kalatra*) is intended to indicate the son and others as well. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"Having thus gratified the gods and the ancestors, the best of the twice-born..."
"A householder, accompanied by his sons, friends, and others, is entitled to eat. Thus [it is said].
He (the same author) states another rule for both the giver and the eater:
"The one who eats at the śrāddha and the one who performs the śrāddha should observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) during that night together."
But if they act otherwise, they shall go to hell.

In the *Matsya Purāṇa* as well: "The performer of a *śrāddha* and the one who eats at a *śrāddha* should both avoid all of this: eating a second time, traveling on a journey, riding in a vehicle, physical exertion, and sexual intercourse."
[413] "Vedic recitation, quarreling, and sleeping during the day as one pleases"—thus [it is said].
Regarding the one who eats at a *śrāddha*, Yama says:
"Eating again, traveling on a road, carrying a load, Vedic study, and sexual intercourse..."
One who eats at a śrāddha feast should avoid these eight: twilight prayers, receiving gifts, and the fire sacrifice.
One should not perform the homa oneself, but rather have it performed by another.

As Kātyāyana has said: "In the case of birth-impurity, while traveling abroad, or being unable to eat at a *śrāddha*, and on other such occasions, one may have [the sacrifice] performed by another, but one must not let it lapse."

The statement "one should cause [the rite] to be omitted," as also stated by Gobhila and others, means that one should have [the rite] performed under such circumstances as these. Regarding the case where no other *hotṛ* (priest) is available, it is declared in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"A twice-born man who has partaken of a *śrāddha* meal shall drink water ten times with the *gāyatrī* mantra;
thereafter he should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*), recite [mantras], and also offer oblations."

Other rules regarding the selection of those who may eat, as stated in the section on invitations, should also be applied here. Regarding the fruit for one who performs the śrāddha in this manner, Hārīta says:
"By performing it according to this procedure, one obtains four boons;
the ancestors bestow wealth, food, sons, and long life upon that person on earth."
Yājñavalkya also says:
"The ancestors, when pleased, bestow upon men longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, happiness, and likewise sovereignty."
Thus ends the section concerning the disposal of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and related matters in the *Smṛticandrikā*, and the ritual procedure for the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha is completed.
Now follows the procedure for performing the *pārvaṇa* rite according to one's capacity. Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"One should perform the obligatory rites in some way or another on the new moon day and other such occasions."
When there is abundance of vessels, materials, and other requisites, one shall obtain the fruit of all desires.

The meaning of the first half-verse is as follows: one should perform, in some manner and according to one's capacity, those obligatory rites such as the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* which are enjoined for times such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), even in the absence of the availability of suitable recipients, materials, and so forth. Regarding the lack of suitable recipients, Devala has stated:
"One should perform the *ṣaṭpiṇḍa-śrāddha* with even a single Brahmin;
one should cause the six *arghya* offerings to be given to him, and likewise provide seats for the six."
The father eats from the hand of the twice-born; the grandfather eats from the mouth;
the great-grandfather is said to eat from the palate, and the maternal grandfather from the throat.

"But the maternal great-grandfather is in the heart, while the maternal grandfather is situated in the navel. Here, "vṛddha" (the elder) refers to the father of the maternal great-grandfather. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:
"If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the portion for the gods (daiva) be provided there?"
Having set aside food from the vessel for all that has been prepared;
"Having performed [the rite] in a temple of the deities, one should then proceed with the *śrāddha*;
one should either cast that food into the fire or give it to a celibate student (*brahmacārin*). Thus it is said.

A *devatāyatana* is the place where the Brahmins intended for the Vaiśvadeva rite are seated. There, prior to the worship of the Brahmins, one should invoke the Viśvedevas upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and perform their propitiation—beginning with the preparation of their seats and ending with incense, lamps, and coverings. After that, having honored the Brahmin seated for the sake of the ancestors, at the time of serving the food, one should take a portion of all the food prepared for the Śrāddha at hand, sprinkle it with water, place it before the propitiated deity in its designated spot, and at the moment of offering the food, first offer this food intending it for the Viśvedevas, and thereafter proceed with the Śrāddha. "One who cooks for oneself is a *svapaca*. In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "A virtuous Śūdra should never feed cooked food to Brahmins; however, he may feed them while they are eating, lest sin should accrue even to him from those holy men."

"With prepared food" means with whatever prepared food is available for the sake of another purpose. The mention of "those without wives" and so forth is intended to include any person lacking the full equipment for cooking and the like. For this very reason, Jamadagni says:

Thus, since that [rule] applies to both the monthly and annual rites, it is intended to prescribe raw materials (*āmadravya*) in every case where cooked food (*pakvānna*) is unavailable; therefore, it is not redundant with the previously cited statement of Jamadagni. For this has been stated by that very [author]. Also in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:

In this case as well, the specific details regarding the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food) should be understood according to what is applicable. One should give grass to a cow, or offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas),

"When one is unable to perform the constituent parts of the *Pitṛyajña*..."
When he causes the Brahmins to recite, "May there be complete success! [then the rite is concluded].

The prayer is: "May there be complete success for the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*), that is, the *śrāddha*, and may all its constituent parts be accomplished; please say so, sirs. The meaning is that one should cause the invited Brahmins to say, "May there be complete success for all the constituent parts of this *śrāddha*. However, if the performance of the *pārvaṇa* rite has been forgotten and is impossible to perform, Vyāsa has stated:

"For one who has abandoned the sacred fires, neither the *pārvaṇa*, nor the *ekoddiṣṭa*, nor the *sapiṇḍana* [is prescribed]. The meaning is as follows: one who has abandoned the sacred fire (*tyaktāgni*)—that is, one who has discarded the fire contrary to the prescribed rule—has no entitlement whatsoever to the śrāddha rites consisting of the *pārvaṇa*, *ekoddiṣṭa*, and *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Therefore, only one who has abandoned the fire should feed [the guests] after making a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). He should perform the śrāddha according to the procedure of formal resolve. When it is asked what the difference is between this procedure of formal resolve and the *pārvaṇa* procedure, he himself says:
When one makes a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), however, one should not perform the filling of the vessel;
nor should one perform the invocation (āvāhana) or the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), and one should not cause the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to be given.

The filling of the vessel is the offering of *arghya*. There is a prohibition against the invocation (*āvāhana*) accompanied by mantras, but not against the mere act of invocation itself; for in its absence, there would be no presence of the gods and ancestors. Therefore, without reciting the mantra of invocation, one should perform the invocation of the gods by saying merely: "I invoke the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava. The same applies to the invocation of the ancestors and others. By the word *caiva* ("and also") in the phrase "and also the rice-balls" (*piṇḍāṃś caiva*), the rice-ball for the leftovers (*ucchiṣṭapiṇḍa*) is also prohibited. For this very reason, it is stated in another *Smṛti*:

It is clearly stated: "If one does not perform the *śrāddha* with a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should not fill the vessels, nor should the scattered offerings (*vikiro*) be given. Thus, even when performing a secondary rite (*anukalpa*), if there is no deceit, the fruit of performing the primary rite (*mukhyakalpa*) is obtained. And so it is said in another *Smṛti*:

"The man who performs a secondary form of the *śrāddha* (anukalpa) in consideration of his caste, condition, and so forth, obtains the entire fruit of the primary form (*mukhyakalpa*) regarding the *śrāddha*. Regarding this, "regarding the *śrāddha*" means in the principal part of the *śrāddha*, whether only the feeding of Brahmins is performed, or only the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) is performed; or "regarding the limbs" means when even a few constituent parts are performed according to one's ability. This is the meaning.
Thus concludes the rule for performing the *pārvaṇa* rite according to one's capacity in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
In this manner, the monthly *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* has been described as it should be performed. Now, the annual *sāṃvatsarika-śrāddha* to be performed every year is discussed.
Regarding this, Lokākṣi says:
One whose father has passed away must personally perform the *śrāddha* ceremony every month on the new moon day, as well as on the anniversary of the death and once a year.

The inclusion of the word "himself" (*svayam*) is for the sake of emphasis, and not for the purpose of excluding the son, disciple, officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), and others; for we observe the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) by another agent in the mantra: "O Father, [Name], this is for you, O Father. According to the mantra "O Father, [Name], this is for you," the officiating priest or others should offer the rice-balls to the sacrificer’s father. In that context, having recited the mantra "O [Name] of such-and-such lineage, [Name], this is for you, O Father," one says "To [Name] of such-and-such lineage, the father of the sacrificer, this rice-ball is for you"—this rice-ball belongs to the sacrificer, not to the sacrificer himself. One should understand the specific rule from another *Smṛti* that "the placing of the rice-ball on the sacred grass (*barhis*) is for the sacrificer," which is mentioned after stating "of the sacrificer. And this agency of another should be understood to apply when the sacrificer is incapable, or when he is preoccupied with other more weighty duties, or in cases where there would be a lapse of the proper time. Regarding the question of how the annual *Śrāddha* should be performed, Jātūkarṇa says:

A son should perform the rites for his father who has joined the company of the ancestors (pitṛgaṇastha) according to the *pārvaṇa* method, both annually and monthly; this is to be known as the eternal rule.

The meaning is that for one who has joined the company of the ancestors—that is, one who has been *sapiṇḍita*—the son should perform the annual (*ābdika*) and monthly (*māsika*) *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death according to the *pārvaṇa* rite. This is what is being stated: just as in the *amāvāsyā* *śrāddha* there is an invocation of the triad consisting of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather during the offering of the *arghya* and other rites, so too in the annual *śrāddha* for the father, the invocation of the triad must be performed.
"When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, the offering should be like that of the *darśa*, with three [deities] designated.

This refers to the monthly offerings (*māsika*). It should be understood that this statement—"one should perform those very same [rites] again"—is intended as an injunction to prescribe that even after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, during the monthly offerings performed in the first year, one should perform them according to the *pārvaṇa* rite with three deities. Nor should it be argued:
"Wherever the fathers (*pitṛ*) are honored, there the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) are certainly [honored too]."
Based on this statement, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather and others must also be performed on the anniversary of the father’s death. As Pāraskara says:
"When the father has attained the state of a deity, [the offering] for the biological son extends to three generations.

"Attained the state of a deity" means having acquired the status of an ancestor (*pitṛ*) through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. The mention of "three generations" is intended to exclude six generations; therefore, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather need not be performed on the anniversary of his death. Kātyāyana also states:
"Excepting the first *ṣoḍaśa-śrāddha* accompanied by the *karṣū*, and the annual (*pratyābdika*) rites, in all other cases there shall be six rice-balls (*piṇḍas*); such is the settled rule.

Here, "accompanied by the *karṣū*" refers to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. By this, it is implied that in the rites beginning with those accompanied by the *karṣū*, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) does not exist. However, the author of the *Saṃgraha* establishes, by means of logic alone, that on the anniversary of the father's death, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather and others should not be performed.
Yājñavalkya has prescribed the time for the ancestral rites (pitrī) and likewise for those of the maternal grandfather (mātāmaha) without distinction, beginning with the new moon day (amāvāsyā).
And he is to be understood as simultaneous from the statement that is about to be spoken;
for the *tantra* indeed exists through the distinction of time and the distinction of place.
Therefore, from the ritual injunctions of the Tantras, simultaneity is understood;
that should be known as occurring at times such as the new moon, but not on the day of death.
"Because the time [of the new moon] and so forth is one, the performance together is appropriate;
but on the day of death, because that [time] is distinct, the performance together would not be fitting.
This is the meaning of the first verse: by means of the new moon and so forth...
The new moon day (amāvāsyā), the eight-day periods (aṣṭakā), the occasion of prosperity (vṛddhi), the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), and the two solstices (ayanadvaya).

By such statements, Yājñavalkya has declared the time for *śrāddha* in general and without distinction for both the ancestral *śrāddha* (*pitrya*) pertaining to the father and the *śrāddha* related to the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*). Regarding the phrase "and that is to be understood as simultaneous," this is the meaning of the quarter-verse: that time declared by Yājñavalkya is not according to a sequential order of parts, as is the case with the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* and the *Darśa-śrāddha*; rather, it is to be understood as occurring simultaneously—once and at the same time—for both the paternal *śrāddha* and the maternal grandfather’s *śrāddha*, without any sequence of parts. Now, one might object: since the previously cited statement prescribing the time lacks words such as "simultaneous" (*yugapat*), how can such an understanding be reached? Anticipating this doubt, it is stated: "from the statement to be mentioned later" (verse 425). The meaning of this is: although such an understanding is not derived from the aforementioned statement prescribing the time itself, nevertheless...
"Likewise for the maternal grandfathers; or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed separately.

Since this will be stated later in this very section on *śrāddha*, such an understanding will arise. Now, one might object: "How can simultaneity be understood from this statement? Anticipating this, he supports his position with the words "by difference of time," etc., noting that this verse has a clear meaning. Thus, where the simultaneity of the paternal *śrāddha* and the maternal grandfather *śrāddha* is perceived at times such as the new moon (*amāvāsya*), it is only there that these two share the same ritual procedure (*samānatantra*), and not on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*). So he says:
"It should be known that [this occurs] on occasions such as the new moon, but not on the day of death."

The intention is that simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is not perceived on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*). But how is simultaneity not perceived on the *mṛtāha*? Anticipating this objection, he says: "At times such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), etc. The meaning of this is as follows: at times such as the new moon, since the *śrāddhas* for the paternal and maternal grandfathers apply without distinction, their performance in a single portion of time is understood due to the unity of the occasion; thus, a common ritual procedure (*samānatantratā*) is appropriate. However, on the *mṛtāha*, because the measure of lifespan differs for each individual, the times for the father and maternal grandfather are distinct. Since the *mṛtāha* of the father is not the time for the maternal grandfather’s *śrāddha*, the unity of the time consisting of that specific portion is utterly remote; therefore, based on that [unity], a common ritual procedure for these two is by no means appropriate. By this same logic, the *mṛtāha* of the father is not the time for the *śrāddha* of the mother and others either, because there is no application of it there. On the *mṛtāha* of the father, the deities are only the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, and not with their wives—this is how it should be understood. Even though by this same logic the *mṛtāha* of the father is not the time for the grandfather’s *śrāddha*, nor is the *mṛtāha* of the mother the time for the grandmother’s *śrāddha*, nevertheless, because of the statement "as in the *pārvaṇa*," the grandfather and great-grandfather are deities on the father’s *mṛtāha*, and the grandmother and great-grandmother are deities on the mother’s *mṛtāha*; it is not so by logical necessity (*nyāyataḥ*), and thus everything is faultless. When the time for the father’s annual *śrāddha* and the time for the mother’s annual *śrāddha* happen to coincide by chance, even then the father’s annual *śrāddha* is not performed with his wife. Rather, the two annual *śrāddhas* for the mother and father must be performed separately—from the invitation of the Brahmins until their dismissal—in the order corresponding to the sequence of their deaths. But when the mother and father die simultaneously and the sequence of priority is unknown, then having first performed the father’s annual *śrāddha*, the mother’s annual *śrāddha* should be performed afterwards, because of the father’s primacy. In such a case, if the days for the annual *śrāddhas* of a brother and others coincide, the various *śrāddhas* must be performed separately according to the order of seniority and so forth. As for that which was stated by Pracetas:
"One should not perform two *śrāddhas* on the same day anywhere.

This statement intends that one should not perform a *śrāddha* repeatedly within the context of a single *śrāddha*. "On the day of death, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) [should be done] collectively, separately..."
The *navaśrāddha* (oblation for the newly deceased) for a couple occurs only upon the practice of *anvārohaṇa* (the wife following her husband onto the funeral pyre).

Thus, by this [text] as well, a *śrāddha* for the deceased together with his wife on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) is not prescribed, such that there would be a contradiction with what was stated previously. What, then, has been stated by this? It is said: when the anniversary of death for the husband and wife occurs on the same day, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is to be performed "in brief" (*samāsena*), that is, concisely. Just as in a *śrāddha* for two fathers, where a single rice-ball is offered for both fathers while designating them as "to so-and-so and to so-and-so," so too here, having made the designation for both parents as "to so-and-so and to so-and-so," only one rice-ball should be given. And the Brahmins should be fed in uneven numbers; just as in the case of the rice-ball offering, they should be fed while designating only the two. This is because the mention of the "offering of the rice-balls" is intended to indicate the *śrāddha* ceremony in general. Thus, since this *śrāddha* possesses the characteristic of an injunction involving the conjunction of multiple objects of dedication, it should be performed according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure by means of a single ritual framework (*tantra*). However, the *nava-śrāddha* (the funeral rites for the newly deceased) for the couple must be performed separately. Consequently, prior to the twelfth day, on the days of the *nava-śrāddha*, two *śrāddhas* in the form of *ekoddiṣṭa* (single dedication) must be performed for the father and the mother. Furthermore, the aforementioned annual *śrāddha* and the *nava-śrāddha* must be performed when the wife has ascended the funeral pyre (*anvārohaṇa*) after her husband; it is stated "only in the case of *anvārohaṇa*" in order to determine that this is not the case otherwise. As for another *smṛti* text:
If a husband and wife have ascended the same funeral pyre and both met their death,
one should perform the śrāddha for them separately, and offer the cooked rice separately for each.

Thus—"rice" means a lump of rice; this should be applied only to the context of the *navaśrāddha* (the nine-day funeral rites). As for those for whom the monthly and annual *śrāddhas* for the mother and father on their death anniversaries are prescribed by the rule of the *ekoddiṣṭa* alone, this applies to that case; therefore, there is no contradiction between this and the previously mentioned specific *sāṃvatsarika-śrāddha*. Furthermore, regarding what was stated by Bhṛgu himself after saying "and annually," namely, "one should conclude the *navaśrāddha* simultaneously," its meaning is as follows: when the death anniversaries of the mother and father coincide, and the mother has performed the *anvārohaṇa* (self-immolation) upon the same funeral pyre as the father, one should perform the father’s *navaśrāddha* at the same time with a single cooking (*ekapāka*)—[or rather, in the absence of separate cooking?]—by way of a *tantra* (combined ritual procedure). Having performed the preliminary set of subsidiary rites (*pūrvāṅga-kalāpa*) before the principal rite, one should first perform the *śrāddha* for the father and afterwards for the mother, and having performed the subsequent set of subsidiary rites (*pāścātyāṅga-kalāpa*), one should do so by way of *tantra*. This is the same even when several mothers have performed the *anvārohaṇa* on the same funeral pyre. One should perform the *navaśrāddha* for the mother immediately after the father, then for the stepmothers in order of seniority, and so forth; and thus says he (Bhṛgu): [The text continues: "If the death anniversaries of the father and mother coincide, and the mother has performed the *anvārohaṇa*, one should perform the *navaśrāddha* for both together with a single cooking, having performed the preliminary rites once, and having performed the *śrāddha* for the father first and the mother afterwards, one should perform the concluding rites once. If several mothers have performed the *anvārohaṇa* on the same pyre, it is exactly the same.
