If many, or even two, have died at the same time,
one should perform the cooking by means of a single tantric rite, but offer the śrāddha separately for each.

"In the case of a conjunction [of deaths], one should first perform [the rite] for the one who died previously, then for the second, and then for the third; this is the sequence. Here, "cooking" (*śrapaṇa*) means the preparation of the food to be offered; the meaning is that it is for the primary [deceased] first, for the secondary in relation to the primary next, and for the tertiary—the most junior—last. However, in the case of *anvārohaṇa* (ascending after death) on a separate funeral pyre (*bhinnacityā*), everything must be performed separately. Thus, the *mṛtāha-śrāddha* (ancestral rite on the anniversary of death) must necessarily be performed according to whichever of the aforementioned rules is applicable, following the established order. And so says Kārṣṇājini:
Just as a seed sown in saline soil does not sprout,
so too shall that which is not given on the day of death be for them.

By this, the intention is that food must necessarily be given on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*). "And that is prescribed as being like the *pārvaṇa* [rite]"—this is the view of Jātūkarṇa and many others. "According to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*"—this is the view of Yājñavalkya and many others. For this very reason, Sumantu says: "O King, the *pārvaṇa* rite must be performed; the *ekoddiṣṭa* should never be done.
They cite very many such statements sung by the sages.
[429] "O King of kings, those who know the Dharma-śāstras declare that there are many more [scriptural statements] that prescribe the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.

Here, the meaning is that in the case of the *pārvaṇa* rite, those learned in the Dharma-śāstras declare—or rather, they proclaim—that there are numerous or several statements that prescribe the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. Therefore, he (the author) states that one should abandon the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite and adopt only the *pārvaṇa* rite: "Therefore, by the force of the scriptural statement, the *pārvaṇa* rite should be performed on the anniversary of death."

The meaning of "by the force of the statements" (*vacanasāmarthyāt*) is "by the force of the majority of statements. This very point was also stated by Jaimini: "In a conflict between contradictory properties, that which belongs to the majority shall prevail. Because they are rooted in direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), the statements of Jātūkarṇya and others are indeed more authoritative. And this is the direct Vedic revelation: "Month after month, at every season, during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons, and every year, let the gods and the ancestors sit together. The meaning is: "Every year on the anniversary of death, let the gods and the ancestors—the Viśvedevas and the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—sit together to partake of the *śrāddha*. By this revelation, it is stated that the *śrāddha* must always be performed according to the *pārvaṇa* rite on the anniversary of death. Therefore, the *pārvaṇa* method alone should be adopted by all, because the statements enjoining the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite are sublated by the statements enjoining the *pārvaṇa* rite. Alternatively, the *pārvaṇa* method may be adopted only by certain [groups]. Thus says another Smṛti:

The two sons— the *kṣetraja* and the *aurasa*— who are conversant with the rules, should perform for their father who has entered the company of the ancestors the rites as prescribed for the new-moon day, both annually and monthly.
The remaining sons should perform [the rite] as in the *ekoddiṣṭa*; this is the sense. For this very reason, Sumantu says:
"Every year, the *kṣetraja* and *aurasa* sons should perform [the rite] by the *pārvaṇa* rule alone;
the other ten sons should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*."

Thus has been explained the systematic arrangement of mutually contradictory Smṛtis according to their distinct spheres of application: "But where there may be two Śrutis [conflicting], both are recorded as Dharma;
however, when there is a conflict between two Smṛtis, their respective spheres must be conceived separately."

Thus it is from the *Smṛti* of Jābāli. Kātyāyana likewise states that this same rule regarding the determination of the subject matter applies even on the anniversary of the mother’s death: "In whatever manner a twice-born son always performs [the rite] for his father every year, in that very same manner should he perform it for his mother—whether as a *pārvaṇa* or otherwise."
As for that which was stated by him [Viṣṇu]:

"For paternal uncles, brothers, and mothers, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is always prescribed," there it is understood from the association with the paternal uncle and others that the word "mother" (*mātṛ*) refers both to the biological mother and the co-wife (*sapatnī*). Therefore, there is no contradiction with the previously cited statement. Furthermore, this mention of "mother" is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for women other than the biological mother. For this very reason, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states:
Every year, men should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for a woman on the anniversary of her death,
according to the rule that has been declared here for men.

Just as the *śrāddha* for men is performed with mantras, so too must the *śrāddha* for twice-born women who have been married be performed with mantras; such is the meaning of the final quarter-verse. However, for unmarried women, because they lack the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), the *śrāddha* is indeed without mantras. The term "of a woman" is intended to mean "of a woman who has no son. For this very reason, Garga says:
"Whatever women or men have died without sons—for them also an *ekoddiṣṭa* should be offered, not a *pārvaṇa*."
Women include the mother’s co-wives and others; men include paternal uncles and others. Or rather:
"By that path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone—by that he should travel the way of the virtuous; going there, he does not come to harm."

Thus, regarding the Śrāddha on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father, one should understand the settled rule (*vyavasthā*) between the *ekoddiṣṭa* and *pārvaṇa* methods—both of which are prescribed by other Smṛtis through the conduct of former sages and accompanied by explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that seem to disparage each other, much like the rules for the *udita* and *anudita* fire-offerings. On this point, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"But those who are divided [in property] should perform the annual and other rites separately;
when it has been performed by even one among those who are undivided, it is as if performed by all."
Thus ends the procedure for the *mṛtahaśrāddha* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the matters concerning the *nityaśrāddha* and other *śrāddhas* that are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *pārvaṇaśrāddha*.

Herein, some statements regarding the *nityaśrāddha*, which is a modification of the *pārvaṇa* mentioned in the section on the classifications of *śrāddhas*, are recorded. Regarding this, Pāraskara says:
That śrāddha which is performed day after day is proclaimed as "nitya" (obligatory);
however, when one is unable [to provide food], it may be performed with water alone, omitting the Vaiśvadeva rite.

"Devoid of the Vaiśvadeva" means it is lacking the performance of the rite dedicated to the Viśvedevas, which would otherwise be obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) of the rules of the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha. By this, it is indicated that the daily (*nitya*) śrāddha is not to be performed according to the *pārvaṇa* model. The phrase "day after day" refers either to one who possesses extreme faith or to one who is very wealthy. As Devala says:
"By this rule, one should perform the śrāddha once a year, or three times, or four times, or according to one's faith, month by month, or day after day."

The meaning is that by this procedure, according to the rules for the *pārvaṇa* rite, one should perform the *nityaśrāddha*—the obligatory ancestral offering—once a year on an auspicious day; or three times a year, once every three months, on an auspicious day; or four times a year, once every four months, on an auspicious day; or month by month on an auspicious day; or even daily, according to one's faith (*yathāśraddham*), that is, in accordance with one's devotion. The phrase "according to one's faith" is intended to indicate "according to one's capacity" (*yathāsāmarthyam*) as well, since it is appropriate to establish the practice based on one's ability. Furthermore, the ritual manual (*kalpa*) for this *nityaśrāddha* has been fully elaborated by us in the *Āhnika*, and thus it is not elaborated here.

The *naimittika* śrāddha, which consists of the *ekoddiṣṭa* and is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *pārvaṇa*, will be described by us in the section on impurity (*āśauca*). However, the *kāmya* śrāddha has been defined by Śātātapa:
"That which is beneficial for a desire is called *kāmya*; it is for the sake of accomplishing a desired object.
That too has been declared according to sequence by means of the *pārvaṇa* procedure. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that even the *kāmya-śrāddha* (optional śrāddha) must be performed according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure, accompanied by the specific rules prescribed for it, and without transgressing the sequence beginning with the invitation of the Brahmins, as stated by the sages. Therefore, the *kāmya-śrāddha* should be performed together with the Viśvedevas named Dhuni and Rocana, as per the statement: "But in the optional [rite], [one should worship] Dhuni and Rocana.
Furthermore, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* (prosperity śrāddha) should also be performed like the *pārvaṇa*, accompanied by the specific rules prescribed for it. And so says the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: [433]
"A man performing a *śrāddha* on an occasion of prosperity (*vṛddhi*) shall always attain prosperity.
Having said this, [the text continues]:
"On an occasion of prosperity, a wise man should always worship the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors."
The specific details have been accomplished; the remainder should be performed as in the Pārvaṇa rite.

Thus it has been stated. The meaning is that "on an occasion of prosperity" refers to an occasion characterized by an increase, such as the birth of a son or a marriage; for the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* states: "The *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is prescribed on the birth of a son, at a marriage, and so forth. Here, the word "man" (*nara*) is intended to mean the father. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:
The father should perform, without omission, the entire cycle of rites for the newborn son, beginning with the birth-rite (jātakarman),
as well as the auspicious śrāddha.
Kātyāyana also says:

"In the rites of consecrating a son, the father should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to his own ancestors until the son's marriage; but in his absence, [the son should do so] according to that same order."

The meaning of this is as follows: during the sacramental rites for a son, such as the *jātakarman* and others, up to the point of his marriage—that is, until the taking of his bride—the father should offer rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) to his own ancestors; the sense is that he should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. However, in the absence of the father, that is, upon the father's death, those rites—namely the *jātakarman* and so forth—must be performed by the brothers who have already been consecrated, for those who have not yet been consecrated are to be consecrated by their elder brothers.

Based on such statements, the eldest brother and others should offer [the śrāddha] to their own ancestors according to that sequence of agents implied by the text. Since the *samāvartana* (the rite of returning home) is also a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for a son preceding marriage, in the case of a *samāvartana* performed while the father is still living, the father himself should offer to his own ancestors. However, one whose father is deceased should offer to his ancestors himself, provided there is no previously consecrated elder brother, because the entitlement to perform rituals has already arisen through the initiation (*upanayana*). This same principle should be understood to apply to marriage as well:
"A wise man should always worship the *nāndīmukha* ancestors during a *vṛddhi* (prosperity) ceremony."

The meaning of this remainder of the passage from the *Viṣṇudharmottara* beginning with these words is as follows: "In the *vṛddhi* [rite], that is, in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, one should worship the ancestors known as the *nāndīmukha*s. The phrase "the special [element] has been accomplished" means that the specific, exceptional rule (*vaiśeṣika-dharma*) consisting of the designation *nāndīmukha* has been established and set forth. "The rest shall be like the *pārvaṇa*" means that all other categories of rules, apart from the specific rule consisting of the designation *nāndīmukha* which has been established, are to be understood here also as being according to the *pārvaṇa* model.

Nor should it be argued that, like the *pārvaṇa* rite, there should be no specific feature here for the Viśvedevas in the form of those known as Purūravas and Ārdrava; for in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, the mention of specific features under the name "Nāndīmukha" is intended to demonstrate the specific features mentioned in other Smṛtis. Therefore, the specific details mentioned in other Smṛtis, such as "Satya, Nāndīmukha, Vasu," and so forth, are to be adopted in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. Regarding this, certain specific features have been stated by Śātātapa:
"The *śrāddha* for the Mothers should come first, and immediately after that, the one for the Fathers."
"Therefore, on the occasion of the anniversary of the maternal grandfathers' deaths, three *śrāddhas* are prescribed.

Thus, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather is performed according to the *pārvaṇa* rite and includes his wives; it is not to be performed separately from the *śrāddhas* for the mother and others as the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather and others might otherwise be understood to be. To express this, it is said that "three *śrāddhas* are prescribed," rather than saying "the *śrāddha* for the mother," which would imply that the *śrāddha* for the mother alone is separately ordained and not for the paternal grandmother and great-grandmother as well. This is because the word "mother" (*mātṛ*) here is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to refer to the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother. For this very reason, it was stated by that same author:
"O twice-born ones, the wives of the three ancestors beginning with the father are to be fed;
since this is for women alone, it is here called the *mātṛśrāddha* (the rite for the mothers). The meaning is:

"O twice-born ones, they are to be fed for the sake of the mothers"—that is, the twice-born are to be fed with reference to the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother. Since this *śrāddha* is performed separately here for the women who are the wives of the triad beginning with the father, it is therefore called the *mātṛśrāddha*; such is the syntactical connection. Gargya states the difference in timing for the three aforementioned *śrāddhas*:

The Śrāddha for the mother is on the day before, that for the paternal ancestors on the very day of the rite, and that for the maternal grandfather on the following day; thus, at a Vṛddhi ceremony, three Śrāddhas are prescribed.
When the practice of performing the *śrāddha* over three days is thus difficult, Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"If one is unable [to perform them] on separate days, one should perform the three *śrāddhas* on a single previous day, including the Vaiśvadeva according to the Tantric method."

The meaning is that, because the fruit, place, time, substance, and deity are common [to all], the rite for the Viśvedevas (vaiśvadaivika) should be performed here by way of a single procedure (tantra). Now, one might ask: how is there a commonality of time here? For it is recorded in the Smṛti: "The Śrāddha for the Mothers is in the forenoon, and likewise the Śrāddha for the Fathers at midday; thereafter, for the maternal grandfathers, three Śrāddhas are prescribed on the occasion of a Vṛddhi."

Thus, since Śātātapa has prescribed distinct times such as the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) and so forth for the *mātṛśrāddha* and other rites, how can there be a single performance (*tantratā*) here? True; according to the practice following the words of Śātātapa, there is no single performance due to the difference in times. However: "A rite for the gods (*daivika*) is to be performed in the forenoon, but that for the ancestors (*paitṛka*) in the afternoon;
the *ekoddiṣṭa* at midday, and that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhi*) in the morning."

Thus, according to the words of Vālmīki, when the performance of three *śrāddhas* occurs on a single day at the time of morning (*prātaḥkāla*), the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *vaiśvadeva* offering shall be common to all, because of the identity of the time. Here, the word "morning" does not intend to exclude the period known as *saṅgava*; for it is said:
"An increase [of prosperity] (*vṛddhi*) should indeed take place in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), except for that occasioned by a birth.
Upon the birth of a son, a wise man should perform the *śrāddha* belonging to that specific time."
Thus it is stated by Atri. Because of its brevity, the performance is currently carried out according to the procedure for the Vaiśvadeva rite. Vṛddha-Śātātapa also states specific details:

"In all three of these [rites], being self-controlled and pure, one should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas, beginning with those for the gods, moving from left to right (pradakṣiṇa) while keeping them on one's left."

The meaning is as follows: two Brāhmaṇas for the rite to the gods (*daiva*); two for the *mātṛ-śrāddha*; two for the *pitṛ-śrāddha*; and two for the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* including the wives of the maternal grandfathers. Thus, having invited at least eight Brāhmaṇas, the performer of the *śrāddha*, moving clockwise from the invitation until the final dismissal, should feed them while remaining endowed with the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) over the left shoulder by means of the left hand, and wearing the upper garment (*uttaravāsa*). In this regard, there is a specific rule stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"O Lord of Men, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas in pairs, facing the east. Pracetas also states a specific rule:

"One should not mutter prayers dedicated to the ancestors (*paitṛka*), nor should one cause meat to be given there. Facing east, with the *devatīrtha*, one should quickly perform the cleansing of the site. Regarding this: "prayers dedicated to the ancestors" refers to those mantras characterized by the ancestors (*pitṛliṅga*) which are prescribed to be muttered at the beginning of the meal and other times; these must not be employed here, because the prohibition here applies specifically to the act of muttering (*japa*). However, even a mantra characterized by the ancestors that serves as an instrument (*karaṇamantra*) must indeed be employed. For this very reason, another Smṛti states:

"Whatever rite has been prescribed by the sages with a mantra addressed to the ancestors (pitṛ-liṅga), that alone should be performed; for [a rite] without a mantra is as if not done at all. Thus it is said.

The meaning of the third quarter [of the verse] is that the performer, facing east, should perform the entire ritual sequence for the ancestors (*paitṛka*) using the *devatīrtha* [finger-tip]. When the twice-born have finished eating, there is a swift cleansing of the place and so forth; in order to sweep those dining areas, the performer’s facing east is appropriate because, while the eaters face north, it is somehow possible for him to be facing toward the Brahmins. However, this is not the case when the eaters face east. Therefore, it should be understood that from this statement the position that one should feed the Brahmins facing north is understood. But regarding the position stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*—"one should feed the Brahmins facing east"—it is appropriate for the performer to somehow face toward the Brahmins if he faces north, but not if he faces east; thus, it should be understood that the position of the performer facing north is understood from that text. And so, it should be understood that when the Brahmins face east, the performer should face north and perform the invocation (*āvahana*) and other rites; but when the Brahmins face north, the performer should face east. For this very reason, the *Āśvalāyanagṛhyapariśiṣṭa* states: "In rites for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), the Brahmins are even in number. The *darbha* grasses are rootless. Facing north, he should give [the offerings] to those facing east; facing east, to those facing north. Two *darbha* blades are the *pavitra*. A specific detail is also mentioned in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*.
One should offer sweet food and should not serve sour food.
One must avoid red flowers, sesame seeds, and the *apasavya* (left-hand) manner.

[438] Regarding the *pārvaṇa* rite, while water-born red flowers are prescribed, other red flowers are prohibited; here, the mention of "red flowers" is intended to prohibit even those red flowers born in water. When the question arises as to how the function of sesame seeds should then be performed, Kātyāyana states: "Barley serves the purpose of sesame."

The meaning is that the function of sesame seeds (*tila*) must be performed with barley (*yava*). And thus, he [the author] says that in the mantra "Thou art sesame, having Soma as thy deity," the modification (*ūha*) "Thou art barley" should be made; he states this as: "In that case, the modification is 'Thou art barley'. This means that when barley is employed for the purpose of the function of sesame seeds, such being the case. He further states that the word *svadhā* should not be used in the offering of food and similar rites: "One should not employ *svadhā*. And thus, in the formula "Svadhā, obeisance," one should instead use the expression "Svāhā, for the *arghya* offerings."

"One should always attend upon the ancestors here with devotion, just as one would the gods," because of this very statement by him [the author]. Since it says "just as the gods," one should not perform the prostration with the left knee on the ground during the services for the ancestors. And so it has been stated by that same author: "Indeed, no prostration with the left knee is ever prescribed."

And thus, wherever in the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* the procedure for the ancestors (*paitṛka-pracāra*) is prescribed as being different from the procedure for the gods (*daivika-pracāra*), there in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the procedure for the gods must be adopted. A specific rule is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "One should offer the *arghya* to two [deities] at a time. The mention of *arghya* is intended to indicate the *pādya* and other offerings as well. For this very reason, it is stated immediately thereafter in that same work:
"The twice-born [guests] should be honored in pairs, preceded by the word *nāndī*."

And the procedure is as follows: for the *daiva* (divine) portion, having invited two Brahmins at a time simultaneously with the words, "May the moment (*kṣaṇa*) be made for the *nāndī* deities," when both Brahmins have replied simultaneously, "Om, so be it," the performer (*kartṛ*) should say, "May you two accept [the invitation]. The two Brahmins, however, should simultaneously give the reply, "We two accept. In the same way, there is the invitation for the *pitrya* (ancestral) portion; however, the specific difference in the *nāndīmukha-śrāddha* is that one says, "May the moment be made for the *nāndīmukha* ancestors. Regarding the manner of performance for the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, Kātyāyana states: "He asks, 'I shall invoke the *nāndīmukha* ancestors,' and in place of the response 'Let there be *svadhā*,' the reply is, 'May the *nāndīmukha* fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and maternal grandfathers be pleased. In place of the request 'I shall cause the *svadhā* to be recited,' he asks, 'I shall cause the *nāndīmukha* ancestors to be recited,' and the reply consists of the formula beginning with 'O *nāndīmukha* fathers' and ending with 'may they be pleased. This means that the Brahmins should speak thus. In place of the question "Are you satisfied? (*tṛptāḥ stha*), he says that one should ask, "Is it complete? (*saṃpannam*): "In place of the question regarding satisfaction, [one says] 'Is it complete? Regarding the substance for the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), he states the specific rule: "The rice-balls are mixed with curd, jujube fruits (*badara*), and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). The word "should be made" (*kāryāḥ*) is to be supplied. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says: [The rice-balls are mixed with curd, jujube fruits, and unbroken rice grains].
Regarding the question of satisfaction, [the response] for the gods is "it is excellent" (*saṃpannam*) or also "it is pleasing" (*rucitam*).
The funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) should be prepared in due order, mixed with curd and *karkandhu* fruits.
*Karkandhū* is the jujube fruit (*badarīphala*). He (the same author) states a specific rule regarding the offering of the funeral cakes:
"Facing east, with the *devatīrtha* [finger-position], upon *kuśa* grass whose tips point eastward, one should offer the *piṇḍas*;
one should not hold the *piṇḍa*-vessel face down.

(440) "In those with tips pointing east" means those with their points directed toward the east. Here, the offering of the *piṇḍas* is not to be performed near the remains of the meal; rather, it should be done outside the dining hall.

"One should offer the *piṇḍas* facing east during a *vṛddhi-śrāddha* by name, outside [the sacrificial ground]," according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Vṛddha-Śātātapa; and because Pracetas has stated: "But outside, on blades of grass with tips pointing east, one should cause the *piṇḍas*—mixed with curd, unbroken rice, and jujube fruits—to be placed. A specific rule is also stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"One should offer one *piṇḍa* by name and another silently, offering the *piṇḍas* separately."

One should offer two balls of rice (piṇḍas) separately for each [deceased person]. In that regard, the meaning is that one should offer the first ball with the name [of the deceased] accompanied by the *gotra* mantra, but the second should be offered silently. However, in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*, it is stated that the offering of the balls of rice here is optional: "O King, O mighty-armed one, one may or may not perform the offering of the balls of rice in a *vṛddhiśrāddha*, having considered the family traditions."

Because of the statement, "having regard for the family customs (*kuladharma*)," those families in whose lineage the entire complex of rites—from the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) up to the dismissal of the Brahmins—is not performed, must perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* ending only with the feeding of the Brahmins. Even in the alternative view where the rite ends with the dismissal of the Brahmins, the mantra for requesting boons from the Mothers should be employed here before the mantra for requesting boons from the Fathers, beginning with "May the givers... This too has been stated in that very same [text]:
"The mother, the paternal grandmother, and likewise the paternal great-grandmother—may these be pleased with me and may they grant me prosperity."
Thus ends the section on the *nitya* (daily) and other types of *śrāddha* within the *śrāddhas* that are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the manual for the performance of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* as taught by Kātyāyana and others.

Now, for the sake of facilitating the practical performance of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* itself, the ritual manual (*prayoga-paddhati*) as taught by Kātyāyana and others is written here. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"Hereafter I shall declare whatever specific details there may be here;
[one should invite] an even number of Brahmins in the morning, both [for the ancestors and the gods]."
"Having seated him, one should indeed give straight blades of kuśa grass with the hand. Thus it is said.

On the previous day, having invited the Brahmins, on the following day in the forenoon, once their feet have been washed, he should seat them upon their seats and perform the preliminary rites such as saying, "I shall perform the ritual," following the procedure for the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha. The specific difference is that for the sake of the Vaiśvadevas and the ancestors (*pitr̥*), he should seat an even number of Brahmins; he should place straight *kuśa* grass—meaning unbroken and with roots—for the seats of the Brahmins facing either east or north, near their right thighs, upon the previously prepared seats. Facing either east or north himself, he should offer this. Then, he should perform the formal invitation (*āmantraṇa*) again for both the divine and ancestral portions according to the method stated in the previous section, beginning with, "May the moment be made for the Nāndī-devas. Then, as in the *pārvaṇa*, having invoked the Viśvedevas once in two Brahmins, he asks the two Brahmins representing the maternal group, "Shall I invoke the mothers, paternal grandmother, and great-paternal grandmother? Having invoked the maternal group once in the two Brahmins with the mantra, "We invoke you, who desire us" (*uśantas tvā havāmahe*), he asks the two Brahmins representing the paternal group, "Shall I invoke the Nāndīmukha ancestors? and should invoke the paternal group in those two Brahmins. There is no invocation here for those accompanied by their wives. Then, having asked the two Brahmins representing the maternal grandfather's group, "Shall I invoke the Nāndīmukha maternal grandfathers along with their wives? he should invoke the maternal grandfather group, including their wives, once in the two Brahmins. Then he should perform the consecration of the water for the *arghya* offering. Regarding the specific details there, the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* states: "Two *darbha* blades serve as the *pavitra*; there are four vessels. Having consecrated the waters with the mantra 'śaṃ no devīḥ,' he pours barley into them, having looked at them with the mantra: 'Barley you are, whose deity is Soma, created by the gods at the Gosava sacrifice; ancient, by the ancients... [etc. ...O Nāndīmukha ancestors, satisfy these worlds for us, svāhā! Svadhā! Arghya! The mantra for bringing [the water] near should also be modified to 'svāhārghyāḥ'. However, regarding the actual offering of the *arghya*, a specific rule has been shown by Kātyāyana.
Having addressed the ancestors by their lineage names, one should offer the *arghya* water;
in this case, neither the practice of wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*) nor the use of the *pitrya* (southern) *tīrtha* is required.
One should indeed have the filling of the vessels and other such acts performed by the deity alone;
[the priests] should have their hands joined with the right hand uppermost, in pairs, with the tips of their fingers touching and the pavitras held at the fingertips.
"Having prepared the *arghya*, it should be offered; it is not given here to only one. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of the passage beginning with *jyeṣṭhottarakarau* is as follows: having joined the hands of two Brāhmaṇas at a time, the offering of the *arghya* (water of respect) should be performed; therein, the subsequent [hand] of the elder Brāhmaṇa should be used. Regarding the end of the *arghya*-offering mantra beginning with *yā divyā āpaḥ*, a specific rule is shown in the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "The offering of the *arghya* is performed according to the gender of the deity, saying: 'O Viśvedevas, this is your *arghya*; O Nāndīmukha ancestors! In the phrase "O Viśvedevas, this is for you," the specific detail mentioned in the preceding section—that the Viśvedevas are those named Satya and Vasu—should be understood. This same specific detail is to be applied wherever the names of the gods are specifically mentioned. Unlike the offering of the *arghya*, the offering of perfumes (*gandha*) and other items is not done by joining the hands of the two Brāhmaṇas; rather, it is done on the hand of each individual as in the *Pārvaṇa* rite, because no specific rule to the contrary is stated. Furthermore, the offering of perfumes and so forth should be made twice for each hand, because the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* states: "The offering of perfumes and so forth is twice, twice. The specific rule for the *agnaukaraṇa* (the offering into the fire) is stated by that same author: "The oblation in the hand is: 'Svāhā to Agni Kavyavahana; Svāhā to Soma Pitṛmat. There is an alternative reading in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "And the *agnaukaraṇa* is constant, and the oblation is performed with the word *svāhā*. Although one might have expected the term "as before" (*pūrvavat*), the authors of the *Pariśiṣṭas* and others use the word "constant" (*nityam*) in various places. Therefore, the meaning is: "The *agnaukaraṇa* is constant, and the *agnaukaraṇa* is exactly as before"—meaning it may be performed either in the fire or in the hand, just as in the *Pārvaṇa*. In place of the mantra for grasping the thumb, *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, another mantra is prescribed in that same work: "'Ataḥ devā avantu naḥ' is the mantra for grasping the thumb. A specific rule regarding the recitation (*japa*) after the offering of water for sipping (*apośana*) has been shown by Kātyāyana.
"One who desires the highest good should mutter three times the words 'Honey, honey' there; for one who avoids the *madhu-mantra* in that regard, the food there [is as if] devoid of the *gāyatrī*.
The *madhu-mantra* refers to the mantra beginning with "The winds are honey," and so forth. This specific mantra to be muttered while the Brahmins are eating has been stated by that very [author].
And while they are eating, one should never recite the *Pitṛsaṃhitā* here;
rather, another auspicious recitation, such as the *Soma-sāman* and so forth, should be performed. Thus it is said.

In the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "One should cause [the officiant] to recite the *Pāvamānī* verses, the *Śaṃvatī* verses, the *Aindrī* verses, and the *Apratiratha*. The *Pāvamānī* verses begin with "svādiṣṭhayā. The *Śaṃvatī* verses begin with "śaṃ na indrāgnī bhavatām avobhiḥ. The *Aindrī* verses begin with "indra tvā vṛṣabhaṃ vayam. The *Apratiratha* is the hymn beginning with "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ. In place of the verse "madhu vātāḥ," one should cause the five "Madhumatī" verses beginning with "upāsmai gāyatā naraḥ" to be recited. Regarding the sixth verse, there is an alternative reading in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "The sixth is 'akṣann amī madanta'. A specific rule concerning the inquiry into satisfaction (*tṛptipraśna*) and other matters has been shown by Kātyāyana.
The question "Is it well-prepared? is prescribed at the point where [the guests] express their satisfaction; when they have replied, "It is very well-prepared," one should offer the remaining food.

"Whatever scattering of food there is there—whether with sesame or with barley—in the vicinity of the leavings, that here [in this rite] is reversed once they are satiated. In this context, regarding the *pārvaṇa* rite, the scattering of food and other items in the vicinity of the leavings—which is prescribed in the relevant *Gṛhyasūtra* as to be performed prior to the questions on satiety—is "reversed" here in the *vṛddhiśrāddha*; the meaning is that it is to be performed after the questions on satiety. A specific rule regarding the offering of the *piṇḍas* has also been shown by that same author.
But upon the darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, having addressed the first [ancestor] as before,
one should pour water without sesame seeds at the root-end, saying, "Be seated."
The second and third [seats] are for the regions of Madhyadeśa and Agradeśa;
however, the maternal grandfather and the others are placed to the left of these very same [seats].
Then, having set aside a portion of all the food and having mixed it with various condiments, well-cooked soups, milk-rice, barley, jujube fruits, and curd, he [should sit] facing the east.
Having offered the rice balls (piṇḍas), each the size of a bilva fruit, just as in the rite of washing the feet,
one should then wash them again with the water used for rinsing that vessel.

In the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), each subsequent ball of rice becomes superior by being offered in successive order; conversely, each preceding one becomes inferior by being placed below.
Therefore, in all śrāddha rites— whether those performed on auspicious occasions or otherwise—
one should offer the rice grains so that they are slightly adhered at the base, middle, and top portions [of the vessel].
"One should offer the perfumes and other items silently, and thereafter cause the twice-born to sip water (ācamana)."

The meaning of the phrase "to the left of these very [places], starting with the maternal grandfather" (*mātāmahaprabhṛtīṃs tu eteṣām eva vāmataḥ*) is as follows: to the north of these places for the water-sprinkling (*avanejana*) intended for the group of mothers, and to the north of the places for the water-sprinkling intended for the group of paternal ancestors, one should sprinkle water for the group beginning with the maternal grandfather. This is what is meant: when the Darbha grass has been spread at the place of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) with the tips pointing eastward, one should first pour water upon the root, middle, and tip sections for the purpose of offering the rice-balls to the group of mothers; then to the north of that for the group of paternal ancestors; and then to the north of that for the group of maternal grandfathers—in this manner one should pour the water. Regarding the phrase "having offered the rice-balls," the words "to the mothers, to the fathers, and to the maternal grandfathers" are to be supplied. Slightly joined, meaning slightly touching one another, two rice-balls each should be offered to the mothers and so forth, and to the fathers and so forth. Among those, the first rice-ball should be offered with the mantra including the name and lineage (*nāmagotra*); the second, however, silently. The remainder should be understood as stated in the preceding section. The specific duties to be performed after the worship of the rice-balls are shown in that very same [section].
In the same way, one should sprinkle the ground twice, saying,
"May it be well-sprinkled," and "May the waters be auspicious," using water to the depth of a yoke.

Immediately after the offering of flowers, one should say, "May there be joy," and one should present the unbroken grains (akṣata) while saying, "May there be well-being and freedom from misfortune. [446] Thus.

The specific rule regarding the recitation of the *svasti* (auspicious benediction) has also been shown by that same authority: "The *svasti* should be pronounced only for an even number [of Brahmins]. Regarding the *akṣayya* (imperishable offering) and the pronouncement of *svadhā*, there is a specific rule: "May the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased. In place of the word *akṣayya*, one asks, "I shall cause the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors to be addressed. By the statement, "May the *Nāndīmukha* fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers be pleased," one should follow what was stated in the preceding section. The remainder is exactly as in the *Pārvaṇa* rite. And the *Pārvaṇa* is of two kinds: the elaborate *Pārvaṇa* and the non-elaborate *Pārvaṇa*. Among these, the non-elaborate *Pārvaṇa* is performed according to the procedure of formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Since the rules of both types of *Pārvaṇa* are extended through the words of the ritual manual regarding the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and so forth, it should be understood that when the performance of the elaborate *Pārvaṇa* rites is impossible, the *Vṛddhi-śrāddha* and other such rites should be performed according to the *Pārvaṇa* rules consisting of the procedure of formal resolve.

Thus concludes the procedure for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* as stated by Kātyāyana and others in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the definition of the *ābhyudayika-karman*. In this context, as an occasion arising from the definition of the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha*, another *ābhyudayika* rite is defined. Regarding this, there is the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
When an auspicious ancestral rite (śrāddha) has arrived, the installation of deities is prescribed;
it is the cause of prosperity for castes, religious duties, families, guilds, and the world.
Three on the father’s side are to be honored, and likewise three on the maternal grandfather’s side;
these are declared to be the Mothers, with the father’s and mother’s sisters as the eighth.

Having first worshipped the seven [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī, as well as Durgā, Kṣetrapāla, and Gaṇādhipa, one should thereafter worship the Nāndīmukha ancestors during rites for prosperity and the like.

"Having honored the maternal ancestors and the paternal ancestors, and then the maternal grandfathers as well, some say that thereafter the maternal grandmothers should be honored; then an even number of twice-born men should be fed."

The meaning of the first half-verse is as follows: when the *ābhyudayika* śrāddha—performed on the occasion of a festival or prosperity (*abhyudaya*)—is due and its performance is about to commence, one must first, for the sake of worshipping the Mothers and others, perform the installation of the deities; that is, the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the deities beginning with the Mothers and ending with the lords of the *gaṇas* upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or similar site. The meaning of the second verse is this: in the paternal line (*pitṛpakṣa*), three women—the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother—are to be worshipped. Likewise, in the maternal line (*mātāmahapakṣa*), three women—the maternal grandmother, maternal great-grandmother, and maternal great-great-grandmother—are to be worshipped. Furthermore, according to the rule "the father’s sister is the eighth," the father’s sister is the seventh and the mother’s sister is the eighth to be worshipped; thus, these eight are declared to be the "mothers of men. Likewise, there are seven "mothers of the gods": Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, Māheśvarī, Aindrī, Vārāhī, Kaumārī, and Cāmuṇḍā. Additionally, one should worship Durgā, the Lord of the Field (*kṣetrapati*), and the Lord of the *Gaṇas*. The meaning of the third verse is that, in rites such as those for prosperity (*vṛddhi*), one should first worship Durgā, the Lord of the Field, and the Lord of the *Gaṇas* with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) prior to the *vṛddhiśrāddha*, and afterwards worship the *nāndīmukha* ancestors in the śrāddha. The remainder is clear. Alternatively, prior to the *vṛddhiśrāddha*, the deities mentioned by Kātyāyana should be worshipped; these are shown in the third verse.
In all rites and other activities, the Mothers together with their lords of the gaṇas must be worshipped with diligence; when they are worshipped, they in turn worship [the worshipper].
And upon pure images, or those depicted on cloth-paintings and the like,
one should worship with perfumes, flowers, consecrated rice, and various kinds of food offerings.
One should cause five streams of clarified butter to flow from the wall of the family-chamber,
or seven streams, which should be neither too low nor too high.
Having recited there with a concentrated mind those mantras that bestow long life for the sake of peace,
one should then proceed to offer the śrāddha to the six ancestors.
The entire ritual procedure taught by Vasiṣṭha should be observed here in its pure form.
[The goddesses are] Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, and Jayā.
Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā, the Mothers, and the Mothers of the World; Dhṛṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi, together with the deities of the self.

"To these one should offer *arghya*, scents, flowers, incense, and lamps. Thus [it is said]. Regarding the rites and so forth, at the commencement of the acts that occasion the *nāndī-śrāddha*, the *āyuṣyāṇi* (longevity-mantras) are those stated beginning with "ā no bhadrāḥ kratavaḥ" and others. One should commence the offering of the *śrāddha* to the six ancestors—namely the paternal ancestors beginning with the father and the maternal ancestors beginning with the maternal grandfather—preceded by the *mātṛ-śrāddha*. The procedure mentioned by Vasiṣṭha refers to the rules set forth by Vasiṣṭha and other authors of the *Smṛtis*. The "deity of oneself" (*ātmadevatā*) is one's own chosen deity.
And in all rites and so forth, the Mothers along with the lords of their hosts [are to be worshipped].
Those who are worthy of worship, when worshipped with effort, in turn worship [the worshipper].
By this [verse], those mentioned previously are to be worshipped:
at the marriages of daughters and sons, upon entering a new house,
at the naming ceremony of children, and at the ceremony of first feeding solid food.
At the parting of the hair ceremony and upon seeing the face of a son or other offspring,
the self-restrained householder should worship the Nāndīmukha group of ancestors.
Now, regarding rites for prosperity that are auspicious and beautiful:
at birth, or at the initiation ceremony, or at the marriage of a son or a daughter.
One should satisfy the ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas according to the prescribed ritual.

Regarding the performance of the *nāndīmukha-śrāddha* mentioned in such passages, he [the author] states that in certain cases it should be performed by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), and not by repetition (*āvṛtti*):
"When rites are performed for a group, the worship of the Mothers is done once;
the *śrāddha* should likewise be performed only once at the beginning, not separately for each."

The meaning of this is as follows: When a person who has gone to another land and whose existence has not been heard of for a long time is presumed dead, and his sons and others have performed the funeral rites (*pretakārya*), and he returns at a later time—then those purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarma*) such as the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) which are performed again by gathering together; likewise, when those rites such as the birth-rite are performed by gathering together for one who has already performed penance (*prāyaścitta*); and likewise, for one who before initiation (*upanayana*) had somehow failed to perform the rites up to the tonsure (*caula*) at their respective times, and those rites prior to initiation are performed by gathering together—in all these cases where the purificatory rites such as the birth-rite are performed collectively in groups, the worship of the mother and others and the *nāndīśrāddha* are performed only once, by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), at the beginning of the first rite that is being performed, and not separately at the beginnings of each individual rite nor by repetition throughout all the purificatory rites. As for that which was stated by him [the author]:

Having first performed the rite of the Mother-sacrifice (mātṛ-yāga), the remaining auspicious rites should be performed after three menstrual periods; no other minor auspicious rite should be done sooner.

Thus, this should be understood as applying to cases other than those previously mentioned, where, even after the lapse of six months, there is no transgression of time regarding all ritual acts of consecration (*saṃskāra*) performed sequentially according to their proper time.
Thus concludes the section on the *ābhyudayika* rites in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the topics concerning the *śrāddha* as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of ritual acts;
specifically, the topics concerning the *śrāddha* as an auxiliary of ritual acts which are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. Regarding this, Pāraskara states:
"At the time of the impregnation rite (niṣeka), during the Soma sacrifice, likewise at the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana),
and at the rite for male offspring (puṃsavana)— it is traditionally taught that the Śrāddha performed as an ancillary to these rites is of an auspicious (vṛddhimat) nature."

The period for conception (*niṣeka*) begins from the time of the wife’s ritual bath after her menses and lasts for sixteen nights. Among these, on a day endowed with a full lunar mansion, the *śrāddha* that is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the rite called *garbhādhāna* (conception) should be performed. Regarding "Soma," which refers to the time of the Soma sacrifice, the *śrāddha* ancillary to that [sacrifice] should be performed on the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth. Here, the word "Soma" is intended as an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and the *agnihotra*. The mention of it being an "ancillary to the rite" is for the purpose of making known that if it is not performed, there is a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in the rite. For this very reason, Śātātapa has shown by way of phrasing that the rite must be performed only after having performed this [śrāddha].

"Having worshipped those ancestors in the sacrifice, one should perform the Vedic rite. Here, "ancestors" refers to those known as *nāndīmukha*. "Vedic rite" refers to such rites as *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *somayāga*, *agnihotra*, and so forth. And this *śrāddha* as an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the rite must be performed only once at the very beginning of rites like the *agnihotra* that are to be performed repeatedly. As Kātyāyana says:
"Those rites which are to be performed repeatedly by the performers of the rituals..."

"And these Mothers, as well as the Śrāddha, should not be performed at every sacrifice. (451) Here, "these" refers to the Mothers who were mentioned along with the lords of the Gaṇas in the verse: "In all rites and so forth, the Mothers together with the lords of the Gaṇas should be worshipped with effort. "Śrāddha" refers to the Śrāddha that is an ancillary part of the ritual. For this very reason, it was stated by that same author immediately thereafter:
"At the consecration of the fires, at the two oblations, and likewise at the Vaiśvadeva..."
In the rite for the deceased, in the New Moon sacrifice, and likewise in the Full Moon sacrifice.
"Regarding all sacrifices, the wise who know sacrifice say thus:
there should be only one *śrāddha* among these, not separate ones for each.

By the phrase "of the two *homas*," because of its mention alongside the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) and because of the dual number, the *karmāṅga-śrāddha* must be performed during the repetition of the morning and evening *agnihotra*. For immediately thereafter, he says:

"There should be no *śrāddha* on the *aṣṭakā* days, nor is a *śrāddha* within another *śrāddha* permitted. Thus it is said. Regarding the specific rules (*viśeṣadharma*) for the *aṣṭakā-śrāddha*, those stated in the respective *Gṛhyasūtras* are to be consulted. The specific injunctions concerning the *goṣṭhī-śrāddha*, the *śuddhyartha-śrāddha*, the *yātrā-śrāddha*, and the *puṣṭyartha-śrāddha* have been shown in this very section on the classification of *śrāddhas* and should be kept in mind. As for the specific injunctions concerning the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa-śrāddha*, we shall present them in the section on impurity (*āśauca*).
Thus ends the section concerning *śrāddha* as an ancillary part of ritual acts in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the sections concerning *tīrtha-śrāddha*;
therein, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states:
Having bathed in all rivers, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
in each such place, one should perform the śrāddha and other rites according to one's means.
Whether it be at an improper time or at the proper time, when men have arrived at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) for a śrāddha ceremony,
they must always perform the libation to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa).
At a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), one should by no means examine Brahmins;
according to the teaching of Manu, one should feed any seeker of food who has arrived there.
The offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be made with roasted grain flour (saktu), or with boiled rice-mash (saṃyāva), or with milk-rice (pāyasa);
it has been observed by the seers that it may also be done with oil-cake (piṇyāka) or with the fruit of the iṅguda tree.
Or with sesame oil-cakes; there, the Śrāddha should be performed by virtuous men together, omitting the offering of water for the Arghya.

"Dogs, crows, vultures, herons, and the like do not destroy [the merit] when they are seen; such are the ritual acts. This means that even if dogs, crows, and other such creatures are seen by the performer of the *śrāddha* or others while the *śrāddha* rites are being performed at a sacred site (*tīrtha*), those ritual acts are not destroyed. Specifically, "with *aiṅguda* oil-cake" refers to an oil-cake produced from *iṅguda* fruits. The meaning is that even if dogs, crows, and so forth are seen by the performers of the *śrāddha*, the *śrāddha* rites being performed at the sacred site are not rendered fruitless.

Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, the section on Śrāddha pertaining to the subject of Tīrtha-Śrāddha has been composed by the illustrious Yājñika Vedāntas for the pleasure of Gadādhara, based upon the statements made by the sages.
Thus ends the Śrāddha-kāṇḍa in the Smṛticandrikā composed by Yājñika Devaṇabhaṭṭopādhyāya Somayājī, son of Śrī Keśavādityabhaṭṭopādhyāya, who was proficient in all branches of learning.
Prosperity.
